entry.article_text: Military Trail has reopened, and the crater left behind by the deadly Learjet crash has been filled, but for families who lived just feet from where the plane came down, the road to recovery is far from over.Mariano Garcia, an attorney with Searcy Denney Scarola Barnhart & Shipley, is representing four families from the Greenacres mobile home community whose homes, vehicles and other property were damaged by crash debris."The immediate need right now is that people who were displaced still have to pay rent. They still have to pay bills. They have to replace food and items that they lost. They have repairs to their homes that need to be made, and so we're dealing with those immediate needs," Garcia said.Those financial concerns have been a part of the aftermath since the first days following the crash.For the four families Garcia represents, the focus is now turning to financial relief for their specific losses.One of those families is a household of eight living in a mobile home roughly 50 feet from the impact site. Garcia said seven members of the family were home when the crash happened, including three who were outside."Dad was on the porch holding his 1-year-old child. Mom was standing nearby when a chunk of sidewalk came busting through their porch, narrowly missing them," Garcia said.Other members of the family were inside."They all felt the explosion, the shock. They breathed all of the residue that was in the air," Garcia said. "It was a very traumatic event for them, as you can imagine."The damage to the family's home was significant."You had chunks of aircraft parts busting through the roofs, you know, allowing the water intrusion into these residences, and when you combine that with the power being out, food spoiling in refrigerators, folks being unable to return to their homes, it had a pretty significant impact on their lives," Garcia said.Power and water have since been restored to the mobile home community, according to Garcia, but the family of eight has not been able to return to its home because the residence remains unsafe. He said the family has been staying in Airbnbs provided through charity.Garcia said there is no lawsuit at this point.Instead, he is communicating with attorneys for Aurora Aviation Inc., which does business as Upper Jets and operated the Learjet, and the company's insurance carrier in an effort to secure immediate financial relief for the four families he represents.When WPTV asked whether the company has been cooperating, Garcia's response was direct."Very much so," he said. "I'm encouraged that at least the company for this charter operator, the insurance company, is responding and acknowledging that there were losses and are doing what they can to advance sums to these families and help them out."An inspector is expected to assess the affected properties as Garcia's team works to determine the extent of the losses.For now, Garcia said the immediate focus is on expenses families are already facing."The immediate need right now is that people who were displaced still have to pay rent. They still have to pay bills. They have to replace food and items that they lost. They have repairs to their homes that need to be made, and so we're dealing with those immediate needs," he said.WPTV previously spoke with Perez, a handyman whose mobile home is about 250 feet from where the Learjet crashed. At the time, he couldn't access his home, vehicle or the tools he depends on for work. Perez is not one of the residents represented by Garcia, but when WPTV recently returned to the neighborhood, our crew found an orange notice on his mobile home that read "UNSAFE.""Working materials are there. My screwdrivers, my drills, my saws, they're stuck there," Perez told WPTV at the time.He worried then about what the disruption would mean financially."We're not asking for nothing else but the necessary that's been lost or gonna get lost because of this, because my job wages, when rent comes down, who is gonna be, is my landlord or the people who I pay for that lot gonna say, ‘Oh, we feel sorry for you to have a discount?’ No, full payments are gonna have to be made," Perez said.Other organizations have also stepped in to address those immediate needs. The Emergency Assistance Foundation, a West Palm Beach-based nonprofit, launched a fund offering $1,000 cash grants to eligible residents impacted by the crash. Other groups have provided food, shelter, supplies and services for displaced residents.But some of what these families experienced is more difficult to measure."The photos and the aerials really don't do justice to just how close these families came to being seriously hurt or killed," Garcia said.He said some of the people he's spoken with are still dealing with the emotional and psychological effects of what they experienced."It's not something you see every day, and so it definitely had an emotional or psychological impact on them," Garcia said. "Many of them are having trouble sleeping, which is a very common report when someone undergoes a very sudden, tragic and unexpected event."Garcia, who has practiced law for 32 years, is also a longtime pilot. He described himself as a commercial multi-engine instrument-rated pilot and said he previously co-owned a flight school and charter service out of Palm Beach International Airport.He said determining the impact of emotional trauma will take time."There's no formula for that, Joel. It really depends upon the degree. We rely on medical experts to make that assessment and then use our judgment based on experience," Garcia said.While representing families impacted on the ground, Garcia stressed the magnitude of the loss suffered by the families of those aboard the Learjet."My heart goes out to the victims on board the plane. They suffered a massive loss, and I think what the public needs to understand is that this had a much broader impact," Garcia said.He said his focus now is helping the families he represents move toward some sense of normalcy."It's such a massive loss, particularly to the families of the occupants of the aircraft. It's hard to put words around what those families must be going through," Garcia said. "I can't imagine what they must be going through. And so if I can do something, even just a little bit to help others who were impacted by it, then, you know, I think that's the right thing to do."WPTV has reached out to Aurora Aviation for comment and is working to hear back.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

entry.title: Indian River County public schools to follow modified schedule Tuesday due to heavy rain threat
entry.summary: The School District of Indian River County will operate on a modified schedule Tuesday as a precaution ahead of expected rain and the potential for heavier rainfall. The district announced the schedule change Monday afternoon for Tuesday, Nov. 17. Under the modified-day schedule, extracurricular activities will conclude by 2:30 p.m. Extended Day will be available Tuesday morning but will be closed Tuesday afternoon, according to the district. The district said families should make decisions based on the conditions in their area. If weather conditions prevent a student from attending school, the resulting absence will be excused. Rain is expected Tuesday, with heavier rainfall possible Tuesday evening. The district also warned that heavier rainfall could continue Wednesday through Friday. The School District of Indian River County said additional updates will be provided by 1 p.m. the day before any additional schedule changes. Families should continue monitoring official district communications for the latest information.

entry.article_text: A major crash blocked two left lanes on southbound I-95 in Martin County beyond Exit 96 for Hobe Sound on Monday morning, according to the Florida Department of Transportation’s FL511 traffic system. The crash was reported at about 11:15 a.m. and was still affecting traffic as of 11:21 a.m. Drivers should expect delays and use caution approaching the area. A second crash nearby has also impacted traffic in the northbound lanes. According to the Florida Highway Patrol, one crash involves a single vehicle, and the second involves three vehicles. No injuries have been reported in either crash. All vehicles have been moved off the roadway. Traffic congestion remains due to the incidents; however, traffic flow is expected to improve shortly. No further details about the crash or any injuries were immediately available. Check FL511 for the latest traffic updates. for the latest traffic updates.

entry.title: Joe Namath's Lucky Shuck coming to Jensen Beach as waterfront village breaks ground - WPEC
entry.summary: Joe Namath's Lucky Shuck coming to Jensen Beach as waterfront village breaks ground    WPEC
entry.article_text: Football legend Joe Namath is bringing his popular Lucky Shuck restaurant to Jensen Beach as a massive waterfront development takes shape along the St. Rio Marine Village , a 30-acre mixed-use development in Martin County, broke ground Thursday, following more than five years of planning. The project will feature 342 apartments, a 131-slip marina, more than a half-mile of public riverwalk, and several waterfront dining and entertainment destinations. Among them is a new location of The Lucky Shuck Oyster Bar & Taphouse , owned by Namath and his business partner Charlie Modica, along with a second, yet-to-be-named outdoor dining concept. See also: New 24/7 animal cruelty hotline launching across Florida "The Lucky Shuck has always been about good food, good people and being on the water," Namath said. "Rio Marine Village gives us a home right on the river, and I can't wait to see boats pulling up and families sitting down together." The development will also feature the Osprey Club, a waterfront wedding and event venue, along with a public park, boardwalk, beach, and kayak and paddleboard rentals. Martin County commissioners unanimously approved the project's first two phases following years of community discussions. Construction is expected to begin this month, with the first phase scheduled for completion in late 2028.

entry.title: What airlines owe you after a canceled flight as FAA ground stop disruptions linger
entry.summary: Flight cancellations are dropping as airlines recover from Friday's nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop , but passengers are still dealing with delays, long layovers and an important question: What does an airline owe you when your flight is canceled? WATCH: Samantha Gutierrez's report for what passengers need to know Flight Canceled After FAA Ground Stop? Know Your Rights | WPTV Federal passenger protections provide a clear right in one key situation. If an airline cancels your flight and you decide not to travel, you are entitled to a refund, regardless of what caused the cancellation. That includes nonrefundable tickets. Hotels, meals and ground transportation are a different story. Because Friday's disruption originated with the FAA rather than an airline, carriers are not universally required to cover those additional expenses, though individual airlines may voluntarily provide assistance. Traveler: 'There's no consequence' At President Donald J. Trump International Airport, passenger Scott Danforth said the disruption left him frustrated by what he sees as an imbalance between the responsibilities of travelers and airlines. 'If we make cancellations, we get to pay a lot of money,' Danforth told WPTV. 'But they can make cancellations, and there's no consequence. That's what I don't like.' Paul Hudson of FlyersRights.org said passengers whose flights are canceled have an important decision to make. 'You can choose the offer of rebooking, or you can get a refund,' Hudson said. Under U.S. Department of Transportation rules, passengers do not have to accept airline credits or travel vouchers in place of a refund when the airline cancels their flight and they decide not to travel. What about hotels and meals? Another family WPTV met at the airport said their journey home now includes a 13-hour layover. 'Maybe they could give us, like, a hotel or something through all this chaos,' traveler Jessica Soros said. Hudson said passengers should ask their airline what assistance is available, but accommodations such as meals, hotel rooms and ground transportation aren't guaranteed when the disruption is outside the carrier's control. 'They may provide it to some passengers ... but they don't have to,' Hudson said. Travelers should still ask their carrier about meal vouchers, hotel assistance, discounted hotel rates and travel waivers. Travel insurance or benefits included with some credit cards may offer another option for qualifying expenses. '

Trump International Airport, passenger Scott Danforth said the disruption left him frustrated by what he sees as an imbalance between the responsibilities of travelers and airlines."If we make cancellations, we get to pay a lot of money," Danforth told WPTV. The continued disruption stems partly from aircraft and flight crews being left out of position following the nationwide stoppage. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said it takes time for airlines to move crews and planes back where they need to be.The FAA has said faulty equipment led to Friday's ground stop, while officials continue investigating the precise cause. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said officials had found no evidence of anything nefarious.A preliminary investigation found that an L3Harris contractor was working at a remote FAA site to replace copper wiring with fiber and replace a router when the router began flooding other routers with data, according to Duffy. The exact cause remains under investigation.U.S. Lois Frankel, D-Fla., said the disruption underscores the importance of ensuring the nation's aviation system remains reliable."We need to take whatever steps we can to make sure people are always safe and on time," Frankel said.While the cancellation numbers are improving, travel disruptions on this scale can take time to fully work through an airline network.For anyone still affected, the key is knowing the distinction: You may be entitled to your money back if the airline canceled your flight and you choose not to travel, but additional expenses such as meals and hotels depend on the circumstances and the airline's policies. entry.title: West Palm Beach neighbors brace for more rain after record flooding left streets underwater for 11 days
entry.summary: The chance of heavy rain this week is lingering over our five-county viewing area days after some communities in West Palm Beach dried out from a major flood event. The Hamilton Bay neighborhood in West Palm Beach was underwater last Monday, a full week after record-breaking rainfall came down. With more heavy rain in the forecast this week, neighbors tell me they're concerned. WATCH REPORT BELOW: West Palm Beach residents fear more flooding if heavy rain returns Late Monday morning, Ashley Debrowski was out strolling the sidewalks of Hamilton Bay with her children. 'A week ago today, I would still be trapped in my house,' Debrowski said. Around the corner, Tushar Bulsara was in his driveway wrapping a vehicle. 'That whole week was just unbelievable. It almost felt like a dream,' Bulsara said. Neighbors told me their community off of Jog Road was underwater for 11 days. 'Eleven days of essentially being afraid to leave the house,' Debrowski said. 'Vehicles have to be able to come in for me to do my work,' Bulsara said. 'And you know, that's business lost.' entry.title: Heavy rain, flooding possible in West Palm Beach this week as city extends state of emergency
entry.summary: West Palm Beach residents are being urged to prepare for another round of heavy rain and possible flooding this week while parts of the city are still recovering from historic rainfall earlier this month. The city said Monday that heavy rainfall and isolated flash flooding are possible from Tuesday through Thursday. According to information provided by the city from the National Weather Service, there is a 40% to 60% chance that 2 to 4 inches of rain could fall across much of South Florida's east coast, with significantly higher amounts possible in isolated locations. Additional rain could worsen flooding in areas where the ground remains saturated from the Nov. 1-2 flooding, particularly in low-lying neighborhoods. Mayor Keith James has extended West Palm Beach's local state of emergency through Sunday, Nov. 22. City officials said the extension allows West Palm Beach to continue emergency measures, coordinate resources and assist residents affected by the flooding. West Palm Beach prepares for additional flooding City crews and emergency personnel are continuing recovery work while preparing for the possibility of more flooding. According to the city, crews are monitoring affected neighborhoods and inspecting and clearing city-maintained storm drain grates. Officials are also evaluating whether garbage, recycling and yard waste collection can be accelerated in western communities hit hardest by the recent flooding to reduce the risk of additional service disruptions. The city is continuing to operate an auxiliary pumping station to lower water levels in the Apoxee Reserve. Water-control structures at Grassy Waters are also being managed to increase available storage capacity ahead of additional rainfall. City staff are meeting daily with regional partners to monitor water levels, review pumping operations and assess the capacity of the drainage system. How residents should prepare for heavy rain West Palm Beach officials are asking residents to prepare now in case flooding makes travel difficult. Residents should: Monitor weather forecasts and official city updates. Avoid driving or walking through flooded areas. Use caution around standing water and storm drains. entry.article_text: Military Trail has reopened, and the crater left behind by the deadly Learjet crash has been filled, but for families who lived just feet from where the plane came down, the road to recovery is far from over.Mariano Garcia, an attorney with Searcy Denney Scarola Barnhart & Shipley, is representing four families from the Greenacres mobile home community whose homes, vehicles and other property were damaged by crash debris.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "The immediate need right now is that people who were displaced still have to pay rent. They still have to pay bills. They have to replace food and items that they lost. They have repairs to their homes that need to be made, and so we're dealing with those immediate needs," Garcia said.Those financial concerns have been a part of the aftermath since the first days following the crash.For the four families Garcia represents, the focus is now turning to financial relief for their specific losses.One of those families is a household of eight living in a mobile home roughly 50 feet from the impact site. Garcia said seven members of the family were home when the crash happened, including three who were outside."Dad was on the porch holding his 1-year-old child. Mom was standing nearby when a chunk of sidewalk came busting through their porch, narrowly missing them," Garcia said.Other members of the family were inside."They all felt the explosion, the shock. They breathed all of the residue that was in the air," Garcia said. "It was a very traumatic event for them, as you can imagine."The damage to the family's home was significant."You had chunks of aircraft parts busting through the roofs, you know, allowing the water intrusion into these residences, and when you combine that with the power being out, food spoiling in refrigerators, folks being unable to return to their homes, it had a pretty significant impact on their lives," Garcia said.Power and water have since been restored to the mobile home community, according to Garcia, but the family of eight has not been able to return to its home because the residence remains unsafe. He said the family has been staying in Airbnbs provided through charity.Garcia said there is no lawsuit at this point.Instead, he is communicating with attorneys for Aurora Aviation Inc., which does business as Upper Jets and operated the Learjet, and the company's insurance carrier in an effort to secure immediate financial relief for the four families he represents.When WPTV asked whether the company has been cooperating, Garcia's response was direct."Very much so," he said. "I'm encouraged that at least the company for this charter operator, the insurance company, is responding and acknowledging that there were losses and are doing what they can to advance sums to these families and help them out."An inspector is expected to assess the affected properties as Garcia's team works to determine the extent of the losses.For now, Garcia said the immediate focus is on expenses families are already facing."The immediate need right now is that people who were displaced still have to pay rent. They still have to pay bills. They have to replace food and items that they lost. They have repairs to their homes that need to be made, and so we're dealing with those immediate needs," he said.WPTV previously spoke with Perez, a handyman whose mobile home is about 250 feet from where the Learjet crashed. At the time, he couldn't access his home, vehicle or the tools he depends on for work. Perez is not one of the residents represented by Garcia, but when WPTV recently returned to the neighborhood, our crew found an orange notice on his mobile home that read "UNSAFE.""Working materials are there. My screwdrivers, my drills, my saws, they're stuck there," Perez told WPTV at the time.He worried then about what the disruption would mean financially."We're not asking for nothing else but the necessary that's been lost or gonna get lost because of this, because my job wages, when rent comes down, who is gonna be, is my landlord or the people who I pay for that lot gonna say, ‘Oh, we feel sorry for you to have a discount?’ No, full payments are gonna have to be made," Perez said.Other organizations have also stepped in to address those immediate needs. The Emergency Assistance Foundation, a West Palm Beach-based nonprofit, launched a fund offering $1,000 cash grants to eligible residents impacted by the crash. Other groups have provided food, shelter, supplies and services for displaced residents.But some of what these families experienced is more difficult to measure."The photos and the aerials really don't do justice to just how close these families came to being seriously hurt or killed," Garcia said.He said some of the people he's spoken with are still dealing with the emotional and psychological effects of what they experienced."It's not something you see every day, and so it definitely had an emotional or psychological impact on them," Garcia said. "Many of them are having trouble sleeping, which is a very common report when someone undergoes a very sudden, tragic and unexpected event."Garcia, who has practiced law for 32 years, is also a longtime pilot. He described himself as a commercial multi-engine instrument-rated pilot and said he previously co-owned a flight school and charter service out of Palm Beach International Airport.He said determining the impact of emotional trauma will take time."There's no formula for that, Joel. It really depends upon the degree. We rely on medical experts to make that assessment and then use our judgment based on experience," Garcia said.While representing families impacted on the ground, Garcia stressed the magnitude of the loss suffered by the families of those aboard the Learjet."My heart goes out to the victims on board the plane. They suffered a massive loss, and I think what the public needs to understand is that this had a much broader impact," Garcia said.He said his focus now is helping the families he represents move toward some sense of normalcy."It's such a massive loss, particularly to the families of the occupants of the aircraft. It's hard to put words around what those families must be going through," Garcia said. "I can't imagine what they must be going through. And so if I can do something, even just a little bit to help others who were impacted by it, then, you know, I think that's the right thing to do."WPTV has reached out to Aurora Aviation for comment and is working to hear back.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: St. Lucie County schools to release students early Tuesday ahead of heavy rain - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County schools to release students early Tuesday ahead of heavy rain    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie Public Schools will dismiss students two hours early Tuesday as rain moves into the area, with heavier rainfall possible in the evening. The district said it made the decision as a precaution based on information from the National Weather Service . Parents and guardians are encouraged to consider conditions in their neighborhoods. Absences caused by weather will be excused, the district said. Heavier rain is possible Wednesday through Friday and could lead to school closures. The district is monitoring conditions with the St. Lucie County Emergency Operations Center and the National Weather Service. The district said it will announce any changes to Tuesday’s after-school activities and athletics based on weather conditions. Families should check the district’s official channels for updates. Neighboring Indian River County schools will also operate on a modified schedule Tuesday, Nov. 17, with students dismissed early, according to the School District of Indian River County. The district announced the following dismissal times: High schools: 12:20 p.m. Middle schools and K-8: 1 p.m. Elementary schools: 1:50 p.m. Wabasso School: 12:30 p.m. Morning arrival times will remain unchanged, and transportation will operate as normal during early dismissal. Extended Day will be available Tuesday morning but closed in the afternoon. All extracurricular activities must conclude by 2:30 p.m. The district said additional updates will be shared as information becomes available. RELATED: Heavy rain returns this week, bringing major threat of flooding across south Florida Palm Beach County schools are still scheduled to open Tuesday, Nov. The district will continue monitoring the weather and share updates if anything changes. The ground is already soaked from the rain we experienced the first weekend of the month, so it won't take much to create flooding concerns. Right now, up to 4-5 inches of rain is possible, but higher isolated amounts can't be ruled out.

entry.article_text: Parents could face criminal charges in a crackdown on illegal e-bikes after a teen was thrown 50 feet in a crash, the Martin County sheriff warned Monday. During a news conference, the sheriff revealed that a 14-year-old Port St. Lucie boy suffered catastrophic injuries in Sunday's crash near U.S. 1 and Northwest Goldenrod Road. The teen was airlifted to St. Mary's Medical Center , where he is now in stable condition. According to the sheriff, the boy and a friend had traveled roughly five miles from home on separate e-bikes when they attempted to cross U.S. See also: Kids, 6,000 fentanyl pills and stolen gun uncovered in massive Florida drug bust The first teen made it across, but the 14-year-old was struck by a northbound vehicle that had a green light. The impact sent the boy flying approximately 50 feet, while his e-bike landed about 100 feet away. "Had he not been wearing a helmet, and had he been hit just a little different, we'd be talking about a 14-year-old die in a fatality crash," the sheriff said. Investigators determined the teen was riding a 3,300-watt electric bike, more than four times the 750-watt limit cited by the sheriff. The motorbike-style vehicle was not street-legal, he said. The crash comes amid growing concerns over e-bike safety in Martin County, where the sheriff reported 41 e-bike crashes this year, involving riders as young as 7 and as old as 80. The sheriff said educational workshops, warnings, and previous enforcement efforts have failed to curb dangerous riding. Now, deputies are considering tougher consequences, including seizing illegal e-bikes and potentially pursuing criminal charges against parents who knowingly allow their children to ride them. I'm not anti-e-bikes, but I'm anti-illegal e-bikes being ridden irresponsibly on our streets." The Florida Highway Patrol is leading the crash investigation, with assistance from the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

entry.title: Jensen Beach residents concerned that forecasted heavy rainfall will cause repeat flooding - WPBF
entry.summary: Jensen Beach residents concerned that forecasted heavy rainfall will cause repeat flooding    WPBF
entry.article_text: As residents in Jensen Beach continue cleaning up after this month’s historic flooding, another round of heavy rainfall is heading their way. Many of the homes on Hyline Drive were flooded for eight long days, and residents are finally starting to get inside to start cleaning up. Related: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes They’re hoping the rain doesn’t ruin their progress. “Eight days of standing water. There was nothing that we could do but watch everything deteriorate and mold,” Susan Destafney said. Destafney’s home sits next to the Hyline Pond and was filled with dirty floodwater for eight days. She said they lost almost everything, and now volunteers are tearing the home down to the studs and treating it for mold. “I've cried more than I've ever cried before. It's just a lot to take in, and it should never have happened,” Destafney said. County officials have pumped water from the neighborhood and the pond, and they have set up a recovery assistance webpage for residents. But Destafney said for their day-to-day needs, they are relying on the volunteers and nonprofits to help them get by. She worries they could be knocked back to square one if the forecasted rainfall this week causes more flooding. I mean, things that I was able to save, I do have on my back porch. So, it's going to be raining. So, what's going to happen to the few things that I was able to save? It's a lot,” Destafney said. Others in the community we spoke to are also concerned about the forecast. We're trying to recover right now. My friends are trying to recover right now. All these efforts for cleanup to get us in a place to where it's dried up, the water is gone, and now they're expecting flash flooding again. So, yeah, we're nervous that this is going to be like what it was a couple of days ago all over again in a few days,” Crystal van Duyme said. WPBF 25 News reached out to the county to see what they’re doing to prep for the upcoming rainfall. The public works director was not available Monday, but we’re hoping to speak with him on Tuesday. However, residents did tell us that crews are currently draining the Hyline Pond again, likely in preparation for that rain. entry.article_text: Football legend Joe Namath is bringing his popular Lucky Shuck restaurant to Jensen Beach as a massive waterfront development takes shape along the St. Rio Marine Village , a 30-acre mixed-use development in Martin County, broke ground Thursday, following more than five years of planning. The project will feature 342 apartments, a 131-slip marina, more than a half-mile of public riverwalk, and several waterfront dining and entertainment destinations. Among them is a new location of The Lucky Shuck Oyster Bar & Taphouse , owned by Namath and his business partner Charlie Modica, along with a second, yet-to-be-named outdoor dining concept. See also: New 24/7 animal cruelty hotline launching across Florida "The Lucky Shuck has always been about good food, good people and being on the water," Namath said. "Rio Marine Village gives us a home right on the river, and I can't wait to see boats pulling up and families sitting down together." The development will also feature the Osprey Club, a waterfront wedding and event venue, along with a public park, boardwalk, beach, and kayak and paddleboard rentals. Martin County commissioners unanimously approved the project's first two phases following years of community discussions. Construction is expected to begin this month, with the first phase scheduled for completion in late 2028.

entry.summary: At 22 games played, the Florida Panthers are a quarter of the way through their regular season. The Panthers have 27 points, tied with Boston for the first Eastern Conference wild card spot. WATCH: Florida Panthers are one-fourth done with their season. Where do they stand? Florida Panthers are one-fourth of the way through their regular season. Where do they stand? The Panthers are currently playing without Captain Alexander Barkov and Brad Marchand. After a 2-1 overtime loss to the Dallas Stars Sunday night, heres what Matthew Tkachuk said about the teams performance so far this season. Fine, you know, it's been OK, some good and some bad, but we're in the fight. That's all you can ask for, and I can promise you it's going to be a fight to the end of this with the division,' Tkachuk told reporters. Tkachuk is having one of the best starts of a season in his career with 5 goals and 25 assists. WPTV Panthers anchor and Panthers 360 host Mike Trim connected with Associated Press reporter Tim Reynolds, who's covered the Panthers for two decades. Trim asked Reynolds who his pick would be for first-quarter team MVP. Seth Jones has been absolutely elite for this team. For me, even with a lot of great statistical numbers, leadership performances, all those things Seth Jones, far and away the most important player for the Panthers to date, Reynolds told Trim. Jones is tied for second on the Panthers with 23 points, notching 20 assists and 3 goals. Tuesday night, the Edmonton Oilers visit Sunrise at Amerant Bank Arena. The Oilers are a team the Panthers are familiar with as they beat them two times in recent years in the Stanley Cup Final. This season, Edmonton is off to a hot start. They have 35 points, which is currently the most in the Western Conference. Through 22 games, Oilers center Connor McDavid has 12 goals and 41 assists. McDavid recently matched former Edmonton captain Wayne Gretzky as the fastest player to 40 assists in a season. The puck drops at 7 p.m. Tuesday evening. The game will air locally on The Spot South Florida.

entry.title: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home - WPTV
entry.summary: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home    WPTV
entry.article_text: A Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding is searching for more permanent housing and money to rebuild after water destroyed much of the inside of their home. Lisa and Jeremy French, who have two young boys, told WPTV's Michael Hoffman they ultimately have one goal: to get their family back home.WATCH REPORT BELOW:WPTV first met the French family shortly after historic rainfall hit South Florida and the Treasure Coast. Floodwater had surrounded their neighborhood, forcing residents to use kayaks to get around and check on neighbors.Days later, much of the water has receded. The damage has not."My floorboards are outside," Lisa French said.Hoffman returned to the French family's Jensen Beach home for an update, but the family said it was not safe to go inside.French said the flooding wiped out much of what her family had accumulated over the years."Our appliances are gone, our cabinets are gone, every piece of furniture," French said.The family is now trying to determine how to pay for repairs while securing a more permanent place to live.WPTV met French again at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach, where a Multi-Agency Resource Center has been helping people looking for assistance following the flooding.French told Hoffman that her home flooded days after the rain had stopped.Martin County told WPTV that the family's home is near the Savannah Preserves, an area where excess water naturally flows from other flooded areas.French, however, questions whether other actions involving water entering the preserve contributed to what happened at her home."They're saying it's from natural rain, but they dumped Monday and Tuesday, nonstop into the savannas," French said.The impact of the flooding extends beyond the physical damage.Through tears, Lisa and Jeremy French pleaded for help before the Martin County Commission as they described what their family is facing."Today we are homeless," Lisa French told commissioners. "We have nowhere to host Thanksgiving. We have nowhere for our boys to have Christmas. We don't have beds to come home to."The couple has two young boys. French said she wants them to continue growing up in the Jensen Beach home the family worked hard to maintain.For now, however, the family says it needs more permanent housing while trying to determine where the money to repair the home will come from.French said the uncertainty surrounding assistance has left her worried there could still be a significant financial gap, even if additional aid becomes available."Who's going to fill in the gaps?" French said. "And, you know, maybe I feel like somebody should take accountability."Despite the uncertainty and extensive damage, the family says it has not given up hope of returning."We just want to go home," French said. "Like, that's at the end, that we just want to be home with our family."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.article_text: A 14-year-old boy was flown to St. Mary’s Medical Center in West Palm Beach after being injured in an illegal e-bike crash at U.S. 1 and NW Goldenrod Road in Jensen Beach over the weekend, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek expressed frustration over the incident and emphasized the risks associated with illegal e-bikes. “We’re not trying to pick on people, but there’s nothing worse than having a child laid up in a trauma center as we go into the holidays,” Budensiek said. The sheriff’s office released footage of the crash, showing two e-bikes attempting to cross U.S. While the first bike crossed safely, the second rider was struck by a vehicle that had a green light. Budensiek highlighted the importance of helmet use in preventing fatalities. “Had he not been wearing a helmet, we’d be talking about a 14-year-old dying in a fatality crash,” Budensiek said. Earlier this year, the sheriff’s office adopted a zero-tolerance policy on illegal e-bike use to address reckless riding and growing safety concerns. However, Budensiek said the message has not been effective. “So, this is serious for us. I know it’s fun for the kids, but our softer approach has not been working. We’ve had 41 e-bike crashes in Martin County this last year,” Budensiek said. Jason Moore, associate trauma medical director at HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce, said his hospital has treated numerous patients injured in e-bike crashes. “Yes, unfortunately we’ve seen a lot of e-bike accident patients. I’d say over the last 12 months we’ve seen hundreds of e-bike accidents,” Moore said. Moore described the severity of injuries resulting from e-bike crashes. “Unfortunately, we’ve seen pretty significant injuries, involving brain injuries, broken bones including those in the neck, the collarbone, the ribs. We see quite a few rib fractures,” Moore said. Budensiek said his office is committed to raising awareness about the dangers of illegal e-bikes and is exploring whether parents who knowingly purchase illegal e-bikes for their children could face criminal prosecution. “Parents are knowingly buying illegal e-bikes, giving them to their kids, and allowing their kids to ride them, so we are looking at criminal prosecution for parents if we can make that stick,” Budensiek said. entry.title: Riviera Beach flood victims seek relief as city weighs $2 million aid plan
entry.summary: Riviera Beach residents demand help after historic flooding Hundreds of Riviera Beach residents packed an emergency City Council meeting seeking financial assistance after November flooding damaged homes, displaced families and left residents questioning how they will pay for repairs. The city discussed setting aside $2 million for a proposed forgivable loan or grant program for residents whose homes were damaged by the flooding. The proposed assistance would help pay for interior and exterior repairs needed to make homes safe and livable. But during the heated meeting, city Finance Director Randy Sherman said the city faces restrictions on using public money to pay for damage to private property, creating uncertainty about how the proposed relief could move forward. Riviera Beach weighs $2M flood relief plan as residents demand help Lone Pine Estates residents press city for financial relief Weeks after floodwaters inundated homes in Lone Pine Estates, residents filled the meeting room, with others standing outside, hoping city leaders would provide a path toward recovery. Keisha Hartys lives in the neighborhood and her home was impacted by the flooding. She summed up the growing frustration in the neighborhood. No help is coming. We are on our own, said Harty. Another resident challenged the city's position that public funding could not be used directly to help private homeowners, pointing to other causes the city has supported. When you say you cant use federal dollars or public funding for private citizens, I have to disagree, the resident said. Im looking for a Lone Pine relief fundraiser. Council member Shirley Lanier argued the flooding and its impact on residents should be treated as a broader public safety concern. That is a public safety issue, Lanier said. There is no way that we cannot use public money for a public concern. Residents describe the toll of the flooding Residents also used the meeting to show city leaders what recovery has looked like on the ground. One woman said firefighters rescued her from floodwaters. entry.article_text: At the podium, she displayed basic items she said she received afterward, including a T-shirt, deodorant and socks.“Why is this being given to a taxpayer on an emergency event?” she asked.The frustrations come as families continue trying to clean up and repair homes weeks after the flooding.Many residents are also concerned about additional rainfall and the possibility that already hard-hit neighborhoods could face more flooding.The Riviera Beach City Council unanimously voted to amend a motion to continue considering the $2 million emergency set-aside while seeking a legal opinion on how the money could be used.The proposal calls for establishing a forgivable loan or grant program specifically for residents whose homes were damaged by the November flooding.City leaders also considered partnerships that could provide emergency shelter, hotel or motel vouchers and temporary housing for displaced residents.Another proposal would allow the city to coordinate mutual aid with neighboring cities, counties and partner agencies for debris removal, collection and other flood recovery needs.The vote does not mean homeowners will immediately receive money. Instead, it keeps the proposed assistance moving forward as city officials examine the legal options available for providing relief.A representative from U.S. Lois Frankel’s office told residents that the office was working with federal and state officials to seek disaster assistance.

entry.title: 37th Stuart Air Show draws big crowds for picture-perfect weekend
entry.summary: The 37th Stuart Air Show brought aviation fans young and old together for a picture-perfect weekend filled with aircraft, family traditions, and appreciation for veterans. Organizers said the weekend got off to a strong start Friday night with a drone and fireworks show and continued with large crowds throughout the weekend. 'Stuart Air Show has had an amazing weekend Friday night with our drone and fireworks show. We had a great turnout,' Chrissy Valvano said. 'Sunday, we're looking at a record turnout for Veterans Appreciation Day, and this weather could not be better.' For some families, attending the Stuart Air Show has become a tradition passed down through the years. 'The Stuart Air Show has been a part of our community for many years,' Sarah Naylor said. 'We have many memories of coming in the past, as long as I can remember.' For younger aviation fans Wyatt and Ivy Rotan, some of the biggest attractions were the military aircraft. 'I like coming to the Stuart Air Show because I like to see the C-17 and the F-16 fly,' Wyatt said. 'I like seeing the C-17,' Ivy added. The event also gave young people a chance to learn more about aviation while honoring those who served. 'You get to have a lot of fun around here, just going around and seeing a bunch of planes,' John Gefell said. 'Also, because I'm working on my aviation merit badge as a Boy Scout and my grandpa was a veteran, so its just real fun to come out here and just have a lot of fun.' With beautiful weather and a strong turnout, the 37th Stuart Air Show once again brought the community together, giving longtime fans and a new generation of aviation enthusiasts a weekend to remember.

entry.summary: Weeks after historic flooding devastated homes in Jensen Beach, Martin County families are still cleaning up and rebuilding, with volunteers, churches, firefighters, contractors and local leaders joining the recovery effort. Water marks remain visible on some homes, showing how high floodwaters rose. Residents are now removing damaged drywall, clearing debris and collecting donated supplies while seeking financial assistance and answers about the area's drainage systems. Jensen Beach families rebuild as neighbors rally after historic flooding Neighbors step in to help Jensen Beach families Before-and-after video from the Jensen Beach neighborhood shows the extent of the flooding, which left several homes under feet of water. Weeks later, homeowner Lisa Marie French said cleaning up has been a major undertaking. We first told you about French's circumstances last week. 'Its a lot of work. entry.article_text: Families across the Treasure Coast are watching the forecast closely after historic flooding overwhelmed parts of Port St. Just as many neighborhoods are drying out, forecasters are warning another 4 to 6 inches of rain could fall over the next few days, raising concerns about renewed flooding in areas still recovering from the record rainfall. The flooding two weeks ago left cars stranded, some families trapped in their homes and others wading through deep water. "It was horrible," said Port St. Lucie resident Crisostomo Santiago Perez. "Water was on top of the cars almost, covering hoods." Among those caught off guard was freshman Noah Julian. 2, Noah stepped off his school bus to find his neighborhood along Coleman Avenue flooded. A video recorded by neighbor Martina Elieson quickly spread on social media, showing the teenager swimming through floodwaters just to reach his driveway. "When I see the video, I'm like, what?" said Noah's father, Romeo Julian. We got alligators here, snakes, sharp objects could have cut him up. A thousand things could've happened to him." With another round of heavy rain in the forecast, residents say they aren't taking any chances." "Today I'm going to get stuff before flood comes," Perez said. See also: From banks to flights, outages leave south Floridians frustrated St. Lucie Public Schools is also preparing ahead of the storm. The district announced a two-hour early release Tuesday in an effort to avoid a repeat of the flooding issues that affected students taking the bus home earlier this month. "But why it always takes one thing to make them wake up." Meanwhile, county crews have been inspecting and clearing canals and drainage systems ahead of the expected rainfall. Officials warn that because the ground is still saturated from recent storms, it will take far less rain than usual to cause flooding in neighborhoods, streets and other low-lying areas. Residents are encouraged to monitor local forecasts and be prepared for changing conditions as the rain moves into the area.

entry.summary: St. Lucie County Prepares for More Rain After Historic Flooding    WPEC
entry.article_text: Crews are clearing drainage systems and checking waterways in St. Lucie County as another round of rain threatens areas still recovering from historic flooding. Lucie Public Schools is releasing students two hours early Tuesday. The district is asking families to monitor its official channels for updates as weather conditions change. Lucie officials say Public Works crews are inspecting drainage systems, clearing blockages and lowering water levels where possible. The ground remains saturated, increasing the risk of flooding even if rainfall is lighter than it was during the early November storms. See also: Heavy rain returns this week, bringing major threat of flooding across South Florida The National Weather Service has issued a flood watch for St. Lucie County from Tuesday afternoon through Friday evening. Forecasters expect 3 to 6 inches of rain across the area, with higher amounts possible in some locations. Two weeks ago, floodwaters stranded cars, trapped families and forced some residents to wade through deep water. Videos from that flooding showed high school freshman Noah Julian swimming from his school bus toward his home in a flooded Port St. Another video showed 7-year-old Ella Ghodooshim walking through chest-deep water with her mother near Oak Hammock K-8. Officials are urging residents to plan ahead, monitor forecasts and local alerts, and limit unnecessary travel. Drivers should never enter standing or moving water. Floodwater can stall a vehicle and cause costly engine damage. If you cannot tell how deep the water is, turn around and find another route. Residents can report flooding concerns to St. Lucie County at flooding@stlucieco.org .

entry.title: Port St. Lucie family offers free heart screenings to honor late daughter - WPBF
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie family offers free heart screenings to honor late daughter    WPBF
entry.article_text: The parents of Jessica Clinton, a Port St. Lucie teen who died of cardiac arrest in 2003, are hosting a free heart screening event this Saturday at the St. Lucie County Health Department to raise awareness about children's heart health. Jessica Clinton's parents Ray and Cheryl Lalloo are preparing for the event, which is expected to draw about 600 children. He stressed the importance of identifying heart problems early. "You hear it all the time. Kids go to sleep, parents come in the morning, they're not awake, and it's now just infants, or SIDS, it's kids that are 10, 12, 13 years old," Ray Lalloo said. Jessica was 17 years old and at cheerleading practice at St. Lucie West Centennial High School when she went into cardiac arrest. At the time, there were no automated external defibrillators (AEDs) on campus, and Jessica died that day. Her parents said she had undergone two sports physicals in the months before her death, but no heart problem was detected. In response to their loss, Jessica's parents founded the Jessica Clinton MVP Foundation and began offering heart screenings 17 years ago. They said the screenings have helped identify previously undiagnosed heart conditions. Last year, they said about 19 children learned they had a condition that had not been detected before. "We've had a couple of kids with pretty significant diagnoses. You know, things like syndrome, the really bad ones, you know," Ray Lalloo said. Cheryl Lalloo is grateful they were able to offer free screenings. "Blessed is the word, Cheryl Lalloo said. "It makes us feel like we also have a lot more work to do. That there's still kids out there that are still diagnosed." The free screenings are available for children and young adults ages 5 to 20 and include an electrocardiogram (EKG) and a check of vital signs. A cardiologist reviews the results, and an Echocardiogram is available if needed. The Lalloos said close to 650 children have signed up for this year's event. Appointments are booked, but families can call to ask about the waiting list. Organizers said they'll try to fill openings if someone cancels or doesn't show up. Jessica's parents hope their efforts will prevent other families from experiencing a loss like theirs. "The one child could be the next president of our country. It could be the person who invents the cure for cancer. So, every life is important. Children should not die like this," Ray Lalloo said. The event will take place Saturday from 8 a.m. Lucie County Health Department, 5150 NW Milner Drive, Port St. The number to call for scheduling is 772-462-3800. entry.title: Jensen Beach neighbors help families rebuild weeks after historic flooding - WFLX
entry.summary: Jensen Beach neighbors help families rebuild weeks after historic flooding    WFLX
entry.article_text: Weeks after historic flooding devastated homes in Jensen Beach, Martin County families are still cleaning up and rebuilding, with volunteers, churches, firefighters, contractors and local leaders joining the recovery effort. Water marks remain visible on some homes, showing how high floodwaters rose. Residents are now removing damaged drywall, clearing debris and collecting donated supplies while seeking financial assistance and answers about the area's drainage systems. Neighbors step in to help Jensen Beach families Before-and-after video from the Jensen Beach neighborhood shows the extent of the flooding, which left several homes under feet of water. Weeks later, homeowner Lisa Marie French said cleaning up has been a major undertaking. We first told you about French's circumstances last week. You first have to empty the houses," French said. "We have to clean the houses; they're filled with mold, we have to take the drywall out." French, whose home was impacted by the flooding, has also helped coordinate community cleanup efforts alongside Christ of Church, Family Church and other organizations. She said neighbors and other volunteers have repeatedly shown up asking what families need and then immediately gotten to work. "People have been just coming and just hands-on," French said. "People are like, 'Hey, are you taking donations? What do you need?' And they get out of their cars, and they start working, and that's our neighbors. It’s pretty amazing." Residents seek answers about flooding and drainage As cleanup continues, residents say they also want answers about what contributed to the severe flooding. Some are questioning how much pumping from Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce into the Savannas Preserve may have contributed to flooding in their neighborhood. Stephen Leighton, chief of staff for U.S. Brian Mast, R-Fla., told WPTV that questions remain as officials work through the recovery process. "There's a lot of answers that these residents need, and hopefully we can do that," Leighton said. Leighton also said the state had taken steps toward an emergency declaration and reached out to the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). Families look for financial assistance For some homeowners, rebuilding also brings financial uncertainty. French said her home is not in a flood zone and she does not have flood insurance, leaving her family dependent on whatever assistance, donated materials and volunteer help becomes available. "We're trying to get any type of help. We don't have flood insurance here," French said. "We're way above sea level; we are not a flood zone. So it's just whatever volunteers and help and materials we can get is what we get." Community calls for more volunteers Residents say more hands are still needed as families work to make their homes livable again. Leighton said a question-and-answer town meeting with residents and county, state and federal officials is planned this week as the community seeks clarity about the flooding and available assistance. For volunteers, Leighton said even small acts can make a difference for families trying to put their lives back together. "To help somebody take that picture off the wall and put it in a box, so they can move on, is a big deal," he said. With Thanksgiving approaching, he said the need for community support remains urgent. "We're two weeks out from Thanksgiving, and we really need the community to come together and help," Leighton said. entry.title: New study shows families are serving up a side dish of financial support this holiday season
entry.summary: This holiday season, many people will sit down with the relatives who helped them cover their rent or groceries this year. A new survey of 1,000 U.S. adults from BestMoney found that family is the first place people turn when they're short on cash. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Study shows families serving up a side dish of financial support The study also revealed people are using the borrowed money to pay for everyday bills rather than one-time emergencies. Some examples beyond groceries and rent include car loans. Of those surveyed, nearly all say they've given or received financial support from someone they know in the past 12 months. A large portion of parents surveyed, nearly 43%, say they've given financial support to their adult child in the past year, compared to just 6 percent of parents who say they received support from a child. Read the full story here.

entry.title: FAU researchers find the best treatment for Childhood Apraxia of Speech could come down to timing
entry.summary: For families with children who have an acute speech disorder known as Child Apraxia of Speech, it's always a race against the clock to find the most optimal therapy. Researchers at Florida Atlantic University may have recently discovered that helping to connect the dots between a child's brain and their speech could come down to the time of day of their therapy. WATCH: The best treatment for complex speech disorder could come down to timing Study: Time of day could make speech therapy more effective Sara Tutoni's daughter was too young to participate in the study, but the family does seek treatment at FAU for CAS. Tutoni says she realized something wasn't right around age 2. 'She could make every sound an animal makes, every sound a car makes, but no words,' Tutoni said. In the study, published in the journal Clinical Linguistics Phonetics , FAU researchers shared a striking difference in how speech-motor learning unfolded for participants with and without CAS. Their findings suggest that the time of day may influence speech-motor learning differently in young people with CAS and could eventually help clinicians identify ways to make therapy more effective without simply adding more hours of treatment. The study consisted of 82 adolescents and young adults ages 12 to 21 with and without CAS. Researchers found that participants with typical speech showed a slight benefit from evening training, while those with CAS performed better after morning training. Dr. Anne van Zelst, one of the lead researchers, says further study is needed, but believes this starting point could be critical to helping families and other stakeholders save time and money on expensive therapies. '(It could save) parents, school districts and insurance companies. It's very demanding on families,' van Zelst said. Tutoni said she wishes she would've had tools like this early on and sees it as a game changer for other families navigating CAS. Her focus is on her daughter and giving her the best chance at success.

entry.title: St. Lucie County prepares for more rain after historic flooding - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County prepares for more rain after historic flooding    WPEC
entry.article_text: Crews are clearing drainage systems and checking waterways in St. Lucie County as another round of rain threatens areas still recovering from historic flooding. Lucie Public Schools is releasing students two hours early Tuesday. The district is asking families to monitor its official channels for updates as weather conditions change. Lucie officials say Public Works crews are inspecting drainage systems, clearing blockages and lowering water levels where possible. The ground remains saturated, increasing the risk of flooding even if rainfall is lighter than it was during the early November storms. See also: Heavy rain returns this week, bringing major threat of flooding across South Florida The National Weather Service has issued a flood watch for St. Lucie County from Tuesday afternoon through Friday evening. Forecasters expect 3 to 6 inches of rain across the area, with higher amounts possible in some locations. Two weeks ago, floodwaters stranded cars, trapped families and forced some residents to wade through deep water. Videos from that flooding showed high school freshman Noah Julian swimming from his school bus toward his home in a flooded Port St. Another video showed 7-year-old Ella Ghodooshim walking through chest-deep water with her mother near Oak Hammock K-8. Officials are urging residents to plan ahead, monitor forecasts and local alerts, and limit unnecessary travel. Drivers should never enter standing or moving water. Floodwater can stall a vehicle and cause costly engine damage. If you cannot tell how deep the water is, turn around and find another route. Residents can report flooding concerns to St. Lucie County at flooding@stlucieco.org .

entry.title: Jensen Beach Festival of Giving brings together more than 50 local nonprofits
entry.summary: More than 50 local nonprofits are coming together for the third annual Festival of Giving at the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast, filling the Jensen Beach museum with holiday displays while allowing community organizations to share the work they do throughout the region. Christina McIntosh, community outreach and events coordinator for the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast, said participating nonprofits come from communities stretching from Palm Beach County north through the Treasure Coast. 'Those are the five counties that our education department here at the museum works with and works with the schools,' McIntosh said. More than Christmas decorations The Festival of Giving uses decorated Christmas trees and holiday displays to introduce visitors to nonprofit organizations serving South Florida and the Treasure Coast. For the organizations involved, the gathering also provides a chance to learn more about one another. Treasure Coast Community Singers is among the nonprofits participating. 'The really great thing about this event is that we get to know other nonprofits,' Sharon Savageaux of Treasure Coast Community Singers said. We get to understand what they do. And we can help spread their word.' The singers also performed at the museum during a festival breakfast event. A Grinch-themed tree with a community mission The GFWC Hobe Sound Womans Club is also participating, decorating its display with a Grinch theme. Sandy Vucik, who represented the organization at the festival, said the money it raises supports several community organizations, including Family Promise, CareBag and Real Life Childrens Ranch in Okeechobee. Vucik said the club is currently helping 19 children at the ranch. 'We're really hoping to give them a nice Christmas,' Vucik said. The holiday setting gives visitors a chance to discover organizations they may not otherwise encounter while allowing nonprofits themselves to make new community connections. Family Night brings Santa, cookies and hot chocolate to Jensen Beach. The festival includes several special events beyond its nonprofit displays. McIntosh said Family Night will include a visit from Santa along with hot chocolate, cookie decorating, and craft activities. 'Santa's coming into town,' McIntosh said. entry.title: Riviera Beach flood victims seek relief as city weighs $2 million aid plan
entry.summary: Riviera Beach residents demand help after historic flooding Hundreds of Riviera Beach residents packed an emergency City Council meeting seeking financial assistance after November flooding damaged homes, displaced families and left residents questioning how they will pay for repairs. The city discussed setting aside $2 million for a proposed forgivable loan or grant program for residents whose homes were damaged by the flooding. The proposed assistance would help pay for interior and exterior repairs needed to make homes safe and livable. But during the heated meeting, city Finance Director Randy Sherman said the city faces restrictions on using public money to pay for damage to private property, creating uncertainty about how the proposed relief could move forward. Riviera Beach weighs $2M flood relief plan as residents demand help Lone Pine Estates residents press city for financial relief Weeks after floodwaters inundated homes in Lone Pine Estates, residents filled the meeting room, with others standing outside, hoping city leaders would provide a path toward recovery. Keisha Harty's lives in the neighborhood and her home was impacted by the flooding. She summed up the growing frustration in the neighborhood. 'No help is coming. We are on our own,' said Harty. 'When you say you can't use federal dollars or public funding for private citizens, I have to disagree,' the resident said. 'I'm looking for a Lone Pine relief fundraiser.' Council member Shirley Lanier argued the flooding and its impact on residents should be treated as a broader public safety concern. 'That is a public safety issue,' Lanier said. entry.article_text: Parents could face criminal charges in a crackdown on illegal e-bikes after a teen was thrown 50 feet in a crash, the Martin County sheriff warned Monday. During a news conference, the sheriff revealed that a 14-year-old Port St. Lucie boy suffered catastrophic injuries in Sunday's crash near U.S. 1 and Northwest Goldenrod Road. The teen was airlifted to St. Mary's Medical Center , where he is now in stable condition. According to the sheriff, the boy and a friend had traveled roughly five miles from home on separate e-bikes when they attempted to cross U.S. See also: Kids, 6,000 fentanyl pills and stolen gun uncovered in massive Florida drug bust The first teen made it across, but the 14-year-old was struck by a northbound vehicle that had a green light. The impact sent the boy flying approximately 50 feet, while his e-bike landed about 100 feet away. "Had he not been wearing a helmet, and had he been hit just a little different, we'd be talking about a 14-year-old die in a fatality crash," the sheriff said. Investigators determined the teen was riding a 3,300-watt electric bike, more than four times the 750-watt limit cited by the sheriff. The motorbike-style vehicle was not street-legal, he said. The crash comes amid growing concerns over e-bike safety in Martin County, where the sheriff reported 41 e-bike crashes this year, involving riders as young as 7 and as old as 80. The sheriff said educational workshops, warnings, and previous enforcement efforts have failed to curb dangerous riding. Now, deputies are considering tougher consequences, including seizing illegal e-bikes and potentially pursuing criminal charges against parents who knowingly allow their children to ride them. I'm not anti-e-bikes, but I'm anti-illegal e-bikes being ridden irresponsibly on our streets." The Florida Highway Patrol is leading the crash investigation, with assistance from the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

entry.title: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in - WPEC
entry.summary: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Treasure Coast is bracing for a soggy stretch as counties prepare for possible flooding from heavy rain. Indian River County The Indian River County Emergency Operations Center remains at Level 2, or partial activation, because of ongoing flooding and the potential for more heavy rain. Emergency services, human services and infrastructure partners are coordinating response and recovery efforts. The county urges residents to avoid flooded roads and floodwaters, watch for rising water in low-lying areas and monitor weather conditions and official updates. Residents with flood-related questions or information can call the Emergency Information Center at 772-226-4000 during operating hours. Heavy rain and gusty winds are forecast in Indian River County from Tuesday, Nov. Solid waste services may be disrupted. Waste Management curbside collections may be delayed, and residents should not put carts in the street if it is flooded. Waste Management collects recycling in blue carts countywide. It collects garbage, yard waste and bulk waste in unincorporated Indian River County, Fellsmere, Sebastian and Indian River Shores. Residents in other cities and towns should check with their local governments for service updates. The county recommends putting carts out by 6 a.m. on collection day, closing lids, bagging garbage and avoiding overfilled carts. Cardboard should be flattened and placed inside recycling carts, and yard waste should stay inside yard waste carts. Residents should bring carts back in as soon as possible after collection. The landfill and all five Customer Convenience Centers may close early or remain closed if conditions become unsafe. The east-central Florida coast faces a Slight Risk, or Level 2 out of 4, for excessive rainfall. Localized flooding is possible, especially along the coast, and some areas could receive 4 inches or more of rain. Martin County Martin County officials expect 3 to 6 inches of rain, with localized amounts of 8 to 12 inches, beginning Tuesday afternoon and continuing through Nov. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office says it is working with the county’s emergency operations center to monitor rainfall and identify roads that could become difficult to pass. The sheriff’s office plans to deploy high-water rescue vehicles in flood-prone areas. Having the vehicles nearby could help deputies reach residents who need assistance and motorists who become stranded, the office said. The sheriff’s office advises residents: If water covers the road, turn around. Standing water may be deeper than it appears and can hide damage to the road. If your usual route home is flooded, take another route or wait somewhere safe. Never drive around a barricade. Stay out of flooded areas and avoid driving to see how high the water is. Keeping roads clear gives deputies and rescue crews room to reach people who need help. Martin County Fire Rescue advises residents to be prepared to evacuate if flooding threatens their homes or neighborhoods. Residents should also have an emergency kit ready for household members and pets. The Community Information Center will be open to provide flood-related information. Okeechobee County Okeechobee County is also preparing for severe flooding. The Okeechobee County Sheriff’s Office says its emergency operations center will remain active as staff coordinate response and recovery efforts from past flooding. Sandbags are available at Okeechobee County Public Works, 804 Northwest Second St. Lucie County Public Safety Department is monitoring the forecast and reminding residents to secure loose items that could be damaged by wind. Gusty northeast winds of 25 to 30 mph are forecast Tuesday and Wednesday, with gusts of 35 to 40 mph along the coast. Residents should secure tarps, patio furniture and unsecured recovery materials. A rip current advisory remains in effect for St. Strong onshore winds can create dangerous rip currents and rough surf. The county has extended the deadline to Nov. 30 for residents to report flood damage through an online survey. The information will help document flooding across the community and inform recovery efforts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants throughout St. Lucie County, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie Village and unincorporated areas. It asks where flooding occurred, how buildings were affected and what impacts residents and businesses experienced. Lucie County asks that the survey be completed by November 30, https://arcg.is/05f4b13 .

entry.title: Trump's Presidential Library foundation amasses $57.6 million
entry.summary: The foundation overseeing President Donald Trumps future presidential library amassed $57.6 million by the end of last year, new tax filings show, as the president turned legal battles with major media and tech companies into an unusual source of funding for the project. The filings do not identify the donors or reveal how much of the money came from controversial settlements. But the documents, provided to CNN by the Donald J. Trump Presidential Library Foundation, confirm the organization has a sizable head start on his unconventional vision for a presidential library a towering Miami skyscraper that he has suggested could also serve as a hotel. RELATED STORY | Eric Trump shares renderings of a proposed Trump presidential library and museum The foundation reported spending just $349,000 during its first seven months. Much of that was paid to Bermello Ajamil Partners, the architecture firm that produced renderings of the proposed 47-story library. It previously told the Internal Revenue Service that it expected to raise about $50 million by the end of 2025. But it anticipated fundraising would accelerate considerably: The organization estimated it will bring in nearly $1 billion by the end of 2027. Its unclear whether the organization remains on track toward reaching that goal. Recently, two of Trumps top political operatives, James Blair and Chris LaCivita, donated to the foundation amid revelations they left the country ahead of the midterms to provide counsel for Republika Srpska, a pro-Russia Balkan government. In the months since Trump circulated renderings for his proposed library including a gilded entranceway and an Air Force One on display he has announced other expensive legacy construction projects, including a White House ballroom that has attracted seven- and eight-figure checks from large companies and political allies. A pro-Trump super PAC, MAGA Inc., closely connected to the president has also brought in hundreds of millions of dollars. Trumps planned library was designated to receive sizable sums from settlements with companies he sued during the presidential campaign and after his first term. ABC News agreed in December 2024 to pay $15 million toward the library, and Meta earmarked $22 million for the library in a January 2025 settlement. In 2025, a $16 million deal with Paramount, the parent company of CBS, agreed to cover legal fees and costs, turning the remainder over to the library foundation. entry.title: Teen arrested in hit-and-run crash that critically injured 24-year-old woman in Port St. Lucie
entry.summary: An 18-year-old driver has been arrested after a hit-and-run crash critically injured a 24-year-old woman on an electric scooter in Port St. Lucie, police said. The incident happened Monday morning near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace, Port St. Lucie police said. According to investigators, the victim was riding an electric scooter westbound on the sidewalk toward Southwest Rosser Boulevard. As the woman on the scooter entered the crosswalk, she was struck by the 18-year-old driver of a gray Chevrolet Tahoe making a left turn onto Southwest Feather Terrace. Police said the driver fled the scene and failed to stop to render aid to the woman. The Port St. Lucie Police Department's Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit identified the driver as Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer and located the vehicle through its investigation. Investigators learned Sanchez-Chasmer had been playing 'ding dong ditch' just before the crash. He was arrested on a charge of leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, police said. The Port St. Lucie Police Department is expected to hold a press conference on Tuesday at 2 p.m. Chief Leo Niemczyk will address the incident, providing additional details about the investigation, the arrest and an update on the victim's condition.

entry.article_text: Families across the Treasure Coast are watching the forecast closely after historic flooding overwhelmed parts of Port St. Just as many neighborhoods are drying out, forecasters are warning another 4 to 6 inches of rain could fall over the next few days, raising concerns about renewed flooding in areas still recovering from the record rainfall. The flooding two weeks ago left cars stranded, some families trapped in their homes and others wading through deep water. "It was horrible," said Port St. Lucie resident Crisostomo Santiago Perez. "Water was on top of the cars almost, covering hoods." Among those caught off guard was freshman Noah Julian. 2, Noah stepped off his school bus to find his neighborhood along Coleman Avenue flooded. A video recorded by neighbor Martina Elieson quickly spread on social media, showing the teenager swimming through floodwaters just to reach his driveway. "When I see the video, I'm like, what?" said Noah's father, Romeo Julian. We got alligators here, snakes, sharp objects could have cut him up. A thousand things could've happened to him." With another round of heavy rain in the forecast, residents say they aren't taking any chances." "Today I'm going to get stuff before flood comes," Perez said. See also: From banks to flights, outages leave south Floridians frustrated St. Lucie Public Schools is also preparing ahead of the storm. The district announced a two-hour early release Tuesday in an effort to avoid a repeat of the flooding issues that affected students taking the bus home earlier this month. "But why it always takes one thing to make them wake up." Meanwhile, county crews have been inspecting and clearing canals and drainage systems ahead of the expected rainfall. Officials warn that because the ground is still saturated from recent storms, it will take far less rain than usual to cause flooding in neighborhoods, streets and other low-lying areas. Residents are encouraged to monitor local forecasts and be prepared for changing conditions as the rain moves into the area.
