entry.title: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in - WPEC
entry.summary: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Treasure Coast is bracing for a soggy stretch as counties prepare for possible flooding from heavy rain. Indian River County The Indian River County Emergency Operations Center remains at Level 2, or partial activation, because of ongoing flooding and the potential for more heavy rain. Emergency services, human services and infrastructure partners are coordinating response and recovery efforts. The county urges residents to avoid flooded roads and floodwaters, watch for rising water in low-lying areas and monitor weather conditions and official updates. Residents with flood-related questions or information can call the Emergency Information Center at 772-226-4000 during operating hours. Due to the heavy rain and gusty winds, solid waste services may be disrupted. Waste Management curbside collections may be delayed, and residents should not put carts in the street if it is flooded. See also: Florida deputies rescue 2-year-old girl found in pond near apartment complex Waste Management collects recycling in blue carts countywide. It collects garbage, yard waste and bulk waste in unincorporated Indian River County, Fellsmere, Sebastian and Indian River Shores. Residents in other cities and towns should check with their local governments for service updates. The county recommends putting carts out by 6 a.m. on collection day, closing lids, bagging garbage, and avoiding overfilled carts. Cardboard should be flattened and placed inside recycling carts, and yard waste should stay inside yard waste carts. Residents should bring carts back in as soon as possible after collection. The landfill and all five Customer Convenience Centers may close early or remain closed if conditions become unsafe. The east-central Florida coast faces a Slight Risk, or Level 2 out of 4, for excessive rainfall. Localized flooding is possible, especially along the coast, and some areas could receive 4 inches or more of rain. Martin County Martin County officials expect 3 to 6 inches of rain, with localized amounts of 8 to 12 inches, beginning Tuesday afternoon and continuing through Nov. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office says it is working with the county’s emergency operations center to monitor rainfall and identify roads that could become difficult to pass. The sheriff’s office plans to deploy high-water rescue vehicles in flood-prone areas. Having the vehicles nearby could help deputies reach residents who need assistance and motorists who become stranded, the office said. The sheriff’s office advises residents to turn around if water covers the road. Standing water may be deeper than it appears and can hide damage. If a regular route is flooded, drivers should take another route or wait somewhere safe. Residents should never drive around barricades or enter flooded areas to see how high the water is. Martin County Fire Rescue also advises residents to be prepared to evacuate if flooding threatens their homes or neighborhoods and to have an emergency kit ready for household members and pets. The Community Information Center will be open to provide flood-related information. Okeechobee County Okeechobee County is also preparing for severe flooding. The Okeechobee County Sheriff’s Office says its emergency operations center will remain active as staff coordinate response and recovery efforts from past flooding. Sandbags are available at Okeechobee County Public Works, 804 Northwest Second St. Lucie County Public Safety Department is monitoring the forecast and reminding residents to secure loose items that could be damaged by wind. Gusty northeast winds of 25 to 30 mph are forecast Tuesday and Wednesday, with gusts of 35 to 40 mph along the coast. Residents should secure tarps, patio furniture and other unsecured items. A rip current advisory remains in effect for St. Strong onshore winds can create dangerous rip currents and rough surf. Lucie County Fire District says its firefighters, paramedics and telecommunicators are prepared to respond as the area faces more heavy rain and recovers from recent flooding. The district has high-water vehicles and a rescue boat available to assist during flood-related emergencies. Free sand is available while supplies last at two self-service locations: County Fairgrounds: 5601 W. Midway Road, Fort Pierce, in the west parking lot Lawnwood Stadium: 2000 Virginia Ave., Fort Pierce Residents should bring their own bags, shovel and other supplies. Residents can use Community Connect to share household information that could help firefighters prepare for an emergency. The county has extended the deadline to Nov. 30 for residents to report flood damage through an online survey. The information will help document flooding across the community and inform recovery efforts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants throughout St. Lucie County, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie Village and unincorporated areas. It asks where flooding occurred, how buildings were affected and what impacts residents and businesses experienced. Residents can complete the flood damage survey by Nov. Officials urge residents across the region to avoid flooded roads and keep roadways clear for emergency responders. If you encounter flooding, turn around and find a safe alternate route.

The project will feature 342 apartments, a 131-slip marina, more than a half-mile of public riverwalk, and several waterfront dining and entertainment destinations. Among them is a new location of The Lucky Shuck Oyster Bar & Taphouse , owned by Namath and his business partner Charlie Modica, along with a second, yet-to-be-named outdoor dining concept. See also: New 24/7 animal cruelty hotline launching across Florida "The Lucky Shuck has always been about good food, good people and being on the water," Namath said. "Rio Marine Village gives us a home right on the river, and I can't wait to see boats pulling up and families sitting down together." The development will also feature the Osprey Club, a waterfront wedding and event venue, along with a public park, boardwalk, beach, and kayak and paddleboard rentals. Martin County commissioners unanimously approved the project's first two phases following years of community discussions. Construction is expected to begin this month, with the first phase scheduled for completion in late 2028.

entry.title: Rough surf and rip currents create dangerous conditions along Treasure Coast - WPBF
entry.summary: Rough surf and rip currents create dangerous conditions along Treasure Coast    WPBF
entry.article_text: Strong winds and high surf are creating dangerous conditions along the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches, with red flag warnings and a high risk of rip currents keeping most beachgoers out of the water. At Stuart Beach, the wind is whipping through the area, churning up rough water conditions. The beach is nearly empty, with no one in the water and only a few people on the sand. "Take advantage of this; it may not be great weather, but there's not a lot of people. So, you got quiet time to yourself. It's beautiful," said Jon Ciffolillo, a beachgoer. Despite the roaring wind, some are still venturing out to enjoy the morning before another round of heavy rain is expected to move through the area. "It's a beautiful day out here. The wind and the surf is just a different view of nature's beauty," said Frank Harvey, who was walking on the beach with his wife, Joan. Joan Harvey added, "A lot of time in your condo is not always ideal. So, you got to take it when it's not raining." Beachgoers are being urged to take caution, as conditions in the water remain dangerous. A high surf advisory is in effect along the Palm Beaches and Treasure Coast, along with a high risk for rip currents. Red flag warnings are also in place along Martin County's beaches, signaling that even experienced swimmers can be pulled away from shore. Martin County Ocean Rescue advises beachgoers to check with lifeguards about water conditions and to swim in guarded areas when conditions improve. The high surf advisory and high risk for rip currents are expected to last through Thursday. You can check the latest beach conditions across Martin County on their Safe Beach Day website. entry.summary: Joe Namath's Lucky Shuck coming to Jensen Beach as waterfront village breaks ground    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Football legend Joe Namath is bringing his popular Lucky Shuck restaurant to Jensen Beach as a massive waterfront development takes shape along the St. Rio Marine Village , a 30-acre mixed-use development in Martin County, broke ground Thursday, following more than five years of planning. The project will feature 342 apartments, a 131-slip marina, more than a half-mile of public riverwalk, and several waterfront dining and entertainment destinations. Among them is a new location of The Lucky Shuck Oyster Bar & Taphouse , owned by Namath and his business partner Charlie Modica, along with a second, yet-to-be-named outdoor dining concept. See also: New 24/7 animal cruelty hotline launching across Florida "The Lucky Shuck has always been about good food, good people and being on the water," Namath said. "Rio Marine Village gives us a home right on the river, and I can't wait to see boats pulling up and families sitting down together." The development will also feature the Osprey Club, a waterfront wedding and event venue, along with a public park, boardwalk, beach, and kayak and paddleboard rentals. Martin County commissioners unanimously approved the project's first two phases following years of community discussions. Construction is expected to begin this month, with the first phase scheduled for completion in late 2028.

entry.article_text: Lucie Police Department provides an update on a hit-and-run crash that left a 24-year-old woman critically injured. The crash happened Monday morning near SW Gatlin Boulevard and SW Feather Terrace, where police say the woman was riding an electric scooter when she was struck by a vehicle. Investigators say the driver fled the scene without stopping to render aid. According to police, detectives with the Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit identified the driver and located the vehicle involved. During the investigation, authorities learned the driver had allegedly been participating in a "ding dong ditch" prank shortly before the crash. Police arrested the 18-year-old driver and charged him with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk is expected to provide additional details about the investigation, discuss the arrest, and share an update on the victim's condition during today's briefing. According to Florida 511 , the crash was reported around 12:40 p.m. in the southbound lanes around Mile Marker 165 near Fort Pierce. Traffic camera footage near mile marker 164.9 shows what appears to be a large pink vehicle or trailer overturned across part of the highway, with several vehicles backed up behind it. The right lane is blocked, according to the latest traffic report. entry.title: Student ACES helping build the next generation of leaders in Palm Beach County
entry.summary: For more than a decade, Student ACES has been working with student-athletes across Palm Beach County, using sports as a starting point to teach lessons that extend far beyond the field. The nonprofit focuses on character and leadership development through interactive programs, including team building, role-playing exercises and real-world case studies. WATCH: Student ACES helping build the next generation of leaders in Palm Beach County WPTV SEASON OF HOPE STUDENT ACES We teach character and leadership to student athletes. We go through team-building, role-play exercises, and case studies. Its very, very interactive, said Krissy Webb, executive director of Student ACES. Webb said the organization has worked with about 60,000 students since it was founded in 2013. Student ACES offers five different programs aimed at helping young people develop leadership skills and prepare for their futures. One of those programs is based at the Student ACES Center in Belle Glade, which serves high school students from Belle Glade, Pahokee and South Bay throughout the year. Students receive mentoring and support in areas including academics, college preparation, career readiness, mental health, health and wellness, entrepreneurship, and character and leadership. WPTV reporter Christy Waite connected with student athletes who say the program is also helping them build confidence and think about what comes after high school. The five Student ACES programs are offered at no cost to students, helping remove a potential barrier for families who want their children to participate. The Student ACES Center (The SAC) in Belle Glade provides year-round afterschool and summer programming for high school students from Belle Glade, Pahokee and South Bay. Students receive mentoring and individualized support focused on academics, college and career preparation, leadership, health and wellness, mental health and entrepreneurship. The ACE Flagship Program brings together high school juniors from across Palm Beach County for character and leadership development. Students take part in mentoring, team-building activities, real-world case studies and leadership challenges. Captains Summits are one-day experiences for team captains and other influential student-athletes. The program focuses on communication, accountability, teamwork and learning how to lead by example. Leadership Workshops bring customized mentoring and leadership programs directly to athletic teams, schools and student groups

entry.summary: One of the greatest to ever do it, Jack Nicklaus was honored by Palm Beach Atlantic University on Tuesday, receiving the school's 2026 Lead Medal during its annual American Free Enterprise Day. Nicklaus, often called the greatest golfer to ever play the game, was recognized in West Palm Beach. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Golf legend Jack Nicklaus honored by Palm Beach Atlantic 'Very nice, very nice honor, you know, Palm Beach Atlantic, being recognized in your own hometown is very special,' Nicklaus said. During the ceremony, Nicklaus shared how his original plan was to become a pharmacist but instead found success on the fairway. 'I guess I was sort of destined to be a golfer or an athlete of some kind, and golf was the one to choose, and I chose the right one for me,' Nicklaus said. Nicklaus had plenty of jokes for the crowd, including a description of his grandson's golf game and advice to golfers who find themselves stuck in a sand trap. 'Play better. Don't hit it there,' Nicklaus said. Nicklaus has been a trailblazer for the sport of golf. He has won 18 majors, which is the most of all time, and has more than 70 PGA Tour wins. While Nicklaus represents golf's legacy, Palm Beach Atlantic University also honored one golfer who is bringing a new era to the game. 'As I first got into YouTube, I would then start running into people that were watching the videos and then it just became more and more and more, and it's been amazing just being able to meet people behind the screen,' Horvat said. entry.title: Martin County residents demand emergency shelter as flooding threatens the Treasure Coast - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County residents demand emergency shelter as flooding threatens the Treasure Coast    WPEC
entry.article_text: Martin County families still recovering from this month’s flooding are bracing for more rain, and on Tuesday, many of them asked county commissioners not to wait on federal help before opening an emergency shelter. Speaker after speaker told commissioners during public comment that water was already back in their streets. Some said their homes took on water earlier this month. Their main request was a public shelter, open before the next round of rain, for both unhoused residents and families who lost their homes in the flooding. Commissioners are discussing funding options at both the local and federal level. Florida has asked President Donald Trump for a major disaster declaration for the flooding, and as of Tuesday, it had not been signed. Once a disaster receives a federal declaration, FEMA must cover 75 percent of state and local response and recovery costs, according to the Florida Policy Institute. Without one, counties pay those costs on their own. Several speakers argued the county does not need to wait for that approval to act. Commissioner, you do not need FEMA’s blessing to open a school. Neighboring counties didn’t wait. Churches didn’t wait, one speaker said. Yamila Rollan Escalona, founder and executive director of Yaya Por Vida, a grassroots harm reduction organization, said she emailed her comments Tuesday morning as water rose in her neighborhood again, then came to speak in person. She said her group has been asking commissioners for emergency shelter for most of the year. See also: Palm Beach County braces for more flooding as cities offer sandbags, prepare for storm Please give us emergency shelter now. It’s no longer about just individuals that are unhoused. It’s also about individuals that just became unhoused because of this tragedy, Rollan Escalona told CBS12 News after the meeting. Rollan Escalona said unhoused residents have nowhere to go, pointing to a 2024 state law that bans sleeping on public property. She said some people are still staying in campsites surrounded by standing water, and some residents have not been accounted for. With drains and the ground already saturated, she said there is no time to wait. She also warned the damage won’t end when the water goes down. Rollan Escalona said mental health services on the Treasure Coast are already hard to access, and she worries the stress and hopelessness of losing everything could lead to more overdoses and people returning to substance use. Other speakers looked further ahead, linking the flooding to development in the county, including a proposed hyperscale data center. They asked commissioners to consider runoff and drainage before approving large projects. Take the 30,000-foot view the next time you look at a large project. How does it affect your neighbors? Martin County Emergency Management Director Sally Waite previously told commissioners the flooding affected 77 homes. Residents whose homes were damaged can report it and fill out a needs survey on the county’s flood recovery page. Ahead of the rain, Martin County is handing out sand and sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park, 8303 SW Lost River Road. Distribution runs from noon to 6 p.m. Each household can take up to 25 sandbags, and residents will be asked for their name and address. The county asks residents to check its map for the exact pickup spot inside the park. CBS12 News will update this story with what commissioners decide on funding and a possible shelter.

entry.title: St. Lucie County prepares for more rain after historic flooding - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County prepares for more rain after historic flooding    WPEC
entry.article_text: Crews are clearing drainage systems and checking waterways in St. Lucie County as another round of rain threatens areas still recovering from historic flooding. Lucie Public Schools is releasing students two hours early Tuesday. The district is asking families to monitor its official channels for updates as weather conditions change. Lucie officials say Public Works crews are inspecting drainage systems, clearing blockages and lowering water levels where possible. The ground remains saturated, increasing the risk of flooding even if rainfall is lighter than it was during the early November storms. See also: Heavy rain returns this week, bringing major threat of flooding across South Florida The National Weather Service has issued a flood watch for St. Lucie County from Tuesday afternoon through Friday evening. Forecasters expect 3 to 6 inches of rain across the area, with higher amounts possible in some locations. Two weeks ago, floodwaters stranded cars, trapped families and forced some residents to wade through deep water. Videos from that flooding showed high school freshman Noah Julian swimming from his school bus toward his home in a flooded Port St. Another video showed 7-year-old Ella Ghodooshim walking through chest-deep water with her mother near Oak Hammock K-8. That mother, Thassia Rodrigues, told CBS12 her only concern was getting her daughter safely across the flooded intersection. "As long as I can get her across and get her to safety, that was my main concern," Rodrigues said. She described how quickly the flooding overwhelmed the neighborhood, leaving parents struggling to reach their children. "It was pretty scary and in a matter of minutes we had everything just flood," she said. Lucie Public Schools told CBS12 News that decisions about closures and early dismissal are based on forecasts and information from the National Weather Service and Emergency Operations Center. The district said the information available before the previous flooding did not indicate schools needed to close or dismiss students earlier. This time, officials said the forecast supported releasing students two hours early to get them home before the heaviest rain. The district said it was awaiting additional updates from the National Weather Service at 2 p.m. and Emergency Operations Center at 4 p.m. Tuesday before making any further decisions about school schedules. Parents picking up their children near Oak Hammock K-8 Tuesday told CBS12 News they welcomed the earlier dismissal. "It's kind of nice that they're doing it early so we have time to get them and not have to rush," said Nathan Leach, whose child attends the school. Rhett Linton, another parent, recalled kayaking through the flooded intersection during the previous storm. "I'm super happy that they are stepping up and taking precautions," Linton said. Rodrigues, who was captured on video helping her daughter through the floodwaters, also praised the district's decision. Lucie County, we appreciate you guys," she said. Officials are urging residents to plan ahead, monitor forecasts and local alerts, and limit unnecessary travel. Drivers should never enter standing or moving water. Floodwater can stall a vehicle and cause costly engine damage. If you cannot tell how deep the water is, turn around and find another route. Residents can report flooding concerns to St. Lucie County at flooding@stlucieco.org .

entry.title: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in - WPEC
entry.summary: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Treasure Coast is bracing for a soggy stretch as counties prepare for possible flooding from heavy rain. Indian River County The Indian River County Emergency Operations Center remains at Level 2, or partial activation, because of ongoing flooding and the potential for more heavy rain. Emergency services, human services and infrastructure partners are coordinating response and recovery efforts. The county urges residents to avoid flooded roads and floodwaters, watch for rising water in low-lying areas and monitor weather conditions and official updates. Residents with flood-related questions or information can call the Emergency Information Center at 772-226-4000 during operating hours. Due to the heavy rain and gusty winds, solid waste services may be disrupted. Waste Management curbside collections may be delayed, and residents should not put carts in the street if it is flooded. See also: Florida deputies rescue 2-year-old girl found in pond near apartment complex Waste Management collects recycling in blue carts countywide. It collects garbage, yard waste and bulk waste in unincorporated Indian River County, Fellsmere, Sebastian and Indian River Shores. Residents in other cities and towns should check with their local governments for service updates. The county recommends putting carts out by 6 a.m. on collection day, closing lids, bagging garbage, and avoiding overfilled carts. Cardboard should be flattened and placed inside recycling carts, and yard waste should stay inside yard waste carts. Residents should bring carts back in as soon as possible after collection. The landfill and all five Customer Convenience Centers may close early or remain closed if conditions become unsafe. The east-central Florida coast faces a Slight Risk, or Level 2 out of 4, for excessive rainfall. Localized flooding is possible, especially along the coast, and some areas could receive 4 inches or more of rain. Martin County Martin County officials expect 3 to 6 inches of rain, with localized amounts of 8 to 12 inches, beginning Tuesday afternoon and continuing through Nov. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office says it is working with the county’s emergency operations center to monitor rainfall and identify roads that could become difficult to pass. The sheriff’s office plans to deploy high-water rescue vehicles in flood-prone areas. Having the vehicles nearby could help deputies reach residents who need assistance and motorists who become stranded, the office said. The sheriff’s office advises residents to turn around if water covers the road. Standing water may be deeper than it appears and can hide damage. If a regular route is flooded, drivers should take another route or wait somewhere safe. Residents should never drive around barricades or enter flooded areas to see how high the water is. Martin County Fire Rescue also advises residents to be prepared to evacuate if flooding threatens their homes or neighborhoods and to have an emergency kit ready for household members and pets. The Community Information Center will be open to provide flood-related information. Okeechobee County Okeechobee County is also preparing for severe flooding. The Okeechobee County Sheriff’s Office says its emergency operations center will remain active as staff coordinate response and recovery efforts from past flooding. Sandbags are available at Okeechobee County Public Works, 804 Northwest Second St. Lucie County Public Safety Department is monitoring the forecast and reminding residents to secure loose items that could be damaged by wind. Gusty northeast winds of 25 to 30 mph are forecast Tuesday and Wednesday, with gusts of 35 to 40 mph along the coast. Residents should secure tarps, patio furniture and other unsecured items. A rip current advisory remains in effect for St. Strong onshore winds can create dangerous rip currents and rough surf. Lucie County Fire District says its firefighters, paramedics and telecommunicators are prepared to respond as the area faces more heavy rain and recovers from recent flooding. The district has high-water vehicles and a rescue boat available to assist during flood-related emergencies. Free sand is available while supplies last at two self-service locations: County Fairgrounds: 5601 W. Midway Road, Fort Pierce, in the west parking lot Lawnwood Stadium: 2000 Virginia Ave., Fort Pierce Residents should bring their own bags, shovel and other supplies. Residents can use Community Connect to share household information that could help firefighters prepare for an emergency. The county has extended the deadline to Nov. 30 for residents to report flood damage through an online survey. The information will help document flooding across the community and inform recovery efforts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants throughout St. Lucie County, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie Village and unincorporated areas. It asks where flooding occurred, how buildings were affected and what impacts residents and businesses experienced. Residents can complete the flood damage survey by Nov. Officials urge residents across the region to avoid flooded roads and keep roadways clear for emergency responders. If you encounter flooding, turn around and find a safe alternate route.

entry.title: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home - WPTV
entry.summary: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home    WPTV
entry.article_text: A Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding is searching for more permanent housing and money to rebuild after water destroyed much of the inside of their home. Lisa and Jeremy French, who have two young boys, told WPTV's Michael Hoffman they ultimately have one goal: to get their family back home.WATCH REPORT BELOW:WPTV first met the French family shortly after historic rainfall hit South Florida and the Treasure Coast. Floodwater had surrounded their neighborhood, forcing residents to use kayaks to get around and check on neighbors.Days later, much of the water has receded. The damage has not."My floorboards are outside," Lisa French said.Hoffman returned to the French family's Jensen Beach home for an update, but the family said it was not safe to go inside.French said the flooding wiped out much of what her family had accumulated over the years."Our appliances are gone, our cabinets are gone, every piece of furniture," French said.The family is now trying to determine how to pay for repairs while securing a more permanent place to live.WPTV met French again at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach, where a Multi-Agency Resource Center has been helping people looking for assistance following the flooding.French told Hoffman that her home flooded days after the rain had stopped.Martin County told WPTV that the family's home is near the Savannah Preserves, an area where excess water naturally flows from other flooded areas.French, however, questions whether other actions involving water entering the preserve contributed to what happened at her home."They're saying it's from natural rain, but they dumped Monday and Tuesday, nonstop into the savannas," French said.The impact of the flooding extends beyond the physical damage.Through tears, Lisa and Jeremy French pleaded for help before the Martin County Commission as they described what their family is facing."Today we are homeless," Lisa French told commissioners. "We have nowhere to host Thanksgiving. We have nowhere for our boys to have Christmas. We don't have beds to come home to."The couple has two young boys. French said she wants them to continue growing up in the Jensen Beach home the family worked hard to maintain.For now, however, the family says it needs more permanent housing while trying to determine where the money to repair the home will come from.French said the uncertainty surrounding assistance has left her worried there could still be a significant financial gap, even if additional aid becomes available."Who's going to fill in the gaps?" French said. "And, you know, maybe I feel like somebody should take accountability."Despite the uncertainty and extensive damage, the family says it has not given up hope of returning."We just want to go home," French said. "Like, that's at the end, that we just want to be home with our family."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.article_text: Palm Beach County homeowners hoping for new financial help after this month's devastating flooding will have to wait a little longer.County commissioners voted 7-0 Tuesday to postpone consideration of a proposed $2 million Flood Disaster Assistance Program, choosing to spend more time working through questions about eligibility, insurance, contractors, temporary housing and how to stretch a limited amount of money among residents who need help.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The proposal is now expected to return to commissioners Dec. 1."We here at the Palm Beach County Commission wanna make sure that we get this right," Commissioner Bobby Powell Jr. told WPTV reporter Joel Lopez after the meeting. "Also, we need to hear from residents. 1 is when we'll have that meeting, and I would look forward to having residents come to that meeting. But also residents should call our offices, talk to us, and let's walk through this and work through it together."The proposed program comes roughly two weeks after extraordinary rainfall left neighborhoods underwater across Palm Beach County.In a previous meeting, county officials said parts of West Palm Beach received more than 22 inches of rain, causing roads to become waterways, leaving vehicles stranded and some residents unable to leave their neighborhoods. In Century Village near West Palm Beach, firefighters responded to more than seventy 911 calls in one night, with nearly 100 residents trapped in stranded vehicles as floodwaters rapidly rose. In Riviera Beach, the county's Swiftwater Response Team evacuated 71 people, conducted two medical rescues and evacuated nine pets.Powell, who represents District 7, was among those rescued during the flooding."Fire Rescue came to get me this morning, so I'm one of the people they had to rescue," Powell told commissioners during the meeting held earlier this month.Now, the county is trying to determine how to help residents recover.County staff proposed using $2 million from the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program to help income-qualified homeowners whose homesteaded properties suffered flood damage.SHIP is a state program funded through documentary stamp taxes that provides money to counties and qualifying municipalities for affordable housing programs.Under the proposal presented Tuesday, eligible homeowners could receive up to $50,000. The money could be used for uninsured structural damage that threatens health or safety, interim repairs to prevent additional damage, insurance deductibles and temporary relocation assistance."It's up to $50,000," Powell said. "Some homeowners may need less, some may need more, but this is a start. What we would like to do is analyze what the needs of the individuals who are requesting funding are so that we can better fulfill their needs."County officials said roughly 80 homes have reported damage so far, although officials noted that number depends on homeowners and municipalities reporting damage.They said they've been communicating with City of Riviera Beach officials who reported closer to 300 homes.The relatively small pool of money compared with the potential need quickly became a major part of Tuesday's discussion.If households received close to the proposed $50,000 maximum, commissioners noted the $2 million could help roughly 40 to 50 households. Some commissioners questioned whether that maximum should be lowered so the county could reach more families.They also raised concerns about whether assistance should simply be distributed on a first-come, first-qualified basis or whether the county should prioritize residents with the greatest need, including seniors and people whose homes are no longer habitable.Powell said what he has seen in some of the hardest-hit communities is difficult to describe."People have worked their entire lives to own a home. Or to get to where they have been in a safe and secure place, people have been put in a position where they no longer feel safe, comfortable, and protected," Powell said. "And able to thrive because their worldly possessions are sitting on the street corner because their house was damaged to an extent that they can no longer inhabit it by an event that they had not anticipated."Commissioners also spent considerable time questioning how the county would handle homeowners with insurance, people without flood insurance, contractor selection and residents who may also qualify for assistance offered by their cities.Temporary housing was another concern.The proposal included up to $10,000 of the $50,000 maximum for temporary relocation assistance for displaced residents for up to six months. Commissioners questioned whether those rules should be flexible enough to allow residents to stay with family members under certain circumstances, particularly given the cost and availability of short-term rentals in Palm Beach County.There were also questions about how the county should coordinate with municipalities such as Riviera Beach, which is exploring its own assistance for flood victims, while making sure residents are not reimbursed twice for the same expense."We have to work together. We have to resolve these issues together. It can be done," Powell said. "We need to work with the citizens, with the cities, the city of Riviera Beach, the city of West Palm Beach, and the county to come up with solutions that actually help people. There's no way around this."Powell acknowledged the frustration facing residents who have been seeking help since the flooding."This has been a problem since Nov. People have been reaching out asking for help, and now we're getting there; we're working on it, but we have to get it right," he said.County administrators originally hoped that, with commission approval Tuesday, applications could begin as soon as Wednesday. Instead, after more than an hour of discussion, commissioners agreed to give staff additional time to refine the proposal and bring it back Dec. 1.The county's efforts come as local leaders continue dealing with the aftermath of a flooding event that prompted Gov. Ron DeSantis to add Palm Beach County to Florida's state of emergency. The declaration provided additional authority and resources for response, recovery and mitigation efforts.For residents still waiting for help, Powell encouraged them to stay involved as county officials rework the program."We will get it right. We'll make sure we get assistance for people, and we'll keep working on it. Keep, keep showing up, keep knocking on doors. I know you're frustrated," Powell said. Do not stop."Powell also encouraged residents affected by the flooding to contact commissioners and participate when the proposal returns Dec. 1."It's our job and those who've been impacted to tell the stories and to show people so that we can make sure that you get the help that is needed and necessary," Powell said.With more rain possible, Powell urged residents to prepare for the possibility of additional flooding."Let's be proactive now we know the rain is coming. Let's do our best to be prepared," Powell said.He also called on government agencies to make sure drainage systems are ready."Let's make sure that every opportunity to drain water is working today so that we're not facing the same thing we saw last time."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. But where others saw aging properties and neglected alleyways, Power saw potential."It spoke to me, and I heard I was once great and now I have fallen into disrepair and not respected at all, and I said we're going to change that," Power told WPTV anchor Meghan McRoberts during a tour of the neighborhood.Power has spent decades creating art and helping develop artistic communities, including an art center in Miami.Now, he's bringing that experience to Vero Beach, with an entire neighborhood as his canvas.Turning Edgewood's alleyways into works of artOne of Power's biggest ambitions is transforming 11 alleyways throughout Edgewood into colorful destinations filled with murals and public art."I'm taking the alleys which are the ugliest part of the neighborhood and turning them into mural opportunities where the alleys are going to be like unbelievable for people to come and visit," Power said."There's a lack of buildings but there's not a lack of fences."Power sees those fences, walls and underused spaces as opportunities to showcase local artists and create an outdoor art experience.But the effort goes beyond beautifying back streets.Special zoning allows artists to live and work in the villageThe city of Vero Beach has established Cultural Arts Village zoning districts designed to encourage artistic businesses while preserving Edgewood's historic residential character.According to the city and the Vero Beach Art Village organization, the zoning creates opportunities for art galleries, studios, live-work spaces and other businesses, depending on the property's classification and applicable approvals.The goal is to create a walkable neighborhood where historic homes can become studios and galleries, and artists can collaborate with their neighbors.“I’ve been working on a bunch of different paintings. And we have projects; there's a bunch of different projects we’ve been working on whether it’s for the city or for trying to save big blue, or our community garden, “ said Linwood Addison Fuller IV, an artist who moved to Edgewood for the focus on art. His wife is also an artist.“It’s so much better to be an artist in a community with other artists,” said sculptor Andrew Draminski. “I’m sitting here working and my neighbors are walking their dog down the alley and come on in and we have a cup of coffee or something like that.”The village's vision extends beyond traditional galleries. Organizers hope to create spaces for music, dance, poetry, photography, workshops and other community events.More galleries, studios and community spaces plannedAccording to the nonprofit Friends of the Vero Beach Art Village, the neighborhood's transformation is a grassroots effort involving artists, residents, businesses and volunteers.The organization highlights ongoing initiatives involving murals, public art, studios, galleries, streetscape improvements and community events.Power says additional galleries, studios, cafes and bed-and-breakfasts are also in the works.For him, the goal isn't simply to attract visitors. entry.title: St. Lucie schools closed Wednesday as more flooding threatens Treasure Coast - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie schools closed Wednesday as more flooding threatens Treasure Coast    WPEC
entry.article_text: Just two weeks after historic flooding forced schools to close for three straight days, St. Lucie County students are getting another day off as more heavy rain threatens the area. Lucie Public Schools announced Tuesday that all schools and district offices will be closed Wednesday due to the threat of significant rainfall and localized flooding. The announcement comes after the district dismissed students two hours early Tuesday as worsening weather conditions raised concerns about flooding. It's the latest disruption for the district, which was forced to close schools for three consecutive days Nov. 4, 5 and 6 after historic flooding left roads underwater and communities struggling to recover. Lucie County clears drains, prepares for more rain after historic flooding Now, with the ground already saturated, district leaders say they aren't taking any chances. According to the district, forecasts from the National Weather Service indicate the potential for significant rainfall, although uncertainty remains about exactly when and where the heaviest rain will fall. "Given the already saturated conditions in our community, the District believes taking a cautious approach is in the best interest of our students, families, and employees," district officials said in a statement. John Carroll High School also announced it will be closed Wednesday, Nov. 18, due to the threat of heavy rainfall and flooding across the region. The decision follows an early dismissal Tuesday and a review of weather forecasts and local flooding conditions. School officials said all Wednesday activities, including athletics, practices, extracurricular programs and other events, have been canceled. John Carroll anticipates reopening Thursday, pending weather and road conditions. Administrators will continue monitoring forecasts and coordinating with local authorities before making further decisions. Updates will be shared through the school's official communication channels. All after-school activities, aftercare programs, and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday have also been canceled. District officials said they will continue monitoring rainfall, flooding, road closures, and access to schools, bus stops, and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. A decision on whether schools will reopen Thursday is expected Wednesday evening. Families are encouraged to monitor the district's official website and social media channels for updates.

entry.article_text: Just weeks after historic flooding destroyed homes and displaced families in Jensen Beach, Martin County residents are bracing for another round of heavy rain — with up to 12 inches forecast over the next three days.For families still struggling to recover, the threat of more flooding comes as county commissioners work to determine what caused the initial disaster and how to help those who lost nearly everything.On Tuesday, flood victims packed a Martin County Commission meeting, pleading for financial assistance and answers.Along Cheri Drive in Jensen Beach, the signs of destruction remain. Dumpsters line driveways, damaged belongings sit outside and families are still trying to salvage what's left of their homes.Lisa French, her husband, Jeremy, and their two young sons are among those displaced after floodwaters rose as high as 3 feet inside some homes two weeks ago."It's like we're kind of stuck," French told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey. French said her home had about 3 to 6 inches of flooding that sat inside for more than a week, causing mold to grow 3 to 4 feet up the walls. "So they, yeah, they tore the walls down in the house," said French. "They just chipped up the last bit of the tile, and it's empty." Now, with more rain approaching, French fears her family could face another disaster before recovering from the first."Of course, we're afraid because we all flooded in our houses," she said.New figures released by Martin County show at least 36 homes sustained damage, with an estimated $3 million in residential losses. Commissioners estimated another $14 million in damage to beaches, and at least $1 million in damage to roadways that now need repairs. For some residents, the destruction represents a lifetime of memories washed away."We've lost everything," one elderly Jensen Beach resident told commissioners. "We have 60 years of our life — kids, grandkids, everything. It's all gone."As residents demand answers about what went wrong, commissioners approved shifting $200,000 from the county's stormwater budget to investigate whether development and changes to local drainage systems contributed to the flooding.Commissioner Blake Capps called the investigation "a good starting point.""It may be that we need to augment the study beyond the $200,000 that we approve today," said Capps. Meanwhile, county crews are working around the clock to prepare for the next storm, lowering retention pond levels, deploying additional pumps and draining flooded properties."We have people 24 hours a day pumping that material down," Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said.Commissioners also approved financial assistance for eligible flood victims through the state's State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program.The assistance includes grants of up to $25,000 for income-eligible homeowners and loans of up to $75,000 secured by liens on their properties.But there's a catch: The grants are reimbursement-based, meaning homeowners must first pay for eligible repairs before receiving the money.For families who lost everything, that presents another obstacle."We don't have $25,000," French said. "A lot of people don't have $25,000, so it's great, and we're appreciative, but I mean, our house is empty, and $25,000 is not going to do much for us." The other problem: the county currently has just $1 million in SHIP funding available, and commissioners warned the money could run out quickly, even with additional state funding promised."They haven't given us the amount yet, but they have assured us that we will be getting some disaster relief funds," said Human Services Director Michelle Miller Strict income limits could also disqualify some flood victims who cannot afford to rebuild on their own. The income cap for a family of one is $86,040. The cap for a family of two is $98,400. For a family of four, it's $122,880. When reporter Kate Hussey asked Capps what would happen to those families, he acknowledged the county needs to explore other options."There are going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where someone barely missed the limit, and we're going to need to take a look at what we can do for those folks," Capps said.For residents like French, the need is immediate."We just need somebody to step up," she said. "We need funding." With another round of heavy rain approaching, Martin County is distributing sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park to help residents protect their properties, with a limit of 25 per person. The County's Emergency Operations Center is scheduled to be staffed beginning Tuesday at 2 p.m., and the county is coordinating with the National Weather Service and Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM).Fire Rescue is also standing by with multiple high-water rescue trucks.Commissioners also said a Federal Emergency Management Agency representative is expected to visit Nov. 30 to assess the damage — a potential step toward securing federal disaster assistance.But for families still displaced and facing the possibility of more flooding, the uncertainty remains.

entry.title: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in - WPEC
entry.summary: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Treasure Coast is bracing for a soggy stretch as counties prepare for possible flooding from heavy rain. Indian River County The Indian River County Emergency Operations Center remains at Level 2, or partial activation, because of ongoing flooding and the potential for more heavy rain. Emergency services, human services and infrastructure partners are coordinating response and recovery efforts. The county urges residents to avoid flooded roads and floodwaters, watch for rising water in low-lying areas and monitor weather conditions and official updates. Residents with flood-related questions or information can call the Emergency Information Center at 772-226-4000 during operating hours. Due to the heavy rain and gusty winds, solid waste services may be disrupted. Waste Management curbside collections may be delayed, and residents should not put carts in the street if it is flooded. See also: Florida deputies rescue 2-year-old girl found in pond near apartment complex Waste Management collects recycling in blue carts countywide. It collects garbage, yard waste and bulk waste in unincorporated Indian River County, Fellsmere, Sebastian and Indian River Shores. Residents in other cities and towns should check with their local governments for service updates. The county recommends putting carts out by 6 a.m. on collection day, closing lids, bagging garbage, and avoiding overfilled carts. Cardboard should be flattened and placed inside recycling carts, and yard waste should stay inside yard waste carts. Residents should bring carts back in as soon as possible after collection. The landfill and all five Customer Convenience Centers may close early or remain closed if conditions become unsafe. The east-central Florida coast faces a Slight Risk, or Level 2 out of 4, for excessive rainfall. Localized flooding is possible, especially along the coast, and some areas could receive 4 inches or more of rain. Martin County Martin County officials expect 3 to 6 inches of rain, with localized amounts of 8 to 12 inches, beginning Tuesday afternoon and continuing through Nov. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office says it is working with the county’s emergency operations center to monitor rainfall and identify roads that could become difficult to pass. The sheriff’s office plans to deploy high-water rescue vehicles in flood-prone areas. Having the vehicles nearby could help deputies reach residents who need assistance and motorists who become stranded, the office said. The sheriff’s office advises residents to turn around if water covers the road. Standing water may be deeper than it appears and can hide damage. If a regular route is flooded, drivers should take another route or wait somewhere safe. Residents should never drive around barricades or enter flooded areas to see how high the water is. Martin County Fire Rescue also advises residents to be prepared to evacuate if flooding threatens their homes or neighborhoods and to have an emergency kit ready for household members and pets. The Community Information Center will be open to provide flood-related information. Okeechobee County Okeechobee County is also preparing for severe flooding. The Okeechobee County Sheriff’s Office says its emergency operations center will remain active as staff coordinate response and recovery efforts from past flooding. Sandbags are available at Okeechobee County Public Works, 804 Northwest Second St. Lucie County Public Safety Department is monitoring the forecast and reminding residents to secure loose items that could be damaged by wind. Gusty northeast winds of 25 to 30 mph are forecast Tuesday and Wednesday, with gusts of 35 to 40 mph along the coast. Residents should secure tarps, patio furniture and other unsecured items. A rip current advisory remains in effect for St. Strong onshore winds can create dangerous rip currents and rough surf. Lucie County Fire District says its firefighters, paramedics and telecommunicators are prepared to respond as the area faces more heavy rain and recovers from recent flooding. The district has high-water vehicles and a rescue boat available to assist during flood-related emergencies. Free sand is available while supplies last at two self-service locations: County Fairgrounds: 5601 W. Midway Road, Fort Pierce, in the west parking lot Lawnwood Stadium: 2000 Virginia Ave., Fort Pierce Residents should bring their own bags, shovel and other supplies. Residents can use Community Connect to share household information that could help firefighters prepare for an emergency. The county has extended the deadline to Nov. 30 for residents to report flood damage through an online survey. The information will help document flooding across the community and inform recovery efforts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants throughout St. Lucie County, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie Village and unincorporated areas. It asks where flooding occurred, how buildings were affected and what impacts residents and businesses experienced. Residents can complete the flood damage survey by Nov. Officials urge residents across the region to avoid flooded roads and keep roadways clear for emergency responders. If you encounter flooding, turn around and find a safe alternate route.

entry.title: Teen arrested in hit-and-run crash that critically injured 24-year-old woman in Port St. Lucie
entry.summary: An 18-year-old driver has been arrested after a hit-and-run crash critically injured a 24-year-old woman on an electric scooter in Port St. Lucie, police said. WATCH: Update from Chief Leo Niemczyk Port St. Lucie police give update on hit-and-run crash The incident happened Monday morning near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace, Port St. Lucie police said. According to investigators, the victim was riding an electric scooter westbound on the sidewalk toward Southwest Rosser Boulevard. As the woman on the scooter entered the crosswalk, she was struck by the 18-year-old driver of a gray Chevrolet Tahoe making a left turn onto Southwest Feather Terrace. Police said the driver fled the scene and failed to stop to render aid to the woman. The Port St. Lucie Police Department's Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit identified the driver as Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer and located the vehicle through its investigation. Investigators learned Sanchez-Chasmer had been playing 'ding dong ditch' just before the crash. entry.title: St. Lucie County prepares for more rain after historic flooding - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County prepares for more rain after historic flooding    WPEC
entry.article_text: Crews are clearing drainage systems and checking waterways in St. Lucie County as another round of rain threatens areas still recovering from historic flooding. Lucie Public Schools is releasing students two hours early Tuesday. The district announced Tuesday afternoon that schools and offices will be closed Wednesday as a precaution. All after-school activities, aftercare programs, and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday are also canceled. District officials will continue monitoring rainfall, flooding, road closures, and the accessibility of schools, bus stops, and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. A decision regarding school operations for Thursday, November 19, will be announced Wednesday evening. Lucie officials say Public Works crews are inspecting drainage systems, clearing blockages and lowering water levels where possible. The ground remains saturated, increasing the risk of flooding even if rainfall is lighter than it was during the early November storms. See also: Heavy rain returns this week, bringing major threat of flooding across South Florida The National Weather Service has issued a flood watch for St. Lucie County from Tuesday afternoon through Friday evening. Forecasters expect 3 to 6 inches of rain across the area, with higher amounts possible in some locations. Two weeks ago, floodwaters stranded cars, trapped families and forced some residents to wade through deep water. Videos from that flooding showed high school freshman Noah Julian swimming from his school bus toward his home in a flooded Port St. Another video showed 7-year-old Ella Ghodooshim walking through chest-deep water with her mother near Oak Hammock K-8. That mother, Thassia Rodrigues, told CBS12 her only concern was getting her daughter safely across the flooded intersection. "As long as I can get her across and get her to safety, that was my main concern," Rodrigues said. She described how quickly the flooding overwhelmed the neighborhood, leaving parents struggling to reach their children. "It was pretty scary and in a matter of minutes we had everything just flood," she said. Lucie Public Schools told CBS12 News that decisions about closures and early dismissal are based on forecasts and information from the National Weather Service and Emergency Operations Center. The district said the information available before the previous flooding did not indicate schools needed to close or dismiss students earlier. This time, officials said the forecast supported releasing students two hours early to get them home before the heaviest rain. The district said it was awaiting additional updates from the National Weather Service at 2 p.m. and Emergency Operations Center at 4 p.m. Tuesday before making any further decisions about school schedules. Parents picking up their children near Oak Hammock K-8 Tuesday told CBS12 News they welcomed the earlier dismissal. "It's kind of nice that they're doing it early so we have time to get them and not have to rush," said Nathan Leach, whose child attends the school. Rhett Linton, another parent, recalled kayaking through the flooded intersection during the previous storm. "I'm super happy that they are stepping up and taking precautions," Linton said. Rodrigues, who was captured on video helping her daughter through the floodwaters, also praised the district's decision. Lucie County, we appreciate you guys," she said. Officials are urging residents to plan ahead, monitor forecasts and local alerts, and limit unnecessary travel. Drivers should never enter standing or moving water. Floodwater can stall a vehicle and cause costly engine damage. If you cannot tell how deep the water is, turn around and find another route. Residents can report flooding concerns to St. Lucie County at flooding@stlucieco.org .

entry.article_text: An 18-year-old is under arrest after police say he was playing a game of ding, dong, ditch with some friends and then hit a woman on an e-scooter and drove away. Police have identified the driver as Tristan Ray Sanchez-Chasmer, 18, of Port St. "Pranks especially at somebody's front door, especially at late hours of the night, early hours of the morning can be very dangerous," said Leo Niemczyk, Port St. Lucie Police say the crash happened Monday, November 16, at about 5:10 am near the intersection of SW Gatlin Blvd. and SW Feather Terrace in Port St. Police say a 24 year old woman on an e-scooter was hit by a vehicle that did not stop. The victim was on her way to a Wendy's where she works and she was in the crosswalk on SW Feather Terrace when she was hit. "I think for somebody to just leave another human being on the side of the road who was possibly injured, to not stop and check on them, it's truly heartbreaking that somebody would make that decision," said Katie Santana, a Port St. Lucie resident who lives near the intersection where the accident happened. We spoke with a high school student who rides an e-scooter in the area where the crash occurred. "I get a little bit fearful sometimes, 'cause I'll see some people going through red lights, not paying attention when they're turning and I've almost been hit a couple times," said John Rogalewski, age 15. See also: Bodycam footage shows deputy fatally shoot armed Florida mother, army veteran outside bar Police say a good Samaritan got the license plate number of the hit and run vehicle and stopped to help the victim. With that information, police determined a Chevy Tahoe struck the woman, and they determined the driver was an 18-year-old. Sanchez-Chasmer is charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. Police say the victim was rushed to a hospital and, at last report, she was hospitalized in critical condition. Police say she is in a coma. If she does not survive, the State Attorney's Office would decide if Sanchez-Chasmer could face a more serious charge. Police say two other individuals who were in the Chevy Tahoe with Sanchez-Chasmer have not been charged.

entry.title: Martin County commissioners approve emergency funding for flood victims - WPBF
entry.summary: Martin County commissioners approve emergency funding for flood victims    WPBF
entry.article_text: Martin County officials announced their plans to support flood victims as they begin the long road to recovery. County commissioners fielded hours of public comment at their meeting Tuesday. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 The county has set up a sandbag distribution site at Halpatiokee Regional Park where folks can fill up to 25 sandbags per household. That is just one part of what they’re doing to prepare for more storms and help residents. “The county needs to help us. Somebody needs to come forward. There's got to be an emergency fund. I can't understand how Martin County, one of the richest counties in Florida, does not have one,” Mary Berner, who lost her home on Hyline Drive in the flood, said. One by one, residents stepped to the podium at the meeting airing their frustrations at the flood disaster response. “We sat there for eight days and didn't have any response until we had a, you know, a meeting and made several phone calls to our commissioner and got no response from her. So, it's hard to not be heard,” Berner said. Commissioners made sure those pleas were heard Tuesday. They approved an increase of an up to $25,000 in grant funding for each eligible household from the county’s SHIP Disaster Assistance fund. Eligibility is determined by household income based on HUD guidelines. “These funds come through the state through something called the Sadowski funds. These funds are captured for each county when there's a real estate transaction, and then the state delivers to each county a certain amount each year to allocate for not only disaster, but things like rehabilitation of your home,” Michelle Miller, Martin County Human Services director, said. The county currently has $900,000 in that fund. “There are certain eligibility uses for that disaster funding, which, again, are expenses to weatherproof your house, rental assistance ... also, emergency hotel vouchers,” Miller said. As far as preps go, Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton told commissioners that right now, crews are pumping several lakes and ponds to create more space for any excess water to go. He said they’re especially focusing on the Hyline Drive area where Berner’s home is and was destroyed. “There's no way to rebuild if you have nothing. And I mean, literally nothing is left. And then, of course, long-term goals, they need to figure out this problem; they need to stop developing in wetlands,” Berner said. To apply for the SHIP emergency funding, applicants should go to the county’s human services office or call 772-320-3169. As for the sandbags, residents can grab them Wednesday from 7 a.m. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

entry.title: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home - WPTV
entry.summary: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home    WPTV
entry.article_text: A Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding is searching for more permanent housing and money to rebuild after water destroyed much of the inside of their home. Lisa and Jeremy French, who have two young boys, told WPTV's Michael Hoffman they ultimately have one goal: to get their family back home.WATCH REPORT BELOW:WPTV first met the French family shortly after historic rainfall hit South Florida and the Treasure Coast. Floodwater had surrounded their neighborhood, forcing residents to use kayaks to get around and check on neighbors.Days later, much of the water has receded. The damage has not."My floorboards are outside," Lisa French said.Hoffman returned to the French family's Jensen Beach home for an update, but the family said it was not safe to go inside.French said the flooding wiped out much of what her family had accumulated over the years."Our appliances are gone, our cabinets are gone, every piece of furniture," French said.The family is now trying to determine how to pay for repairs while securing a more permanent place to live.WPTV met French again at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach, where a Multi-Agency Resource Center has been helping people looking for assistance following the flooding.French told Hoffman that her home flooded days after the rain had stopped.Martin County told WPTV that the family's home is near the Savannah Preserves, an area where excess water naturally flows from other flooded areas.French, however, questions whether other actions involving water entering the preserve contributed to what happened at her home."They're saying it's from natural rain, but they dumped Monday and Tuesday, nonstop into the savannas," French said.The impact of the flooding extends beyond the physical damage.Through tears, Lisa and Jeremy French pleaded for help before the Martin County Commission as they described what their family is facing."Today we are homeless," Lisa French told commissioners. "We have nowhere to host Thanksgiving. We have nowhere for our boys to have Christmas. We don't have beds to come home to."The couple has two young boys. French said she wants them to continue growing up in the Jensen Beach home the family worked hard to maintain.For now, however, the family says it needs more permanent housing while trying to determine where the money to repair the home will come from.French said the uncertainty surrounding assistance has left her worried there could still be a significant financial gap, even if additional aid becomes available."Who's going to fill in the gaps?" French said. "And, you know, maybe I feel like somebody should take accountability."Despite the uncertainty and extensive damage, the family says it has not given up hope of returning."We just want to go home," French said. "Like, that's at the end, that we just want to be home with our family."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Martin County residents demand emergency shelter as flooding threatens the Treasure Coast - cw34.com
entry.summary: Martin County residents demand emergency shelter as flooding threatens the Treasure Coast    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Martin County families still recovering from this month’s flooding are bracing for more rain, and on Tuesday, many of them asked county commissioners not to wait on federal help before opening an emergency shelter. Speaker after speaker told commissioners during public comment that water was already back in their streets. Some said their homes took on water earlier this month. Their main request was a public shelter, open before the next round of rain, for both unhoused residents and families who lost their homes in the flooding. Commissioners are discussing funding options at both the local and federal level. Florida has asked President Donald Trump for a major disaster declaration for the flooding, and as of Tuesday, it had not been signed. Once a disaster receives a federal declaration, FEMA must cover 75 percent of state and local response and recovery costs, according to the Florida Policy Institute. Without one, counties pay those costs on their own. Several speakers argued the county does not need to wait for that approval to act. Commissioner, you do not need FEMA’s blessing to open a school. Neighboring counties didn’t wait. Churches didn’t wait, one speaker said. Yamila Rollan Escalona, founder and executive director of Yaya Por Vida, a grassroots harm reduction organization, said she emailed her comments Tuesday morning as water rose in her neighborhood again, then came to speak in person. She said her group has been asking commissioners for emergency shelter for most of the year. See also: Palm Beach County braces for more flooding as cities offer sandbags, prepare for storm Please give us emergency shelter now. It’s no longer about just individuals that are unhoused. It’s also about individuals that just became unhoused because of this tragedy, Rollan Escalona told CBS12 News after the meeting. Rollan Escalona said unhoused residents have nowhere to go, pointing to a 2024 state law that bans sleeping on public property. She said some people are still staying in campsites surrounded by standing water, and some residents have not been accounted for. With drains and the ground already saturated, she said there is no time to wait. She also warned the damage won’t end when the water goes down. Rollan Escalona said mental health services on the Treasure Coast are already hard to access, and she worries the stress and hopelessness of losing everything could lead to more overdoses and people returning to substance use. Other speakers looked further ahead, linking the flooding to development in the county, including a proposed hyperscale data center. They asked commissioners to consider runoff and drainage before approving large projects. Take the 30,000-foot view the next time you look at a large project. How does it affect your neighbors? Martin County Emergency Management Director Sally Waite previously told commissioners the flooding affected 77 homes. Residents whose homes were damaged can report it and fill out a needs survey on the county’s flood recovery page. Ahead of the rain, Martin County is handing out sand and sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park, 8303 SW Lost River Road. Distribution runs from noon to 6 p.m. Each household can take up to 25 sandbags, and residents will be asked for their name and address. The county asks residents to check its map for the exact pickup spot inside the park. CBS12 News will update this story with what commissioners decide on funding and a possible shelter.

entry.article_text: Lucie County residents are preparing for heavy rainfall this week, with officials offering free self-serve sandbag stations and working to clear drainage systems to address potential flooding. Dreamland Park in Fort Pierce, residents were seen filling sandbags to protect their homes. Resident Lisa Powell is concerned. "My ditches are full from the last storm, they haven't gone down, so this could be very bad. The water is just still standing there, up to the yard." Another resident shared their concerns, saying, "My crawlspace got a foot of water in there, so trying to get all these bags to try and cover up the opening, you know." Public works crews in St. Lucie County are actively checking and clearing swales and drainage systems as the area braces for more severe weather. Recent flooding left parts of the county submerged, with residents in the Creekside development trapped inside, some using kayaks to navigate flooded streets while others waded through the water. Fredrick Reeves, a resident whose home was previously flooded, is preparing for the upcoming rain by using sandbags and mulch to block water from entering his house. "It was pretty bad, and the house itself, once it started coming in, I thought maybe we would be alright. I threw down all my clothes trying to soak it up, but that didn't do anything. The next thing you knew, it was in the house," Reeves said. He described the situation as "overwhelming." The City of Fort Pierce is offering free self-serve sandbag stations at Martin Luther King Jr. Dreamland Park and Jaycee Park. Residents are advised to bring their own bags and shovels. Both parks are open daily from dawn to dusk. Lucie County has also set up self-service sandbag distribution points at the St. Lucie County Fairgrounds West Parking Lot and Lawnwood Stadium Parking Lot, thanks to donations of sand from Dickerson Infrastructure and Stewart Materials. Residents must bring their own supplies and fill their own bags. For updates about the precautions residents should take, please visit St. Lucie County’s emergency management portal at: www.readystlucie.org. For more information, residents can contact the Public Works Department or visit the county’s emergency management portal.
