entry.article_text: Crews are clearing drainage systems and checking waterways in St. Lucie County as another round of rain threatens areas still recovering from historic flooding. Lucie Public Schools is releasing students two hours early Tuesday. The district announced Tuesday afternoon that schools and offices will be closed Wednesday as a precaution. All after-school activities, aftercare programs, and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday are also canceled. District officials will continue monitoring rainfall, flooding, road closures, and the accessibility of schools, bus stops, and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. A decision regarding school operations for Thursday, November 19, will be announced Wednesday evening. Lucie officials say Public Works crews are inspecting drainage systems, clearing blockages and lowering water levels where possible. The ground remains saturated, increasing the risk of flooding even if rainfall is lighter than it was during the early November storms. See also: Heavy rain returns this week, bringing major threat of flooding across South Florida The National Weather Service has issued a flood watch for St. Lucie County from Tuesday afternoon through Friday evening. Forecasters expect 3 to 6 inches of rain across the area, with higher amounts possible in some locations. Two weeks ago, floodwaters stranded cars, trapped families and forced some residents to wade through deep water. Videos from that flooding showed high school freshman Noah Julian swimming from his school bus toward his home in a flooded Port St. Another video showed 7-year-old Ella Ghodooshim walking through chest-deep water with her mother near Oak Hammock K-8. That mother, Thassia Rodrigues, told CBS12 her only concern was getting her daughter safely across the flooded intersection. "As long as I can get her across and get her to safety, that was my main concern," Rodrigues said. She described how quickly the flooding overwhelmed the neighborhood, leaving parents struggling to reach their children. "It was pretty scary and in a matter of minutes we had everything just flood," she said. Lucie Public Schools told CBS12 News that decisions about closures and early dismissal are based on forecasts and information from the National Weather Service and Emergency Operations Center. The district said the information available before the previous flooding did not indicate schools needed to close or dismiss students earlier. This time, officials said the forecast supported releasing students two hours early to get them home before the heaviest rain. The district said it was awaiting additional updates from the National Weather Service at 2 p.m. and Emergency Operations Center at 4 p.m. Tuesday before making any further decisions about school schedules. Parents picking up their children near Oak Hammock K-8 Tuesday told CBS12 News they welcomed the earlier dismissal. "It's kind of nice that they're doing it early so we have time to get them and not have to rush," said Nathan Leach, whose child attends the school. Rhett Linton, another parent, recalled kayaking through the flooded intersection during the previous storm. "I'm super happy that they are stepping up and taking precautions," Linton said. Rodrigues, who was captured on video helping her daughter through the floodwaters, also praised the district's decision. Lucie County, we appreciate you guys," she said. Officials are urging residents to plan ahead, monitor forecasts and local alerts, and limit unnecessary travel. Drivers should never enter standing or moving water. Floodwater can stall a vehicle and cause costly engine damage. If you cannot tell how deep the water is, turn around and find another route. Residents can report flooding concerns to St. Lucie County at flooding@stlucieco.org .

entry.title: From unrecruited walk-on to NFL hopeful: FAU's Easton Messer eyes becoming NFL draft pick
entry.summary: After back-to-back 1,000-yard receiving seasons, FAU wide receiver Easton Messer is on several NFL Draft boards and looks to be the Owls' first draft pick in six years. I sat down with the FAU Owls standout for a one-on-one conversation about his journey one that spanned multiple countries before leading him to South Florida. WATCH REPORT BELOW: FAU's Easton Messer aims to become Owls' first NFL Draft pick since 2020 Messer moved around a lot over the years. 'My first place was Costa Rica, then I moved back to Louisville, then Panama, and lastly Malaysia,' Messer said. Growing up, he played both soccer and American football a combination he credits with shaping his footwork and technique. 'I really haven't thought about the fact that soccer helped out my feet and helped me play receiver, but soccer is big pretty much everywhere but the U.S. Just being over in those places and trying to get integrated into the culture,' Messer said. Football, though, was always his sport. 'Growing up, that was my sport. I played football, basketball and a little bit of baseball, but football was my favorite one. I went to high school at Christian Academy in Louisville,' Messer said. In high school, Messer was a standout receiver but felt he was under-recruited. 'It was pretty short; it wasn't a ton of recruiting with me being undersized and not passing the eye test. I had a couple offers, and I wasn't sure if they were commitable, and I ended up having to walk on at Western Kentucky,' Messer said. After standing out over three years at Western Kentucky, Messer entered the transfer portal and ultimately arrived at FAU. 'My transfer portal recruitment wasn't really popping either; not a lot of people reached out,' Messer said. Since 2020, no Owls player has heard their name called in the NFL Draft. Messer could change that in a few months. 'Personally, for me, going from a walk-on and not really getting recruited to possibly getting my name called on draft night, it doesn't even feel real at this point, but we got some other guys too,' Messer said. entry.article_text: Just weeks after historic flooding destroyed homes and displaced families in Jensen Beach, Martin County residents are bracing for another round of heavy rain — with up to 12 inches forecast over the next three days.For families still struggling to recover, the threat of more flooding comes as county commissioners work to determine what caused the initial disaster and how to help those who lost nearly everything.On Tuesday, flood victims packed a Martin County Commission meeting, pleading for financial assistance and answers.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Along Cheri Drive in Jensen Beach, the signs of destruction remain. Dumpsters line driveways, damaged belongings sit outside and families are still trying to salvage what's left of their homes.Lisa French, her husband, Jeremy, and their two young sons are among those displaced after floodwaters rose as high as 3 feet inside some homes two weeks ago."It's like we're kind of stuck," French told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey. French said her home had about 3 to 6 inches of flooding that sat inside for more than a week, causing mold to grow 3 to 4 feet up the walls. "So they, yeah, they tore the walls down in the house," said French. "They just chipped up the last bit of the tile, and it's empty." Now, with more rain approaching, French fears her family could face another disaster before recovering from the first."Of course, we're afraid because we all flooded in our houses," she said.New figures released by Martin County show at least 36 homes sustained damage, with an estimated $3 million in residential losses. Commissioners estimated another $14 million in damage to beaches, and at least $1 million in damage to roadways that now need repairs. For some residents, the destruction represents a lifetime of memories washed away."We've lost everything," one elderly Jensen Beach resident told commissioners. "We have 60 years of our life — kids, grandkids, everything. It's all gone."As residents demand answers about what went wrong, commissioners approved shifting $200,000 from the county's stormwater budget to investigate whether development and changes to local drainage systems contributed to the flooding.Commissioner Blake Capps called the investigation "a good starting point.""It may be that we need to augment the study beyond the $200,000 that we approve today," said Capps. Meanwhile, county crews are working around the clock to prepare for the next storm, lowering retention pond levels, deploying additional pumps and draining flooded properties."We have people 24 hours a day pumping that material down," Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said.Commissioners also approved financial assistance for eligible flood victims through the state's State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program.The assistance includes grants of up to $25,000 for income-eligible homeowners and loans of up to $75,000 secured by liens on their properties.But there's a catch: The grants are reimbursement-based, meaning homeowners must first pay for eligible repairs before receiving the money.For families who lost everything, that presents another obstacle."We don't have $25,000," French said. "A lot of people don't have $25,000, so it's great, and we're appreciative, but I mean, our house is empty, and $25,000 is not going to do much for us." The other problem: the county currently has just $1 million in SHIP funding available, and commissioners warned the money could run out quickly, even with additional state funding promised."They haven't given us the amount yet, but they have assured us that we will be getting some disaster relief funds," said Human Services Director Michelle Miller Strict income limits could also disqualify some flood victims who cannot afford to rebuild on their own. The income cap for a family of one is $86,040. The cap for a family of two is $98,400. For a family of four, it's $122,880. When reporter Kate Hussey asked Capps what would happen to those families, he acknowledged the county needs to explore other options."There are going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where someone barely missed the limit, and we're going to need to take a look at what we can do for those folks," Capps said.For residents like French, the need is immediate."We just need somebody to step up," she said. "We need funding." With another round of heavy rain approaching, Martin County is distributing sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park to help residents protect their properties, with a limit of 25 per person. The County's Emergency Operations Center is scheduled to be staffed beginning Tuesday at 2 p.m., and the county is coordinating with the National Weather Service and Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM).Fire Rescue is also standing by with multiple high-water rescue trucks.Commissioners also said a Federal Emergency Management Agency representative is expected to visit Nov. 30 to assess the damage — a potential step toward securing federal disaster assistance.But for families still displaced and facing the possibility of more flooding, the uncertainty remains.

The victim was on her way to a Wendy's where she works and she was in the crosswalk on SW Feather Terrace when she was hit. "I think for somebody to just leave another human being on the side of the road who was possibly injured, to not stop and check on them, it's truly heartbreaking that somebody would make that decision," said Katie Santana, a Port St. Lucie resident who lives near the intersection where the accident happened. We spoke with a high school student who rides an e-scooter in the area where the crash occurred. "I get a little bit fearful sometimes, 'cause I'll see some people going through red lights, not paying attention when they're turning and I've almost been hit a couple times," said John Rogalewski, age 15. See also: Bodycam footage shows deputy fatally shoot armed Florida mother, army veteran outside bar Police say a good Samaritan got the license plate number of the hit and run vehicle and stopped to help the victim. With that information, police determined a Chevy Tahoe struck the woman, and they determined the driver was an 18-year-old. Sanchez-Chasmer is charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. Police say the victim was rushed to a hospital and, at last report, she was hospitalized in critical condition. Police say she is in a coma. If she does not survive, the State Attorney's Office would decide if Sanchez-Chasmer could face a more serious charge. Police say two other individuals who were in the Chevy Tahoe with Sanchez-Chasmer have not been charged.

entry.title: St. Lucie County superintendent of schools promises review of district policies after historic flooding - WPBF
entry.summary: St. Lucie County superintendent of schools promises review of district policies after historic flooding    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie County Schools Superintendent Dr. Jon Prince apologized to the district Tuesday night and promised a review of all decisions and actions from the historic flooding on Nov. "It was very stressful for our families, and I certainly apologize for the stress that they went through on that day," Prince said. A video from that day shows a boy getting off a school bus on SW Coleman Avenue in Port St. Lucie and walking through flood waters that reach as high as his chest. Critics have pointed to that video and questioned the actions of the school district. In an exclusive interview, Prince expressed regret over the events of Nov. 2, stating that decisions were made based on the information available at the time. He emphasized that the flooding was unexpected. "The bottom line is I don't know of anything that could have predicted what transpired as the day progressed," Prince said. Prince assured that every decision made that day is being analyzed. "We are going to review all our procedures, our policies to make sure that if there's anything that we could have done differently, that moving forward we will," he said. With heavy rain in the forecast, St. Lucie County Schools decided to cancel classes for Wednesday. Prince said he hopes the decision is an overreaction. At the same time, though, he does not want to take any chances. "The ground is so saturated, but if the conditions worsen tomorrow, we don't want a repeat of what happened November 2," Prince said. Prince said the district will monitor the weather Wednesday and decide late Wednesday afternoon if classes should be canceled again Thursday. He said they'll follow that model until they are sure it's safe for students to return to class. entry.title: Riviera Beach residents brace for more rain weeks after homes flooded
entry.summary: Residents in Riviera Beach are preparing for another round of rain weeks after floodwaters damaged or destroyed hundreds of homes, including properties in Lone Pine Estates. With families still recovering, residents lined up for sandbags Tuesday as city leaders worked to identify financial assistance for homeowners. For families who recently watched water enter their homes, the possibility of more rain is bringing back fears of another flood. Keeping my fingers crossed, said Keisha Harty while preparing for the rain. WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache reconnected with the Harty family, who were waiting in line for sandbags while still recovering from the previous flooding. We need sandbags to put in front, just in case, Harty said. I dont want another flood. Not another one again. Lone Pine Estates was among the Riviera Beach communities hit by the recent flooding, which left hundreds of homes damaged or destroyed. Homeowner Guy Volel said his house flooded on consecutive days. Last week my house got flooded both days, Volel said. All the stuff inside my house is falling apart. Riviera Beach considers $2 million relief proposal The preparations come after an emergency meeting Monday night as residents continued pressing city leaders for help. Riviera Beach Mayor Douglas Lawson told WPTV that city officials are looking for ways to get financial assistance to affected homeowners. Residents are hurting and were trying to find every vehicle to help them to get the resources they need to rebuild their homes, Lawson said. City leaders are considering a $2 million relief proposal for residents affected by the flooding. Lawson said officials directed staff to move quickly and hoped to have more information before the Thanksgiving break. We demanded that staff comes back as quickly as possible, Lawson said. So hopefully by next week, prior to the Thanksgiving break, well have some answers for our residents to be able to disseminate some of this money weve allocated for them. entry.title: Mary Peltola projected to flip Alaska Senate seat, giving Democrats 56-44 majority
entry.summary: Democrat Mary Peltola is projected to defeat Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, according to the Associated Press, delivering a significant pickup for Democrats. Peltola's victory marks the first time since 2008 that a Democrat has won a U.S. Senate election in Alaska, and gives Democrats a 56-44 majority in the Senate though two lawmakers identify as Independents and simply caucus with the Democrats. 'As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first,' Peltola said in a statement. 'As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaskas working families. Thank you Alaska. Lets get to work. Peltola, who made history in 2022 as the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, focused her Senate campaign on lowering the cost of living and addressing economic challenges facing everyday Alaskans. She previously served in the U.S. House of Representatives, where she became known for emphasizing issues important to Alaska, including the state's fishing industry and economic development. The race drew national attention as Republicans fought to defend their Senate majority. Sullivan, a military veteran seeking a third term, received support from President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance. Sullivan aligned his campaign with the Trump administration's tax and spending priorities and advocated for expanding fossil fuel production. The race in Alaska was complicated by the presence of another Dan Sullivan on the ballot. Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, ran as a long shot Democratic candidate for Senate. Both Dan Sullivans running prompted a legal fight early in the campaign, and President Donald Trump later called the former teacher's campaign 'fake' and 'a hoax by the Democrats.'

entry.article_text: The Treasure Coast is bracing for a soggy stretch as counties prepare for possible flooding from heavy rain. Indian River County The Indian River County Emergency Operations Center remains at Level 2, or partial activation, because of ongoing flooding and the potential for more heavy rain. Emergency services, human services and infrastructure partners are coordinating response and recovery efforts. The county urges residents to avoid flooded roads and floodwaters, watch for rising water in low-lying areas and monitor weather conditions and official updates. Residents with flood-related questions or information can call the Emergency Information Center at 772-226-4000 during operating hours. Due to the heavy rain and gusty winds, solid waste services may be disrupted. Waste Management curbside collections may be delayed, and residents should not put carts in the street if it is flooded. See also: Florida deputies rescue 2-year-old girl found in pond near apartment complex Waste Management collects recycling in blue carts countywide. It collects garbage, yard waste and bulk waste in unincorporated Indian River County, Fellsmere, Sebastian and Indian River Shores. Residents in other cities and towns should check with their local governments for service updates. The county recommends putting carts out by 6 a.m. on collection day, closing lids, bagging garbage, and avoiding overfilled carts. Cardboard should be flattened and placed inside recycling carts, and yard waste should stay inside yard waste carts. Residents should bring carts back in as soon as possible after collection. The landfill and all five Customer Convenience Centers may close early or remain closed if conditions become unsafe. The east-central Florida coast faces a Slight Risk, or Level 2 out of 4, for excessive rainfall. Localized flooding is possible, especially along the coast, and some areas could receive 4 inches or more of rain. Martin County Martin County officials expect 3 to 6 inches of rain, with localized amounts of 8 to 12 inches, beginning Tuesday afternoon and continuing through Nov. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office says it is working with the county’s emergency operations center to monitor rainfall and identify roads that could become difficult to pass. The sheriff’s office plans to deploy high-water rescue vehicles in flood-prone areas. Having the vehicles nearby could help deputies reach residents who need assistance and motorists who become stranded, the office said. The sheriff’s office advises residents to turn around if water covers the road. Standing water may be deeper than it appears and can hide damage. If a regular route is flooded, drivers should take another route or wait somewhere safe. Residents should never drive around barricades or enter flooded areas to see how high the water is. Martin County Fire Rescue also advises residents to be prepared to evacuate if flooding threatens their homes or neighborhoods and to have an emergency kit ready for household members and pets. The Community Information Center will be open to provide flood-related information. Okeechobee County Okeechobee County is also preparing for severe flooding. The Okeechobee County Sheriff’s Office says its emergency operations center will remain active as staff coordinate response and recovery efforts from past flooding. Sandbags are available at Okeechobee County Public Works, 804 Northwest Second St. Lucie County Public Safety Department is monitoring the forecast and reminding residents to secure loose items that could be damaged by wind. Gusty northeast winds of 25 to 30 mph are forecast Tuesday and Wednesday, with gusts of 35 to 40 mph along the coast. Residents should secure tarps, patio furniture and other unsecured items. A rip current advisory remains in effect for St. Strong onshore winds can create dangerous rip currents and rough surf. Lucie County Fire District says its firefighters, paramedics and telecommunicators are prepared to respond as the area faces more heavy rain and recovers from recent flooding. The district has high-water vehicles and a rescue boat available to assist during flood-related emergencies. Free sand is available while supplies last at two self-service locations: County Fairgrounds: 5601 W. Midway Road, Fort Pierce, in the west parking lot Lawnwood Stadium: 2000 Virginia Ave., Fort Pierce Residents should bring their own bags, shovel and other supplies. Residents can use Community Connect to share household information that could help firefighters prepare for an emergency. The county has extended the deadline to Nov. 30 for residents to report flood damage through an online survey. The information will help document flooding across the community and inform recovery efforts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants throughout St. Lucie County, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie Village and unincorporated areas. It asks where flooding occurred, how buildings were affected and what impacts residents and businesses experienced. Residents can complete the flood damage survey by Nov. Officials urge residents across the region to avoid flooded roads and keep roadways clear for emergency responders. If you encounter flooding, turn around and find a safe alternate route.

entry.title: Martin County residents demand emergency shelter as flooding threatens the Treasure Coast - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County residents demand emergency shelter as flooding threatens the Treasure Coast    WPEC
entry.article_text: Martin County families still recovering from this month’s flooding are bracing for more rain, and on Tuesday, many of them asked county commissioners not to wait on federal help before opening an emergency shelter. Speaker after speaker told commissioners during public comment that water was already back in their streets. Some said their homes took on water earlier this month. Their main request was a public shelter, open before the next round of rain, for both unhoused residents and families who lost their homes in the flooding. Commissioners are discussing funding options at both the local and federal level. Florida has asked President Donald Trump for a major disaster declaration for the flooding, and as of Tuesday, it had not been signed. Once a disaster receives a federal declaration, FEMA must cover 75 percent of state and local response and recovery costs, according to the Florida Policy Institute. Without one, counties pay those costs on their own. Several speakers argued the county does not need to wait for that approval to act. Commissioner, you do not need FEMA’s blessing to open a school. Neighboring counties didn’t wait. Churches didn’t wait, one speaker said. Yamila Rollan Escalona, founder and executive director of Yaya Por Vida, a grassroots harm reduction organization, said she emailed her comments Tuesday morning as water rose in her neighborhood again, then came to speak in person. She said her group has been asking commissioners for emergency shelter for most of the year. See also: Palm Beach County braces for more flooding as cities offer sandbags, prepare for storm Please give us emergency shelter now. It’s no longer about just individuals that are unhoused. It’s also about individuals that just became unhoused because of this tragedy, Rollan Escalona told CBS12 News after the meeting. Rollan Escalona said unhoused residents have nowhere to go, pointing to a 2024 state law that bans sleeping on public property. She said some people are still staying in campsites surrounded by standing water, and some residents have not been accounted for. With drains and the ground already saturated, she said there is no time to wait. She also warned the damage won’t end when the water goes down. Rollan Escalona said mental health services on the Treasure Coast are already hard to access, and she worries the stress and hopelessness of losing everything could lead to more overdoses and people returning to substance use. Other speakers looked further ahead, linking the flooding to development in the county, including a proposed hyperscale data center. They asked commissioners to consider runoff and drainage before approving large projects. Take the 30,000-foot view the next time you look at a large project. How does it affect your neighbors? Martin County Emergency Management Director Sally Waite previously told commissioners the flooding affected 77 homes. Residents whose homes were damaged can report it and fill out a needs survey on the county’s flood recovery page. Ahead of the rain, Martin County is handing out sand and sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park, 8303 SW Lost River Road. Distribution runs from noon to 6 p.m. Each household can take up to 25 sandbags, and residents will be asked for their name and address. The county asks residents to check its map for the exact pickup spot inside the park. CBS12 News will update this story with what commissioners decide on funding and a possible shelter.

Police have identified the driver as Tristan Ray Sanchez-Chasmer, 18, of Port St. "Pranks especially at somebody's front door, especially at late hours of the night, early hours of the morning can be very dangerous," said Leo Niemczyk, Port St. Lucie Police say the crash happened Monday, November 16, at about 5:10 am near the intersection of SW Gatlin Blvd. and SW Feather Terrace in Port St. Police say a 24 year old woman on an e-scooter was hit by a vehicle that did not stop. The victim was on her way to a Wendy's where she works and she was in the crosswalk on SW Feather Terrace when she was hit. "I think for somebody to just leave another human being on the side of the road who was possibly injured, to not stop and check on them, it's truly heartbreaking that somebody would make that decision," said Katie Santana, a Port St. Lucie resident who lives near the intersection where the accident happened. We spoke with a high school student who rides an e-scooter in the area where the crash occurred. "I get a little bit fearful sometimes, 'cause I'll see some people going through red lights, not paying attention when they're turning and I've almost been hit a couple times," said John Rogalewski, age 15. With that information, police determined a Chevy Tahoe struck the woman, and they determined the driver was an 18-year-old. entry.summary: 18-year-old charged in Port St. Lucie hit-and-run that critically injured woman riding e-scooter    WFLX
entry.article_text: An 18-year-old driver has been arrested after Port St. Lucie Police Department investigators say he struck a 24-year-old woman riding an electric scooter to work and left the scene, leaving her critically injured. Police say the driver had been playing a "ding-dong-ditch" prank with friends shortly before Monday morning's crash. WATCH: E-Scooter Hit-and-Run in Port St. Lucie Police identified the driver as Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer. He was arrested on a felony charge of leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, according to the department. The crash happened near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. Investigators said the woman was traveling west on the sidewalk toward Southwest Rosser Boulevard and had entered a crosswalk when she was hit by a gray Chevrolet Tahoe making a left turn onto Southwest Feather Terrace. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said Tuesday the woman remained unconscious and in critical condition. "We're deeply concerned for her recovery, and our thoughts are with her loved ones," Niemczyk said. Police said a witness stopped to help the woman, called 911 and was able to get the SUV's license plate information. Investigators used that information to identify the vehicle and the driver. Investigators said Sanchez-Chasmer had two friends with him and had been playing "ding-dong-ditch" shortly before the crash. "They were specifically playing, I'll call it ring and run, ding-dong-ditch, at a house that belonged to a friend of theirs, and apparently the mother came to the door and they fled the scene," Niemczyk told WPTV. Niemczyk said investigators believe the people inside the SUV realized a collision had occurred. "They're aware that they hit something. According to Niemczyk, Sanchez-Chasmer and the two passengers did not call 911. Niemczyk said the decision to leave the scene was key to the criminal investigation. "Had they remained on scene, provided aid, it would have been a very different criminal outcome," Niemczyk said. "There probably wouldn't have been criminal charges at that point." Sanchez-Chasmer was charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. According to published reports citing law enforcement records, he was being held on a $5,000 bond. Police have not announced charges against the two passengers. WPTV returned to the intersection after the crash and spoke with 15-year-old John Rogalewski, who said he rides an e-scooter to school and is sometimes on the road early in the morning. "I'm looking at my surroundings almost the whole time," Rogalewski said. "I'm making sure every time I have to cross the street that there's not a car coming up, and that it is my sign to go, no matter how long I have to wait to cross." Police said the 24-year-old woman was wearing a helmet when she was struck. The investigation remains active, according to police, and toxicology results are still pending. entry.summary: Joe Namath's Lucky Shuck coming to Jensen Beach as waterfront village breaks ground    WPEC
entry.article_text: Football legend Joe Namath is bringing his popular Lucky Shuck restaurant to Jensen Beach as a massive waterfront development takes shape along the St. Rio Marine Village , a 30-acre mixed-use development in Martin County, broke ground Thursday, following more than five years of planning. The project will feature 342 apartments, a 131-slip marina, more than a half-mile of public riverwalk, and several waterfront dining and entertainment destinations. Among them is a new location of The Lucky Shuck Oyster Bar & Taphouse , owned by Namath and his business partner Charlie Modica, along with a second, yet-to-be-named outdoor dining concept. See also: New 24/7 animal cruelty hotline launching across Florida "The Lucky Shuck has always been about good food, good people and being on the water," Namath said. "Rio Marine Village gives us a home right on the river, and I can't wait to see boats pulling up and families sitting down together." The development will also feature the Osprey Club, a waterfront wedding and event venue, along with a public park, boardwalk, beach, and kayak and paddleboard rentals. Martin County commissioners unanimously approved the project's first two phases following years of community discussions. Construction is expected to begin this month, with the first phase scheduled for completion in late 2028.

entry.title: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home - WPTV
entry.summary: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home    WPTV
entry.article_text: A Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding is searching for more permanent housing and money to rebuild after water destroyed much of the inside of their home. Lisa and Jeremy French, who have two young boys, told WPTV's Michael Hoffman they ultimately have one goal: to get their family back home.WATCH REPORT BELOW:WPTV first met the French family shortly after historic rainfall hit South Florida and the Treasure Coast. Floodwater had surrounded their neighborhood, forcing residents to use kayaks to get around and check on neighbors.Days later, much of the water has receded. The damage has not."My floorboards are outside," Lisa French said.Hoffman returned to the French family's Jensen Beach home for an update, but the family said it was not safe to go inside.French said the flooding wiped out much of what her family had accumulated over the years."Our appliances are gone, our cabinets are gone, every piece of furniture," French said.The family is now trying to determine how to pay for repairs while securing a more permanent place to live.WPTV met French again at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach, where a Multi-Agency Resource Center has been helping people looking for assistance following the flooding.French told Hoffman that her home flooded days after the rain had stopped.Martin County told WPTV that the family's home is near the Savannah Preserves, an area where excess water naturally flows from other flooded areas.French, however, questions whether other actions involving water entering the preserve contributed to what happened at her home."They're saying it's from natural rain, but they dumped Monday and Tuesday, nonstop into the savannas," French said.The impact of the flooding extends beyond the physical damage.Through tears, Lisa and Jeremy French pleaded for help before the Martin County Commission as they described what their family is facing."Today we are homeless," Lisa French told commissioners. "We have nowhere to host Thanksgiving. We have nowhere for our boys to have Christmas. We don't have beds to come home to."The couple has two young boys. French said she wants them to continue growing up in the Jensen Beach home the family worked hard to maintain.For now, however, the family says it needs more permanent housing while trying to determine where the money to repair the home will come from.French said the uncertainty surrounding assistance has left her worried there could still be a significant financial gap, even if additional aid becomes available."Who's going to fill in the gaps?" French said. "And, you know, maybe I feel like somebody should take accountability."Despite the uncertainty and extensive damage, the family says it has not given up hope of returning."We just want to go home," French said. "Like, that's at the end, that we just want to be home with our family."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Rough surf and rip currents create dangerous conditions along Treasure Coast - WPBF
entry.summary: Rough surf and rip currents create dangerous conditions along Treasure Coast    WPBF
entry.article_text: Strong winds and high surf are creating dangerous conditions along the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches, with red flag warnings and a high risk of rip currents keeping most beachgoers out of the water. At Stuart Beach, the wind is whipping through the area, churning up rough water conditions. The beach is nearly empty, with no one in the water and only a few people on the sand. "Take advantage of this; it may not be great weather, but there's not a lot of people. So, you got quiet time to yourself. It's beautiful," said Jon Ciffolillo, a beachgoer. Despite the roaring wind, some are still venturing out to enjoy the morning before another round of heavy rain is expected to move through the area. "It's a beautiful day out here. The wind and the surf is just a different view of nature's beauty," said Frank Harvey, who was walking on the beach with his wife, Joan. Joan Harvey added, "A lot of time in your condo is not always ideal. So, you got to take it when it's not raining." Beachgoers are being urged to take caution, as conditions in the water remain dangerous. A high surf advisory is in effect along the Palm Beaches and Treasure Coast, along with a high risk for rip currents. Red flag warnings are also in place along Martin County's beaches, signaling that even experienced swimmers can be pulled away from shore. Martin County Ocean Rescue advises beachgoers to check with lifeguards about water conditions and to swim in guarded areas when conditions improve. The high surf advisory and high risk for rip currents are expected to last through Thursday. You can check the latest beach conditions across Martin County on their Safe Beach Day website. entry.title: New survey shows people plan to forgo future savings to pay for holiday costs
entry.summary: People are sacrificing their long-term savings to afford the holidays this year. A new survey of 1,000 people by USA Capitol Gold found 42% of Americans plan to cut back on or draw from their savings and investments to afford holiday expenses. WATCH: New survey shows people plan to dig into savings to afford holiday purchases Survey: People plan to dig into savings for holiday spending Nearly 1 in 5 say they expect to take on debt to cover holiday costs. Of those who plan to take on debt, 16% of those surveyed say they plan to charge it to their credit card, whereas 10% say they'll rely on buy now, pay later options to make purchases. The poll set out to understand how rising costs and economic pressures are affecting consumers' savings, retirement plans, investment decisions, and long-term financial goals. The study also reflects a growing habit of more people investing less money each month to pay for everyday expenses.

entry.title: St. Lucie County clears drains, prepares for more rain after historic flooding - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County clears drains, prepares for more rain after historic flooding    WPEC
entry.article_text: Crews are clearing drainage systems and checking waterways in St. Lucie County as another round of rain threatens areas still recovering from historic flooding. Lucie Public Schools is releasing students two hours early Tuesday. The district announced Tuesday afternoon that schools and offices will be closed Wednesday as a precaution. All after-school activities, aftercare programs, and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday are also canceled. District officials will continue monitoring rainfall, flooding, road closures, and the accessibility of schools, bus stops, and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. A decision regarding school operations for Thursday, November 19, will be announced Wednesday evening. Lucie officials say Public Works crews are inspecting drainage systems, clearing blockages and lowering water levels where possible. The ground remains saturated, increasing the risk of flooding even if rainfall is lighter than it was during the early November storms. See also: Heavy rain returns this week, bringing major threat of flooding across South Florida The National Weather Service has issued a flood watch for St. Lucie County from Tuesday afternoon through Friday evening. Forecasters expect 3 to 6 inches of rain across the area, with higher amounts possible in some locations. Two weeks ago, floodwaters stranded cars, trapped families and forced some residents to wade through deep water. Videos from that flooding showed high school freshman Noah Julian swimming from his school bus toward his home in a flooded Port St. Another video showed 7-year-old Ella Ghodooshim walking through chest-deep water with her mother near Oak Hammock K-8. That mother, Thassia Rodrigues, told CBS12 her only concern was getting her daughter safely across the flooded intersection. "As long as I can get her across and get her to safety, that was my main concern," Rodrigues said. She described how quickly the flooding overwhelmed the neighborhood, leaving parents struggling to reach their children. "It was pretty scary and in a matter of minutes we had everything just flood," she said. Lucie Public Schools told CBS12 News that decisions about closures and early dismissal are based on forecasts and information from the National Weather Service and Emergency Operations Center. The district said the information available before the previous flooding did not indicate schools needed to close or dismiss students earlier. This time, officials said the forecast supported releasing students two hours early to get them home before the heaviest rain. The district said it was awaiting additional updates from the National Weather Service at 2 p.m. and Emergency Operations Center at 4 p.m. Tuesday before making any further decisions about school schedules. Parents picking up their children near Oak Hammock K-8 Tuesday told CBS12 News they welcomed the earlier dismissal. "It's kind of nice that they're doing it early so we have time to get them and not have to rush," said Nathan Leach, whose child attends the school. Rhett Linton, another parent, recalled kayaking through the flooded intersection during the previous storm. "I'm super happy that they are stepping up and taking precautions," Linton said. Rodrigues, who was captured on video helping her daughter through the floodwaters, also praised the district's decision. Lucie County, we appreciate you guys," she said. Officials are urging residents to plan ahead, monitor forecasts and local alerts, and limit unnecessary travel. Drivers should never enter standing or moving water. Floodwater can stall a vehicle and cause costly engine damage. If you cannot tell how deep the water is, turn around and find another route. Residents can report flooding concerns to St. Lucie County at flooding@stlucieco.org .

entry.title: Martin County Teacher of the Year Richard Acosta celebrates educators who inspire students - WPTV
entry.summary: Martin County Teacher of the Year Richard Acosta celebrates educators who inspire students    WPTV
entry.article_text: Pinewood Elementary School science teacher Richard Acosta has been named the 2026-27 Martin County Teacher of the Year, earning the opportunity to represent the county in the Florida Department of Education’s statewide Teacher of the Year competition.The Education Foundation of Martin County announced Acosta as the overall winner during its Teacher of the Year Award Celebration on Nov. 6 at the MIDFLORIDA Event Center in Port St. Lucie.Acosta was also named Elementary Teacher of the Year.“This is phenomenal,” Acosta said after the honor was revealed. “I feel incredibly invigorated and inspired to go to the next level and represent Martin County at the state competition.”Acosta was among three educators recognized with top honors.Miriam Hernández, an intensive reading teacher at Indiantown Middle School, was named Middle School Teacher of the Year.Marc Turull, who teaches International Baccalaureate physics and chemistry at South Fork High School, was named High School Teacher of the Year.Turull said the award also represents the people he works alongside.“It’s such an honor,” Turull said. “I teach physics, and I work with amazing people, so to represent them and be Teacher of the Year makes me so grateful.”Hernández described the recognition as both a privilege and an honor.During the celebration, the three teachers emphasized the importance of educators at every stage of a student's education.“The fact is that it takes all three of us for excellence in Martin County schools,” Acosta said. “We start with the foundation in elementary school. We move on to middle school intensive reading, and then we finish at the high school at South Fork. So we, we feel very blessed to be working together.”The Education Foundation said Acosta’s 35-year career in education can be traced partly to his own experience as a teenager.According to the Education Foundation of Martin County, at 16, Acosta was struggling with confidence and direction when he entered teacher John Lynskey’s American history class. According to the foundation, Lynskey’s storytelling and encouragement helped Acosta develop a love of learning.Acosta still keeps two history books Lynskey gave him.His path toward teaching became clearer when Acosta later tutored a younger student after school and watched the child's confidence and enthusiasm for learning grow, according to the foundation.Today, Acosta teaches science to students from prekindergarten through fifth grade at Pinewood Elementary.“I love what I do, and I love energizing the classroom and engaging them to the greatest possibility,” Acosta said.His lessons include hands-on investigations tied to the natural environment around Martin County. The Education Foundation said students have examined sea turtle skull models, shells and other materials connected to the Indian River Lagoon while studying how adaptations help turtles survive.Acosta also helped develop a “Birds of the Everglades” curriculum with environmental partners and has been involved with schoolwide science initiatives and family STEAM events.For Acosta, the recognition provides another opportunity beyond representing Martin County at the state level.“I feel very blessed to be in this position because I get to mentor other teachers from other schools,” Acosta said.Acosta also receives a one-year vehicle lease provided through Audi Stuart and Infiniti Stuart.“That is amazing and spectacular,” Acosta said. “I cannot wait to pick out a car on Saturday.”The celebration recognized 24 school-level Teachers of the Year who were selected by their peers. According to the Education Foundation, nominees submitted application portfolios and participated in interviews before a panel of judges.Felix A. Williams Elementary School also won the Spirit Award for its enthusiasm, interpretation of the event's theme, and props.The recognition comes as Martin County educators continue the everyday work behind the awards: helping children learn, building their confidence and creating connections that can influence students long after they leave the classroom.For Acosta, that circle is especially meaningful. A teacher once helped him see greater possibilities for his own future. Decades later, he is working to create those possibilities for another generation.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: St. Lucie County schools closed as families prepare for more heavy rain - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County schools closed as families prepare for more heavy rain    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County schools and district offices are closed Wednesday as families prepare for more heavy rain, two weeks after flooding left roads underwater and damaged homes. All aftercare programs, after-school activities and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday are also canceled. See also: Flood risk continues for the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches through Friday evening The school district said forecasts show the potential for significant rainfall and localized flooding. With the ground already saturated, the district said closing schools was the cautious choice for students, families and employees. Officials are monitoring rainfall, flooding, road closures and access to schools, bus stops and transportation routes. The district plans to announce Wednesday evening whether schools will reopen Thursday. Across the Treasure Coast, some residents are filling sandbags to protect their homes. Others are stocking up on groceries and preparing to stay home if roads flood again. Lucie says floodwater rose to his knees two weeks ago, damaging his garage and guitars. He filled sandbags at the St. Lucie County Fairgrounds and is adding more around his home. We had a lot of water go into the garage and we just got over the fact that it stopped smelling like mold in there, Vargas said. And then here we go again with this inclement weather. Lucie County set up self-service sand distribution sites at the county fairgrounds in Fort Pierce and the Lawnwood Stadium parking lot. Residents need to bring their own bags and shovels and fill the bags themselves. Sand is available while supplies last. Tuesday, the two truckloads at Lawnwood Stadium were nearly gone. Glen Ferlance was out for a morning walk Wednesday morning when he spoke with CBS12. He said the flooding two weeks ago kept him from reaching his children. I could not get to cross over to go and see my kids, Ferlance said. I had to park in the um the plaza here and just look on. Ferlance said he lives in Port St. Lucie and he’s preparing for more rain, but hopes the flooding won’t be as severe this time. I just hope that is not too bad like last time. Yes, I’m prepared, he said. I’m going to get something to eat, and I’m running back home in my bed to watch TV and relax until all this is over. He also said he’s glad St. Lucie County schools are closed. I just thank God they’re not school today, so the kids then should be more safe at home, he said. Some residents are also stocking up on food and supplies. Shoppers told CBS12 they’re preparing to stay home if roads flood again. The district said updates about school operations will be shared on its website and social media channels. Martin County canceled after-school activities. Schools in Indian River and Okeechobee counties remain open as of Wednesday morning. Palm Beach County schools and offices are open Wednesday, but the district canceled all after-school activities and athletics because of the afternoon forecast. Aftercare families must pick up their children by 4 p.m., the district said.

entry.title: New 24/7 animal cruelty hotline in Florida already getting results just hours after its launch
entry.summary: A new 24/7 animal cruelty hotline in Florida is already getting results just hours after its launch was announced. Big Dog Ranch Rescue CEO and founder Lauree Simmons said the hotline went live Monday, and the organization received more than 30 calls. It also led to the rescue of an abandoned and neglected dog in Bay County. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Big Dog Ranch applauds Florida's new animal cruelty hotline The hotline gives people a place to report suspected animal abuse, including cruelty, abandonment and dog fighting. The reports are then turned over to law enforcement, animal control or a government agency for possible investigation. 'These animals can't call you can. You see an animal being neglected, starved, call and report it,' Simmons said. The Florida Statewide Animal Cruelty Hotline is operated by Big Dog Ranch Rescue, located in Loxahatchee Groves, and funded through the state. The hotline number is 844-4-SOSPET (844-476-7738). People can report anonymously, and it's available 24/7.

entry.title: Woman dies after Port St. Lucie hit-and-run; police say driver was playing 'ding dong ditch' beforehand
entry.summary: A 24-year-old woman has died from injuries she suffered after she was struck while riding an electric scooter in a hit-and-run crash in Port St. Lucie , police said Wednesday. The woman died at approximately 9:23 p.m. Tuesday, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Teen Charged in Port St. Lucie E-Scooter Hit-and-Run | WPTV The crash happened around 5:10 a.m. Monday near the intersection of Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. Police said the woman was riding an electric scooter when a vehicle struck her. Investigators allege the driver left the scene without stopping to help her or notify law enforcement. The department's Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit later identified the vehicle as a gray Chevrolet Tahoe and located it at a Port St. Lucie home, according to police. Investigators identified the alleged driver as 18-year-old Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer. Police said investigators learned Sanchez-Chasmer had been playing 'ding dong ditch' with friends shortly before the crash. According to the department, the group was leaving a home where they had been participating in the prank when the vehicle struck the woman. Sanchez-Chasmer was arrested and charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, a second-degree felony, police said. Following the woman's death, police said they anticipate the State Attorney's Office will pursue enhanced or additional charges as appropriate based on the circumstances and the outcome of the investigation. Police did not identify the woman in Wednesday's news release.

The district is also encouraging families to monitor their children's bus routes in real time through the free Here Comes the Bus app. District officials said they are monitoring the forecast for Thursday, Nov. 19, and plan to provide an update later Wednesday about school operations. The district said student and staff safety remains its top priority as officials continue to monitor weather conditions.

entry.summary: Jensen Beach Festival of Giving brings together more than 50 local nonprofits    WPTV
entry.article_text: More than 50 local nonprofits are coming together for the third annual Festival of Giving at the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast, filling the Jensen Beach museum with holiday displays while allowing community organizations to share the work they do throughout the region.Christina McIntosh, community outreach and events coordinator for the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast, said participating nonprofits come from communities stretching from Palm Beach County north through the Treasure Coast."Those are the five counties that our education department here at the museum works with and works with the schools," McIntosh said. More than Christmas decorationsThe Festival of Giving uses decorated Christmas trees and holiday displays to introduce visitors to nonprofit organizations serving South Florida and the Treasure Coast.For the organizations involved, the gathering also provides a chance to learn more about one another.Treasure Coast Community Singers is among the nonprofits participating."The really great thing about this event is that we get to know other nonprofits," Sharon Savageaux of Treasure Coast Community Singers said. “We get to understand what they do. "He loves this event, so the kids will be able to visit with him."Family Night is scheduled for Tuesday evening on Nov. 17, at the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast.An adult holiday pajama party follows FridayThe celebration takes a turn for the grown-ups Friday with an adult holiday pajama party."We will be a museum full of adults dressed in their holiday pajamas because who doesn’t want to go to a party and go home and go right to bed," McIntosh said.The festival continues through Saturday, Nov. 21, at 2 p.m., according to McIntosh. The Children’s Museum of the Treasure Coast is located at 1707 NE Indian River Drive in Jensen Beach.Click here for more information.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home - WPTV
entry.summary: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home    WPTV
entry.article_text: A Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding is searching for more permanent housing and money to rebuild after water destroyed much of the inside of their home. Lisa and Jeremy French, who have two young boys, told WPTV's Michael Hoffman they ultimately have one goal: to get their family back home.WATCH REPORT BELOW:WPTV first met the French family shortly after historic rainfall hit South Florida and the Treasure Coast. Floodwater had surrounded their neighborhood, forcing residents to use kayaks to get around and check on neighbors.Days later, much of the water has receded. The damage has not."My floorboards are outside," Lisa French said.Hoffman returned to the French family's Jensen Beach home for an update, but the family said it was not safe to go inside.French said the flooding wiped out much of what her family had accumulated over the years."Our appliances are gone, our cabinets are gone, every piece of furniture," French said.The family is now trying to determine how to pay for repairs while securing a more permanent place to live.WPTV met French again at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach, where a Multi-Agency Resource Center has been helping people looking for assistance following the flooding.French told Hoffman that her home flooded days after the rain had stopped.Martin County told WPTV that the family's home is near the Savannah Preserves, an area where excess water naturally flows from other flooded areas.French, however, questions whether other actions involving water entering the preserve contributed to what happened at her home."They're saying it's from natural rain, but they dumped Monday and Tuesday, nonstop into the savannas," French said.The impact of the flooding extends beyond the physical damage.Through tears, Lisa and Jeremy French pleaded for help before the Martin County Commission as they described what their family is facing."Today we are homeless," Lisa French told commissioners. "We have nowhere to host Thanksgiving. We have nowhere for our boys to have Christmas. We don't have beds to come home to."The couple has two young boys. French said she wants them to continue growing up in the Jensen Beach home the family worked hard to maintain.For now, however, the family says it needs more permanent housing while trying to determine where the money to repair the home will come from.French said the uncertainty surrounding assistance has left her worried there could still be a significant financial gap, even if additional aid becomes available."Who's going to fill in the gaps?" French said. "And, you know, maybe I feel like somebody should take accountability."Despite the uncertainty and extensive damage, the family says it has not given up hope of returning."We just want to go home," French said. "Like, that's at the end, that we just want to be home with our family."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: South Florida Water Management District authorizes emergency pumping as flooding threat continues
entry.summary: The South Florida Water Management District has issued an emergency order allowing certain pumping and water-management measures as communities contend with saturated ground and the threat of additional heavy rainfall. The emergency final order, signed by Executive Director Drew Bartlett, is intended to help address flooding caused by the heavy rainfall that has hit portions of Florida beginning Oct. 31. The district said some impacted areas received more than 10 inches of rain in 36 hours, causing widespread flooding and leaving standing water and saturated ground. WATCH BELOW: Flood victims worried as Martin County braces for more rain Flood victims worried as Martin County braces for more rain The order comes as additional localized heavy rain threatens areas already hit hard by flooding. The district said those conditions create an 'imminent threat' of additional significant flooding and damage to life and property. The emergency action stems from state-of-emergency declarations issued by Gov. Ron DeSantis on Nov. 2 and Nov. 4 in response to the flooding. Under the order, water can be moved from flooded portions of a property, including roadways, parking lots and swales, to ponds, lakes or other areas on the same property without notifying the district, as long as the water is not being discharged off-site. Moving floodwater off-site requires more oversight. The district must approve such discharges after a field inspection, and the flooding must pose an immediate threat to public health, safety or welfare. The order specifically says minor flooding, such as standing water in roads, swales or yards, does not qualify as an immediate threat. Local governments and water control districts can also receive authorization to discharge water beyond their normal district-permitted operating schedules to prepare for or reduce flooding. They must notify the district's Emergency Operations Center and receive authorization from district staff. WATCH BELOW: Flooding threat collides with St. Lucie County budget concerns Flooding threat collides with St. Lucie County budget concerns The district said all emergency activities must be carried out in ways that minimize impacts to water quality and quantity. Those carrying out pumping or discharges must also correct any erosion, sediment or water-quality problems resulting from the work. The order specifically says minor flooding, such as standing water in roads, swales or yards, does not qualify as an immediate threat. Local governments and water control districts can also receive authorization to discharge water beyond their normal district-permitted operating schedules to prepare for or reduce flooding. They must notify the district's Emergency Operations Center and receive authorization from district staff. WATCH BELOW: Flooding threat collides with St. Lucie County budget concernsThe district said all emergency activities must be carried out in ways that minimize impacts to water quality and quantity. Those carrying out pumping or discharges must also correct any erosion, sediment or water-quality problems resulting from the work. The order temporarily suspends certain permitting and notice requirements when necessary for the specifically authorized emergency activities. However, it does not eliminate requirements imposed by other federal, state or local agencies. The emergency order took effect immediately upon its execution and is scheduled to expire Jan. 1, 2027, unless it is extended or ended earlier by the district's executive director or Governing Board.The district said its emergency operations center remains at Level 2 partial activation. They also remind everyone to avoid floodwaters resulting from heavy rains. If you face life-threatening flooding or are in imminent danger, call 9-1-1Avoid driving through flooded areas. entry.summary: A massive indoor pickleball facility is opening its doors in Boca Raton. Boca Paddle by City Pickle is officially welcoming players to 25 brand-new courts. It's the city's first fully climate-controlled indoor pickleball and padel club. Day passes cost $40, with Boca Raton residents getting $5 off. The center also features a restaurant and bar, a shop, and fitness and recovery spaces like a sauna and cold plunge. One of its co-founders says Boca Paddle is unlike anything else in the city. Boca Raton's mayor says the city is the right fit for this type of facility. The area that we're in right now, here in North Park, is in need of revitalization. And this facility, by itself, takes a huge step in that direction to help revitalize this part of the city,' Boca Raton Mayor Andy Thomson said. The facility will also be the home of a new professional team. 'I'm excited that we're a home for the Palm Beach Royals , which is major league pickleball's newest franchise. They paid $16 million last year. They're going to be based here,' Boca Paddle Co-Founder Brian Levine said. By the numbers, the facility spans 100,000 square feet and cost around $20 million to build. It has 14 indoor pickleball courts and nine outdoor courts, along with two padel courts. entry.article_text: Due to anticipated rainfall, at least one public-school district and a private school on the Treasure Coast will close. LUCIE COUNTY A spokesperson for the St. Lucie County Public Schools announced that the school district will be closed to students and employees on Wednesday, Nov. "While there remains some uncertainty regarding the exact timing, location, and amount of rainfall, current forecasts from the National Weather Service indicate the potential for significant rainfall and localized flooding. Given the already saturated conditions in our community, the District believes taking a cautious approach is in the best interest of our students, families, and employees," the school district spokesperson said in a statement. All after-school activities, after-care programs and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday were canceled. The spokesperson added that school district officials will continue to monitor rainfall, flooding, road closures and the accessibility of schools, bus stops and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. A decision about school reopening on Thursday will be announced on Wednesday evening. The school district said it will provide updates on its website and social media platforms. John Carroll High School: The private school in Fort Pierce announced it will be closed on Wednesday because of the potential for heavy rainfall and flooding throughout the region. "The decision follows today's early dismissal and a review of current weather forecasts and local flooding conditions. School officials determined that closing campus is the best course of action to ensure the safety of students, faculty, staff, and families," the school said in a statement to WPBF 25 News on Tuesday evening. "All school-sponsored activities scheduled for Wednesday, including athletics, practices, extracurricular programs, and other events, have been canceled." The school added it anticipates resuming normal operations on Thursday, Nov. 19, pending weather and road conditions. "Administrators will continue to monitor forecasts and remain in communication with local authorities before making any further decisions regarding school operations," the school said. "Updates will be shared through the school’s official communication channels as conditions warrant." Boys Girls Club of Palm Beach County: All Boys Girls Club school sites in Palm Beach County are closed November 18 due to weather concerns, while other club sites remain open. Lucie County: All after-school programs and Clubhouse locations will be closed on Wednesday, Nov. MARTIN COUNTY The Martin County School District said that school and Extended Day will be open to students on Wednesday, but all other after-school activities, athletic practices and events are canceled for Wednesday. Officials in Martin County will monitor weather conditions. Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County: All Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County locations will reopen on Wednesday, Nov. 18, and resume normal operating hours. INDIAN RIVER COUNTY The School District of Indian River County announced on Tuesday afternoon that there will be a regular school schedule for students and employees, including Extended Day and extracurricular activities, on Wednesday, Nov. "District teams found no standing water affecting safe routes to bus stops. Families are encouraged to make the best decision for their circumstances," a spokesperson for the school district said in a statement on Tuesday. "Weather-related absences will follow standard attendance procedures and will not be excused solely due to weather." entry.title: Mary Peltola projected to flip Alaska Senate seat, giving Democrats 56-44 majority
entry.summary: Democrat Mary Peltola is projected to defeat Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, according to the Associated Press, delivering a significant pickup for Democrats. ANALYSIS | The significance of Peltola's election win The significance of Peltola's election win Peltola's victory marks the first time since 2008 that a Democrat has won a U.S. Senate election in Alaska, and gives Democrats a 56-44 majority in the Senate though two lawmakers identify as Independents and simply caucus with the Democrats. 'As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first,' Peltola said in a statement. 'As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaskas working families. Thank you Alaska. Lets get to work. Peltola, who made history in 2022 as the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, focused her Senate campaign on lowering the cost of living and addressing economic challenges facing everyday Alaskans. She previously served in the U.S. House of Representatives, where she became known for emphasizing issues important to Alaska, including the state's fishing industry and economic development. The race drew national attention as Republicans fought to defend their Senate majority. Sullivan, a military veteran seeking a third term, received support from President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance. Sullivan aligned his campaign with the Trump administration's tax and spending priorities and advocated for expanding fossil fuel production. The race in Alaska was complicated by the presence of another Dan Sullivan on the ballot. Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, ran as a long shot Democratic candidate for Senate. Both Dan Sullivans running prompted a legal fight early in the campaign, and President Donald Trump later called the former teacher's campaign 'fake' and 'a hoax by the Democrats.'

entry.summary: As the threat of another round of November rain and flooding takes aim at Florida's east coast, many local governments are once again preparing for what may be ahead. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Flooding and Budget Worries on Treasure Coast He said crews are being deployed across the county as they were two weeks ago. 'There were probably 50 to 100 staff members out there, including crews in public works, out in the field working during the storm. That's unbudgeted overtime,' Gill said. This week, the county offered free sand , donated by Dickerson Infrastructure and Stewart Materials, for residents to bag. 'We're looking at the early estimates in this next upcoming fiscal year to be about a $60 million shortfall and then about $120 million once the exemption goes up.'

entry.article_text: Just weeks after historic flooding destroyed homes and displaced families in Jensen Beach, Martin County residents are bracing for another round of heavy rain — with up to 12 inches forecast over the next three days.For families still struggling to recover, the threat of more flooding comes as county commissioners work to determine what caused the initial disaster and how to help those who lost nearly everything.On Tuesday, flood victims packed a Martin County Commission meeting, pleading for financial assistance and answers.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Along Cheri Drive in Jensen Beach, the signs of destruction remain. Dumpsters line driveways, damaged belongings sit outside and families are still trying to salvage what's left of their homes.Lisa French, her husband, Jeremy, and their two young sons are among those displaced after floodwaters rose as high as 3 feet inside some homes two weeks ago."It's like we're kind of stuck," French told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey. French said her home had about 3 to 6 inches of flooding that sat inside for more than a week, causing mold to grow 3 to 4 feet up the walls. "So they, yeah, they tore the walls down in the house," said French. "They just chipped up the last bit of the tile, and it's empty." Now, with more rain approaching, French fears her family could face another disaster before recovering from the first."Of course, we're afraid because we all flooded in our houses," she said.New figures released by Martin County show at least 36 homes sustained damage, with an estimated $3 million in residential losses. Commissioners estimated another $14 million in damage to beaches, and at least $1 million in damage to roadways that now need repairs. For some residents, the destruction represents a lifetime of memories washed away."We've lost everything," one elderly Jensen Beach resident told commissioners. "We have 60 years of our life — kids, grandkids, everything. It's all gone."As residents demand answers about what went wrong, commissioners approved shifting $200,000 from the county's stormwater budget to investigate whether development and changes to local drainage systems contributed to the flooding.Commissioner Blake Capps called the investigation "a good starting point.""It may be that we need to augment the study beyond the $200,000 that we approve today," said Capps. Meanwhile, county crews are working around the clock to prepare for the next storm, lowering retention pond levels, deploying additional pumps and draining flooded properties."We have people 24 hours a day pumping that material down," Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said.Commissioners also approved financial assistance for eligible flood victims through the state's State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program.The assistance includes grants of up to $25,000 for income-eligible homeowners and loans of up to $75,000 secured by liens on their properties.But there's a catch: The grants are reimbursement-based, meaning homeowners must first pay for eligible repairs before receiving the money.For families who lost everything, that presents another obstacle."We don't have $25,000," French said. "A lot of people don't have $25,000, so it's great, and we're appreciative, but I mean, our house is empty, and $25,000 is not going to do much for us." The other problem: the county currently has just $1 million in SHIP funding available, and commissioners warned the money could run out quickly, even with additional state funding promised."They haven't given us the amount yet, but they have assured us that we will be getting some disaster relief funds," said Human Services Director Michelle Miller Strict income limits could also disqualify some flood victims who cannot afford to rebuild on their own. The income cap for a family of one is $86,040. The cap for a family of two is $98,400. For a family of four, it's $122,880. When reporter Kate Hussey asked Capps what would happen to those families, he acknowledged the county needs to explore other options."There are going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where someone barely missed the limit, and we're going to need to take a look at what we can do for those folks," Capps said.For residents like French, the need is immediate."We just need somebody to step up," she said. "We need funding." With another round of heavy rain approaching, Martin County is distributing sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park to help residents protect their properties, with a limit of 25 per person. The County's Emergency Operations Center is scheduled to be staffed beginning Tuesday at 2 p.m., and the county is coordinating with the National Weather Service and Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM).Fire Rescue is also standing by with multiple high-water rescue trucks.Commissioners also said a Federal Emergency Management Agency representative is expected to visit Nov. 30 to assess the damage — a potential step toward securing federal disaster assistance.But for families still displaced and facing the possibility of more flooding, the uncertainty remains.

entry.summary: Joe Namath's Lucky Shuck coming to Jensen Beach as waterfront village breaks ground    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Football legend Joe Namath is bringing his popular Lucky Shuck restaurant to Jensen Beach as a massive waterfront development takes shape along the St. Rio Marine Village , a 30-acre mixed-use development in Martin County, broke ground Thursday, following more than five years of planning. The project will feature 342 apartments, a 131-slip marina, more than a half-mile of public riverwalk, and several waterfront dining and entertainment destinations. Among them is a new location of The Lucky Shuck Oyster Bar & Taphouse , owned by Namath and his business partner Charlie Modica, along with a second, yet-to-be-named outdoor dining concept. See also: New 24/7 animal cruelty hotline launching across Florida "The Lucky Shuck has always been about good food, good people and being on the water," Namath said. "Rio Marine Village gives us a home right on the river, and I can't wait to see boats pulling up and families sitting down together." The development will also feature the Osprey Club, a waterfront wedding and event venue, along with a public park, boardwalk, beach, and kayak and paddleboard rentals. Martin County commissioners unanimously approved the project's first two phases following years of community discussions. Construction is expected to begin this month, with the first phase scheduled for completion in late 2028.
