entry.title: Flooded roads reported in Vero Lake Estates as Indian River County schools close - cw34.com
entry.summary: Flooded roads reported in Vero Lake Estates as Indian River County schools close    cw34.com
entry.article_text: The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office is reporting more flooded roads in the Vero Lake Estates area as heavy rain moves through the county Thursday. The sheriff’s office urged drivers to stay off flooded roads, warning that water can be deeper than it appears and can stall vehicles. High-water vehicles are in the area, and anyone who becomes stranded should call 911. Ryan Lloyd, Indian River County’s emergency management chief, told CBS12 News the county has received about 5 to 7 inches of rain so far. He said the north end of the county, including Sebastian, Fellsmere and Vero Lake Estates, has gotten more than the rest. Another 3 to 5 inches is expected by midnight Friday, Lloyd said, and the area is still at risk for pockets of 10 to 12 inches or more falling in a short time. Lloyd said the county’s water management systems are full and the ground is essentially saturated, so new rain is running off onto roads. The county’s emergency operations center is at a Level 2 partial activation, and National Guard members are there with high-water vehicles. Lloyd said there had been no requests for high-water rescues as of Thursday afternoon. He urged residents to avoid nonessential travel, turn around at flooded roads and never drive around barricades. Please do not drive to neighborhoods that are flooded because that can actually push floodwaters into homes and create a bigger problem than what some of those residents may already be facing, Lloyd said. The weather prompted the School District of Indian River County to close all public schools and district offices Thursday. The district said saturated ground and expected rain could make travel unsafe for students and staff. Lloyd said schools will also be closed Friday. A Vero Beach football game scheduled for Friday night has been moved to Saturday at 7 p.m., he said. CHIME IN: Send in your weather photos and videos The National Weather Service issued a flood advisory Thursday morning for eastern Indian River and northeastern St. Lucie counties, reporting that 2 to 4 inches of rain had fallen in parts of the area. The advisory warned of minor flooding in low-lying and poorly drained areas. A flood watch remains in effect for Indian River County through Friday evening, with more showers and thunderstorms possible. See also: Flood risk lingers across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches before a drier weekend The county’s road closure map , viewed at 2:47 p.m. Thursday, listed 13 road closures and six lane closures. Among the roads marked closed were 100th Court, 103rd Avenue, 104th Avenue, 83rd Street and 87th Street. The map also showed a long-term closure on 13th Street Southwest, scheduled to remain in place until Jan. Lane-closure listings included 101st Avenue, West 98th Avenue and two locations near Barber Street and U.S. The county also warned that heavy rain and gusty winds could disrupt trash collection. Residents whose streets are flooded were asked not to put carts in the water; the landfill and customer convenience centers could close early if conditions become unsafe. The City of Fellsmere also urged drivers to use extreme caution, identifying two potential trouble spots: New York Avenue near Hickory Street and North Broadway. The city said those roads could close if rain continues. City Hall remains open and operating normally. Lloyd said there are no known water main breaks or significant power outages in the county. The county’s Emergency Information Center, at 772-226-4000, will be open overnight Thursday for questions and flooding reports, and the county will decide Friday whether to keep it running. Residents can report flood damage to homes and businesses through the county’s emergency management website .

entry.article_text: Home Business News and Economic Updates in Sebastian, Florida Indian River County remains under Flood Watch as more rain possible by Andy Hodges Nov 19, 2026 / 5:51 PM A A A A Reset Indian River County remains under a Flood Watch Share on Twitter Share via Email INDIAN RIVER COUNTY — Indian River County remains under a Flood Watch, with a continued risk of excessive rainfall through Saturday, the National Weather Service said Thursday. There is a medium chance — 40% to 60% — of 3 to 6 inches of additional rainfall along the east-central Florida coast through Saturday, according to the National Weather Service office in Melbourne. Because the soil is already saturated from recent heavy rain, many areas are more prone to flooding. Officials said precise locations of the heaviest rainfall remain uncertain. If the most likely rainfall totals materialize, scattered pockets of flooding may develop along the coast, the forecast said. There is a 10% chance of higher-end totals of 8 to 10 inches or more in some locations. Those amounts would bring a risk of impactful flash flooding. The Indian River County Emergency Operations Center continues to monitor weather and road conditions. Officials urged residents to stay home if they do not need to travel. Floodwater and road damage can be difficult to see after dark, the EOC said. Residents should check the county’s road closure map before traveling and never drive through flooded roadways or around barricades. A road may be unsafe even if it is not shown as closed on the map. Multiple roads in the Vero Lake Estates area and elsewhere in the county have already seen closures or standing water this week because of the saturated ground. entry.title: Related Ross shares new details on CityPlace movie theater
entry.summary: Three years after the movie theater at CityPlace was demolished, the big screen is planned to make a comeback in downtown West Palm Beach. WATCH: Related Ross shares new details on CityPlace movie theater Related Ross shares new details on CityPlace movie theater Developer Related Ross is working to bring a new movie theater to downtown as part of its planned 515 Fern building, near the Brightline station. Current plans call for eight auditoriums and about 800 seats. For people who live in and frequent downtown West Palm Beach, the announcement answers something many say has been missing. Hannah Alexander lived downtown for two years before recently moving to Boynton Beach. She said going to the movies while living downtown often meant leaving the city. We actually used to live right in downtown, and we'd have to travel all the way to Palm Beach Gardens to watch movies, and so I think it would be great, Alexander said. We're actually here just to hang out in this area because we really like it, so wed definitely come. Alexander said she used to go to the movies a couple of times a month, but the lack of a nearby theater has made that more difficult. Honestly, recently I haven't gone to the movies because I don't want to have to drive to the movie theaters, she said. Her boyfriend, Alec Estrill, agreed. Yeah, the commute is kind of annoying, you know, especially when you're so close to downtown, you would like something more local to attend, Estrill said. Even after moving to Boynton Beach, the couple said a movie theater could give them another reason to return downtown. Of course, yes, definitely, Alexander said. I think it'd also be cool for the residents because when we lived here we did a lot of things just walking in the area and be able to commute by bike or walking. That would be great for the residents that are still here. Residents asked for the movies to come back Jordan Rathlev, executive vice president of Related Ross, said those reactions mirror what the developer has been hearing over the past year. It's amazing, the reception, Rathlev said. I think we anticipated they were going to embrace this. This is an exciting opportunity for us to bring a great entertainment complex back to the downtown. entry.article_text: Three years after the movie theater at CityPlace was demolished, the big screen is planned to make a comeback in downtown West Palm Beach.WATCH: Related Ross shares new details on CityPlace movie theaterDeveloper Related Ross is working to bring a new movie theater to downtown as part of its planned 515 Fern building, near the Brightline station. Current plans call for eight auditoriums and about 800 seats.For people who live in and frequent downtown West Palm Beach, the announcement answers something many say has been missing.Hannah Alexander lived downtown for two years before recently moving to Boynton Beach. She said going to the movies while living downtown often meant leaving the city.“We actually used to live right in downtown, and we'd have to travel all the way to Palm Beach Gardens to watch movies, and so I think it would be great,” Alexander said. “We're actually here just to hang out in this area because we really like it, so we’d definitely come.”Alexander said she used to go to the movies a couple of times a month, but the lack of a nearby theater has made that more difficult.“Honestly, recently I haven't gone to the movies because I don't want to have to drive to the movie theaters,” she said.Her boyfriend, Alec Estrill, agreed.“Yeah, the commute is kind of annoying, you know, especially when you're so close to downtown, you would like something more local to attend,” Estrill said.Even after moving to Boynton Beach, the couple said a movie theater could give them another reason to return downtown.“Of course, yes, definitely,” Alexander said. “I think it'd also be cool for the residents because when we lived here we did a lot of things just walking in the area and be able to commute by bike or walking. That would be great for the residents that are still here.”Jordan Rathlev, executive vice president of Related Ross, said those reactions mirror what the developer has been hearing over the past year.“It's amazing, the reception,” Rathlev said. “I think we anticipated they were going to embrace this. This is an exciting opportunity for us to bring a great entertainment complex back to the downtown.”Rathlev said the decision followed months of conversations with people living in West Palm Beach.“We've been meeting with a number of groups, including the Downtown Neighborhood Association and the West Palm Beach Resident Coalition, and they've all said, ‘We want a theater, we want more entertainment, we want more things that our residents, our neighbors can go to.’ And we said, ‘Yeah, we agree with you.’”Rathlev, who also lives in West Palm Beach, said the desire for more family-friendly entertainment downtown became personal.“I mean, frankly, I'm a resident. I've lived here for almost 10 years. I have a 9- and 7-year-old. They want to go to the movies,” Rathlev said. “So we said, look, where can we find opportunities for things that families can do? Not just businesses and people from out of town, but what can the local residents really enjoy? And theater continued to be one of those things that we heard continuously from people that they wanted back here.”That's one of the biggest remaining questions.Related Ross has not selected an operator for the theater, but Rathlev said conversations are underway.“We're talking to all the operators. They see a tremendous opportunity with everything that's happening in and around West Palm,” Rathlev said. “So we're excited that we'll be able to announce one of the great premier operators in the country wanting to plant their flag here in West Palm.”When asked whether a decision has been made, Rathlev responded, “No decision made yet.”But some potential moviegoers already have a wish list.Downtown resident Rob Coppinger said he would like to see something beyond a traditional movie theater.“A higher-end theater, like an iPic-type thing, where they're serving food, things like that, would be great,” Coppinger said.And when it comes to the screen?“I guess the bigger screens, the better, right?” he said.Caleb Suppner, who was visiting CityPlace with his daughter Mia, also said he would like to see a dine-in experience.“Yeah, I mean, she loves the dine-in kind of vibe ones, like the new ones, you know, where you can have lunch, dinner, even the adults can grab a drink,” Suppner said.Mia had an even more specific request.“I like the 3D ones when it feels like when the chairs are moving and it looks like when the stuff come out in real life,” she said.WPTV took that request directly to Rathlev, asking if a theater with a big screen and moving seats could happen.“We're definitely open to it. We'll look at all opportunities,” Rathlev said. “We want to make every resident feel like this is their theater and really embrace it, and we're looking forward to it.”Rathlev said the developer wants the new theater to take advantage of how much the movie-going experience has evolved.“The technology is evolving so much, whether it's the seats or the way you watch the screens, whether it's 3D, whether it's interactive,” he said. “We're looking at all options, and we think this is an opportunity to really take advantage of the emerging technologies in the theater business.”Moviegoers will still have to wait.The 515 Fern building had previously been approved, but Related Ross is now going back through the approval process to incorporate the movie theater into the project.“We just started the reapproval process of the building,” Rathlev said. “It was approved two years ago, but we're now integrating this theater concept into it. We hope to have the approvals by the end of next year to be open in 2030.”For Rathlev, there's already one thing he's looking forward to most if those plans become reality.“Take my kids to the movies,” he said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Loxahatchee Groves nursery floods again as conditions were starting to improve
entry.summary: Just as Gardino Nursery was beginning to recover from weeks of flooding, another round of rain has left the Loxahatchee Groves business underwater again. WPTV reporter Christy Waite has been following the flooding's impact on the nursery, touring the property several times and seeing the changing conditions firsthand. Watch report from Christy Waite: Local Nursery Floods Again When Waite first visited Gardino Nursery a few weeks ago, floodwater covered much of the property. Water reached up to her shins in some areas, and fish could even be seen swimming through the floodwater. On Wednesday, Waite returned and found a much different scene. The standing water had largely receded, though thick mud still covered parts of the nursery. Owner Sid Gardino said at the time that conditions were finally improving. But the relief didn't last. After more rain fell, Gardino Nursery flooded again. Waite returned to the property and found plants submerged and standing water once again covering areas that had only recently begun drying out. 'This is the worst that I have seen on this property,' Gardino said. Sid Gardino, owner of Gardino, said it was especially frustrating to see the flooding return after conditions had finally started moving in the right direction. 'We dried out a little bit, it started looking good and then the rain comes again and floods the whole place again,' he said. The flooding is only the latest weather challenge for Gardino Nursery, an appointment-only plant nursery specializing in Hoyas, orchids, rare and unusual tropicals, fragrant plants and pre-bonsai. A year of weather extremes, including freezes, drought and repeated flooding, has kept the nursery closed to visitors since October. 'This is the 5th time that this has happened,' Gardino said. During Waite's previous visit, Gardino told WPTV that the prolonged closure had already cost the business several thousand dollars in revenue. Now, he's also dealing with damage to some of the plants and trees he has spent years growing. 'I'm frustrated because it never ends. I lost a few very important trees here, I lost them because the water saturated the roots,' he added. The repeated flooding has left Gardino with few options other than waiting for conditions to improve. 'I have to be patient and get a few good days so things can dry out and we can go back to full-time work because right now it is impossible,' Gardino said.

entry.article_text: A controversial proposal to build a more than 5.7 million-square-foot data center just half a mile from an elementary school is drawing growing opposition in Martin County, where residents are raising concerns about everything from environmental impacts to whether they'll have a say in the project's approval.WATCH: 'We need answers': Martin Co. officials address outrage over proposed data centerOn Friday morning, a small but vocal group of residents gathered outside the Martin County Administrative Center, demanding answers about the massive development proposed for a parcel of land off Kanner Highway, west of Interstate 95.They had planned to attend a meeting with the county's Growth Management Department. But less than 17 hours before it was scheduled to begin, the county canceled it, citing overwhelming public interest.Residents showed up anyway."We need answers, and we need them quick," said Chris McIntyre, whose son graduated from nearby Crystal Lake Elementary School. "This story cannot die, or else this is the death of Crystal Lake School."McIntyre, who goes by Coach Mack, became emotional discussing what the proposed development could mean for the school and surrounding neighborhoods."Now that's the death of an A-rated elementary school that I love," he said, his voice breaking.He's far from alone.Residents have raised concerns about potential noise pollution, water consumption, increased electricity demand, higher utility bills, wildlife displacement, declining property values and possible health impacts on children attending Crystal Lake Elementary.Michael Panella, another resident opposing the project, became emotional while explaining why the fight is so personal."It's life. These little ones are innocent," Panella said, referring also to students of Crystal Lake. Dan Wilson, president of the Locks Landing homeowners association, represents a community less than two miles from the proposed site.“They’re probably dropping now because, oh, the data center going there. We don’t want to move there,” Wilson said of property values."We have residences right here, tons of residents. We're all going to have to deal with this."Residents acknowledge they don't yet know for sure what the long-term consequences of the project might be. They don't know whether electricity bills will increase, how much noise the facility could generate or what wildlife habitat might be lost.But they do know that once something of this magnitude is built, there's no easy way to undo it.The controversy intensified Thursday evening when Martin County announced the cancellation of an informal Growth Management meeting scheduled for 9:30 a.m. 19, the Martin County Board of County Commissioners posted the following message online:For residents who had planned to attend, the cancellation only added to their frustration."The thing that frustrates me the most about this is the fact that they were willing to do this meeting in private," said resident Alisha Gibbs.Gibbs described herself as "disgusted" and "absolutely appalled" by the situation.But Martin County Deputy Growth Management Director Pete Walden told WPTV Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey that the meeting was never intended to be a formal public hearing or a decision-making session.Instead, Walden said, it was an informal meeting requested by members of the public who wanted to ask county staff questions about the development — something his department routinely accommodates for other projects.He said information about the meeting circulated online, creating the impression that county officials were privately considering a decision on the data center.When interest grew beyond what the county could accommodate, officials decided to cancel."We could not accommodate that. We didn't have any rooms or anything available for that size," Walden explained. "So we had to cancel, and we'll do some workshops in the future. I believe the applicant is also going to reach out for some public presentations on the subject." When asked why residents weren't being given more opportunities to weigh in, Walden maintained the county has been transparent."We are transparent through the process, and everything can be made available to anyone that is interested," he said.Walden said additional public meetings and workshops will be scheduled to allow residents to ask questions and learn more about the project.But the canceled meeting is only one of several controversies surrounding the development.Another major point of contention is the timing of the developer's application.On Oct. 27, Martin County commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on data centers, temporarily restricting new applications while the county reviews its development regulations.But records show the application for this project was submitted the day before the moratorium was proposed on October 13. That timing means the project is not subject to the temporary restriction, according to county officials.Walden acknowledged the timing but said the county cannot control when developers submit applications."They obviously saw like everybody else that a moratorium was coming, and they got their application in ahead of time," Walden said. "We don't direct applicants ... and we certainly can't pick and choose when these things happen."WPTV reached out to the project applicant and the law firm representing it, requesting comment on the timing of the application and residents' environmental, energy and health concerns.Neither responded by publication time.Perhaps the most significant concern for opponents is whether residents will have any formal say in the project's approval.Under a county ordinance adopted in 2010, during the Great Recession, Martin County established an administrative approval process for certain targeted industries to encourage economic development.Data centers fall within the county's targeted industry classifications. According to Walden, the proposed development is also covered by an existing planned unit development, or PUD, agreement that allows qualifying targeted industries on platted industrial lots to receive administrative approval.That means the project could potentially move forward without a public hearing or recorded vote by county commissioners.For residents demanding a voice in the decision, that distinction is critical.Hussey asked Walden whether there was anything the county could do to give residents more of a say in whether the development is approved."With the moratorium, we'll be looking at our code to make revisions so everything is appropriately reviewed as it comes in," Walden said."To give the public more of a say in future projects?" Hussey asked. "Correct," Walden responded. Residents are also demanding answers about how a development of this size could affect surrounding neighborhoods, wildlife and students at Crystal Lake Elementary School.The proposal initially called for just under 1 million square feet of development. An updated application brings the total to approximately 1.6 million square feet, including an existing warehouse.Among the concerns raised by residents are the potential effects of noise from cooling equipment, increased water and electricity consumption, wildlife habitat loss and possible impacts on nearby property values.Those concerns remain questions, not established consequences of the proposed development.Walden said the county will review the project's potential impacts before making any approval decision.He also emphasized that despite speculation circulating in the community, the data center has not been approved."There is a misconception that this project was already approved — that's very far from the truth," Walden said."This is our first data center to be reviewed. We're going to take our time ... and make sure everything is properly vetted."The county says a staff report examining the project is expected to be released in December.Following that report, officials plan to schedule a public forum, likely including a presentation from the applicant, where residents can ask questions and learn more about the development.No date for that meeting has been announced.For opponents, the controversy goes beyond whether a data center belongs on acres of industrial land.It's about who gets to decide what their community becomes — and whether the people who will live with the consequences have a meaningful opportunity to influence that decision.The residents who gathered outside the county building Friday made clear that canceling a meeting would not end their opposition."If they want to actually please the public, they would deny this proposal," Gibbs said.

entry.article_text: Indian River and Palm Beach counties saw the highest totals The highest report among the five counties came from The Acreage in Palm Beach County, where 12.92 inches were reported since Tuesday morning. Other notable Palm Beach County reports included 7.91 inches in Royal Palm Beach, 7.30 inches in Haverhill and 7.20 inches in Sandalfoot Cove. Indian River County also saw several high totals. Sebastian Inlet reported 10.29 inches, while Vero Lake Estates had reports of 8.49 and 7.51 inches. Other reports included 7.23 inches in Fellsmere and 6.90 inches in Roseland. Totals varied across the Treasure Coast In St. Lucie County, the highest report was 6.24 inches at the county fairgrounds. Indrio reported 4.92 inches, while Tradition and Paradise Park received 4.70 and 4.68 inches, respectively. Martin County’s highest report was 5.11 inches at Philo Farms. Other reports included 3.79 inches in Indiantown, 3.72 inches in Caloosa and 3.28 inches in Palm City. Okeechobee County had lower totals Rainfall reports in Okeechobee County were lower overall. The highest listed total was 2.81 inches in Kissimmee Prairie, followed by 2.32 inches in Country Hills. Okeechobee reported 1.58 inches. Heavy rain was concentrated in pockets These reports show how unevenly the rain fell. Most locations across the five counties saw totals of only a few inches, while certain communities caught repeated or heavier downpours that pushed their totals much higher. The highest localized amounts were concentrated in Indian River and Palm Beach counties.

entry.title: Indian River County schools closed Thursday as heavy rain raises flooding concerns
entry.summary: All School District of Indian River County public schools and district offices will be closed Thursday, Nov. 19, because of expected heavy rain and potential flooding, district officials announced Wednesday. Officials cited already saturated ground and concerns about whether students and employees could safely travel to and from schools. The storm system is expected to affect Indian River, Brevard and Volusia counties between 3 a.m. and 3 p.m. Thursday, according to the district. Saturated ground raises travel concerns Indian River County remains under a flood watch as another round of rain moves through the Treasure Coast. The National Weather Service forecast calls for a 95% chance of precipitation Thursday, with about 1.74 inches of rain possible. The district said saturated conditions were a key factor in its decision to cancel classes and close offices. 'With ground conditions already saturated, we cannot be confident that students and staff will be able to travel safely to and from school,' the district said. 'Weather conditions may also affect staff members' ability to report to work.' The closure comes about two weeks after prolonged rainfall caused significant flooding in Indian River County. Flood watch remains in effect A flood watch for Indian River County remains in effect through Friday evening. The National Weather Service is also reporting a high surf advisory and rip current statement for the area. Indian River County officials have warned residents that roads not officially listed as closed could still have standing water or other hazards. Drivers should obey barricades and never attempt to drive through floodwater. The school district said student, family and employee safety remains its highest priority. Officials will continue monitoring conditions and said any additional information will be released through official district communication channels. entry.summary: In Tuesdays Florida Panthers matchup against the Edmonton Oilers, Palm Beach County veteran and retired Lieutenant Colonel Jeffrey Garten was honored. Before the national anthem, Garten was honored as the Panthers Hero Among Us. WPTV Panthers Anchor and Panthers 360 host Mike Trim connected with Garten at the WPTV studios in West Palm Beach. WATCH: Palm Beach County veteran honored as Florida Panthers Hero Among Us Palm Beach County veteran honored as Florida Panthers Hero Among Us My mom and my brother had come in and surprised me. When you're looking at 20,000 people standing up looking at you, that means a lot, that America, even after all these years, they still remember the veterans, and that's what's really important, Garten told Trim, reflecting on the moment. Garten continues to serve in the South Florida veterans community with Wreaths Across America, the Patriot Guard and many more organizations. Trim asked Garten, Why is that so important to you to continue on serving the local veterans community? Garten replied, I couldnt give it up, even after retirement. Its my way of continuing to serve the veterans because theres a need. Garten was in the Army Special Forces, known to many as a Green Beret. An accomplishment that means the most to me was earning the green beret. Its a specialized unit, they can go behind enemy lines if need be, they can train foreign troops. The most important mission we ever did is a humanitarian mission to El Salvador in 1984, we built a two room schoolhouse in a little village. The appreciation from the kids and the parents, I mean it was really just an amazing mission down there, Garten told Trim. Garten, who admittedly hasnt watch a lot of hockey said hes now proud to call himself a Panthers fan. The game, unfortunately the Panthers lost but, good showing. Were already planning on our next game, Garten told Trim. Since 2013 the Florida Panthers have honored more than 500 veterans in the Heroes Among Us program.

entry.title: Flooding leads to partial road collapse in Port St. Lucie - WPBF
entry.summary: Flooding leads to partial road collapse in Port St. Lucie    WPBF
entry.article_text: A road and nearby property in Port St. Lucie have partially collapsed following historic flooding, leaving residents concerned about the growing damage and the safety of surrounding homes. “All this was flooded,” said Yoshi Duran, a neighbor who showed the damaged area near her home. From aerial views, the extent of the collapse is clear, with sections of the road and property having fallen into the hole. “It’s not anything to laugh about. It is a dangerous situation because they’re not knowing when it can cave in,” Duran said. The collapse occurred during the flooding, as water poured in and the land buckled until it finally gave way. Duran said the hole has been expanding daily since then. Because what’s going to happen, you know? What’s going to happen to the houses that are around this area?” Duran said. City officials are aware of the issue and are working to address it. “We want to repair these as quickly as we possibly can. Unfortunately, it takes some time,” said Scott Samples, public information officer for Port St. Samples explained the damage was caused by excess water both on the road and in a culvert below it. He said the city is currently determining the best way to fix the problem. “You want to make sure you’re doing it as well and as correctly as you possibly can. So that may require some studies to take place before you actually start the work,” Samples said. For Duran, that work can’t come soon enough. We understand everybody is short-staffed. But we need answers,” Duran said. City officials said there is no timeline for the repairs since they're still trying to figure out the best way to fix the problem. entry.article_text: Nearly three weeks after historic flooding forced families from their homes and caused millions of dollars in damage across Martin County, residents are still waiting for a federal disaster declaration that could unlock critical financial assistance.Now, after a WPTV report on the delays and growing frustration among flood victims, Florida's top emergency management official is responding to questions about the state's recovery efforts—and what help families can expect if FEMA funding never arrives.Watch more from Kate Hussey:In an exclusive interview with WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey, Jared Perdue, director of the Florida Division of Emergency Management, confirmed the state submitted an expedited federal disaster declaration request Nov. 9, one week after the initial flooding.But nearly two weeks after that request, a decision remains pending."We've been very engaged with FEMA, and we did actually submit an expedited disaster declaration request to FEMA on November the ninth," Perdue said. "FEMA has been very closely coordinating with us in reviewing that, and I'm sure they're going to make quick work of it."The uncertainty comes as Martin County estimates approximately $18 million in residential and public infrastructure damage, with families still struggling to afford repairs and another round of historic rainfall complicating recovery efforts.Along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach, the devastation is still visible.Dumpsters line driveways, waterlogged belongings have been discarded and homes have been stripped down to their frames.For Linda Weisbecker, whose home was among those severely damaged, the destruction has been overwhelming."It's like an apocalypse here," Weisbecker told WPTV in an earlier interview.For nine days, Weisbecker and her neighbors navigated waist-deep floodwaters before they could begin salvaging what remained of their homes."Once we got through that and the water came out, we just all started pitching in, going in to see what we can salvage from each home," she said.But much of what Weisbecker lost cannot be replaced."We are fully gutted. Our house is empty," she said. "We lost everything, from pictures of our children and their lives, our friends, our grandkids, now we have great-grandkids. Everything [my husband] had since he was 13 on is gone."Weisbecker has been approved for a $25,000 grant through Florida's State Housing Initiatives Partnership, or SHIP, program. But for families facing tens of thousands of dollars in repairs, that assistance may cover only a fraction of the cost.And not everyone will qualify."You do think about that process and you sit there and you say to yourself, how am I gonna do this?" Weisbecker said.That question is at the center of WPTV's ongoing investigation.Martin County estimates the flooding caused:$14 million in beach damage.Nearly $1 million in damaged roads requiring repaving.$3 million in residential losses.Additional expenses associated with county staff overtime and emergency response.A federal major disaster declaration could make certain public infrastructure repairs eligible for FEMA reimbursement and potentially open the door to individual assistance for qualifying residents.But approval is not guaranteed.When WPTV initially contacted FEMA, the agency confirmed it had received the disaster declaration request and that it remained under review. FEMA referred additional questions about the response and recovery timeline to the Florida Division of Emergency Management.Hussey subsequently pressed Perdue on what would happen if the federal government denied the request."If FEMA ultimately denies federal assistance, does Florida have a Plan B, or are these families simply on their own?" Hussey asked.Perdue did not identify a specific alternative state funding program, instead emphasizing Florida's experience responding to natural disasters and its ongoing coordination with federal and local officials."This is something that we're very used to doing. I mean, in Florida, we deal with natural disasters all the time," Perdue said. "We have a great relationship with FEMA, and usually those things go very well."He added that the state remains focused on immediate response efforts, including search and rescue operations and meeting residents' emergency needs.In the meantime, Martin County is working to distribute approximately $1 million in available SHIP funding to qualifying residents.Eligible homeowners may receive grants of up to $25,000, with additional assistance potentially available through loans of up to $75,000. However, those loans come with repayment requirements and liens.Income eligibility restrictions could also leave some families without assistance, even if they cannot afford to rebuild on their own."There's going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where somebody barely missed the limit," Commissioner Blake Capps said during a recent Martin County Commission meeting.Capps proposed establishing a separate county-funded emergency assistance program for residents who fall through the cracks.But when WPTV asked where that money would come from, Capps acknowledged a funding source had not yet been identified."Well, that would be ... we'd have to talk to staff," he said.County Human Services Director Michelle Miller previously told commissioners the state had promised additional disaster relief funding, although neither the amount nor the timeline had been confirmed."They haven't confirmed the amount yet but has assured us we will be getting some disaster relief funds," Miller told Hussey.Hussey raised those concerns directly with Perdue, asking whether the state had other programs available for families who earn too much to qualify for existing assistance but not enough to pay for repairs.Perdue pointed to the state's partnerships with nonprofit organizations and its deployment of emergency personnel to assist with cleanup."We've actually activated the National Guard, and are also partnering with nonprofits to do what they call the muck and gut of homes that have been flooded," Perdue said.That work includes removing damaged drywall and other waterlogged materials to help prevent mold growth."We're providing the assistance that we can and partnering with those nonprofit organizations as well," he said.However, Perdue did not identify a specific funding program to cover rebuilding costs for homeowners who do not qualify for existing assistance.The financial uncertainty extends beyond individual homeowners.Martin County faces approximately $15 million in combined beach and road damage, with additional emergency response expenses still being assessed.County spokesperson Martha Ann Kniess previously told WPTV that without federal reimbursement, Martin County could be left responsible for covering those costs, potentially forcing officials to redirect money from elsewhere in the budget or identify other funding sources.Hussey asked Perdue whether the state would help cover those expenses if FEMA denied federal assistance — or whether the financial burden could ultimately fall on local taxpayers.Perdue did not commit to providing state funding for those repairs."We are and have been doing damage assessments ever since we submitted the first disaster declaration request," he said."As those damage assessments come in, we'll continue to coordinate with FEMA and make sure all that information is submitted."The state's response follows an emotional Martin County Commission meeting Tuesday, where residents pleaded with elected officials to do more to secure recovery funding."Please. Fight for us!" one resident urged commissioners.Others questioned why families were being asked to wait even longer for answers."And the answer from this dais is wait 13 more days?!?" another resident asked.Commissioner Eileen Vargas said she had reached out to FEMA through personal contacts in an effort to expedite the process."I did, through contacts, reach out to FEMA to try and get this going," Vargas said.Vargas also told residents she expected a new FEMA director to take office Nov. 30 and hoped that development could help move the disaster declaration forward.But even if a declaration is approved, not all losses or recovery expenses would necessarily qualify for federal assistance.As Martin County continues to recover from the Nov. 2 flooding, Perdue said the state is also responding to another significant rainfall event affecting communities across Florida.According to Perdue, Gov. Ron DeSantis expanded the state's emergency executive order to include 21 counties.The state has mobilized resources from the National Guard, State Guard, Florida Highway Patrol and Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, among other agencies."We're actively still responding to the previous flooding event on November 2, and now we're actively dealing with a current, another historic rain event that's brought record amount of flooding in many counties throughout the state," Perdue said.The overlapping disasters have added urgency to recovery efforts, particularly for residents whose homes remain exposed after being gutted.Perdue said state resources remain available for immediate needs, including food, water, shelter and emergency medical assistance."We're committed. We're fully mobilized," he said. We're going to be with you till the very end, and we're going to make sure we help everybody get back on their feet."Despite those assurances, several critical questions remain unresolved.FEMA has not announced a decision on Florida's expedited disaster declaration request. The state has not identified a specific alternative rebuilding assistance program for homeowners who do not qualify for existing aid, nor has it committed to covering Martin County's public infrastructure losses if federal funding is denied.For residents like Weisbecker, the uncertainty is more than a question of government funding.It's a question of whether they can afford to return to the homes they've spent years building their lives in."This is very urgent for people to get back into their daily lives," Weisbecker said. entry.article_text: A controversial proposal to build a more than 1.6 million-square-foot data center just half a mile from an elementary school is drawing growing opposition in Martin County, where residents are raising concerns about everything from environmental impacts to whether they'll have a say in the project's approval.WATCH: 'We need answers': Martin Co. officials address outrage over proposed data centerOn Friday morning, a small but vocal group of residents gathered outside the Martin County Administrative Center, demanding answers about the massive development proposed for a parcel of land off Kanner Highway, west of Interstate 95.They had planned to attend a meeting with the county's Growth Management Department. But less than 17 hours before it was scheduled to begin, the county canceled it, citing overwhelming public interest.Residents showed up anyway."We need answers, and we need them quick," said Chris McIntyre, whose son graduated from nearby Crystal Lake Elementary School. "This story cannot die, or else this is the death of Crystal Lake School."McIntyre, who goes by Coach Mack, became emotional discussing what the proposed development could mean for the school and surrounding neighborhoods."Now that's the death of an A-rated elementary school that I love," he said, his voice breaking.He's far from alone.Residents have raised concerns about potential noise pollution, water consumption, increased electricity demand, higher utility bills, wildlife displacement, declining property values and possible health impacts on children attending Crystal Lake Elementary.Michael Panella, another resident opposing the project, became emotional while explaining why the fight is so personal."It's life. These little ones are innocent," Panella said, referring also to students of Crystal Lake. Dan Wilson, president of the Locks Landing homeowners association, represents a community less than two miles from the proposed site.“They’re probably dropping now because, oh, the data center going there. We don’t want to move there,” Wilson said of property values."We have residences right here, tons of residents. We're all going to have to deal with this."Residents acknowledge they don't yet know for sure what the long-term consequences of the project might be. They don't know whether electricity bills will increase, how much noise the facility could generate or what wildlife habitat might be lost.But they do know that once something of this magnitude is built, there's no easy way to undo it.The controversy intensified Thursday evening when Martin County announced the cancellation of an informal Growth Management meeting scheduled for 9:30 a.m. 19, the Martin County Board of County Commissioners posted the following message online:For residents who had planned to attend, the cancellation only added to their frustration."The thing that frustrates me the most about this is the fact that they were willing to do this meeting in private," said resident Alisha Gibbs.Gibbs described herself as "disgusted" and "absolutely appalled" by the situation.But Martin County Deputy Growth Management Director Pete Walden told WPTV Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey that the meeting was never intended to be a formal public hearing or a decision-making session.Instead, Walden said, it was an informal meeting requested by members of the public who wanted to ask county staff questions about the development — something his department routinely accommodates for other projects.He said information about the meeting circulated online, creating the impression that county officials were privately considering a decision on the data center.When interest grew beyond what the county could accommodate, officials decided to cancel."We could not accommodate that. We didn't have any rooms or anything available for that size," Walden explained. "So we had to cancel, and we'll do some workshops in the future. I believe the applicant is also going to reach out for some public presentations on the subject." When asked why residents weren't being given more opportunities to weigh in, Walden maintained the county has been transparent."We are transparent through the process, and everything can be made available to anyone that is interested," he said.Walden said additional public meetings and workshops will be scheduled to allow residents to ask questions and learn more about the project.But the canceled meeting is only one of several controversies surrounding the development.Another major point of contention is the timing of the developer's application.On Oct. 27, Martin County commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on data centers, temporarily restricting new applications while the county reviews its development regulations.But records show the application for this project was submitted the day before the moratorium was proposed on October 13. That timing means the project is not subject to the temporary restriction, according to county officials.Walden acknowledged the timing but said the county cannot control when developers submit applications."They obviously saw like everybody else that a moratorium was coming, and they got their application in ahead of time," Walden said. "We don't direct applicants ... and we certainly can't pick and choose when these things happen."WPTV reached out to the project applicant and the law firm representing it, requesting comment on the timing of the application and residents' environmental, energy and health concerns.Neither responded by publication time.Perhaps the most significant concern for opponents is whether residents will have any formal say in the project's approval.Under a county ordinance adopted in 2010, during the Great Recession, Martin County established an administrative approval process for certain targeted industries to encourage economic development.Data centers fall within the county's targeted industry classifications. According to Walden, the proposed development is also covered by an existing planned unit development, or PUD, agreement that allows qualifying targeted industries on platted industrial lots to receive administrative approval.That means the project could potentially move forward without a public hearing or recorded vote by county commissioners.For residents demanding a voice in the decision, that distinction is critical.Hussey asked Walden whether there was anything the county could do to give residents more of a say in whether the development is approved."With the moratorium, we'll be looking at our code to make revisions so everything is appropriately reviewed as it comes in," Walden said."To give the public more of a say in future projects?" Hussey asked. "Correct," Walden responded. Residents are also demanding answers about how a development of this size could affect surrounding neighborhoods, wildlife and students at Crystal Lake Elementary School.The proposal initially called for just under 1 million square feet of development. An updated application brings the total to approximately 1.6 million square feet, including an existing warehouse.Among the concerns raised by residents are the potential effects of noise from cooling equipment, increased water and electricity consumption, wildlife habitat loss and possible impacts on nearby property values.Those concerns remain questions, not established consequences of the proposed development.Walden said the county will review the project's potential impacts before making any approval decision.He also emphasized that despite speculation circulating in the community, the data center has not been approved."There is a misconception that this project was already approved — that's very far from the truth," Walden said."This is our first data center to be reviewed. We're going to take our time ... and make sure everything is properly vetted."The county says a staff report examining the project is expected to be released in December.Following that report, officials plan to schedule a public forum, likely including a presentation from the applicant, where residents can ask questions and learn more about the development.No date for that meeting has been announced.For opponents, the controversy goes beyond whether a data center belongs on acres of industrial land.It's about who gets to decide what their community becomes — and whether the people who will live with the consequences have a meaningful opportunity to influence that decision.The residents who gathered outside the county building Friday made clear that canceling a meeting would not end their opposition."If they want to actually please the public, they would deny this proposal," Gibbs said.

entry.article_text: Cars were still getting through when CBS12 News reached one of the spots Port St. Lucie police had flagged for high water Thursday. Water pooled along Port St. Lucie Boulevard, and nearby driveways were dry. Earlier, water had made a lane impassable in two places on Village Parkway, and crews were pumping it off Tradition Parkway. Two weeks ago, floodwater stranded drivers across the city. Near Oak Hammock K 8, video showed a mother and daughter wading through chest-deep water. Lucie recorded 16.7 inches of rain over 60 hours during that storm. Where police reported flooding Port St. Lucie Boulevard: Crews were putting up barricades at McCorkle Avenue, at Alcantara Boulevard and along the stretch from Southwest Liberty Drive to Firestone. Northbound Village Parkway: The right lane was impassable south of the fire station and south of Discovery Way. Water was spreading into a second lane near Discovery Way. Tradition Parkway east of Hazel Drive: Crews were pumping water off the road after the outside lanes flooded in both directions. Police said more closures could be needed as rain continued. The Florida Department of Transportation also had overnight closures scheduled this week on Port St. Lucie Boulevard between Southwest Fisherman and Southwest Liberty avenues for drainage work tied to a widening project. Where to fill sandbags St. Lucie County says sand is still available while supplies last at the St. Lucie County Fairgrounds’ west parking lot, 15601 W. Midway Road in Fort Pierce. The Lawnwood Stadium site has run out. The fairgrounds site is self-service. Bring a shovel and plan to fill your own bags. The county has a limited supply of bags and encourages residents to bring their own. Residents in unincorporated St. Lucie County can report flooding that threatens homes, businesses or personal safety to flooding@stlucieco.gov. What was different this time Port St. Lucie crews started lowering water levels in stormwater basins Sunday to make room for more rain. They also cleared drains and checked canals and culverts. A lot of it just depends on how much rain you get at a given time, city spokesperson Scott Samples said. 1 3 storm, Samples said, rain came down so quickly that the drainage system needed longer to move it. This week, he said, less rain had fallen all at once. We’ve been fortunate that so far we haven’t had that kind of rain, he said. Samples said homeowners associations and community development districts manage drainage in parts of Tradition. The city helped pump water out of a neighborhood there after the first storm, he said. It’s really a very collective stormwater system. A flood watch remains in effect for St. Lucie County through 7 p.m. The National Weather Service issued a separate advisory Thursday morning after radar and gauges indicated 2 to 4 inches had fallen across parts of northeastern St. Lucie County and eastern Indian River County. forecast.weather.gov See also: Who’s responsible for improving drainage after St. Lucie County’s historic flooding? Lucie Public Schools reopened on a regular schedule Thursday after closing Wednesday over flooding concerns. Aftercare, sports and other activities were scheduled to resume. The district said weather-related absences would be excused with a note from a parent or guardian. In neighboring Indian River County, public schools and district offices were closed Thursday. More rain on already-soaked ground A flood watch covers St. Lucie County through 7 p.m. The National Weather Service issued a separate advisory Thursday morning for northeastern St. Lucie County and eastern Indian River County after radar and gauges indicated 2 to 4 inches had already fallen across that area. 1 3 storm, one location in Port St. Lucie recorded 16.7 inches of rain over 60 hours. Lucie County had received at least 472 preliminary reports of property damage from that storm. The county is accepting damage reports from the earlier storm through Nov.

entry.article_text: Last week's FAA ground stop uprooted plans and wreaked havoc for so many people across the U.S. But for one Hobe Sound woman, it led to what could be her big break.WATCH: FAA ground stop leads to surprise duet for Hobe Sound singer in JupiterWhen the FAA grounded flights across the U.S., it cast a dark cloud over the Maltz Jupiter Theatre, where Broadway and "Glee" star Matthew Morrison was scheduled to perform this weekend. Much of his ensemble couldn't make it here.But with storms come rainbows. And one local singer can attest.Emily Rynasko, who said she watched "Glee" when she was younger, said she would have never expected a text from the actor who played William Schuester, asking her to sing a duet with him on stage."I found out about 9:30 in the morning, and the show was at 7:30 that night," Emily Rynasko said.It was a moment Rynasko had been working toward her whole life."Learning sight-reading music and just using my ear. It's being a trained musician that's part of your job," Rynasko said.Rynasko, who grew up in Hobe Sound, started that training as a kid at the Maltz Jupiter Theatre."They raised me. The Maltz Jupiter Theater is my, my home, and that is truly my family. They have made me the woman I am," Rynasko said.So when Rynasko stepped into the spotlight to sing Somewhere Over the Rainbow, she treated it like a professional and felt right at home next to Morrison."I was a lot calmer than I thought I would be because I treated it like any other show that I had done," Rynasko said.After all, there's no place like home."To also honor everyone that has been part of your journey, whether it's been a teacher, your community, your friends and family," Rynasko said. "That's what brings me joy and carries me through."This story was reported on-air by journalist Jamie Ostroff and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Recent rainfall worsens Hurricane Milton damage at Port St. Lucie home - WPTV
entry.summary: Recent rainfall worsens Hurricane Milton damage at Port St. Lucie home    WPTV
entry.article_text: Lucie homeowner says recent heavy rain is worsening damage left behind by Hurricane Milton more than two years ago, as she continues waiting for repairs through the state's Rebuild Florida Housing Repair and Replacement Program. A repair assessment reviewed by WPTV documents unrepaired storm damage and work needed inside her home.WATCH: Recent rainfall worsens Hurricane Milton damage at Port St. Lucie homeCaryn McGregor contacted WPTV asking for help as water continued entering her house through the ceiling, windows and vents. During WPTV's visit, rainwater could be seen dripping inside the home."I'm scared my ceiling's gonna come down," McGregor said.Buckets and towels have become a temporary solution while she waits for more permanent repairs."Water is coming in our house, and we're experiencing so much now," McGregor said. "I just can't believe the events that are happening."Assessment documents unrepaired Hurricane Milton damageMcGregor said her roof was damaged when Hurricane Milton struck Florida in October 2024. She said she initially contacted her insurance company but couldn't afford the deductible and later sought help through Rebuild Florida.A repair assessment reviewed by WPTV lists Oct. 9, 2024, as the date of loss and says McGregor's home was inspected Jan. 6, 2026.The assessment documents unrepaired storm damage and says McGregor reported plumbing problems since the hurricane. The proposed scope of work includes repairs involving ceilings, walls, plumbing, siding, appliances, drywall and doors.The document helps establish the damage identified during the Rebuild Florida assessment, but it does not establish whether the proposed repairs were ultimately approved or funded.Recent rain adds to homeowner's concernsMcGregor told WPTV the continued water intrusion has left her worried that parts of the ceiling could collapse."I can't even have my son living here because the ceiling, I'm scared of it falling on him and hurting him," McGregor said. She also expressed concerns about water and mold.McGregor said water has damaged appliances in the home, including her washer, dryer and dishwasher."The water is ruining everything," she said.Homeowner says she's waiting on permits and repairsMcGregor said Rebuild Florida inspected the home in January but the repairs have not been completed."They were supposed to help," she said. "However they were going to rebuild or replace it, they were supposed to do that."McGregor said she has been told the project is waiting on permits before work can move forward. The documents reviewed by WPTV do not establish which permits remain outstanding, when they were requested or when construction is expected to begin.For McGregor, recent rainfall has added urgency to a problem she says has already kept her family from returning to normal."I want them to help us fix our house," she said. "They said they were going to."WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache reached out to Rebuild Florida seeking answers about the delay, the permitting process and when work could begin. Rebuild Florida acknowledged receiving WPTV's request, but a response addressing those questions had not been received by the time of reporting.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

entry.title: St. Lucie County schools closed as families prepare for more heavy rain - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County schools closed as families prepare for more heavy rain    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County schools and district offices are closed Wednesday as families prepare for more heavy rain, two weeks after flooding left roads underwater and damaged homes. All aftercare programs, after-school activities and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday are also canceled. See also: Flood risk continues for the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches through Friday evening The school district said forecasts show the potential for significant rainfall and localized flooding. With the ground already saturated, the district said closing schools was the cautious choice for students, families and employees. Officials are monitoring rainfall, flooding, road closures and access to schools, bus stops and transportation routes. The district plans to announce Wednesday evening whether schools will reopen Thursday. Across the Treasure Coast, some residents are filling sandbags to protect their homes. Others are stocking up on groceries and preparing to stay home if roads flood again. Lucie says floodwater rose to his knees two weeks ago, damaging his garage and guitars. He filled sandbags at the St. Lucie County Fairgrounds and is adding more around his home. We had a lot of water go into the garage and we just got over the fact that it stopped smelling like mold in there, Vargas said. And then here we go again with this inclement weather. Lucie County set up self-service sand distribution sites at the county fairgrounds in Fort Pierce and the Lawnwood Stadium parking lot. Residents need to bring their own bags and shovels and fill the bags themselves. Sand is available while supplies last. Tuesday, the two truckloads at Lawnwood Stadium were nearly gone. Glen Ferlance was out for a morning walk Wednesday morning when he spoke with CBS12. He said the flooding two weeks ago kept him from reaching his children. I could not get to cross over to go and see my kids, Ferlance said. I had to park in the um the plaza here and just look on. Ferlance said he lives in Port St. Lucie and he’s preparing for more rain, but hopes the flooding won’t be as severe this time. I just hope that is not too bad like last time. Yes, I’m prepared, he said. I’m going to get something to eat, and I’m running back home in my bed to watch TV and relax until all this is over. He also said he’s glad St. Lucie County schools are closed. I just thank God they’re not school today, so the kids then should be more safe at home, he said. Some residents are also stocking up on food and supplies. Shoppers told CBS12 they’re preparing to stay home if roads flood again. The district said updates about school operations will be shared on its website and social media channels. Martin County canceled after-school activities. entry.title: Florida emergency management director responds to FEMA delays as Jensen Beach flood victims wait for help - WFLX
entry.summary: Florida emergency management director responds to FEMA delays as Jensen Beach flood victims wait for help    WFLX
entry.article_text: Nearly three weeks after historic flooding forced families from their homes and caused millions of dollars in damage across Martin County, residents are still waiting for a federal disaster declaration that could unlock critical financial assistance. Now, after a WPTV report on the delays and growing frustration among flood victims, Florida's top emergency management official is responding to questions about the state's recovery efforts—and what help families can expect if FEMA funding never arrives. Watch more from Kate Hussey: In an exclusive interview with WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey, Jared Perdue, director of the Florida Division of Emergency Management, confirmed the state submitted an expedited federal disaster declaration request Nov. 9, one week after the initial flooding. But nearly two weeks after that request, a decision remains pending. "We've been very engaged with FEMA, and we did actually submit an expedited disaster declaration request to FEMA on November the ninth," Perdue said. "FEMA has been very closely coordinating with us in reviewing that, and I'm sure they're going to make quick work of it." The uncertainty comes as Martin County estimates approximately $18 million in residential and public infrastructure damage, with families still struggling to afford repairs and another round of historic rainfall complicating recovery efforts. Along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach, the devastation is still visible. Dumpsters line driveways, waterlogged belongings have been discarded and homes have been stripped down to their frames. For Linda Weisbecker, whose home was among those severely damaged, the destruction has been overwhelming. "It's like an apocalypse here," Weisbecker told WPTV in an earlier interview. For nine days, Weisbecker and her neighbors navigated waist-deep floodwaters before they could begin salvaging what remained of their homes. "Once we got through that and the water came out, we just all started pitching in, going in to see what we can salvage from each home," she said. But much of what Weisbecker lost cannot be replaced. Our house is empty," she said. "We lost everything, from pictures of our children and their lives, our friends, our grandkids, now we have great-grandkids. Everything [my husband] had since he was 13 on is gone." Weisbecker has been approved for a $25,000 grant through Florida's State Housing Initiatives Partnership, or SHIP, program. But for families facing tens of thousands of dollars in repairs, that assistance may cover only a fraction of the cost. And not everyone will qualify. "You do think about that process and you sit there and you say to yourself, how am I gonna do this?" Weisbecker said. That question is at the center of WPTV's ongoing investigation. Martin County estimates the flooding caused: A federal major disaster declaration could make certain public infrastructure repairs eligible for FEMA reimbursement and potentially open the door to individual assistance for qualifying residents. But approval is not guaranteed. When WPTV initially contacted FEMA, the agency confirmed it had received the disaster declaration request and that it remained under review. FEMA referred additional questions about the response and recovery timeline to the Florida Division of Emergency Management. Hussey subsequently pressed Perdue on what would happen if the federal government denied the request. "If FEMA ultimately denies federal assistance, does Florida have a Plan B, or are these families simply on their own?" Hussey asked. Perdue did not identify a specific alternative state funding program, instead emphasizing Florida's experience responding to natural disasters and its ongoing coordination with federal and local officials. "This is something that we're very used to doing. I mean, in Florida, we deal with natural disasters all the time," Perdue said. "We have a great relationship with FEMA, and usually those things go very well." He added that the state remains focused on immediate response efforts, including search and rescue operations and meeting residents' emergency needs. In the meantime, Martin County is working to distribute approximately $1 million in available SHIP funding to qualifying residents. Eligible homeowners may receive grants of up to $25,000, with additional assistance potentially available through loans of up to $75,000. However, those loans come with repayment requirements and liens. Income eligibility restrictions could also leave some families without assistance, even if they cannot afford to rebuild on their own. "There's going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where somebody barely missed the limit," Commissioner Blake Capps said during a recent Martin County Commission meeting. Capps proposed establishing a separate county-funded emergency assistance program for residents who fall through the cracks. But when WPTV asked where that money would come from, Capps acknowledged a funding source had not yet been identified. we'd have to talk to staff," he said. County Human Services Director Michelle Miller previously told commissioners the state had promised additional disaster relief funding, although neither the amount nor the timeline had been confirmed. "They haven't confirmed the amount yet but has assured us we will be getting some disaster relief funds," Miller told Hussey. Hussey raised those concerns directly with Perdue, asking whether the state had other programs available for families who earn too much to qualify for existing assistance but not enough to pay for repairs. Perdue pointed to the state's partnerships with nonprofit organizations and its deployment of emergency personnel to assist with cleanup. "We've actually activated the National Guard, and are also partnering with nonprofits to do what they call the muck and gut of homes that have been flooded," Perdue said. That work includes removing damaged drywall and other waterlogged materials to help prevent mold growth. "We're providing the assistance that we can and partnering with those nonprofit organizations as well," he said. However, Perdue did not identify a specific funding program to cover rebuilding costs for homeowners who do not qualify for existing assistance. The financial uncertainty extends beyond individual homeowners. Martin County faces approximately $15 million in combined beach and road damage, with additional emergency response expenses still being assessed. County spokesperson Martha Ann Kniess previously told WPTV that without federal reimbursement, Martin County could be left responsible for covering those costs, potentially forcing officials to redirect money from elsewhere in the budget or identify other funding sources. Hussey asked Perdue whether the state would help cover those expenses if FEMA denied federal assistance — or whether the financial burden could ultimately fall on local taxpayers. Perdue did not commit to providing state funding for those repairs. "We are and have been doing damage assessments ever since we submitted the first disaster declaration request," he said. "As those damage assessments come in, we'll continue to coordinate with FEMA and make sure all that information is submitted." The state's response follows an emotional Martin County Commission meeting Tuesday, where residents pleaded with elected officials to do more to secure recovery funding. Fight for us!" one resident urged commissioners. Others questioned why families were being asked to wait even longer for answers. "And the answer from this dais is wait 13 more days?!?" another resident asked. Commissioner Eileen Vargas said she had reached out to FEMA through personal contacts in an effort to expedite the process. "I did, through contacts, reach out to FEMA to try and get this going," Vargas said. Vargas also told residents she expected a new FEMA director to take office Nov. 30 and hoped that development could help move the disaster declaration forward. But even if a declaration is approved, not all losses or recovery expenses would necessarily qualify for federal assistance. As Martin County continues to recover from the Nov. 2 flooding, Perdue said the state is also responding to another significant rainfall event affecting communities across Florida. Ron DeSantis expanded the state's emergency executive order to include 21 counties. The state has mobilized resources from the National Guard, State Guard, Florida Highway Patrol and Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, among other agencies. "We're actively still responding to the previous flooding event on November 2, and now we're actively dealing with a current, another historic rain event that's brought record amount of flooding in many counties throughout the state," Perdue said. The overlapping disasters have added urgency to recovery efforts, particularly for residents whose homes remain exposed after being gutted. Perdue said state resources remain available for immediate needs, including food, water, shelter and emergency medical assistance. We're fully mobilized," he said. We're going to be with you till the very end, and we're going to make sure we help everybody get back on their feet." Despite those assurances, several critical questions remain unresolved. FEMA has not announced a decision on Florida's expedited disaster declaration request. The state has not identified a specific alternative rebuilding assistance program for homeowners who do not qualify for existing aid, nor has it committed to covering Martin County's public infrastructure losses if federal funding is denied. For residents like Weisbecker, the uncertainty is more than a question of government funding. It's a question of whether they can afford to return to the homes they've spent years building their lives in. "This is very urgent for people to get back into their daily lives," Weisbecker said. "This is total devastation.

entry.title: PSL police have a GTA VI release-day warning: Port St. Lucie is not Vice City - WPEC
entry.summary: PSL police have a GTA VI release-day warning: Port St. Lucie is not Vice City    WPEC
entry.article_text: The wanted level in Port St. Lucie should stay at zero, police say. As Grand Theft Auto VI arrives Thursday, the Port St. Lucie Police Department posted a playful safety briefing reminding fans that real life doesn’t come with a respawn button and that U.S. 1 and Crosstown are not racetracks. Five stars might be impressive in GTA , but trust us, you don’t want that kind of attention in Port St. Lucie, the department wrote. Its other reminders: patrol vehicles aren’t available for test drives, red lights aren’t suggestions, sidewalks aren’t shortcuts and the SWAT team isn’t a feature anyone wants to unlock. What happens in Vice City stays in Vice City, the post said. Lucie might come with a police report. The game officially launches Nov. 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. Rockstar’s fictional state of Leonida draws on Florida , with Vice City serving as its Miami-inspired centerpiece. The game follows Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, whose criminal plans pull them into a conspiracy spanning the state. CBS12 has been following the Sunshine State’s transformation into a real-life part of the game’s promotion. In September, a giant pink Welcome to Vice City sign went up on Miami’s Kaseya Center as part of a deal between Miami-Dade County and Rockstar Games. County officials said the arrangement was expected to bring in nearly $1 million in revenue and create marketing opportunities. Miami has also leaned into the Vice City connection with release-week events. The Miami Heat held a Night in Vice City celebration Wednesday, the night before launch. A release-day party is planned Thursday at the Clevelander South Beach, and Rockstar’s GTA VI : The Festival is scheduled for Saturday, Nov. See also: Who’s responsible for improving drainage after St. Lucie County’s historic flooding? Police in other cities have also used the GTA VI release to remind players to keep the game’s crime on screen. The Atlanta Police Department posted that GTA is not a real place, but Atlanta is! and warned that reckless driving, drunk driving, auto theft and violence have real consequences. Keep it in the game, the department wrote . In South Florida, law enforcement leaders raised a different concern before release day. The Miami-Dade Association of Chiefs of Police opposed plans to promote the county as Vice City, saying the game depicts violence against women and law enforcement. Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz also questioned whether public agencies should promote a game built around crimes her department works to prevent. For drivers tempted to bring a little of the game’s chaos onto local roads, PSLPD’s advice is simpler: drive safe, play smart and leave the wanted level in the game. Could 'sick days' coincide with release? The release could affect more than gamers’ free time. A GameSquare survey of 1,000 U.S. employees found that 10% of full-time employees surveyed who identify as gamers planned to skip work on launch day, while another 30% were considering taking time off. Of those considering time off, 36% said they would call in sick. The survey also found that 42% expected the game to make them less productive at work. Surveyed gamers expected to spend about $400 on the game and related purchases, and anticipated playing a median of 15 hours during the opening weekend. The survey found 70% might skip watching sports to spend more time gaming, while 42% said they’d be less likely to watch NFL games that weekend. I ndian River County students have Thursday off , giving young GTA VI fans an unexpected chance to spend part of release day in Vice City. The district closed schools because of forecast conditions and flooding concerns, while St. Lucie schools reopened and Palm Beach County schools remained open, except for West Boca High School, which is closed because of heavy flooding in the parking lot. entry.article_text: From cheering in the stands to making big plays under the Friday night lights, Latravious Woods is living out his childhood dream. The Vero Beach High School wide receiver now plays for the same Fighting Indians team he grew up watching. But the junior has an even bigger goal: bringing a state championship home. See Also: Tennis Star Coco Gauff Returns Home for Billie Jean King Cup Since joining the team as a freshman, Woods has grown into a key playmaker and leader his coaches and teammates can count on, both on and off the field.
