entry.title: Martin County flood victims fear more devastation as county braces for another foot of rain - WPTV
entry.summary: Martin County flood victims fear more devastation as county braces for another foot of rain    WPTV
entry.article_text: Just weeks after historic flooding destroyed homes and displaced families in Jensen Beach, Martin County residents are bracing for another round of heavy rain — with up to 12 inches forecast over the next three days.For families still struggling to recover, the threat of more flooding comes as county commissioners work to determine what caused the initial disaster and how to help those who lost nearly everything.On Tuesday, flood victims packed a Martin County Commission meeting, pleading for financial assistance and answers.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Along Cheri Drive in Jensen Beach, the signs of destruction remain. Dumpsters line driveways, damaged belongings sit outside and families are still trying to salvage what's left of their homes.Lisa French, her husband, Jeremy, and their two young sons are among those displaced after floodwaters rose as high as 3 feet inside some homes two weeks ago."It's like we're kind of stuck," French told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey. French said her home had about 3 to 6 inches of flooding that sat inside for more than a week, causing mold to grow 3 to 4 feet up the walls. "So they, yeah, they tore the walls down in the house," said French. "They just chipped up the last bit of the tile, and it's empty." Now, with more rain approaching, French fears her family could face another disaster before recovering from the first."Of course, we're afraid because we all flooded in our houses," she said.New figures released by Martin County show at least 36 homes sustained damage, with an estimated $3 million in residential losses. Commissioners estimated another $14 million in damage to beaches, and at least $1 million in damage to roadways that now need repairs. For some residents, the destruction represents a lifetime of memories washed away."We've lost everything," one elderly Jensen Beach resident told commissioners. "We have 60 years of our life — kids, grandkids, everything. It's all gone."As residents demand answers about what went wrong, commissioners approved shifting $200,000 from the county's stormwater budget to investigate whether development and changes to local drainage systems contributed to the flooding.Commissioner Blake Capps called the investigation "a good starting point.""It may be that we need to augment the study beyond the $200,000 that we approve today," said Capps. Meanwhile, county crews are working around the clock to prepare for the next storm, lowering retention pond levels, deploying additional pumps and draining flooded properties."We have people 24 hours a day pumping that material down," Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said.Commissioners also approved financial assistance for eligible flood victims through the state's State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program.The assistance includes grants of up to $25,000 for income-eligible homeowners and loans of up to $75,000 secured by liens on their properties.But there's a catch: The grants are reimbursement-based, meaning homeowners must first pay for eligible repairs before receiving the money.For families who lost everything, that presents another obstacle."We don't have $25,000," French said. "A lot of people don't have $25,000, so it's great, and we're appreciative, but I mean, our house is empty, and $25,000 is not going to do much for us." The other problem: the county currently has just $1 million in SHIP funding available, and commissioners warned the money could run out quickly, even with additional state funding promised."They haven't given us the amount yet, but they have assured us that we will be getting some disaster relief funds," said Human Services Director Michelle Miller Strict income limits could also disqualify some flood victims who cannot afford to rebuild on their own. The income cap for a family of one is $86,040. The cap for a family of two is $98,400. For a family of four, it's $122,880. When reporter Kate Hussey asked Capps what would happen to those families, he acknowledged the county needs to explore other options."There are going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where someone barely missed the limit, and we're going to need to take a look at what we can do for those folks," Capps said.For residents like French, the need is immediate."We just need somebody to step up," she said. "We need funding." With another round of heavy rain approaching, Martin County is distributing sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park to help residents protect their properties, with a limit of 25 per person. The County's Emergency Operations Center is scheduled to be staffed beginning Tuesday at 2 p.m., and the county is coordinating with the National Weather Service and Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM).Fire Rescue is also standing by with multiple high-water rescue trucks.Commissioners also said a Federal Emergency Management Agency representative is expected to visit Nov. 30 to assess the damage — a potential step toward securing federal disaster assistance.But for families still displaced and facing the possibility of more flooding, the uncertainty remains.

entry.title: How much rain did we get? See the highest totals across Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches - WPEC
entry.summary: How much rain did we get? See the highest totals across Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches    WPEC
entry.article_text: Indian River and Palm Beach counties saw the highest totals The highest report among the five counties came from The Acreage in Palm Beach County, where 12.92 inches were reported since Tuesday morning. Other notable Palm Beach County reports included 7.91 inches in Royal Palm Beach, 7.30 inches in Haverhill and 7.20 inches in Sandalfoot Cove. Indian River County also saw several high totals. Sebastian Inlet reported 10.29 inches, while Vero Lake Estates had reports of 8.49 and 7.51 inches. Other reports included 7.23 inches in Fellsmere and 6.90 inches in Roseland. Totals varied across the Treasure Coast In St. Lucie County, the highest report was 6.24 inches at the county fairgrounds. Indrio reported 4.92 inches, while Tradition and Paradise Park received 4.70 and 4.68 inches, respectively. Martin County’s highest report was 5.11 inches at Philo Farms. Other reports included 3.79 inches in Indiantown, 3.72 inches in Caloosa and 3.28 inches in Palm City. Okeechobee County had lower totals Rainfall reports in Okeechobee County were lower overall. The highest listed total was 2.81 inches in Kissimmee Prairie, followed by 2.32 inches in Country Hills. Okeechobee reported 1.58 inches. Heavy rain was concentrated in pockets These reports show how unevenly the rain fell. Most locations across the five counties saw totals of only a few inches, while certain communities caught repeated or heavier downpours that pushed their totals much higher. The highest localized amounts were concentrated in Indian River and Palm Beach counties.

entry.title: New memorial honors two Indian River County deputies killed in line of duty - WFLX
entry.summary: New memorial honors two Indian River County deputies killed in line of duty    WFLX
entry.article_text: The sound of bagpipes and taps filled the air Saturday as the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office unveiled a new memorial honoring two deputies killed in the line of duty. The memorial, located outside the sheriff’s office’s new administration building, honors Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow and Cpl. Their deaths happened 40 years apart. Now, their names have a permanent place together. WATCH: New memorial honors two Indian River County deputies killed in line of duty The unveiling came exactly one year after Sweeting-Mashkow was killed while serving an eviction notice at a home in the Bermuda Club community. 47-year-old Sweeting-Mashkow was one of three deputies serving the eviction notice on Nov. 21, 2025, when authorities said 37-year-old Michael Halberstam retrieved a weapon and opened fire. Sweeting-Mashkow was killed, and Deputy Florentino Arizpe was shot in the shoulder. A locksmith who was there for the eviction, David Long, was also critically wounded and later died from his injuries. Sweeting-Mashkow had served with the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office for more than 25 years. Her death marked the second line-of-duty death in the 100-year history of the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. For those who gathered Saturday, the passage of a year has not made that loss feel distant. “It’s an honor to be out here but also very sad,” community member Joanne Knott said. “To think that it happened a year ago is strange because it feels like it was yesterday.” The memorial also reaches back four decades, honoring Cpl. Richard Raczkoski, who was killed in the line of duty 40 years ago. “The two heroes that are on this memorial are two people that our community will remember forever,” Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said. Hundreds of family members, friends, law enforcement officers and community members gathered for Saturday’s unveiling, paying their respects. “I am so glad that they did this for Terri and Raczkoski,” one community member said. For those at the ceremony, the memorial is also a reminder of the risks law enforcement officers face each time they go to work. “All of these officers that step out into the community, they never know what their day is going to bring,” says Knott. Flowers hopes the two names on the memorial will be the only ones it ever bears: “I hope we never have to add names to this memorial again."

entry.article_text: The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office is reporting more flooded roads in the Vero Lake Estates area as heavy rain moves through the county Thursday. The sheriff’s office urged drivers to stay off flooded roads, warning that water can be deeper than it appears and can stall vehicles. High-water vehicles are in the area, and anyone who becomes stranded should call 911. Ryan Lloyd, Indian River County’s emergency management chief, told CBS12 News the county has received about 5 to 7 inches of rain so far. He said the north end of the county, including Sebastian, Fellsmere and Vero Lake Estates, has gotten more than the rest. Another 3 to 5 inches is expected by midnight Friday, Lloyd said, and the area is still at risk for pockets of 10 to 12 inches or more falling in a short time. Lloyd said the county’s water management systems are full and the ground is essentially saturated, so new rain is running off onto roads. The county’s emergency operations center is at a Level 2 partial activation, and National Guard members are there with high-water vehicles. Lloyd said there had been no requests for high-water rescues as of Thursday afternoon. He urged residents to avoid nonessential travel, turn around at flooded roads and never drive around barricades. Please do not drive to neighborhoods that are flooded because that can actually push floodwaters into homes and create a bigger problem than what some of those residents may already be facing, Lloyd said. The weather prompted the School District of Indian River County to close all public schools and district offices Thursday. The district said saturated ground and expected rain could make travel unsafe for students and staff. Lloyd said schools will also be closed Friday. A Vero Beach football game scheduled for Friday night has been moved to Saturday at 7 p.m., he said. CHIME IN: Send in your weather photos and videos The National Weather Service issued a flood advisory Thursday morning for eastern Indian River and northeastern St. Lucie counties, reporting that 2 to 4 inches of rain had fallen in parts of the area. The advisory warned of minor flooding in low-lying and poorly drained areas. A flood watch remains in effect for Indian River County through Friday evening, with more showers and thunderstorms possible. See also: Flood risk lingers across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches before a drier weekend The county’s road closure map , viewed at 2:47 p.m. Thursday, listed 13 road closures and six lane closures. Among the roads marked closed were 100th Court, 103rd Avenue, 104th Avenue, 83rd Street and 87th Street. The map also showed a long-term closure on 13th Street Southwest, scheduled to remain in place until Jan. Lane-closure listings included 101st Avenue, West 98th Avenue and two locations near Barber Street and U.S. The county also warned that heavy rain and gusty winds could disrupt trash collection. Residents whose streets are flooded were asked not to put carts in the water; the landfill and customer convenience centers could close early if conditions become unsafe. The City of Fellsmere also urged drivers to use extreme caution, identifying two potential trouble spots: New York Avenue near Hickory Street and North Broadway. The city said those roads could close if rain continues. City Hall remains open and operating normally. Lloyd said there are no known water main breaks or significant power outages in the county. The county’s Emergency Information Center, at 772-226-4000, will be open overnight Thursday for questions and flooding reports, and the county will decide Friday whether to keep it running. Residents can report flood damage to homes and businesses through the county’s emergency management website .

All after-school activities, aftercare programs, and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday are also canceled. District officials will continue monitoring rainfall, flooding, road closures, and the accessibility of schools, bus stops, and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. A decision regarding school operations for Thursday, November 19, will be announced Wednesday evening. Forecasters expect 3 to 6 inches of rain across the area, with higher amounts possible in some locations. Two weeks ago, floodwaters stranded cars, trapped families and forced some residents to wade through deep water. Videos from that flooding showed high school freshman Noah Julian swimming from his school bus toward his home in a flooded Port St. Another video showed 7-year-old Ella Ghodooshim walking through chest-deep water with her mother near Oak Hammock K-8. That mother, Thassia Rodrigues, told CBS12 her only concern was getting her daughter safely across the flooded intersection. "As long as I can get her across and get her to safety, that was my main concern," Rodrigues said. She described how quickly the flooding overwhelmed the neighborhood, leaving parents struggling to reach their children. "It was pretty scary and in a matter of minutes we had everything just flood," she said. Lucie Public Schools told CBS12 News that decisions about closures and early dismissal are based on forecasts and information from the National Weather Service and Emergency Operations Center. The district said the information available before the previous flooding did not indicate schools needed to close or dismiss students earlier. This time, officials said the forecast supported releasing students two hours early to get them home before the heaviest rain. The district said it was awaiting additional updates from the National Weather Service at 2 p.m. and Emergency Operations Center at 4 p.m. Tuesday before making any further decisions about school schedules. Parents picking up their children near Oak Hammock K-8 Tuesday told CBS12 News they welcomed the earlier dismissal. "It's kind of nice that they're doing it early so we have time to get them and not have to rush," said Nathan Leach, whose child attends the school. Rhett Linton, another parent, recalled kayaking through the flooded intersection during the previous storm. "I'm super happy that they are stepping up and taking precautions," Linton said. Rodrigues, who was captured on video helping her daughter through the floodwaters, also praised the district's decision. Lucie County, we appreciate you guys," she said. Officials are urging residents to plan ahead, monitor forecasts and local alerts, and limit unnecessary travel. Drivers should never enter standing or moving water. Floodwater can stall a vehicle and cause costly engine damage. If you cannot tell how deep the water is, turn around and find another route. Residents can report flooding concerns to St. Lucie County at flooding@stlucieco.org .

entry.title: 'We need answers': Martin County officials address outrage over proposed data center - WFLX
entry.summary: 'We need answers': Martin County officials address outrage over proposed data center    WFLX
entry.article_text: A controversial proposal to build a more than 1.6 million-square-foot data center just half a mile from an elementary school is drawing growing opposition in Martin County, where residents are raising concerns about everything from environmental impacts to whether they'll have a say in the project's approval. WATCH: 'We need answers': Martin Co. officials address outrage over proposed data center On Friday morning, a small but vocal group of residents gathered outside the Martin County Administrative Center, demanding answers about the massive development proposed for a parcel of land off Kanner Highway, west of Interstate 95. They had planned to attend a meeting with the county's Growth Management Department. But less than 17 hours before it was scheduled to begin, the county canceled it, citing overwhelming public interest. Residents showed up anyway. "We need answers, and we need them quick," said Chris McIntyre, whose son graduated from nearby Crystal Lake Elementary School. "This story cannot die, or else this is the death of Crystal Lake School." McIntyre, who goes by Coach Mack, became emotional discussing what the proposed development could mean for the school and surrounding neighborhoods. "Now that's the death of an A-rated elementary school that I love," he said, his voice breaking. Residents have raised concerns about potential noise pollution, water consumption, increased electricity demand, higher utility bills, wildlife displacement, declining property values and possible health impacts on children attending Crystal Lake Elementary. Michael Panella, another resident opposing the project, became emotional while explaining why the fight is so personal. These little ones are innocent," Panella said, referring also to students of Crystal Lake. Dan Wilson, president of the Locks Landing homeowners association, represents a community less than two miles from the proposed site. “They’re probably dropping now because, oh, the data center going there. We don’t want to move there,” Wilson said of property values. "We have residences right here, tons of residents. We're all going to have to deal with this." Residents acknowledge they don't yet know for sure what the long-term consequences of the project might be. They don't know whether electricity bills will increase, how much noise the facility could generate or what wildlife habitat might be lost. But they do know that once something of this magnitude is built, there's no easy way to undo it. The controversy intensified Thursday evening when Martin County announced the cancellation of an informal Growth Management meeting scheduled for 9:30 a.m. 19, the Martin County Board of County Commissioners posted the following message online: "This meeting has been canceled. Due to the level of public interest, a more formal meeting will be scheduled and publicly noticed in advance to accommodate any and all residents who wish to attend, learn more, and share their thoughts. Stay tuned to our website and social media as meeting details are finalized." For residents who had planned to attend, the cancellation only added to their frustration. "The thing that frustrates me the most about this is the fact that they were willing to do this meeting in private," said resident Alisha Gibbs. Gibbs described herself as "disgusted" and "absolutely appalled" by the situation. But Martin County Deputy Growth Management Director Pete Walden told WPTV Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey that the meeting was never intended to be a formal public hearing or a decision-making session. Instead, Walden said, it was an informal meeting requested by members of the public who wanted to ask county staff questions about the development — something his department routinely accommodates for other projects. He said information about the meeting circulated online, creating the impression that county officials were privately considering a decision on the data center. When interest grew beyond what the county could accommodate, officials decided to cancel. "We could not accommodate that. We didn't have any rooms or anything available for that size," Walden explained. "So we had to cancel, and we'll do some workshops in the future. I believe the applicant is also going to reach out for some public presentations on the subject." When asked why residents weren't being given more opportunities to weigh in, Walden maintained the county has been transparent. "We are transparent through the process, and everything can be made available to anyone that is interested," he said. Walden said additional public meetings and workshops will be scheduled to allow residents to ask questions and learn more about the project. But the canceled meeting is only one of several controversies surrounding the development. Another major point of contention is the timing of the developer's application. 27, Martin County commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on data centers, temporarily restricting new applications while the county reviews its development regulations. But records show the application for this project was submitted the day before the moratorium was proposed on October 13. That timing means the project is not subject to the temporary restriction, according to county officials. Walden acknowledged the timing but said the county cannot control when developers submit applications. "They obviously saw like everybody else that a moratorium was coming, and they got their application in ahead of time," Walden said. "We don't direct applicants ... and we certainly can't pick and choose when these things happen." WPTV reached out to the project applicant and the law firm representing it, requesting comment on the timing of the application and residents' environmental, energy and health concerns. Neither responded by publication time. Perhaps the most significant concern for opponents is whether residents will have any formal say in the project's approval. Under a county ordinance adopted in 2010, during the Great Recession, Martin County established an administrative approval process for certain targeted industries to encourage economic development. Data centers fall within the county's targeted industry classifications. According to Walden, the proposed development is also covered by an existing planned unit development, or PUD, agreement that allows qualifying targeted industries on platted industrial lots to receive administrative approval. That means the project could potentially move forward without a public hearing or recorded vote by county commissioners. For residents demanding a voice in the decision, that distinction is critical. Hussey asked Walden whether there was anything the county could do to give residents more of a say in whether the development is approved. "With the moratorium, we'll be looking at our code to make revisions so everything is appropriately reviewed as it comes in," Walden said. "To give the public more of a say in future projects?" Hussey asked. "Correct," Walden responded. Residents are also demanding answers about how a development of this size could affect surrounding neighborhoods, wildlife and students at Crystal Lake Elementary School. The proposal initially called for just under 1 million square feet of development. An updated application brings the total to approximately 1.6 million square feet, including an existing warehouse. Among the concerns raised by residents are the potential effects of noise from cooling equipment, increased water and electricity consumption, wildlife habitat loss and possible impacts on nearby property values. Those concerns remain questions, not established consequences of the proposed development. Walden said the county will review the project's potential impacts before making any approval decision. He also emphasized that despite speculation circulating in the community, the data center has not been approved. "There is a misconception that this project was already approved — that's very far from the truth," Walden said. "This is our first data center to be reviewed. We're going to take our time ... and make sure everything is properly vetted." The county says a staff report examining the project is expected to be released in December. Following that report, officials plan to schedule a public forum, likely including a presentation from the applicant, where residents can ask questions and learn more about the development. No date for that meeting has been announced. For opponents, the controversy goes beyond whether a data center belongs on acres of industrial land. It's about who gets to decide what their community becomes — and whether the people who will live with the consequences have a meaningful opportunity to influence that decision. The residents who gathered outside the county building Friday made clear that canceling a meeting would not end their opposition. "If they want to actually please the public, they would deny this proposal," Gibbs said.

entry.title: NWS confirms Saturday evening EF-1 tornado in Palm Beach County
entry.summary: Saturday evening's severe weather produced a confirmed EF-1 tornado in southern Palm Beach County. WATCH: NWS confirms Saturday evening tornado in Palm Beach County The National Weather Service began tracking a rotating thunderstorm near Boca Raton before issuing updates as the storm moved toward Delray Beach. At 6:19 p.m. Saturday, the Weather Service confirmed a tornado over Kings Point, moving northeast at 15 miles per hour. The storm prompted tornado warnings across portions of southern and eastern Palm Beach County, with reports of downed trees, damage to homes and power outages . A tornado watch was also issued for Palm Beach County and surrounding areas through 10 p.m. Saturday night. Following the NWS survey performed on Sunday - meteorologists confirmed an EF-1 tornado was responsible for the damage. The tornado had peak winds around 102 mph and followed a 7 1/2 mile path from near Whisper Walk in Boca Raton north to western Boynton Beach near the Westchester Country Club.

entry.title: EF-1 tornado damages communities in southern Palm Beach County with 102 mph winds
entry.summary: An EF-1 tornado that touched down in southern Palm Beach County left residents in west Boca Raton and west Delray Beach cleaning up damaged homes, downed trees and crushed vehicles after the storm tore through the area Saturday. The National Weather Service confirmed the tornado touched down along the Kings Point area. WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache spoke with residents who described how quickly conditions changed and how close some came to being caught in the storm. EF-1 tornado with 102 mph winds hits southern Palm Beach County Tornado leaves trail of damage in west Boca Raton In west Boca Raton, WPTV found a massive uprooted tree that lifted concrete in a parking lot and fell onto three parked vehicles. Video shared with WPTV also showed intense winds as the tornado moved through the area. At Boca Gardens, Thulio Dos Santos, 19, said he was walking home with his brother when he received an alert warning him to take shelter. 'After that, we started seeing the wind pick up and then the rain started going,' Dos Santos said. Dos Santos said he began running for safety as conditions deteriorated. During the storm, a branch struck him in the back of the head. He described the experience as something out of a movie. 'Honestly, I'm grateful that nothing major happened,' Dos Santos said. 'I only got hit in the head, but everything is fine.' He also expressed relief that there were no deaths in his immediate area. Resident loses only car after tree comes crashing down For Alvaro Villa Correa, the storm left behind a different challenge. His vehicle was among those crushed by a fallen tree in west Boca Raton. 'Honestly, I didn't realize just how powerful and dangerous a tornado could be,' Villa Correa told WPTV. He moved to Florida from Venezuela four years ago unaware of tornado impacts. Villa Correa said he had stepped outside and was heading toward his car when the tornado struck. He did not make it to the vehicle before the tree came down. 'Fortunately, I didn't have time to make it to my car,' he said in Spanish. 'It's probably for the best, because I might not be here to tell the story.' WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache spoke with residents who described how quickly conditions changed and how close some came to being caught in the storm.In west Boca Raton, WPTV found a massive uprooted tree that lifted concrete in a parking lot and fell onto three parked vehicles. Video shared with WPTV also showed intense winds as the tornado moved through the area.At Boca Gardens, Thulio Dos Santos, 19, said he was walking home with his brother when he received an alert warning him to take shelter."After that, we started seeing the wind pick up and then the rain started going," Dos Santos said.Dos Santos said he began running for safety as conditions deteriorated. During the storm, a branch struck him in the back of the head.He described the experience as something out of a movie."Honestly, I'm grateful that nothing major happened," Dos Santos said. "I only got hit in the head, but everything is fine."He also expressed relief that there were no deaths in his immediate area.For Alvaro Villa Correa, the storm left behind a different challenge.His vehicle was among those crushed by a fallen tree in west Boca Raton."Honestly, I didn't realize just how powerful and dangerous a tornado could be," Villa Correa told WPTV.He moved to Florida from Venezuela four years ago — unaware of tornado impacts. Villa Correa said he had stepped outside and was heading toward his car when the tornado struck. He did not make it to the vehicle before the tree came down."Fortunately, I didn't have time to make it to my car," he said in Spanish. "It's probably for the best, because I might not be here to tell the story."Villa Correa said the vehicle was his only car and he is still making payments on it. He is now worried about how insurance will handle the loss and how he will get to work.But amid that uncertainty, he said neighbors have already offered to help by giving him rides."I'm scared, surprised and amazed, all three at once," he said.WPTV also documented storm damage at the Gleneagles community in west Delray Beach.For residents accustomed to preparing for hurricanes, the tornado came as a shock.Dos Santos said a tornado hitting so close to home was something he never expected."Crazy, because like 15 seconds did a lot of damage, but when I was there, it felt like a long time," he said.For residents such as Villa Correa, the aftermath now means dealing with damaged property and unexpected expenses while also reflecting on how much worse the tornado could have been.The National Weather Service Miami confirmed the tornado was an EF-1 with estimated peak winds of 102 mph. The tornado traveled about 7.64 miles through southern Palm Beach County, reaching a maximum width of 500 yards, according to a preliminary damage survey released Sunday evening.The National Weather Service said the tornado began around 6:04 p.m. Saturday in the Boca Gardens area and remained on the ground until about 6:31 p.m., eventually lifting as the storm moved over western Boynton Beach.No injuries or fatalities were reported, according to the National Weather Service.Robert Garcia, a warning coordination meteorologist with National Weather Service Miami, was among those who surveyed the tornado damage Sunday.Survey crews found widespread tree damage along the tornado's path, along with occasional roof damage. Damage became more scattered toward the northern end of the surveyed area.According to the National Weather Service, crews were unable to access some gated communities and relied in part on residents to learn about damage in those locations.Meteorologists said the tornado developed after a cell merger and a surge in the storm's rear-flank downdraft allowed its rotating mesocyclone to reach the surface. entry.title: Florida emergency management director responds to FEMA delays as Jensen Beach flood victims wait for help - WFLX
entry.summary: Florida emergency management director responds to FEMA delays as Jensen Beach flood victims wait for help    WFLX
entry.article_text: Nearly three weeks after historic flooding forced families from their homes and caused millions of dollars in damage across Martin County, residents are still waiting for a federal disaster declaration that could unlock critical financial assistance. Now, after a WPTV report on the delays and growing frustration among flood victims, Florida's top emergency management official is responding to questions about the state's recovery efforts—and what help families can expect if FEMA funding never arrives. Watch more from Kate Hussey: In an exclusive interview with WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey, Jared Perdue, director of the Florida Division of Emergency Management, confirmed the state submitted an expedited federal disaster declaration request Nov. 9, one week after the initial flooding. But nearly two weeks after that request, a decision remains pending. "We've been very engaged with FEMA, and we did actually submit an expedited disaster declaration request to FEMA on November the ninth," Perdue said. "FEMA has been very closely coordinating with us in reviewing that, and I'm sure they're going to make quick work of it." The uncertainty comes as Martin County estimates approximately $18 million in residential and public infrastructure damage, with families still struggling to afford repairs and another round of historic rainfall complicating recovery efforts. Along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach, the devastation is still visible. Dumpsters line driveways, waterlogged belongings have been discarded and homes have been stripped down to their frames. For Linda Weisbecker, whose home was among those severely damaged, the destruction has been overwhelming. "It's like an apocalypse here," Weisbecker told WPTV in an earlier interview. For nine days, Weisbecker and her neighbors navigated waist-deep floodwaters before they could begin salvaging what remained of their homes. "Once we got through that and the water came out, we just all started pitching in, going in to see what we can salvage from each home," she said. But much of what Weisbecker lost cannot be replaced. Our house is empty," she said. "We lost everything, from pictures of our children and their lives, our friends, our grandkids, now we have great-grandkids. Everything [my husband] had since he was 13 on is gone." Weisbecker has been approved for a $25,000 grant through Florida's State Housing Initiatives Partnership, or SHIP, program. But for families facing tens of thousands of dollars in repairs, that assistance may cover only a fraction of the cost. And not everyone will qualify. "You do think about that process and you sit there and you say to yourself, how am I gonna do this?" Weisbecker said. That question is at the center of WPTV's ongoing investigation. Martin County estimates the flooding caused: A federal major disaster declaration could make certain public infrastructure repairs eligible for FEMA reimbursement and potentially open the door to individual assistance for qualifying residents. But approval is not guaranteed. When WPTV initially contacted FEMA, the agency confirmed it had received the disaster declaration request and that it remained under review. FEMA referred additional questions about the response and recovery timeline to the Florida Division of Emergency Management. Hussey subsequently pressed Perdue on what would happen if the federal government denied the request. "If FEMA ultimately denies federal assistance, does Florida have a Plan B, or are these families simply on their own?" Hussey asked. Perdue did not identify a specific alternative state funding program, instead emphasizing Florida's experience responding to natural disasters and its ongoing coordination with federal and local officials. "This is something that we're very used to doing. I mean, in Florida, we deal with natural disasters all the time," Perdue said. "We have a great relationship with FEMA, and usually those things go very well." He added that the state remains focused on immediate response efforts, including search and rescue operations and meeting residents' emergency needs. In the meantime, Martin County is working to distribute approximately $1 million in available SHIP funding to qualifying residents. Eligible homeowners may receive grants of up to $25,000, with additional assistance potentially available through loans of up to $75,000. However, those loans come with repayment requirements and liens. Income eligibility restrictions could also leave some families without assistance, even if they cannot afford to rebuild on their own. "There's going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where somebody barely missed the limit," Commissioner Blake Capps said during a recent Martin County Commission meeting. Capps proposed establishing a separate county-funded emergency assistance program for residents who fall through the cracks. But when WPTV asked where that money would come from, Capps acknowledged a funding source had not yet been identified. we'd have to talk to staff," he said. County Human Services Director Michelle Miller previously told commissioners the state had promised additional disaster relief funding, although neither the amount nor the timeline had been confirmed. "They haven't confirmed the amount yet but has assured us we will be getting some disaster relief funds," Miller told Hussey. Hussey raised those concerns directly with Perdue, asking whether the state had other programs available for families who earn too much to qualify for existing assistance but not enough to pay for repairs. Perdue pointed to the state's partnerships with nonprofit organizations and its deployment of emergency personnel to assist with cleanup. "We've actually activated the National Guard, and are also partnering with nonprofits to do what they call the muck and gut of homes that have been flooded," Perdue said. That work includes removing damaged drywall and other waterlogged materials to help prevent mold growth. "We're providing the assistance that we can and partnering with those nonprofit organizations as well," he said. However, Perdue did not identify a specific funding program to cover rebuilding costs for homeowners who do not qualify for existing assistance. The financial uncertainty extends beyond individual homeowners. Martin County faces approximately $15 million in combined beach and road damage, with additional emergency response expenses still being assessed. County spokesperson Martha Ann Kniess previously told WPTV that without federal reimbursement, Martin County could be left responsible for covering those costs, potentially forcing officials to redirect money from elsewhere in the budget or identify other funding sources. Hussey asked Perdue whether the state would help cover those expenses if FEMA denied federal assistance — or whether the financial burden could ultimately fall on local taxpayers. Perdue did not commit to providing state funding for those repairs. "We are and have been doing damage assessments ever since we submitted the first disaster declaration request," he said. "As those damage assessments come in, we'll continue to coordinate with FEMA and make sure all that information is submitted." The state's response follows an emotional Martin County Commission meeting Tuesday, where residents pleaded with elected officials to do more to secure recovery funding. Fight for us!" one resident urged commissioners. Others questioned why families were being asked to wait even longer for answers. "And the answer from this dais is wait 13 more days?!?" another resident asked. Commissioner Eileen Vargas said she had reached out to FEMA through personal contacts in an effort to expedite the process. "I did, through contacts, reach out to FEMA to try and get this going," Vargas said. Vargas also told residents she expected a new FEMA director to take office Nov. 30 and hoped that development could help move the disaster declaration forward. But even if a declaration is approved, not all losses or recovery expenses would necessarily qualify for federal assistance. As Martin County continues to recover from the Nov. 2 flooding, Perdue said the state is also responding to another significant rainfall event affecting communities across Florida. Ron DeSantis expanded the state's emergency executive order to include 21 counties. The state has mobilized resources from the National Guard, State Guard, Florida Highway Patrol and Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, among other agencies. "We're actively still responding to the previous flooding event on November 2, and now we're actively dealing with a current, another historic rain event that's brought record amount of flooding in many counties throughout the state," Perdue said. The overlapping disasters have added urgency to recovery efforts, particularly for residents whose homes remain exposed after being gutted. Perdue said state resources remain available for immediate needs, including food, water, shelter and emergency medical assistance. We're fully mobilized," he said. We're going to be with you till the very end, and we're going to make sure we help everybody get back on their feet." Despite those assurances, several critical questions remain unresolved. FEMA has not announced a decision on Florida's expedited disaster declaration request. The state has not identified a specific alternative rebuilding assistance program for homeowners who do not qualify for existing aid, nor has it committed to covering Martin County's public infrastructure losses if federal funding is denied. For residents like Weisbecker, the uncertainty is more than a question of government funding. It's a question of whether they can afford to return to the homes they've spent years building their lives in. "This is very urgent for people to get back into their daily lives," Weisbecker said. "This is total devastation.

entry.title: Vance, El-Sayed move toward meeting after contentious midterm election
entry.summary: Vice President JD Vance and Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed are preparing to meet, the incoming Democratic lawmaker and the White House said, after a bitter campaign season that featured sharp and at-times personal attacks between the two men. The circumstances of the would-be meeting were not immediately clear, nor was it certain on whose initiative it was being set. And Vance will ultimately preside over El-Sayeds swearing-in Jan. 3. El-Sayed said in a Tuesday interview on MSNOW that his team was contacted by Vance's office for a meeting. Vances office said Wednesday that it had contacted El-Sayeds staff after being told the Democrat sought time with the vice president. Both men have in recent days expressed willingness to attempt to find common ground after their heated criticism albeit on their own terms. entry.article_text: The National Weather Service canceled a Flood Watch for Indian River County Friday morning, but additional showers remain possible and flooding continues to affect roads across the county. See also: DeSantis expands Florida emergency order to 21 counties amid flooding The heaviest rainfall threat is farther north, according to an update from Indian River County Emergency Services. Officials are asking drivers to check road conditions before traveling, allow extra time for detours and never drive through flooded roads. As of 9 a.m. Friday, flooding or roadway damage was affecting these locations: U.S. 1 near Barber Street: Partial blockage Old Dixie Highway SW: Flooding and partial blockages at several locations 82nd Avenue at the entrance to Heritage Plantation: Partial blockage Skyline Drive, from Periwinkle to Barber Street: Partial blockage 130th Street: Closed 79th Street west of 130th Avenue: Closed because of a roadway washout 13th Street SW east of 66th Avenue SW: Closed because of roadway damage Vero Lake Estates: 104th Avenue between 87th and 93rd streets, and 83rd Street between 91st and 93rd avenues, are closed The county said the list includes selected locations. Drivers can check the live road closure map for additional closures and updates. Officials said water needs time to recede and damaged roads must be assessed and repaired before they can safely reopen. Crews are working in affected areas, and drivers are asked to give them room and follow barricades. Facility and school updates The Indian River County Shooting Range, Gifford Aquatic Center and North County Aquatic Center are open Friday. Marian Fell Library and the Veterans Services office in Sebastian remain closed. The School District of Indian River County is closed Friday. Check the district website for updates. The county said the Indian River County Fairgrounds may be used in the coming days to support emergency management missions for communities to the north, where the threat of heavy rain and flooding is greater.

entry.article_text: A controversial proposal to build a more than 1.6 million-square-foot data center just half a mile from an elementary school is drawing growing opposition in Martin County, where residents are raising concerns about everything from environmental impacts to whether they'll have a say in the project's approval.WATCH: 'We need answers': Martin Co. officials address outrage over proposed data centerOn Friday morning, a small but vocal group of residents gathered outside the Martin County Administrative Center, demanding answers about the massive development proposed for a parcel of land off Kanner Highway, west of Interstate 95.They had planned to attend a meeting with the county's Growth Management Department. But less than 17 hours before it was scheduled to begin, the county canceled it, citing overwhelming public interest.Residents showed up anyway."We need answers, and we need them quick," said Chris McIntyre, whose son graduated from nearby Crystal Lake Elementary School. "This story cannot die, or else this is the death of Crystal Lake School."McIntyre, who goes by Coach Mack, became emotional discussing what the proposed development could mean for the school and surrounding neighborhoods."Now that's the death of an A-rated elementary school that I love," he said, his voice breaking.He's far from alone.Residents have raised concerns about potential noise pollution, water consumption, increased electricity demand, higher utility bills, wildlife displacement, declining property values and possible health impacts on children attending Crystal Lake Elementary.Michael Panella, another resident opposing the project, became emotional while explaining why the fight is so personal."It's life. These little ones are innocent," Panella said, referring also to students of Crystal Lake. Dan Wilson, president of the Locks Landing homeowners association, represents a community less than two miles from the proposed site.“They’re probably dropping now because, oh, the data center going there. We don’t want to move there,” Wilson said of property values."We have residences right here, tons of residents. We're all going to have to deal with this."Residents acknowledge they don't yet know for sure what the long-term consequences of the project might be. They don't know whether electricity bills will increase, how much noise the facility could generate or what wildlife habitat might be lost.But they do know that once something of this magnitude is built, there's no easy way to undo it.The controversy intensified Thursday evening when Martin County announced the cancellation of an informal Growth Management meeting scheduled for 9:30 a.m. Friday.At 4:55 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 19, the Martin County Board of County Commissioners posted the following message online:For residents who had planned to attend, the cancellation only added to their frustration."The thing that frustrates me the most about this is the fact that they were willing to do this meeting in private," said resident Alisha Gibbs.Gibbs described herself as "disgusted" and "absolutely appalled" by the situation.But Martin County Deputy Growth Management Director Pete Walden told WPTV Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey that the meeting was never intended to be a formal public hearing or a decision-making session.Instead, Walden said, it was an informal meeting requested by members of the public who wanted to ask county staff questions about the development — something his department routinely accommodates for other projects.He said information about the meeting circulated online, creating the impression that county officials were privately considering a decision on the data center.When interest grew beyond what the county could accommodate, officials decided to cancel."We could not accommodate that. We didn't have any rooms or anything available for that size," Walden explained. "So we had to cancel, and we'll do some workshops in the future. I believe the applicant is also going to reach out for some public presentations on the subject." When asked why residents weren't being given more opportunities to weigh in, Walden maintained the county has been transparent."We are transparent through the process, and everything can be made available to anyone that is interested," he said.Walden said additional public meetings and workshops will be scheduled to allow residents to ask questions and learn more about the project.But the canceled meeting is only one of several controversies surrounding the development.Another major point of contention is the timing of the developer's application.On Oct. 27, Martin County commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on data centers, temporarily restricting new applications while the county reviews its development regulations.But records show the application for this project was submitted the day before the moratorium was proposed on October 13. That timing means the project is not subject to the temporary restriction, according to county officials.Walden acknowledged the timing but said the county cannot control when developers submit applications."They obviously saw like everybody else that a moratorium was coming, and they got their application in ahead of time," Walden said. "We don't direct applicants ... and we certainly can't pick and choose when these things happen."WPTV reached out to the project applicant and the law firm representing it, requesting comment on the timing of the application and residents' environmental, energy and health concerns.Neither responded by publication time.Perhaps the most significant concern for opponents is whether residents will have any formal say in the project's approval.Under a county ordinance adopted in 2010, during the Great Recession, Martin County established an administrative approval process for certain targeted industries to encourage economic development.Data centers fall within the county's targeted industry classifications. According to Walden, the proposed development is also covered by an existing planned unit development, or PUD, agreement that allows qualifying targeted industries on platted industrial lots to receive administrative approval.That means the project could potentially move forward without a public hearing or recorded vote by county commissioners.For residents demanding a voice in the decision, that distinction is critical.Hussey asked Walden whether there was anything the county could do to give residents more of a say in whether the development is approved."With the moratorium, we'll be looking at our code to make revisions so everything is appropriately reviewed as it comes in," Walden said."To give the public more of a say in future projects?" Hussey asked. "Correct," Walden responded. Residents are also demanding answers about how a development of this size could affect surrounding neighborhoods, wildlife and students at Crystal Lake Elementary School.The proposal initially called for just under 1 million square feet of development. An updated application brings the total to approximately 1.6 million square feet, including an existing warehouse.Among the concerns raised by residents are the potential effects of noise from cooling equipment, increased water and electricity consumption, wildlife habitat loss and possible impacts on nearby property values.Those concerns remain questions, not established consequences of the proposed development.Walden said the county will review the project's potential impacts before making any approval decision.He also emphasized that despite speculation circulating in the community, the data center has not been approved."There is a misconception that this project was already approved — that's very far from the truth," Walden said."This is our first data center to be reviewed. We're going to take our time ... and make sure everything is properly vetted."The county says a staff report examining the project is expected to be released in December.Following that report, officials plan to schedule a public forum, likely including a presentation from the applicant, where residents can ask questions and learn more about the development.No date for that meeting has been announced.For opponents, the controversy goes beyond whether a data center belongs on acres of industrial land.It's about who gets to decide what their community becomes — and whether the people who will live with the consequences have a meaningful opportunity to influence that decision.The residents who gathered outside the county building Friday made clear that canceling a meeting would not end their opposition."If they want to actually please the public, they would deny this proposal," Gibbs said.

entry.title: Man found guilty of murder in 2023 Riviera Beach shooting of woman
entry.summary: A jury has found a man guilty of first-degree murder in connection with the 2023 shooting of a Riviera Beach woman who remained on life support for months before dying from her injuries. Christopher Lane Jr. was convicted of first-degree murder with a firearm and shooting into an occupied vehicle in the death of Lauren St. Fort, according to the Riviera Beach Police Department. The shooting happened March 11, 2023, in the 1400 block of West 36th Street. When officers arrived, they found 27-year-old St. Fort inside her car with two gunshot wounds, one near the base of her neck and another in her thigh. Investigators said the shooting was connected to a drug deal. Witnesses told police they saw a man flag down St. Fort's car before forcing his way into the driver's side. They heard him demand, 'give me that,' followed by several gunshots. The man then ran away, witnesses told investigators. St. Fort was rushed to St. Mary's Medical Center, where she remained on a ventilator after being paralyzed from the neck down. In April 2023, family members and community supporters organized a fundraiser to help pay for her mounting medical expenses and long-term care. Her sisters said at the time that as long as she kept fighting for her life, they would keep fighting for her. Lane was arrested in May 2023, about two months after the shooting. Investigators said fingerprints recovered from St. Fort's car matched his. St. Fort remained on life support for months before dying from her injuries on Jan. 9, 2024. Following her death, the case was referred to the State Attorney's Office Homicide Unit for prosecution. 'We thank everyone who helped bring justice to Lauren St. Fort and her family,' Riviera Beach Police Chief Michael Coleman said in a statement. Lane remains in custody and is scheduled to be sentenced Jan. 5, 2027.

entry.title: Delray Beach Arts, Inc. takes step to bring back St. Patrick's Day Parade
entry.summary: Delray Beach Arts, Inc. has submitted an application to put on the 59th Annual Delray Beach St. Patrick's Day Parade after a new Florida law prompted the city to announce it would cancel the event. The nonprofit submitted the Special Event application in hopes of being granted permission to the parade in 2027. New legislation restricts local governments from funding, promoting or taking official actions related to certain diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) activities. Delray Beach Arts said that bringing the parade to life will require community support from sponsors, businesses, and community participation. They created a GoFundMe campaign and said they are actively seeking corporate sponsors and community partners for the event. 'Together, we can keep the tradition alive and make the 59th Annual Delray Beach St. Patricks Day Parade a celebration our community can be proud of,' the nonprofit said. When we spoke with Delray Beach Mayor Tom Carney earlier this month, he said he's confident the St. Patrick's Day Parade will go on as scheduled in 2027. Senate Bill 1143 takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.

entry.title: St. Lucie County schools closed Friday as heavy rain threatens morning commute
entry.summary: St. Lucie Public Schools will be closed Friday, Nov. 20, because additional heavy rainfall is expected overnight and into the morning, district officials announced Thursday. ADDITIONAL CLOSURES: Indian River County schools closed Friday due to flooding, heavy rain Palm Beach County schools to close Friday amid heavy rain, flood watches The district said it made the decision out of an abundance of caution because heavy rain could coincide with the morning arrival period while areas throughout the county are already saturated. More heavy rain expected After a break from the rain Thursday afternoon, the district said the National Weather Service is forecasting an additional 3 to 4 inches or more of rainfall, with the heaviest rain expected around the time students and staff would normally be traveling to school. The safety of our students and staff is at the forefront of this decision, Superintendent Dr. Jon R. Prince said. Given the potential for heavy rainfall during the morning arrival period and the already saturated conditions throughout our community, we believe closing schools is the safest decision for our students, families, and employees. After-school activities also canceled All after-school programs scheduled for Friday are canceled, including aftercare, activities and athletic events, according to the district. Some closures are limited to today, while others remain in effect until conditions improve. Check with the agency before heading out, since updates may change. Palm Beach County West Palm Beach: The city canceled in-person meetings and events scheduled for Thursday, including Clematis by Night. The city also canceled in-person meetings and events scheduled to begin or continue after 5 p.m. Wednesday. The city's local state of emergency is extended through Nov. 22 as the city continues recovery from earlier flooding and prepares for more rain. Schools: Palm Beach County public schools are open Thursday, but will be closed on Friday, according to the district. Only West Boca High is closed Thursday because of flooding in the parking lot. Martin County MARTY transit: The county’s current notice says ADA paratransit service has been restored and fixed-route service has resumed on the U.S. 1 corridor. Riders can call 772-463-2860 for updates. Schools: Martin County schools and after-school activities are scheduled to resume Thursday after activities were canceled Wednesday. Indian River County Schools and district offices: Closed Thursday and Friday because of weather impacts. County government offices, courthouses and Indian River State College campuses are listed as open. Schools will also be closed for Thanksgiving break from Nov. 23 through Nov. 27. They are scheduled to reopen Monday, Nov. 30. Waste services: The Roseland Customer Convenience Center is closed today because flooding on 130th Street makes it unsafe to reach. The landfill, Gifford and Winter Beach centers are open; curbside collection is running, though routes may be affected by flooded streets. Okeechobee County Okeechobee County’s local state of emergency was extended through Nov. 21. entry.title: 'We need answers': Martin County officials address outrage over proposed data center - WFLX
entry.summary: 'We need answers': Martin County officials address outrage over proposed data center    WFLX
entry.article_text: A controversial proposal to build a more than 1.6 million-square-foot data center just half a mile from an elementary school is drawing growing opposition in Martin County, where residents are raising concerns about everything from environmental impacts to whether they'll have a say in the project's approval. WATCH: 'We need answers': Martin Co. officials address outrage over proposed data center On Friday morning, a small but vocal group of residents gathered outside the Martin County Administrative Center, demanding answers about the massive development proposed for a parcel of land off Kanner Highway, west of Interstate 95. They had planned to attend a meeting with the county's Growth Management Department. But less than 17 hours before it was scheduled to begin, the county canceled it, citing overwhelming public interest. Residents showed up anyway. "We need answers, and we need them quick," said Chris McIntyre, whose son graduated from nearby Crystal Lake Elementary School. "This story cannot die, or else this is the death of Crystal Lake School." McIntyre, who goes by Coach Mack, became emotional discussing what the proposed development could mean for the school and surrounding neighborhoods. "Now that's the death of an A-rated elementary school that I love," he said, his voice breaking. Residents have raised concerns about potential noise pollution, water consumption, increased electricity demand, higher utility bills, wildlife displacement, declining property values and possible health impacts on children attending Crystal Lake Elementary. Michael Panella, another resident opposing the project, became emotional while explaining why the fight is so personal. These little ones are innocent," Panella said, referring also to students of Crystal Lake. Dan Wilson, president of the Locks Landing homeowners association, represents a community less than two miles from the proposed site. “They’re probably dropping now because, oh, the data center going there. We don’t want to move there,” Wilson said of property values. "We have residences right here, tons of residents. We're all going to have to deal with this." Residents acknowledge they don't yet know for sure what the long-term consequences of the project might be. They don't know whether electricity bills will increase, how much noise the facility could generate or what wildlife habitat might be lost. But they do know that once something of this magnitude is built, there's no easy way to undo it. The controversy intensified Thursday evening when Martin County announced the cancellation of an informal Growth Management meeting scheduled for 9:30 a.m. Friday. At 4:55 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 19, the Martin County Board of County Commissioners posted the following message online: "This meeting has been canceled. Due to the level of public interest, a more formal meeting will be scheduled and publicly noticed in advance to accommodate any and all residents who wish to attend, learn more, and share their thoughts. Stay tuned to our website and social media as meeting details are finalized." For residents who had planned to attend, the cancellation only added to their frustration. "The thing that frustrates me the most about this is the fact that they were willing to do this meeting in private," said resident Alisha Gibbs. Gibbs described herself as "disgusted" and "absolutely appalled" by the situation. But Martin County Deputy Growth Management Director Pete Walden told WPTV Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey that the meeting was never intended to be a formal public hearing or a decision-making session. Instead, Walden said, it was an informal meeting requested by members of the public who wanted to ask county staff questions about the development — something his department routinely accommodates for other projects. He said information about the meeting circulated online, creating the impression that county officials were privately considering a decision on the data center. When interest grew beyond what the county could accommodate, officials decided to cancel. "We could not accommodate that. We didn't have any rooms or anything available for that size," Walden explained. "So we had to cancel, and we'll do some workshops in the future. I believe the applicant is also going to reach out for some public presentations on the subject." When asked why residents weren't being given more opportunities to weigh in, Walden maintained the county has been transparent. "We are transparent through the process, and everything can be made available to anyone that is interested," he said. Walden said additional public meetings and workshops will be scheduled to allow residents to ask questions and learn more about the project. But the canceled meeting is only one of several controversies surrounding the development. Another major point of contention is the timing of the developer's application. On Oct. 27, Martin County commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on data centers, temporarily restricting new applications while the county reviews its development regulations. But records show the application for this project was submitted the day before the moratorium was proposed on October 13. That timing means the project is not subject to the temporary restriction, according to county officials. Walden acknowledged the timing but said the county cannot control when developers submit applications. "They obviously saw like everybody else that a moratorium was coming, and they got their application in ahead of time," Walden said. "We don't direct applicants ... and we certainly can't pick and choose when these things happen." WPTV reached out to the project applicant and the law firm representing it, requesting comment on the timing of the application and residents' environmental, energy and health concerns. Neither responded by publication time. Perhaps the most significant concern for opponents is whether residents will have any formal say in the project's approval. Under a county ordinance adopted in 2010, during the Great Recession, Martin County established an administrative approval process for certain targeted industries to encourage economic development. Data centers fall within the county's targeted industry classifications. According to Walden, the proposed development is also covered by an existing planned unit development, or PUD, agreement that allows qualifying targeted industries on platted industrial lots to receive administrative approval. That means the project could potentially move forward without a public hearing or recorded vote by county commissioners. For residents demanding a voice in the decision, that distinction is critical. Hussey asked Walden whether there was anything the county could do to give residents more of a say in whether the development is approved. "With the moratorium, we'll be looking at our code to make revisions so everything is appropriately reviewed as it comes in," Walden said. "To give the public more of a say in future projects?" Hussey asked. "Correct," Walden responded. Residents are also demanding answers about how a development of this size could affect surrounding neighborhoods, wildlife and students at Crystal Lake Elementary School. The proposal initially called for just under 1 million square feet of development. An updated application brings the total to approximately 1.6 million square feet, including an existing warehouse. Among the concerns raised by residents are the potential effects of noise from cooling equipment, increased water and electricity consumption, wildlife habitat loss and possible impacts on nearby property values. Those concerns remain questions, not established consequences of the proposed development. Walden said the county will review the project's potential impacts before making any approval decision. He also emphasized that despite speculation circulating in the community, the data center has not been approved. "There is a misconception that this project was already approved — that's very far from the truth," Walden said. "This is our first data center to be reviewed. We're going to take our time ... and make sure everything is properly vetted." The county says a staff report examining the project is expected to be released in December. Following that report, officials plan to schedule a public forum, likely including a presentation from the applicant, where residents can ask questions and learn more about the development. No date for that meeting has been announced. For opponents, the controversy goes beyond whether a data center belongs on acres of industrial land. It's about who gets to decide what their community becomes — and whether the people who will live with the consequences have a meaningful opportunity to influence that decision. The residents who gathered outside the county building Friday made clear that canceling a meeting would not end their opposition. "If they want to actually please the public, they would deny this proposal," Gibbs said.

The closures are impacting travel to and from the Seaway Drive Bridge. Officials are directing drivers to use Avenue C or the Citrus Avenue Bridge as alternate routes. The Fort Pierce Police Department is continuing its investigation and is expected to provide additional details as they become available.

entry.summary: Boil water notice lifted for 21,000 Port St. Lucie customers after water main break    WPEC
entry.article_text: Thousands of Port St. Lucie residents can put away their pots after city officials lifted a precautionary boil water notice Saturday afternoon. The City of Port St. Lucie announced the all-clear at 3:15 p.m. Saturday after water quality tests confirmed the water was safe to drink. The notice affected approximately 21,000 customers in Tradition and areas west of Interstate 95 following a water main break Tuesday near Glades Cut Off Road. See also: A helping of hope: 600 turkeys bring Thanksgiving cheer to South Florida families Residents in the following communities no longer need to boil their water: Tradition Western Grove Riverland Wilson Grove Southern Grove Copper Creek Wylder Verano The affected area stretched west of I-95 south to Becker Road, including communities along Glades Cut Off Road. According to city officials, the break occurred when a contractor working on a construction project unrelated to the city damaged a 36-inch water main. City crews responded immediately and completed repairs within hours. Flushing and required water quality testing followed. After tests confirmed the water was safe, officials lifted the precautionary notice. The city thanked the roughly 21,000 affected customers for their patience throughout the disruption.

entry.title: Flooded roads snarl travel across Port St. Lucie - WPEC
entry.summary: Flooded roads snarl travel across Port St. Lucie    WPEC
entry.article_text: Cars were still getting through when CBS12 News reached one of the spots Port St. Lucie police had flagged for high water Thursday. Water pooled along Port St. Lucie Boulevard, and nearby driveways were dry. Earlier, water had made a lane impassable in two places on Village Parkway, and crews were pumping it off Tradition Parkway. Two weeks ago, floodwater stranded drivers across the city. Near Oak Hammock K 8, video showed a mother and daughter wading through chest-deep water. One location in Port St. Lucie recorded 16.7 inches of rain over 60 hours during that storm. Where police reported flooding Port St. Lucie Boulevard: Crews were putting up barricades at McCorkle Avenue, at Alcantara Boulevard and along the stretch from Southwest Liberty Drive to Firestone. Northbound Village Parkway: The right lane was impassable south of the fire station and south of Discovery Way. Water was spreading into a second lane near Discovery Way. Tradition Parkway east of Hazel Drive: Crews were pumping water off the road after the outside lanes flooded in both directions. Police said more closures could be needed as rain continued. The Florida Department of Transportation also had overnight closures scheduled this week on Port St. Lucie Boulevard between Southwest Fisherman and Southwest Liberty avenues for drainage work tied to a widening project. Where to fill sandbags St. Lucie County says sand is still available while supplies last at the St. Lucie County Fairgrounds’ west parking lot, 15601 W. Midway Road in Fort Pierce. The Lawnwood Stadium site has run out. The fairgrounds site is self-service. Bring a shovel and plan to fill your own bags. The county has a limited supply of bags and encourages residents to bring their own. Residents in unincorporated St. Lucie County can report flooding that threatens homes, businesses or personal safety to flooding@stlucieco.gov. What was different this time Port St. Lucie crews started lowering water levels in stormwater basins Sunday to make room for more rain. They also cleared drains and checked canals and culverts. A lot of it just depends on how much rain you get at a given time, city spokesperson Scott Samples said. During the Nov. 1 3 storm, Samples said, rain came down so quickly that the drainage system needed longer to move it. This week, he said, less rain had fallen all at once. We’ve been fortunate that so far we haven’t had that kind of rain, he said. Samples said homeowners associations and community development districts manage drainage in parts of Tradition. The city helped pump water out of a neighborhood there after the first storm, he said. It’s really a very collective stormwater system. A flood watch remains in effect for St. Lucie County through 7 p.m. Friday. The National Weather Service issued a separate advisory Thursday morning after radar and gauges indicated 2 to 4 inches had fallen across parts of northeastern St. Lucie County and eastern Indian River County. forecast.weather.gov See also: Who’s responsible for improving drainage after St. Lucie County’s historic flooding? St. Lucie schools reopen St. Lucie Public Schools reopened on a regular schedule Thursday after closing Wednesday over flooding concerns. Aftercare, sports and other activities were scheduled to resume. The district said weather-related absences would be excused with a note from a parent or guardian. In neighboring Indian River County, public schools and district offices were closed Thursday. More rain on already-soaked ground A flood watch covers St. Lucie County through 7 p.m. Friday. The National Weather Service issued a separate advisory Thursday morning for northeastern St. Lucie County and eastern Indian River County after radar and gauges indicated 2 to 4 inches had already fallen across that area. During the Nov. 1 3 storm, one location in Port St. Lucie recorded 16.7 inches of rain over 60 hours. By Nov. 12, St. Lucie County had received at least 472 preliminary reports of property damage from that storm. The county is accepting damage reports from the earlier storm through Nov. 30.
