entry.title: St. Lucie County schools closed as families prepare for more heavy rain - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County schools closed as families prepare for more heavy rain    WPEC
entry.article_text: St. Lucie County schools and district offices are closed Wednesday as families prepare for more heavy rain, two weeks after flooding left roads underwater and damaged homes. All aftercare programs, after-school activities and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday are also canceled. See also: Flood risk continues for the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches through Friday evening The school district said forecasts show the potential for significant rainfall and localized flooding. With the ground already saturated, the district said closing schools was the cautious choice for students, families and employees. Officials are monitoring rainfall, flooding, road closures and access to schools, bus stops and transportation routes. The district plans to announce Wednesday evening whether schools will reopen Thursday. Across the Treasure Coast, some residents are filling sandbags to protect their homes. Others are stocking up on groceries and preparing to stay home if roads flood again. Leo Vargas of Port St. Lucie says floodwater rose to his knees two weeks ago, damaging his garage and guitars. He filled sandbags at the St. Lucie County Fairgrounds and is adding more around his home. We had a lot of water go into the garage and we just got over the fact that it stopped smelling like mold in there, Vargas said. And then here we go again with this inclement weather. St. Lucie County set up self-service sand distribution sites at the county fairgrounds in Fort Pierce and the Lawnwood Stadium parking lot. Residents need to bring their own bags and shovels and fill the bags themselves. Sand is available while supplies last. By 6 p.m. Tuesday, the two truckloads at Lawnwood Stadium were nearly gone. Glen Ferlance was out for a morning walk Wednesday morning when he spoke with CBS12. He said the flooding two weeks ago kept him from reaching his children. I could not get to cross over to go and see my kids, Ferlance said. I had to park in the um the plaza here and just look on. Ferlance said he lives in Port St. Lucie and he’s preparing for more rain, but hopes the flooding won’t be as severe this time. I just hope that is not too bad like last time. Yes, I’m prepared, he said. I’m going to get something to eat, and I’m running back home in my bed to watch TV and relax until all this is over. He also said he’s glad St. Lucie County schools are closed. I just thank God they’re not school today, so the kids then should be more safe at home, he said. Some residents are also stocking up on food and supplies. Shoppers told CBS12 they’re preparing to stay home if roads flood again. The district said updates about school operations will be shared on its website and social media channels. Martin County canceled after-school activities. Schools in Indian River and Okeechobee counties remain open as of Wednesday morning. Palm Beach County schools and offices are open Wednesday, but the district canceled all after-school activities and athletics because of the afternoon forecast. Aftercare families must pick up their children by 4 p.m., the district said.

entry.title: 'Overwhelming': St. Lucie County residents prepare for heavy rainfall with sandbag stations - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Overwhelming': St. Lucie County residents prepare for heavy rainfall with sandbag stations    WPBF
entry.article_text: St. Lucie County residents are preparing for heavy rainfall this week, with officials offering free self-serve sandbag stations and working to clear drainage systems to address potential flooding. Dreamland Park in Fort Pierce, residents were seen filling sandbags to protect their homes. Resident Lisa Powell is concerned. "My ditches are full from the last storm, they haven't gone down, so this could be very bad. The water is just still standing there, up to the yard." Another resident shared their concerns, saying, "My crawlspace got a foot of water in there, so trying to get all these bags to try and cover up the opening, you know." Public works crews in St. Lucie County are actively checking and clearing swales and drainage systems as the area braces for more severe weather. Recent flooding left parts of the county submerged, with residents in the Creekside development trapped inside, some using kayaks to navigate flooded streets while others waded through the water. Fredrick Reeves, a resident whose home was previously flooded, is preparing for the upcoming rain by using sandbags and mulch to block water from entering his house. "It was pretty bad, and the house itself, once it started coming in, I thought maybe we would be alright. I threw down all my clothes trying to soak it up, but that didn't do anything. The next thing you knew, it was in the house," Reeves said. He described the situation as "overwhelming." The City of Fort Pierce is offering free self-serve sandbag stations at Martin Luther King Jr. Dreamland Park and Jaycee Park. Residents are advised to bring their own bags and shovels. Both parks are open daily from dawn to dusk. St. Lucie County has also set up self-service sandbag distribution points at the St. Lucie County Fairgrounds West Parking Lot and Lawnwood Stadium Parking Lot, thanks to donations of sand from Dickerson Infrastructure and Stewart Materials. Residents must bring their own supplies and fill their own bags. For updates about the precautions residents should take, please visit St. Lucie County’s emergency management portal at: www.readystlucie.org. For more information, residents can contact the Public Works Department or visit the county’s emergency management portal. entry.title: Port St. Lucie family waits years for swale liner as standing water brings mosquitoes
entry.summary: A Port St. Lucie family says it has spent nearly four years trying to get a swale liner installed to keep stagnant water from lingering in its yard, a problem the family says leaves water sitting for days and turns the property into what they jokingly call a 'mosquito hotel.' Oprah Fasulo and her mother, Divika Todd, brought the problem to WPTV's Michael Hoffman after meeting him at WPTV's Let's Hear It community meetup in Jensen Beach. Their frustration centers on a yearslong wait and changing rules over who is responsible for installing the swale liner. Now, the city says the family is not alone and that it recently received approval to add a contractor to help speed up installations. Port St. Lucie family waits years for swale liner as standing water brings mosquitoesFamily says home fell between changing city rules Fasulo and Todd told Hoffman their problem dates back to when their Port St. Lucie home was built. At the time, the city was changing its rules surrounding responsibility for installing swale liners, which are designed to help keep water moving rather than allowing it to remain on properties. According to the family, installation had been the city's responsibility before shifting to builders. It has since shifted back to the city. Their house, they said, was built between those changes and never received one. The family eventually contacted Port St. Lucie. 'They said that they have to install it. The homeowners are not allowed to install it,' Fasulo said. Fasulo said she understood that requirement. What frustrated her was how long her family was told it would take. 'I understand that totally, but they told us that it was three years; it would be done,' she said. Now, Fasulo said the family has been told it could take another two years. That's when they turned to WPTV. 'We've seen you guys get results,' Fasulo told Hoffman. entry.title: Port St. Lucie extends boil water notice for 21,000 customers after main break
entry.summary: About 21,000 customers in Port St. Lucie remain under a precautionary boil water notice after a contractor damaged a water main earlier this week. The city announced it is extending the notice for the Tradition and west Port St. Lucie areas following Tuesday's water main break near Glades Cut Off Road. The notice covers all of Tradition, including Western Grove, Riverland, Wilson Grove and Southern Grove, as well as areas west of Interstate 95 south to Becker Road. Communities along Glades Cut Off Road, including Copper Creek, Wylder and Verano, are also affected. City officials said the notice will remain in place until water quality testing is successfully completed and the city determines it is safe to lift. With an estimated 21,000 customers affected, officials said a significant number of water samples must be collected and tested to ensure the water is safe. The city is asking residents not to tamper with clearly marked hydrants or pipes that are flushing water, warning that interference could delay testing and extend the notice. According to officials, the break was caused by a contractor working on a construction project unrelated to the city. Crews responded and repaired the damaged 36-inch water main within hours before beginning the required flushing process. The city is investigating the incident and expects to pursue appropriate action to recover costs from those responsible. There is no estimated time for when the boil water notice will be lifted. Residents can find updates at CityofPSL.com .

entry.title: DeSantis says Florida will seek another federal disaster declaration after historic flooding
entry.summary: Gov. Ron DeSantis said Florida is preparing to seek additional federal disaster assistance after a second round of historic flooding inundated communities across the state, with the St. Johns River reaching record levels and hundreds of people requiring rescue. Speaking Monday in Brevard County alongside state and local emergency officials, DeSantis said parts of Cocoa Beach and surrounding communities received 15 to 20 inches of rain in recent days. Many of those areas were still recovering from severe flooding earlier this month. WATCH BELOW: Florida seeking more federal aid after historic flooding, according to DeSantis DeSantis says Florida seeking more federal aid after historic flooding DeSantis said the St. Johns River near Cocoa reached nearly 19 feet on Saturday, surpassing the previous record by more than a foot. He warned that because the river moves slowly, flooding could take weeks or even months to fully recede. 'There could be more flooding that happens in the near future,' DeSantis said. 'The St. Johns River is a major concern just given how high it has gotten.' Florida preparing another disaster declaration request Florida previously requested a major federal disaster declaration following the first round of flooding earlier this month. DeSantis said that request is awaiting action from the federal government. The state is now collecting damage assessments from the latest flooding and plans to submit another request for a major disaster declaration. DeSantis said the second request will cover a broader area because more counties and communities were affected by the latest rainfall. Florida Division of Emergency Management Executive Director Jared Perdue said the state could have enough damage information to move forward with the request as soon as Monday or Tuesday. DeSantis said he expects the request to warrant federal approval. 'It's basically just the damage assessments trying to show that there's been enough damage to justify federal intervention,' DeSantis said. 'And I think in this case that that has been the case.' DeSantis also said individual assistance included in the state's initial request could provide some relief to residents with damaged homes, including those who did not carry flood insurance. However, he cautioned that federal assistance may not cover the full amount of a homeowner's losses. However, he cautioned that federal assistance may not cover the full amount of a homeowner's losses.State agencies, including the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, Florida National Guard, Florida State Guard and Florida Highway Patrol, have completed nearly 500 floodwater rescues, according to DeSantis.The Florida National Guard has mobilized 421 personnel and conducted 417 welfare checks, while deploying 54 high-water vehicles across six counties.Another 173 FWC officers are deployed, along with more than 200 FHP troopers assisting flooded communities, stranded motorists and disabled vehicles.Nearly 160 Florida State Guard personnel have also been mobilized. State Guard crews have helped with "muck and gut" operations at more than 250 properties in Brevard and Okeechobee counties, removing water-damaged material from flooded homes.The state has distributed more than 22,000 boxes of water, 7,500 ready-to-eat meals, 1,200 flood cleanup buckets and 1,300 tarps to affected communities, according to Perdue.Emergency officials warned that high water remains a threat even as conditions begin to improve.Perdue said State Road 50 in Brevard County and State Road 46 in Seminole County remained underwater as of Monday."If there are any state roads or local roads that are underwater, please do not drive or walk through the water," Perdue said. "It can be very dangerous. You just can't see what's down there."The Florida Division of Emergency Management has deployed more than 10,000 feet of temporary flood barriers to protect critical infrastructure, including government buildings and lift stations in Seminole County and HCA Florida Lake Monroe Hospital in Sanford.The state has also deployed 90 pumps and 22 vacuum trucks during the response in Brevard, Broward, Indian River, Flagler, Palm Beach, St. Lucie and Volusia counties.FDOT has more than 750 personnel working on flood assessments and pumping operations across Central and South Florida, DeSantis said.A shelter remains open at the Joseph N. Davis Community Center in Melbourne.Four multi-agency resource centers have also been established across three counties, including two in Brevard County. DeSantis said more than 1,600 residents have already received assistance through the centers. The centers will be closed on Thanksgiving.Residents whose homes are uninhabitable because of flooding can also apply for the state's temporary travel trailer program through emergencyRV.org.DeSantis said state resources will remain in affected communities throughout the recovery."Our folks aren't going anywhere," DeSantis said. We're going to see through the federal assistance and make sure that people can get back on their feet."

entry.title: Driving for Thanksgiving? Check these parts of your car before hitting the road
entry.summary: If you're driving for Thanksgiving, don't wait until the last minute to make sure your car is ready for the trip. Before packing the car and hitting the road, take a few minutes to check your vehicle. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Before you travel for Thanksgiving, make sure your car is road-trip ready Start with the tires . Check the air pressure on all four tires, including the spare. Look for low tread, cracks or other signs of damage that could cause trouble during a long drive. Next, pop the hood and check your oil, coolant and windshield-washer fluid . Make sure everything is at the proper level before leaving home. Drivers should also check their headlights, brake lights and turn signals to make sure they're working properly. Don't forget about the battery . If your vehicle is slow to start or the battery is several years old, consider having it tested before your Thanksgiving trip. It's also a good idea to pack an emergency kit with water, a flashlight, phone charger and basic first-aid supplies. Taking a few minutes to inspect your vehicle before leaving could help prevent a breakdown and keep your Thanksgiving road trip from ending on the side of the road.

entry.title: Palm Beach County partners help families facing food insecurity this Thanksgiving
entry.summary: Hundreds of Palm Beach County families are getting help putting Thanksgiving dinner on the table through SPECTRA, the nonprofit arm of the Palm Beach County Housing Authority, as community partners work to address food insecurity during the holiday season. SPECTRA recently helped distribute 300 frozen turkeys and is now preparing Thanksgiving fixings for families in South Bay, according to Naderge Alcime, ROSS coordinator with the Palm Beach County Housing Authority. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Community partners help bring Thanksgiving dinner to Palm Beach County families The assistance comes as the Housing Authority says more than 280 additional families are on its waiting list for help. Filling needs beyond housing SPECTRA was created to help address needs that extend beyond putting a roof over someone's head. 'SPECTRA is our not-for-profit arm of the Housing Authority,' Chief Financial Officer Tad Fuller said. 'The Housing Authority, of course, houses individuals and families within our county. SPECTRA's job is to fill in those missing middle pieces.' Fuller said those needs can include food, transportation and other services for residents. For some families, food insecurity can mean making difficult choices between basic necessities. entry.title: WPTV Anchor Hollani Davis emcees 2026 Black Chamber of Palm Beach County Ascension Awards
entry.summary: More than 150 people turned out for the 14 th Annual Black Chamber of Commerce Ascension Awards. The Awards recognize small minority owned businesses and business owners that continue to help sustain Palm Beach County. WPTV Morning Anchor Hollani Davis was the emcee of the annual brunch, this year held at the Wellington National Golf Club. Nearly 30 professionals and businesses in restaurant/dining, marketing, human resources, consulting services, mentoring, public relations, legal and more were honored. The 2026 Ascension Award winners are: Nonprofit/Public Sector Organization of the Year - NAACP West Palm Beach Chapter Emerging Black Business of the Year - Kitty Lundan (Pop Star Productions) Distinguished Black Business of the Year - Dr. J. Sheree (Evolve Total Health) Young Professional of the Year - Ray Nelson Dicky Sykes Social Justice Advocate Award - Telsula Morgan (Partner, Lewis Longman Walker PA) The President's Award - John Carpenter (FAU Associate Director of Executive Education). This year's awards also paid tribute to Leontyne Brown. The Palm Beach County natives work included spearheading initiatives like 'Pretty Girls Vote'. Brown served on the Board of Directors of the Black Chamber for nearly 15 years. She is the longest-serving Board Secretary and was posthumously recognized as Secretary Emeritus through a special resolution by the Board. Brown passed away this past Spring.

entry.summary: Pedestrian killed in train incident in Fort Pierce, several crossings blocked    WPEC
entry.article_text: A pedestrian was killed Sunday morning in an incident involving a freight train at the Seaway Drive railroad crossing in Fort Pierce, authorities said. The incident was reported at about 7:16 a.m. Nov. 22. The St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said it was assisting the Fort Pierce Police Department, the lead agency investigating. A southbound freight train about 2 miles long was stopped, blocking Seaway Drive and affecting crossings at Avenue H, Old Dixie Highway and Chamberlain Boulevard. Motorists traveling to or from the Seaway Drive Bridge were advised to use the Avenue C or Citrus Avenue bridges as alternate routes and avoid the affected crossings. Fort Pierce police will release additional information about the investigation.

See also: DeSantis expands Florida emergency order to 21 counties amid flooding The heaviest rainfall threat is farther north, according to an update from Indian River County Emergency Services. Officials are asking drivers to check road conditions before traveling, allow extra time for detours and never drive through flooded roads. As of 9 a.m. Friday, flooding or roadway damage was affecting these locations: U.S. 1 near Barber Street: Partial blockage Old Dixie Highway SW: Flooding and partial blockages at several locations 82nd Avenue at the entrance to Heritage Plantation: Partial blockage Skyline Drive, from Periwinkle to Barber Street: Partial blockage 130th Street: Closed 79th Street west of 130th Avenue: Closed because of a roadway washout 13th Street SW east of 66th Avenue SW: Closed because of roadway damage Vero Lake Estates: 104th Avenue between 87th and 93rd streets, and 83rd Street between 91st and 93rd avenues, are closed The county said the list includes selected locations. Drivers can check the live road closure map for additional closures and updates. Officials said water needs time to recede and damaged roads must be assessed and repaired before they can safely reopen. Crews are working in affected areas, and drivers are asked to give them room and follow barricades. Facility and school updates The Indian River County Shooting Range, Gifford Aquatic Center and North County Aquatic Center are open Friday. Marian Fell Library and the Veterans Services office in Sebastian remain closed. The School District of Indian River County is closed Friday. Check the district website for updates. The county said the Indian River County Fairgrounds may be used in the coming days to support emergency management missions for communities to the north, where the threat of heavy rain and flooding is greater.

entry.article_text: A controversial proposal to build a more than 1.6 million-square-foot data center just half a mile from an elementary school is drawing growing opposition in Martin County, where residents are raising concerns about everything from environmental impacts to whether they'll have a say in the project's approval.WATCH: 'We need answers': Martin Co. officials address outrage over proposed data centerOn Friday morning, a small but vocal group of residents gathered outside the Martin County Administrative Center, demanding answers about the massive development proposed for a parcel of land off Kanner Highway, west of Interstate 95.They had planned to attend a meeting with the county's Growth Management Department. But less than 17 hours before it was scheduled to begin, the county canceled it, citing overwhelming public interest.Residents showed up anyway."We need answers, and we need them quick," said Chris McIntyre, whose son graduated from nearby Crystal Lake Elementary School. "This story cannot die, or else this is the death of Crystal Lake School."McIntyre, who goes by Coach Mack, became emotional discussing what the proposed development could mean for the school and surrounding neighborhoods."Now that's the death of an A-rated elementary school that I love," he said, his voice breaking.He's far from alone.Residents have raised concerns about potential noise pollution, water consumption, increased electricity demand, higher utility bills, wildlife displacement, declining property values and possible health impacts on children attending Crystal Lake Elementary.Michael Panella, another resident opposing the project, became emotional while explaining why the fight is so personal."It's life. These little ones are innocent," Panella said, referring also to students of Crystal Lake. Dan Wilson, president of the Locks Landing homeowners association, represents a community less than two miles from the proposed site.“They’re probably dropping now because, oh, the data center going there. We don’t want to move there,” Wilson said of property values."We have residences right here, tons of residents. We're all going to have to deal with this."Residents acknowledge they don't yet know for sure what the long-term consequences of the project might be. They don't know whether electricity bills will increase, how much noise the facility could generate or what wildlife habitat might be lost.But they do know that once something of this magnitude is built, there's no easy way to undo it.The controversy intensified Thursday evening when Martin County announced the cancellation of an informal Growth Management meeting scheduled for 9:30 a.m. Friday.At 4:55 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 19, the Martin County Board of County Commissioners posted the following message online:For residents who had planned to attend, the cancellation only added to their frustration."The thing that frustrates me the most about this is the fact that they were willing to do this meeting in private," said resident Alisha Gibbs.Gibbs described herself as "disgusted" and "absolutely appalled" by the situation.But Martin County Deputy Growth Management Director Pete Walden told WPTV Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey that the meeting was never intended to be a formal public hearing or a decision-making session.Instead, Walden said, it was an informal meeting requested by members of the public who wanted to ask county staff questions about the development — something his department routinely accommodates for other projects.He said information about the meeting circulated online, creating the impression that county officials were privately considering a decision on the data center.When interest grew beyond what the county could accommodate, officials decided to cancel."We could not accommodate that. We didn't have any rooms or anything available for that size," Walden explained. "So we had to cancel, and we'll do some workshops in the future. I believe the applicant is also going to reach out for some public presentations on the subject." When asked why residents weren't being given more opportunities to weigh in, Walden maintained the county has been transparent."We are transparent through the process, and everything can be made available to anyone that is interested," he said.Walden said additional public meetings and workshops will be scheduled to allow residents to ask questions and learn more about the project.But the canceled meeting is only one of several controversies surrounding the development.Another major point of contention is the timing of the developer's application.On Oct. 27, Martin County commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on data centers, temporarily restricting new applications while the county reviews its development regulations.But records show the application for this project was submitted the day before the moratorium was proposed on October 13. That timing means the project is not subject to the temporary restriction, according to county officials.Walden acknowledged the timing but said the county cannot control when developers submit applications."They obviously saw like everybody else that a moratorium was coming, and they got their application in ahead of time," Walden said. "We don't direct applicants ... and we certainly can't pick and choose when these things happen."WPTV reached out to the project applicant and the law firm representing it, requesting comment on the timing of the application and residents' environmental, energy and health concerns.Neither responded by publication time.Perhaps the most significant concern for opponents is whether residents will have any formal say in the project's approval.Under a county ordinance adopted in 2010, during the Great Recession, Martin County established an administrative approval process for certain targeted industries to encourage economic development.Data centers fall within the county's targeted industry classifications. According to Walden, the proposed development is also covered by an existing planned unit development, or PUD, agreement that allows qualifying targeted industries on platted industrial lots to receive administrative approval.That means the project could potentially move forward without a public hearing or recorded vote by county commissioners.For residents demanding a voice in the decision, that distinction is critical.Hussey asked Walden whether there was anything the county could do to give residents more of a say in whether the development is approved."With the moratorium, we'll be looking at our code to make revisions so everything is appropriately reviewed as it comes in," Walden said."To give the public more of a say in future projects?" Hussey asked. "Correct," Walden responded. Residents are also demanding answers about how a development of this size could affect surrounding neighborhoods, wildlife and students at Crystal Lake Elementary School.The proposal initially called for just under 1 million square feet of development. An updated application brings the total to approximately 1.6 million square feet, including an existing warehouse.Among the concerns raised by residents are the potential effects of noise from cooling equipment, increased water and electricity consumption, wildlife habitat loss and possible impacts on nearby property values.Those concerns remain questions, not established consequences of the proposed development.Walden said the county will review the project's potential impacts before making any approval decision.He also emphasized that despite speculation circulating in the community, the data center has not been approved."There is a misconception that this project was already approved — that's very far from the truth," Walden said."This is our first data center to be reviewed. We're going to take our time ... and make sure everything is properly vetted."The county says a staff report examining the project is expected to be released in December.Following that report, officials plan to schedule a public forum, likely including a presentation from the applicant, where residents can ask questions and learn more about the development.No date for that meeting has been announced.For opponents, the controversy goes beyond whether a data center belongs on acres of industrial land.It's about who gets to decide what their community becomes — and whether the people who will live with the consequences have a meaningful opportunity to influence that decision.The residents who gathered outside the county building Friday made clear that canceling a meeting would not end their opposition."If they want to actually please the public, they would deny this proposal," Gibbs said.

entry.title: Jensen Beach Festival of Giving brings together more than 50 local nonprofits - WFLX
entry.summary: Jensen Beach Festival of Giving brings together more than 50 local nonprofits    WFLX
entry.article_text: More than 50 local nonprofits are coming together for the third annual Festival of Giving at the Children’s Museum of the Treasure Coast, filling the Jensen Beach museum with holiday displays while allowing community organizations to share the work they do throughout the region. Christina McIntosh, community outreach and events coordinator for the Children’s Museum of the Treasure Coast, said participating nonprofits come from communities stretching from Palm Beach County north through the Treasure Coast. “Those are the five counties that our education department here at the museum works with and works with the schools,” McIntosh said. More than Christmas decorations The Festival of Giving uses decorated Christmas trees and holiday displays to introduce visitors to nonprofit organizations serving South Florida and the Treasure Coast. For the organizations involved, the gathering also provides a chance to learn more about one another. Treasure Coast Community Singers is among the nonprofits participating. “The really great thing about this event is that we get to know other nonprofits,” Sharon Savageaux of Treasure Coast Community Singers said. “We get to understand what they do. And we can help spread their word.” The singers also performed at the museum during a festival breakfast event. A Grinch-themed tree with a community mission The GFWC Hobe Sound Woman’s Club is also participating, decorating its display with a Grinch theme. Sandy Vucik, who represented the organization at the festival, said the money it raises supports several community organizations, including Family Promise, CareBag and Real Life Children’s Ranch in Okeechobee. Vucik said the club is currently helping 19 children at the ranch. “We’re really hoping to give them a nice Christmas,” Vucik said. The holiday setting gives visitors a chance to discover organizations they may not otherwise encounter while allowing nonprofits themselves to make new community connections. The festival includes several special events beyond its nonprofit displays. “Santa’s coming into town,” McIntosh said. “He loves this event, so the kids will be able to visit with him.” Family Night is scheduled for Tuesday evening on Nov. 17, at the Children’s Museum of the Treasure Coast. An adult holiday pajama party follows Friday The celebration takes a turn for the grown-ups Friday with an adult holiday pajama party. “We will be a museum full of adults dressed in their holiday pajamas because who doesn’t want to go to a party and go home and go right to bed,” McIntosh said. The festival continues through Saturday, Nov. 21, at 2 p.m., according to McIntosh. The Children’s Museum of the Treasure Coast is located at 1707 NE Indian River Drive in Jensen Beach. entry.title: 1 dead, passenger critically injured in 4-vehicle crash near I-95 in Riviera Beach
entry.summary: One person was killed and another suffered life-threatening injuries in a four-vehicle crash near Interstate 95 in Riviera Beach early Sunday morning, police said. The Riviera Beach Police Department said officers and Riviera Beach Fire Rescue responded to the intersection of West Blue Heron Boulevard and I-95 around 5:32 a.m. after the city's communications center received multiple 911 calls reporting a crash. Police said investigators determined that a 2022 Nissan Altima exited the northbound I-95 ramp and continued across the median, striking a 2021 Acura ILX that was stopped at a red light while facing west and waiting to turn onto southbound I-95. The initial impact led to a chain-reaction crash involving two other vehicles, according to police. The driver of the Acura was pronounced dead at the scene. A 26-year-old passenger had to be extricated from the vehicle and was taken to a hospital with life-threatening injuries. Police said the driver and passenger of the Nissan were also taken to a hospital with injuries that were not considered life-threatening. The names of those involved have not been released pending notification of their families. The Riviera Beach Police Department's Traffic Homicide Unit is investigating the crash. Police said criminal charges are pending. Anyone with information about the crash is asked to contact Riviera Beach police at 561-845-4123.

Rose and her team have been tracking the Trump administration's use of 287(g) agreements. entry.article_text: New research shows Florida law enforcement agencies could earn more than $1 billion in federal funding through next year for helping the Department of Homeland Security with immigration enforcement operations — far beyond what any other state could receive for its participation.Since February 2025, every law enforcement agency in Florida is required to have a 287(g) agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The agreement allows state and local law enforcement officers to conduct immigration enforcement activities on ICE's behalf. The 287(g) program has been around for 30 years."(It's) basically a program that if someone came into the jail, then the jail could run their information through an immigration database and alert ICE if they had an immigration detainer or some civil immigration issue, and then ICE could come and pick them up," said Felicity Rose, vice president of research and policy at fwd.us, a bipartisan advocacy organization that focuses on immigration and criminal justice. Rose and her team have been tracking the Trump administration's use of 287(g) agreements. They recently published a report using public and leaked records to estimate how much money local law enforcement agencies are getting from ICE in exchange for participating in 287(g)."Those partnerships are both sending billions of dollars to state and local law enforcement with very little oversight," Rose said.I asked Rose for her data on each sheriff's office in our five-county viewing area. In Palm Beach County, the report estimates more than $16 million in available funding for fiscal year 2026. In Martin County, the estimate is nearly $1.8 million, along with $5.3 million in St. Lucie County, $1.7 million in Okeechobee County and $880,000 in Indian River County."After the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act in the summer of 2025 passed, they gave $191 billion to (the U.S. Department of Homeland Security). One thing they decided to do with that was start paying people who signed up for the task force model," Rose explained.ICE breaks down its 287(g) task force payment structure on its website: initial stipends of $100,000, plus $7,500 per credentialed officer. Then, quarterly stipends of $15,000 per officer per quarter. That's on top of salary reimbursement for officers' time working immigration enforcement, plus "quarterly monetary performance awards based on the successful location of illegal aliens.""That money led to a major change in the number of agencies signing up and, very importantly, the number of arrests that they were making," Rose said.The Florida Department of Law Enforcement tracks 287(g) arrests throughout the state. Their data states that since August 2025, the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office had 361, the Okeechobee County Sheriff's Office carried out 37, Indian River County had 38 and St. Lucie County had 15. The Martin County Sheriff's Office had 1,095 287(g) arrests.The Martin County Sheriff's Office declined an interview for this story, but Sheriff John Budensiek spoke to us in December 2025 about accepting funding to help with immigration detention."I don't think our taxpayers should be taxed again. I think the federal government, if they're going to use us as a tool, should pay for their portion of that," Budensiek said.A spokeswoman for MCSO told me in a statement that "The Martin County Sheriff's Office has not conducted any recent immigration enforcement operations under the 287(g) program. Individuals without lawful immigration status who are arrested on local criminal charges in Martin County are booked into the Martin County Jail. The number of those bookings is substantially lower than the figure you cited."Mariana Blanco and her team at the Guatemalan Maya Center in Lake Worth Beach have also been tracking immigration arrests and working with the families impacted by them."When you begin monetizing these arrests, now you lose sight of the protection of the people, and that's exactly what we're seeing," Blanco said.She tells me she's noticed a change in how and where those arrests have happened in recent months in Palm Beach County."So they're not just taking the driver in the vehicle; they're taking the passengers as well," Blanco said."When (people) called to report crimes, (deputies) have been arresting them because of their — due to their immigration status," Blanco said.I asked her if the person who called to report the crime gets arrested, and she confirmed that they do.I asked Blanco whether she worries about the impact that will have on crime overall in Lake Worth."Crime has been heavily under-reported in Lake Worth and I know that because PBSO has asked us for help in ... giving a sense of security for the people to report crimes," Blanco said. "We said, well, respectfully, we don't trust you, and so how would we tell the people that they could trust you?" The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office didn't respond to my requests for comment.The fwd.us report estimates law enforcement agencies across Florida could be eligible for a total of up to $1.4 billion through fiscal year 2027 from the federal government. The report also estimates that Florida has deputized 9,021 law enforcement officers under the 287(g) task force model and conducted 15,164 arrests since January 2025.To compare, the report shows Texas, the state believed to be eligible for the second-highest payday through 287(g), is estimated to qualify for roughly $421 million through FY 2027. The state is estimated to have deputized 4,082 officers and conducted 9,138 arrests through the program (although Rose noted that Florida provides more data on 287(g) than other states).I filed public records requests with our five local sheriff's offices to see how they were spending that money, beyond reimbursement for deputies' time. Those requests are still pending.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

entry.title: Riviera Beach mayor calls on community to help rebuild Lone Pine Estates after severe flooding
entry.summary: Riviera Beach Mayor Douglas Lawson is asking businesses, nonprofits, faith groups and volunteers to help families in Lone Pine Estates repair their homes after severe flooding earlier this month. Lawson announced the 'Rebuild Lone Pine Together' initiative Monday, calling on community partners to donate building materials and supplies, provide volunteers and offer other resources to residents recovering from the flooding. WATCH BELOW: Riviera Beach weighs flood relief plan Riviera Beach weighs $2M flood relief plan as residents demand help Heavy rain this month flooded homes and left neighborhood streets underwater, forcing some residents from their homes, according to the city. Riviera Beach declared a state of emergency on Nov. 2 as crews worked to pump water from flooded areas and assess the damage. City officials said some families continue to deal with flood damage as they work toward returning home. WATCH BELOW: Riviera Beach residents rescued from floodwaters Riviera Beach residents rescued from flooding 'These families need more than words. They need building materials, helping hands, and neighbors who will stand with them. I'm asking our community to answer that call,' Lawson said in a statement. Through Rebuild Lone Pine Together, the mayor's office is seeking help from businesses, nonprofits, faith organizations, service groups and individual residents. People and organizations can assist by donating building materials and other supplies, volunteering to help with recovery efforts or providing other resources that could help affected families repair their homes. Those interested in helping can contact the Riviera Beach Mayor's Office at 561-845-4145 or the Sincere 2000 Foundation at 561-385-4469. The initiative comes as residents of Lone Pine Estates continue recovering from a month marked by significant rainfall and flooding across parts of South Florida.

entry.title: Nearly 1.8 million chickens to be depopulated after bird flu detected at Okeechobee County facility
entry.summary: Nearly 1.8 million chickens will be depopulated after highly pathogenic avian influenza, commonly known as bird flu, was detected at a Cal-Maine Foods facility in Okeechobee County. Cal-Maine Foods announced Nov. 18 that the facility tested positive for highly pathogenic avian influenza, or HPAI. The company said the outbreak will lead to the depopulation of approximately 1.4 million laying hens and 360,000 pullets, representing about 2.7% of the company's total flock. Production at the Okeechobee County facility has temporarily stopped while Cal-Maine follows protocols established by the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services has established a quarantine area following the detection, according to St. Lucie County government. The poultry quarantine extends from Okeechobee County into a rural portion of western St. Lucie County north of State Road 70 near the county line. People who own or care for poultry within the affected area are being advised to review the state's quarantine restrictions, which include limits on moving poultry and poultry products without FDACS authorization. Residents can check whether they are within the affected area using the state's interactive quarantine map. Cal-Maine said it is coordinating production and distribution among its other facilities in an effort to maintain its egg supply and minimize disruptions for customers. The company also said it maintains biosecurity programs at its facilities but noted that no farm is immune to HPAI. The virus remains present among wild birds, and the risk of outbreaks can increase during bird migration seasons. Health officials say the detection does not mean consumers should stop eating eggs. According to information provided by the company, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention considers the health risk from HPAI viruses to the general U.S. public to be low. The USDA also says HPAI is not transmitted through properly handled and cooked eggs. Cal-Maine said there is no known HPAI risk associated with eggs currently on the market and that no eggs have been recalled because of the outbreak. Cal-Maine said it is working with federal, state and local officials as it responds to the outbreak and works to reduce the risk of additional infections. entry.title: WPTV anchor Hollani Davis emcees 2026 Black Chamber of Palm Beach County Ascension Awards
entry.summary: More than 150 people turned out for the 14th Annual Black Chamber of Commerce Ascension Awards. The Awards recognize small minority-owned businesses and business owners who continue to help sustain Palm Beach County. WPTV Morning anchor Hollani Davis was the emcee of the annual brunch, this year held at the Wellington National Golf Club. Nearly 30 professionals and businesses in restaurant/dining, marketing, human resources, consulting services, mentoring, public relations, legal and more were honored. The 2026 Ascension Award winners are: Nonprofit/Public Sector Organization of the Year - NAACP West Palm Beach Chapter Emerging Black Business of the Year - Kitty Lundan (Pop Star Productions) Distinguished Black Business of the Year - Dr. J. Sheree (Evolve Total Health) Young Professional of the Year - Ray Nelson Dicky Sykes Social Justice Advocate Award - Telsula Morgan (Partner, Lewis Longman Walker PA) The President's Award - John Carpenter (FAU Associate Director of Executive Education). This year's awards also paid tribute to Leontyne Brown. The Palm Beach County natives work included spearheading initiatives like 'Pretty Girls Vote'. Brown served on the Board of Directors of the Black Chamber for nearly 15 years. She is the longest-serving Board Secretary and was posthumously recognized as Secretary Emeritus through a special resolution by the Board. Brown passed away this past Spring.

entry.title: New memorial honors two Indian River County deputies killed in line of duty
entry.summary: The sound of bagpipes and taps filled the air Saturday as the Indian River County Sheriffs Office unveiled a new memorial honoring two deputies killed in the line of duty. The memorial, located outside the sheriffs offices new administration building, honors Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow and Cpl. Richard Raczkoski. Their deaths happened 40 years apart. Now, their names have a permanent place together. WATCH: New memorial honors two Indian River County deputies killed in line of duty New memorial honors fallen deputies The unveiling came exactly one year after Sweeting-Mashkow was killed while serving an eviction notice at a home in the Bermuda Club community. 47-year-old Sweeting-Mashkow was one of three deputies serving the eviction notice on Nov. 21, 2025, when authorities said 37-year-old Michael Halberstam retrieved a weapon and opened fire. Sweeting-Mashkow was killed, and Deputy Florentino Arizpe was shot in the shoulder. A locksmith who was there for the eviction, David Long, was also critically wounded and later died from his injuries. Sweeting-Mashkow had served with the Indian River County Sheriffs Office for more than 25 years. Her death marked the second line-of-duty death in the 100-year history of the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. For those who gathered Saturday, the passage of a year has not made that loss feel distant. Its an honor to be out here but also very sad, community member Joanne Knott said. To think that it happened a year ago is strange because it feels like it was yesterday. The memorial also reaches back four decades, honoring Cpl. Richard Raczkoski, who was killed in the line of duty 40 years ago. The two heroes that are on this memorial are two people that our community will remember forever, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said. Hundreds of family members, friends, law enforcement officers and community members gathered for Saturdays unveiling, paying their respects. I am so glad that they did this for Terri and Raczkoski, one community member said. For those at the ceremony, the memorial is also a reminder of the risks law enforcement officers face each time they go to work. All of these officers that step out into the community, they never know what their day is going to bring, says Knott. Flowers hopes the two names on the memorial will be the only ones it ever bears: I hope we never have to add names to this memorial again.'

entry.title: St. Lucie County commissioners to consider Port of Fort Pierce master plan Dec. 1 - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County commissioners to consider Port of Fort Pierce master plan Dec. 1    WPEC
entry.article_text: St. Lucie County commissioners are scheduled to consider adopting the final draft of the 2026 Port of Fort Pierce Master Plan during their Dec. 1 meeting. County Port, Inlet and Beaches staff will present the plan at the meeting, which begins at 6 p.m. Commissioners can ask questions and approve the document as presented or amend it before adoption, according to the county. The update builds on the port’s 2020 master plan and incorporates feedback from residents and industry stakeholders since commissioners last reviewed the draft on Aug. 11. The plan is intended to guide future development and help the county seek state and federal grants for port improvements. Among the long-term opportunities in the draft is a Launch Vehicle Recovery Facility to support offshore rocket recovery operations, including drone ships and other support vessels. As CBS12 previously reported, the proposed facility could position Fort Pierce to support recovery work tied to Florida’s growing space industry . The plan describes it as one part of a broader working waterfront vision, alongside mega-yacht services, marine research and workforce training, recreation and public access. The rocket-recovery proposal is one part of a broader vision for the Port of Fort Pierce as a mixed-use working waterfront. The plan also outlines Harbour Pointe as a public-facing district, with a regional boat ramp, waterfront dining and commercial space, an entertainment pavilion, a shared-use path and a living shoreline. The update also envisions a marine research and workforce training campus focused on marine science, environmental education and training for waterfront jobs. It calls for continued growth of the port’s mega-yacht maintenance and repair operations, as well as a marina at Museum Pointe where yachts could dock temporarily for crew changes, provisioning or staging before service. The plan includes infrastructure and access projects, such as a new road to Harbour Pointe, stormwater improvements and a possible connection to the regional Sun Trail. It also proposes a future Port to Park link to improve access between the waterfront and Franklin Park. See also: 3 auto insurers directed to refund $122 million in excess profits to Florida customers The 2026 update supplements the port’s 2020 master plan rather than replacing it. The document lays out a long-term vision for development; proposed zoning changes and the Port Overlay District remain under discussion. The county says commissioners will consider the plan during their regular meeting in the Commission Chambers on the third floor of the Roger Poitras Administration Annex, 2300 Virginia Ave. in Fort Pierce. The meeting will also be streamed on the county’s website and YouTube channel. Residents can review the draft plan on the county’s Port Master Plan webpage .

entry.article_text: New research shows Florida law enforcement agencies could earn more than $1 billion in federal funding through next year for helping the Department of Homeland Security with immigration enforcement operations — far beyond what any other state could receive for its participation.Since February 2025, every law enforcement agency in Florida is required to have a 287(g) agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The agreement allows state and local law enforcement officers to conduct immigration enforcement activities on ICE's behalf. The 287(g) program has been around for 30 years."(It's) basically a program that if someone came into the jail, then the jail could run their information through an immigration database and alert ICE if they had an immigration detainer or some civil immigration issue, and then ICE could come and pick them up," said Felicity Rose, vice president of research and policy at fwd.us, a bipartisan advocacy organization that focuses on immigration and criminal justice. Rose and her team have been tracking the Trump administration's use of 287(g) agreements. They recently published a report using public and leaked records to estimate how much money local law enforcement agencies are getting from ICE in exchange for participating in 287(g)."Those partnerships are both sending billions of dollars to state and local law enforcement with very little oversight," Rose said.I asked Rose for her data on each sheriff's office in our five-county viewing area. In Palm Beach County, the report estimates more than $16 million in available funding for fiscal year 2026. In Martin County, the estimate is nearly $1.8 million, along with $5.3 million in St. Lucie County, $1.7 million in Okeechobee County and $880,000 in Indian River County."After the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act in the summer of 2025 passed, they gave $191 billion to (the U.S. Department of Homeland Security). One thing they decided to do with that was start paying people who signed up for the task force model," Rose explained.ICE breaks down its 287(g) task force payment structure on its website: initial stipends of $100,000, plus $7,500 per credentialed officer. Then, quarterly stipends of $15,000 per officer per quarter. That's on top of salary reimbursement for officers' time working immigration enforcement, plus "quarterly monetary performance awards based on the successful location of illegal aliens.""That money led to a major change in the number of agencies signing up and, very importantly, the number of arrests that they were making," Rose said.The Florida Department of Law Enforcement tracks 287(g) arrests throughout the state. Their data states that since August 2025, the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office had 361, the Okeechobee County Sheriff's Office carried out 37, Indian River County had 38 and St. Lucie County had 15. The Martin County Sheriff's Office had 1,095 287(g) arrests.The Martin County Sheriff's Office declined an interview for this story, but Sheriff John Budensiek spoke to us in December 2025 about accepting funding to help with immigration detention."I don't think our taxpayers should be taxed again. I think the federal government, if they're going to use us as a tool, should pay for their portion of that," Budensiek said.A spokeswoman for MCSO told me in a statement that "The Martin County Sheriff's Office has not conducted any recent immigration enforcement operations under the 287(g) program. Individuals without lawful immigration status who are arrested on local criminal charges in Martin County are booked into the Martin County Jail. The number of those bookings is substantially lower than the figure you cited."Mariana Blanco and her team at the Guatemalan Maya Center in Lake Worth Beach have also been tracking immigration arrests and working with the families impacted by them."When you begin monetizing these arrests, now you lose sight of the protection of the people, and that's exactly what we're seeing," Blanco said.She tells me she's noticed a change in how and where those arrests have happened in recent months in Palm Beach County."So they're not just taking the driver in the vehicle; they're taking the passengers as well," Blanco said."When (people) called to report crimes, (deputies) have been arresting them because of their — due to their immigration status," Blanco said.I asked her if the person who called to report the crime gets arrested, and she confirmed that they do.I asked Blanco whether she worries about the impact that will have on crime overall in Lake Worth."Crime has been heavily under-reported in Lake Worth and I know that because PBSO has asked us for help in ... giving a sense of security for the people to report crimes," Blanco said. "We said, well, respectfully, we don't trust you, and so how would we tell the people that they could trust you?" The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office didn't respond to my requests for comment.The fwd.us report estimates law enforcement agencies across Florida could be eligible for a total of up to $1.4 billion through fiscal year 2027 from the federal government. The report also estimates that Florida has deputized 9,021 law enforcement officers under the 287(g) task force model and conducted 15,164 arrests since January 2025.To compare, the report shows Texas, the state believed to be eligible for the second-highest payday through 287(g), is estimated to qualify for roughly $421 million through FY 2027. The state is estimated to have deputized 4,082 officers and conducted 9,138 arrests through the program (although Rose noted that Florida provides more data on 287(g) than other states).I filed public records requests with our five local sheriff's offices to see how they were spending that money, beyond reimbursement for deputies' time. Those requests are still pending.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

entry.title: William T. Dwyer cements status as golf powerhouse with back-to-back state championships
entry.summary: For years, when you thought of sports at William T. Dwyer, you thought of football, basketball and baseball. However, for the past two years, Dwyer has been a statewide golf powerhouse, securing back-to-back state championships. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Dwyer captures second straight state golf title Dwyer golfers capture second straight state championship 'It was really cool; it was really fun. We had an early pretty big lead, and it kind of got closer at the end,' said sophomore golfer Matthew Marigliano. With the boys giving up an early lead on the greens, the ship was righted by a stellar freshman, Martin Bustos, who shot an even par in his final round. 'It was pretty awesome; it was pretty great we had a great team this year, and it was pretty fun,' said Bustos. Pretty fun might be an understatement; this season, the team lost only once. But when it mattered most, they won districts, regionals and their second straight state crown, defeating Beachside High School with a final score of 584. To cap off the amazing weekend, William Cui, the outstanding junior, sank a clutch 15-foot birdie to capture an individual state championship. 'It was really nice to win individually. This was my third time playing in states, so it's a course I like and know well. So I got pretty aggressive out there and hit some good shots, and it worked out well,' said Cui.

entry.title: Thanksgiving airfare jumps 17% as travelers face higher prices, potential delays
entry.summary: The holiday rush to the airport for Thanksgiving is underway , and passengers are paying more this year to fly. According to AAA, the average domestic round-trip flight is costing $800. That figure is up 17% from a year ago, largely because of jet fuel costs. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Thanksgiving Travel Begins With Higher Airfares and Concern Over Delays 'We've seen increases this year anywhere between 20 and 30%,' said Clint Henderson at The Points Guy website. 'My fear is, the CEOs are basically getting used to these higher costs, and they've suggested that even if the cost of jet fuel drops, they may not lower prices that much.' entry.article_text: New research shows Florida law enforcement agencies could earn more than $1 billion in federal funding through next year for helping the Department of Homeland Security with immigration enforcement operations — far beyond what any other state could receive for its participation.Since February 2025, every law enforcement agency in Florida is required to have a 287(g) agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The agreement allows state and local law enforcement officers to conduct immigration enforcement activities on ICE's behalf. The 287(g) program has been around for 30 years.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "(It's) basically a program that if someone came into the jail, then the jail could run their information through an immigration database and alert ICE if they had an immigration detainer or some civil immigration issue, and then ICE could come and pick them up," said Felicity Rose, vice president of research and policy at fwd.us, a bipartisan advocacy organization that focuses on immigration and criminal justice. Rose and her team have been tracking the Trump administration's use of 287(g) agreements. They recently published a report using public and leaked records to estimate how much money local law enforcement agencies are getting from ICE in exchange for participating in 287(g)."Those partnerships are both sending billions of dollars to state and local law enforcement with very little oversight," Rose said.I asked Rose for her data on each sheriff's office in our five-county viewing area. In Palm Beach County, the report estimates more than $16 million in available funding for fiscal year 2026. In Martin County, the estimate is nearly $1.8 million, along with $5.3 million in St. Lucie County, $1.7 million in Okeechobee County and $880,000 in Indian River County.PREVIOUS COVERAGE: Several local police departments are enrolled in 287(g) program"After the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act in the summer of 2025 passed, they gave $191 billion to (the U.S. Department of Homeland Security). One thing they decided to do with that was start paying people who signed up for the task force model," Rose explained.ICE breaks down its 287(g) task force payment structure on its website: initial stipends of $100,000, plus $7,500 per credentialed officer. Then, quarterly stipends of $15,000 per officer per quarter. That's on top of salary reimbursement for officers' time working immigration enforcement, plus "quarterly monetary performance awards based on the successful location of illegal aliens.""That money led to a major change in the number of agencies signing up and, very importantly, the number of arrests that they were making," Rose said.The Florida Department of Law Enforcement tracks 287(g) arrests throughout the state. Their data states that since August 2025, the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office had 361, the Okeechobee County Sheriff's Office carried out 37, Indian River County had 38 and St. Lucie County had 15. The Martin County Sheriff's Office had 1,095 287(g) arrests.The Martin County Sheriff's Office declined an interview for this story, but Sheriff John Budensiek spoke to us in December 2025 about accepting funding to help with immigration detention."I don't think our taxpayers should be taxed again. I think the federal government, if they're going to use us as a tool, should pay for their portion of that," Budensiek said.A spokeswoman for MCSO told me in a statement that "The Martin County Sheriff's Office has not conducted any recent immigration enforcement operations under the 287(g) program. Individuals without lawful immigration status who are arrested on local criminal charges in Martin County are booked into the Martin County Jail. The number of those bookings is substantially lower than the figure you cited."Mariana Blanco and her team at the Guatemalan Maya Center in Lake Worth Beach have also been tracking immigration arrests and working with the families impacted by them."When you begin monetizing these arrests, now you lose sight of the protection of the people, and that's exactly what we're seeing," Blanco said.She tells me she's noticed a change in how and where those arrests have happened in recent months in Palm Beach County."So they're not just taking the driver in the vehicle; they're taking the passengers as well," Blanco said."When (people) called to report crimes, (deputies) have been arresting them because of their — due to their immigration status," Blanco said.I asked her if the person who called to report the crime gets arrested, and she confirmed that they do.I asked Blanco whether she worries about the impact that will have on crime overall in Lake Worth."Crime has been heavily under-reported in Lake Worth and I know that because PBSO has asked us for help in ... giving a sense of security for the people to report crimes," Blanco said. "We said, well, respectfully, we don't trust you, and so how would we tell the people that they could trust you?" The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office didn't respond to my requests for comment.The fwd.us report estimates law enforcement agencies across Florida could be eligible for a total of up to $1.4 billion through fiscal year 2027 from the federal government. The report also estimates that Florida has deputized 9,021 law enforcement officers under the 287(g) task force model and conducted 15,164 arrests since January 2025.To compare, the report shows Texas, the state believed to be eligible for the second-highest payday through 287(g), is estimated to qualify for roughly $421 million through FY 2027. The state is estimated to have deputized 4,082 officers and conducted 9,138 arrests through the program (although Rose noted that Florida provides more data on 287(g) than other states).I filed public records requests with our five local sheriff's offices to see how they were spending that money, beyond reimbursement for deputies' time. Those requests are still pending.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

entry.title: Nearly 1.8 million chickens to be depopulated after bird flu detected at Okeechobee County facility
entry.summary: Nearly 1.8 million chickens will be depopulated after highly pathogenic avian influenza, commonly known as bird flu, was detected at a Cal-Maine Foods facility in Okeechobee County. Cal-Maine Foods announced Nov. 18 that the facility tested positive for highly pathogenic avian influenza, or HPAI. The company said the outbreak will lead to the depopulation of approximately 1.4 million laying hens and 360,000 pullets, representing about 2.7% of the company's total flock. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Bird flu detected at Okeechobee County poultry facility Production at the Okeechobee County facility has temporarily stopped while Cal-Maine follows protocols established by the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services has established a quarantine area following the detection, according to St. Lucie County government. The poultry quarantine extends from Okeechobee County into a rural portion of western St. Lucie County north of State Road 70 near the county line. People who own or care for poultry within the affected area are being advised to review the state's quarantine restrictions, which include limits on moving poultry and poultry products without FDACS authorization. Residents can check whether they are within the affected area using the state's interactive quarantine map. Cal-Maine said it is coordinating production and distribution among its other facilities in an effort to maintain its egg supply and minimize disruptions for customers. The company also said it maintains biosecurity programs at its facilities but noted that no farm is immune to HPAI. The virus remains present among wild birds, and the risk of outbreaks can increase during bird migration seasons. Health officials say the detection does not mean consumers should stop eating eggs. According to information provided by the company, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention considers the health risk from HPAI viruses to the general U.S. public to be low. The USDA also says HPAI is not transmitted through properly handled and cooked eggs. Cal-Maine said there is no known HPAI risk associated with eggs currently on the market and that no eggs have been recalled because of the outbreak. Cal-Maine said it is working with federal, state and local officials as it responds to the outbreak and works to reduce the risk of additional infections. entry.title: 'Don't come here and do stupid things': Two accused of breaking into Martin County business to play games - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Don't come here and do stupid things': Two accused of breaking into Martin County business to play games    WPBF
entry.article_text: Two men are facing felony burglary charges after allegedly breaking into a Hutchinson Island business to play video games after hours, the Martin County Sheriff's Office said. The incident occurred late Saturday into early Sunday morning at the Indian River Plantation Shopping Plaza, according to Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek. A security guard on patrol noticed something unusual and called 911. "He happens upon an individual that had the back door of a restaurant/bowling alley game room, and as he tried to confront that individual, he fled," Budensiek said. Footage from the sheriff's Air One unit showed deputies tracking a suspect from above. "He should be coming up on your right side. Stop, stop the car," a deputy said in the video. Deputies located one man walking down the road and another emerging from the woods with an electric scooter. "Facedown, facedown, all the way down," a deputy said during the arrest. The sheriff said the suspects were identified as 29-year-old Ferdinand Schoedinger IV of New Hampshire and 33-year-old James Bolon of Ohio. Both men were reportedly placed at Local Lanes Duckpin Bowling and Eatery on Hutchinson Island. The sheriff said one of the suspects admitted they broke into the business because they wanted to play video games after it had closed. "They had been there earlier, had enjoyed it, were trying to come back and continue playing Pac-Man. And ended up in a serious game of hide-and-go-seek with the Martin County Sheriff's Office," Budensiek said. Budensiek also issued a warning to visitors. "Don't come here and do stupid things; definitely don't come here and try to victimize our citizens," he said. Both suspects have bonded out but face felony burglary charges. entry.summary: Boil water notice lifted for 21,000 Port St. Lucie customers after water main break    WPEC
entry.article_text: Thousands of Port St. Lucie residents can put away their pots after city officials lifted a precautionary boil water notice Saturday afternoon. The City of Port St. Lucie announced the all-clear at 3:15 p.m. Saturday after water quality tests confirmed the water was safe to drink. The notice affected approximately 21,000 customers in Tradition and areas west of Interstate 95 following a water main break Tuesday near Glades Cut Off Road. See also: A helping of hope: 600 turkeys bring Thanksgiving cheer to South Florida families Residents in the following communities no longer need to boil their water: Tradition Western Grove Riverland Wilson Grove Southern Grove Copper Creek Wylder Verano The affected area stretched west of I-95 south to Becker Road, including communities along Glades Cut Off Road. According to city officials, the break occurred when a contractor working on a construction project unrelated to the city damaged a 36-inch water main. City crews responded immediately and completed repairs within hours. Flushing and required water quality testing followed. After tests confirmed the water was safe, officials lifted the precautionary notice. The city thanked the roughly 21,000 affected customers for their patience throughout the disruption.

entry.summary: Cleanup crews and residents are continuing to clear damage left behind by an EF-1 tornado that tore through southern Palm Beach County on Saturday evening, toppling trees and damaging homes, vehicles and other property from west Boca Raton through west Delray Beach. WATCH: EF-1 tornado cleanup continues in Delray Beach EF-1 Tornado Leaves Trail of Damage in Delray Beach | WPTV The National Weather Service said the tornado reached peak winds of 102 mph and traveled 7.64 miles after first touching down around 6:04 p.m. near Boca Gardens. It remained on the ground until about 6:31 p.m., ending southwest of Boynton Beach. No deaths or injuries were reported. WPTV crews surveying damage in the Delray Beach area found a massive tree that came crashing down and crushed a stone wall. Landscaping crews said they have been clearing damaged and fallen trees since Sunday. Resident describes hearing 'a train coming through' Tony Symia lives in an apartment just feet from where the tornado passed. He told WPTV the storm announced itself with a sound he had never experienced before. 'Well, we heard it was like a train coming through,' Symia said. 'It was pretty rumbling when it came through, and I rushed my wife into the bathroom, and it only lasted about a minute.' 'I kind of think I reacted late because it all started prior to me getting her into the bathroom,' he said. entry.title: St. Lucie County commissioners to consider Port of Fort Pierce master plan Dec. 1 - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County commissioners to consider Port of Fort Pierce master plan Dec. 1    WPEC
entry.article_text: St. Lucie County commissioners are scheduled to consider adopting the final draft of the 2026 Port of Fort Pierce Master Plan during their Dec. 1 meeting. County Port, Inlet and Beaches staff will present the plan at the meeting, which begins at 6 p.m. Commissioners can ask questions and approve the document as presented or amend it before adoption, according to the county. The update builds on the port’s 2020 master plan and incorporates feedback from residents and industry stakeholders since commissioners last reviewed the draft on Aug. 11. The plan is intended to guide future development and help the county seek state and federal grants for port improvements. Among the long-term opportunities in the draft is a Launch Vehicle Recovery Facility to support offshore rocket recovery operations, including drone ships and other support vessels. As CBS12 previously reported, the proposed facility could position Fort Pierce to support recovery work tied to Florida’s growing space industry . The plan describes it as one part of a broader working waterfront vision, alongside mega-yacht services, marine research and workforce training, recreation and public access. The rocket-recovery proposal is one part of a broader vision for the Port of Fort Pierce as a mixed-use working waterfront. The plan also outlines Harbour Pointe as a public-facing district, with a regional boat ramp, waterfront dining and commercial space, an entertainment pavilion, a shared-use path and a living shoreline. The update also envisions a marine research and workforce training campus focused on marine science, environmental education and training for waterfront jobs. It calls for continued growth of the port’s mega-yacht maintenance and repair operations, as well as a marina at Museum Pointe where yachts could dock temporarily for crew changes, provisioning or staging before service. The plan includes infrastructure and access projects, such as a new road to Harbour Pointe, stormwater improvements and a possible connection to the regional Sun Trail. It also proposes a future Port to Park link to improve access between the waterfront and Franklin Park. See also: 3 auto insurers directed to refund $122 million in excess profits to Florida customers The 2026 update supplements the port’s 2020 master plan rather than replacing it. The document lays out a long-term vision for development; proposed zoning changes and the Port Overlay District remain under discussion. The county says commissioners will consider the plan during their regular meeting in the Commission Chambers on the third floor of the Roger Poitras Administration Annex, 2300 Virginia Ave. in Fort Pierce. The meeting will also be streamed on the county’s website and YouTube channel. Residents can review the draft plan on the county’s Port Master Plan webpage .
