entry.article_text: A water meter data collection issue in Martin County caused some utility customers to receive unusually high water bills, according to Martin County Utilities. The county said the problem dates back about five months and affected the reporting of water usage for some customers. After the issue was corrected, water usage that had not previously been reported was reflected on a single month's bill, resulting in a higher-than-normal charge for affected customers. Martin County Utilities said the issue affects some customers in these communities: Customers with questions about their bills or who need assistance can contact Martin County Utilities customer service at cservice@martin.fl.us. The county said a customer service representative can work with affected residents to establish a payment arrangement. Martin County Utilities said it has since implemented additional training and safeguards within its data collection software. Let us know on our Facebook page!

entry.title: St. Lucie County commissioners to consider Port of Fort Pierce master plan Dec. 1 - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County commissioners to consider Port of Fort Pierce master plan Dec. 1    WPEC
entry.article_text: St. Lucie County commissioners are scheduled to consider adopting the final draft of the 2026 Port of Fort Pierce Master Plan during their Dec. 1 meeting. County Port, Inlet and Beaches staff will present the plan at the meeting, which begins at 6 p.m. Commissioners can ask questions and approve the document as presented or amend it before adoption, according to the county. The update builds on the port’s 2020 master plan and incorporates feedback from residents and industry stakeholders since commissioners last reviewed the draft on Aug. 11. The plan is intended to guide future development and help the county seek state and federal grants for port improvements. Among the long-term opportunities in the draft is a Launch Vehicle Recovery Facility to support offshore rocket recovery operations, including drone ships and other support vessels. As CBS12 previously reported, the proposed facility could position Fort Pierce to support recovery work tied to Florida’s growing space industry . The plan describes it as one part of a broader working waterfront vision, alongside mega-yacht services, marine research and workforce training, recreation and public access. The rocket-recovery proposal is one part of a broader vision for the Port of Fort Pierce as a mixed-use working waterfront. The plan also outlines Harbour Pointe as a public-facing district, with a regional boat ramp, waterfront dining and commercial space, an entertainment pavilion, a shared-use path and a living shoreline. The update also envisions a marine research and workforce training campus focused on marine science, environmental education and training for waterfront jobs. It calls for continued growth of the port’s mega-yacht maintenance and repair operations, as well as a marina at Museum Pointe where yachts could dock temporarily for crew changes, provisioning or staging before service. The plan includes infrastructure and access projects, such as a new road to Harbour Pointe, stormwater improvements and a possible connection to the regional Sun Trail. It also proposes a future Port to Park link to improve access between the waterfront and Franklin Park. See also: 3 auto insurers directed to refund $122 million in excess profits to Florida customers The 2026 update supplements the port’s 2020 master plan rather than replacing it. The document lays out a long-term vision for development; proposed zoning changes and the Port Overlay District remain under discussion. The county says commissioners will consider the plan during their regular meeting in the Commission Chambers on the third floor of the Roger Poitras Administration Annex, 2300 Virginia Ave. in Fort Pierce. The meeting will also be streamed on the county’s website and YouTube channel. Residents can review the draft plan on the county’s Port Master Plan webpage .

entry.title: Dolphins bring energy to Thanksgiving week practice as they prepare for Jets rematch
entry.summary: The Miami Dolphins were on the practice field Wednesday as they prepare for Sunday's battle against the New York Jets. The rain forced the team indoors, but that didn't stop the Fins from bringing nonstop energy at practice. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Rain can't dampen Dolphins' energy as team preps for Jets On the injury front, cornerback Juju Brents was out Wednesday, but everyone else was a full go. Although the rain tore through South Florida on Thanksgiving Eve, the Dolphins laced up their cleats to prepare for the New York Jets. 'This is going to be a long season, and there is always going to be a Thanksgiving, there is always going to be a Thanksgiving, a Christmas, and other holidays, and you have to push through,' head coach Jeff Hafley said. Rain stormed through South Florida this week, but it didn't slow the grind for new quarterback Kyle McCord, who's learning the NFL game on the fly as he and the Fins welcome the Jets to Hard Rock Stadium this Sunday. In Week 7, the Dolphins beat the Jets 28-25 at MetLife Stadium to earn their only win of the season. 'It's just another great opportunity to keep growing and keep rolling and keep getting better,' McCord said. With two starts under his belt, McCord credits rookie wide receiver Caleb Douglas with helping ease him into a new role. 'There's a reason we try to get him the ball; he's a great player, but at the same time we're both young players in the league and continuing to grow,' McCord said. For Douglas, he's shown the most promise on offense, but like any rookie, he's had some growing pains, including drops. So Wednesday afternoon, he worked with specialized glasses to help with vision, but number seven has his eyes set on Sunday's game against their division rival. 'I'm really excited and blessed with another opportunity to go out there and keep proving it,' said Douglas. With Thanksgiving on Thursday, we wanted to know what these guys have on their plates. 'I'm getting a little bit of everything, you know. I'm getting some Turkey, some ham, mac and cheese, some collard greens,' offensive lineman Austin Jackson said. 'I hope I go home today and Ma Duke's got the kitchen good, man. I can't wait to get that first scoop of macaroni and greens,' running back Ollie Gordon said.

entry.title: Top American golf courses rated, where do Florida courses rank?
entry.summary: What is the best golf course in America? Golf.com broke down the top 100 courses, which they call a 'Top 100 Courses in the U.S. for 2026-27: The ultimate bucket list for American golf' . So, how do they determine the list? It's a democratic vote with the panelists. Golf.com said each panelist gets a ballot with hundreds of courses. Beside the list of courses are 11 groupings. If a panelist considers a course to be among the top three in the U.S., they tick the first column. If they believe the course to be among Nos. 4-10, they check that column, followed by 11-25 and so on. They even have a column for remove.  The organization is also careful with panelist selections to include a variety of input and to avoid anyone with ties to any of the courses. Research shows golf is experiencing a resurgence as a hobby. The National Golf Foundation reports that 30.6 million Americans play golf, that's up 1.7 million from the previous year and a new record. Did any Florida courses make the list? Course: TPC Sawgrass (Players Stadium) , Ponte Vedra Beach Rank: 53 Built: 1981 Designer : Pete Dye Course : Seminole , Juno Beach Rank: 17 Built: 1926 Designer: Donald Ross

entry.title: 4 men arrested after attempted home invasion at Martin County’s Evergreen Club - cw34.com
entry.summary: 4 men arrested after attempted home invasion at Martin County’s Evergreen Club    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A Palm City teenager's quick thinking may have stopped four men from breaking into his family's home at the Evergreen Club community off Murphy Road. The Martin County Sheriff's Office says the 17-year-old boy heard a noise outside their home on SW Bimini Circle at 3 a.m. Tuesday. He alerted his parents who called 911, interrupting the home invasion. When deputies arrived at the scene, the four suspects, three men and a teenager from Jacksonville, ran away in different directions. The sheriff's office says deputies set up a perimeter around the neighborhood with help from its aviation team, K-9 unit, and the Stuart Police Department. K9's were able to track down all four suspects hiding in separate locations throughout the community. The teen was found hiding in a bush outside the community. Two of the men were found hiding under a nearby bridge off Murphy Road. The fourth person was in a nearby parking lot who detectives believe was the getaway driver. The sheriff's office says at least one of the suspects was armed with a handgun. Sheriff John Budensiek said three of the four suspects have violent criminal histories. "These are bad, bad individuals who drove at least three and a half hours to Martin County to victimize a family that was going throughout their normal nightly routines," Budensiek said. Investigators said the suspects parked along the canal and walked half a mile into the neighborhood to target the home. The group is seen on home security video around 3 a.m. wearing dark clothing, masks and gloves. The sheriff said they tried to break in through a back door and covered a surveillance camera lens with a sticker. Deputies found masks, gloves and a firearm that had been stolen. Homeowners at the Evergreen Club community were shaken up. "I immediately woke up to Facebook and texts this morning, friends and family asked me if I was okay," said resident Katherine Willis. "Absolutely shocked that they would try to come in here. What are you going to get out of here? It's just very out of the ordinary for sure." The suspects were identified as: Nathaniel Phillip Wise Jr, 22 Za'kyri Isreal Emmanuel Crews, 21 Cameron Elijah Mapson, 21 Teenage boy, 16 All four were charged with attempted home invasion. Wise faces an additional charge of grand theft and possession of a firearm. They're all being held in the Martin County Jail without bond. See also: Boca Raton police arrest man after reported assault on El Rio Trail The agency is asking Palm City residents to check their homes and vehicles for missing property or signs of a break-in. Anyone who finds anything missing should call the sheriff’s office at 772-220-7060. "The Martin County Sheriff's Office is heavily invested in protecting our community," Budensiek said. "To these traveling criminals, we're gonna put you away forever if we can."

entry.title: Treasure Coast beaches under advisory due to high bacteria levels - WPBF
entry.summary: Treasure Coast beaches under advisory due to high bacteria levels    WPBF
entry.article_text: Health officials are warning swimmers to avoid water-related activities at several locations along the Treasure Coast due to elevated bacteria levels following recent heavy rain and flooding. Jetty Park Beach in Fort Pierce is among the affected areas, where advisory signs have been posted to alert visitors. "Heavy amounts of rain that we've experienced here in St. Lucie County, really here on the Treasure Coast, have resulted in higher bacteria levels in our waterways," Erick Gill, Communications Director at St. Lucie County Board of County Commissioners said. The Florida Department of Health reported that tests conducted Monday revealed enterococcus bacteria levels exceeding state guidelines at eight locations in St. Lucie County and three in Martin County. "A lot of it is the heavy rainfall and the runoff that we're getting, and agricultural as well as some septic tanks that may have been impacted by the amount of rain and flooding that we've gotten over the last couple of weeks," Gill said. Health officials are advising against swimming and other water-related activities at the affected locations due to an increased risk of illness. For some beach visitors, like Enma Kennedy, the advisories are not a deterrent to enjoying the scenery. "We get to enjoy it regardless of what's going. We have family that just flew in yesterday from California, their first time here, and look where we are. Rather rain or shine, we're here," Kennedy said. In St. Lucie County, advisories remain in effect at Jetty Park Beach, South Beach Causeway, Little Jim Bridge, Jaycee Park, Surfside Park, Walton Rocks Beach, Blue Heron, and Frederick Douglass Memorial Park. Health officials said the advisories will remain in place until bacteria levels fall below accepted health standards. Gill is also warning everyone to be look out for fire ants. "In addition to the bacteria levels residents should be aware that there are a lot of fire ants out there and other wildlife out there that might be seeking drier grounds so be cautious, when you're out hiking or playing in the back yard because fire ants are seeking shelter as well," Gill said. entry.title: Port St. Lucie man sentenced to nearly 4 years in $260K AI cryptocurrency fraud scheme - WPTV
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie man sentenced to nearly 4 years in $260K AI cryptocurrency fraud scheme    WPTV
entry.article_text: A Port St. Lucie man has been sentenced to nearly four years in federal prison for using artificial intelligence to impersonate a popular online streamer as part of a cryptocurrency fraud scheme that authorities say cost victims about $260,000.David Anthony Sanchez, 36, was sentenced to 47 months in federal prison after pleading guilty to money laundering and aggravated identity theft, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida.Federal prosecutors said Sanchez, who also went by "Dave the Jewler," "Rueben Alexis De Jesus Santana" and other aliases, impersonated online streamer N3ON to convince organizers of a cryptocurrency memecoin project that the streamer had agreed to endorse and participate in it.According to court records, Sanchez created online accounts designed to look as though they belonged to N3ON and communicated with the project's organizers while posing as both the streamer and his representative.Prosecutors said Sanchez also executed agreements using N3ON's identity and sent organizers an AI-generated voice recording that mimicked the streamer's voice to falsely confirm his participation.Believing the representations were legitimate, the victims transferred approximately $260,000 in cryptocurrency to accounts controlled by Sanchez, according to prosecutors.Authorities said Sanchez later converted a substantial portion of the cryptocurrency into U.S. dollars through transactions designed to conceal the source and ownership of the money. Prosecutors said he used the proceeds for his personal benefit."Behind every fraud scheme are real people who suffer real financial harm," Acting U.S. Attorney Yara Lorenzo Klukas said in the release. She said Sanchez exploited artificial intelligence to manipulate victims' trust and take their money.In addition to his 47-month prison sentence, Sanchez was ordered to pay restitution to the victims. The amount of restitution was not specified in the release.The FBI's Miami Field Office investigated the case.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie woman says flood damage left her 'landlocked' as road caved due to flooding - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie woman says flood damage left her 'landlocked' as road caved due to flooding    WPEC
entry.article_text: Frances Bertino has lived on Lakehurst Drive for nearly 30 years. For the past three weeks, a hole in the road outside her home has kept her from making the right turn out of her driveway. "I've been here since 1996 when we built the house," Bertino said. "I never had any problems until that. Until now." The hole is about five feet wide and sits in the middle of the road. It opened during the Nov. 2 storm that flooded much of St. Lucie County. The City of Port St. Lucie's flooded streets dashboard lists Lakehurst Drive between Sandia Drive and Prinville Street as "closed indefinitely due to infrastructure damage." Bertino said that when the road first closed, the barricades blocked her driveway. "They said if I got out of it, I was going to get arrested," she said. "I couldn't sleep at night thinking I'm landlocked." The barricades were later moved back. Now she turns around and drives out the other way. It seems funny at first," she said. Her neighbor, who often gives her rides, has had to change how he gets in and out. "Now he pulls in the driveway, now backs up and pulls out." See also: Travelers pack DJT airport ahead of Thanksgiving amid jitters over recent outages Bertino said she reported the damage to the city and was told a water pipe was involved. Asked whether she had heard anything since, she said, "No, I have heard nothing." On Wednesday afternoon, while CBS12 was interviewing her, city crews arrived to inspect the hole. "This is the first time they've been out to inspect it that I know of, because I didn't see anybody here," Bertino said. Three weeks." Asked whether the inspection gave her confidence the road would be fixed soon, she said, "I hope so." City spokesperson Scott Samples said a temporary fix for Lakehurst Drive is expected sometime next week. "The long-term fixes may take a little bit longer, but our goal is to try to get those temporary fixes in place as quickly as we can to make sure that people have access in and out of their homes," Samples said. Samples said the early November storm forced five road closures in the city, and two are still closed. The other is Ann Arbor between Pier Court and Jerico Lane. He said crews decide which roads to fix first based on how bad the damage is and how many people depend on that road. He said the repeated rain has slowed the work. Wednesday's Flood Watch is the third the city has prepared for since the start of the month. "This kind of weather makes it harder to continue to do those kinds of repairs," Samples said. He said supplies are another problem. Flooding up and down Florida's east coast has put many communities in need of the same repair materials at once. "A lot of those materials that we require to be able to fix those roads, it makes it harder to obtain those," he said. The storm also filled the swale outside her home. Bertino said she had seen water that high only once before, during Hurricanes Frances and Jeanne in 2004. "It was all the way to the top. I could not believe it," she said. "We're talking about Frances and Jeanne. And this is just a storm." Lakehurst Drive is one of two streets the city lists as closed indefinitely for infrastructure damage. The other is Ann Arbor between Pier Court and Jerico Lane. The closures come as federal help begins to reach the region. President Donald Trump approved Florida's request for a Major Disaster Declaration for the flooding that began Oct. 31. That makes FEMA individual assistance available to residents of St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River, Okeechobee, Palm Beach and Brevard counties. The aid can help pay for temporary housing, home repairs, and uninsured property losses. Homeowners, renters and small businesses can also apply for low-interest SBA disaster loans. FEMA says families should file insurance claims first, then apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or by calling 1-800-621-3362. The declaration does not yet cover St. Lucie County's local governments. Five of the six counties were also approved for FEMA public assistance, which pays local governments back for debris removal and emergency work. St. Lucie County was not on that list. The National Weather Service in Melbourne has St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River, Okeechobee and Brevard counties under a Flood Watch until 1 a.m. Thursday. Forecasters say 1 to 3 inches of rain is most likely, with 4 to 5 inches or more possible in some spots. They warn that heavy rain on already soaked ground could flood roads and low-lying areas.

entry.title: Martin County flood victims fear more devastation as county braces for another foot of rain - WPTV
entry.summary: Martin County flood victims fear more devastation as county braces for another foot of rain    WPTV
entry.article_text: Just weeks after historic flooding destroyed homes and displaced families in Jensen Beach, Martin County residents are bracing for another round of heavy rain — with up to 12 inches forecast over the next three days.For families still struggling to recover, the threat of more flooding comes as county commissioners work to determine what caused the initial disaster and how to help those who lost nearly everything.On Tuesday, flood victims packed a Martin County Commission meeting, pleading for financial assistance and answers.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Along Cheri Drive in Jensen Beach, the signs of destruction remain. Dumpsters line driveways, damaged belongings sit outside and families are still trying to salvage what's left of their homes.Lisa French, her husband, Jeremy, and their two young sons are among those displaced after floodwaters rose as high as 3 feet inside some homes two weeks ago."It's like we're kind of stuck," French told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey. French said her home had about 3 to 6 inches of flooding that sat inside for more than a week, causing mold to grow 3 to 4 feet up the walls. "So they, yeah, they tore the walls down in the house," said French. "They just chipped up the last bit of the tile, and it's empty." Now, with more rain approaching, French fears her family could face another disaster before recovering from the first."Of course, we're afraid because we all flooded in our houses," she said.New figures released by Martin County show at least 36 homes sustained damage, with an estimated $3 million in residential losses. Commissioners estimated another $14 million in damage to beaches, and at least $1 million in damage to roadways that now need repairs. For some residents, the destruction represents a lifetime of memories washed away."We've lost everything," one elderly Jensen Beach resident told commissioners. "We have 60 years of our life — kids, grandkids, everything. It's all gone."As residents demand answers about what went wrong, commissioners approved shifting $200,000 from the county's stormwater budget to investigate whether development and changes to local drainage systems contributed to the flooding.Commissioner Blake Capps called the investigation "a good starting point.""It may be that we need to augment the study beyond the $200,000 that we approve today," said Capps. Meanwhile, county crews are working around the clock to prepare for the next storm, lowering retention pond levels, deploying additional pumps and draining flooded properties."We have people 24 hours a day pumping that material down," Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said.Commissioners also approved financial assistance for eligible flood victims through the state's State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program.The assistance includes grants of up to $25,000 for income-eligible homeowners and loans of up to $75,000 secured by liens on their properties.But there's a catch: The grants are reimbursement-based, meaning homeowners must first pay for eligible repairs before receiving the money.For families who lost everything, that presents another obstacle."We don't have $25,000," French said. "A lot of people don't have $25,000, so it's great, and we're appreciative, but I mean, our house is empty, and $25,000 is not going to do much for us." The other problem: the county currently has just $1 million in SHIP funding available, and commissioners warned the money could run out quickly, even with additional state funding promised."They haven't given us the amount yet, but they have assured us that we will be getting some disaster relief funds," said Human Services Director Michelle Miller Strict income limits could also disqualify some flood victims who cannot afford to rebuild on their own. The income cap for a family of one is $86,040. The cap for a family of two is $98,400. For a family of four, it's $122,880. When reporter Kate Hussey asked Capps what would happen to those families, he acknowledged the county needs to explore other options."There are going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where someone barely missed the limit, and we're going to need to take a look at what we can do for those folks," Capps said.For residents like French, the need is immediate."We just need somebody to step up," she said. "We need funding." With another round of heavy rain approaching, Martin County is distributing sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park to help residents protect their properties, with a limit of 25 per person. The County's Emergency Operations Center is scheduled to be staffed beginning Tuesday at 2 p.m., and the county is coordinating with the National Weather Service and Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM).Fire Rescue is also standing by with multiple high-water rescue trucks.Commissioners also said a Federal Emergency Management Agency representative is expected to visit Nov. 30 to assess the damage — a potential step toward securing federal disaster assistance.But for families still displaced and facing the possibility of more flooding, the uncertainty remains.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie woman says flood damage left her 'landlocked' as road caved due to flooding - cw34.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie woman says flood damage left her 'landlocked' as road caved due to flooding    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Frances Bertino has lived on Lakehurst Drive for nearly 30 years. For the past three weeks, a hole in the road outside her home has kept her from making the right turn out of her driveway. "I've been here since 1996 when we built the house," Bertino said. "I never had any problems until that. Until now." The hole is about five feet wide and sits in the middle of the road. It opened during the Nov. 2 storm that flooded much of St. Lucie County. The City of Port St. Lucie's flooded streets dashboard lists Lakehurst Drive between Sandia Drive and Prinville Street as "closed indefinitely due to infrastructure damage." Bertino said that when the road first closed, the barricades blocked her driveway. "They said if I got out of it, I was going to get arrested," she said. "I couldn't sleep at night thinking I'm landlocked." The barricades were later moved back. Now she turns around and drives out the other way. It seems funny at first," she said. Her neighbor, who often gives her rides, has had to change how he gets in and out. "Now he pulls in the driveway, now backs up and pulls out." See also: Travelers pack DJT airport ahead of Thanksgiving amid jitters over recent outages Bertino said she reported the damage to the city and was told a water pipe was involved. Asked whether she had heard anything since, she said, "No, I have heard nothing." On Wednesday afternoon, while CBS12 was interviewing her, city crews arrived to inspect the hole. "This is the first time they've been out to inspect it that I know of, because I didn't see anybody here," Bertino said. Three weeks." Asked whether the inspection gave her confidence the road would be fixed soon, she said, "I hope so." City spokesperson Scott Samples said a temporary fix for Lakehurst Drive is expected sometime next week. "The long-term fixes may take a little bit longer, but our goal is to try to get those temporary fixes in place as quickly as we can to make sure that people have access in and out of their homes," Samples said. Samples said the early November storm forced five road closures in the city, and two are still closed. The other is Ann Arbor between Pier Court and Jerico Lane. He said crews decide which roads to fix first based on how bad the damage is and how many people depend on that road. He said the repeated rain has slowed the work. Wednesday's Flood Watch is the third the city has prepared for since the start of the month. "This kind of weather makes it harder to continue to do those kinds of repairs," Samples said. He said supplies are another problem. Flooding up and down Florida's east coast has put many communities in need of the same repair materials at once. "A lot of those materials that we require to be able to fix those roads, it makes it harder to obtain those," he said. The storm also filled the swale outside her home. Bertino said she had seen water that high only once before, during Hurricanes Frances and Jeanne in 2004. "It was all the way to the top. I could not believe it," she said. "We're talking about Frances and Jeanne. And this is just a storm." Lakehurst Drive is one of two streets the city lists as closed indefinitely for infrastructure damage. The other is Ann Arbor between Pier Court and Jerico Lane. The closures come as federal help begins to reach the region. President Donald Trump approved Florida's request for a Major Disaster Declaration for the flooding that began Oct. 31. That makes FEMA individual assistance available to residents of St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River, Okeechobee, Palm Beach and Brevard counties. The aid can help pay for temporary housing, home repairs, and uninsured property losses. Homeowners, renters and small businesses can also apply for low-interest SBA disaster loans. FEMA says families should file insurance claims first, then apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or by calling 1-800-621-3362. The declaration does not yet cover St. Lucie County's local governments. Five of the six counties were also approved for FEMA public assistance, which pays local governments back for debris removal and emergency work. St. Lucie County was not on that list. The National Weather Service in Melbourne has St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River, Okeechobee and Brevard counties under a Flood Watch until 1 a.m. Thursday. Forecasters say 1 to 3 inches of rain is most likely, with 4 to 5 inches or more possible in some spots. They warn that heavy rain on already soaked ground could flood roads and low-lying areas.

entry.title: Businesses report fake City of Stuart invoice emails seeking thousands in project fees - WPEC
entry.summary: Businesses report fake City of Stuart invoice emails seeking thousands in project fees    WPEC
entry.article_text: The City of Stuart is warning local businesses and contractors about a fraudulent email scam involving fake invoices for development, building, planning, or project-related fees. According to the City, several businesses with active projects and applications have recently reported receiving emails claiming to be from the City of Stuart and requesting thousands of dollars in fees. In some cases recipients were instructed to wire funds. The City says it does not send invoices by email for these purposes, and that all official City development and permitting fees must be paid through the City’s official OpenGov application portal. One of the fraudulent email addresses reported to the City is: commissions.stuartfl.gov@usa.com. The City encourages applicants with active projects to remain vigilant and carefully review all correspondence related to their projects to prevent getting scammed.

[fsis.usda.gov]De Almeida also cautioned against washing a raw turkey because water that touches the bird can contaminate the sink and surrounding areas."Heat from the cooking process is sufficient to kill the bacteria," de Almeida said. "Washing the bird is OK, but you have to keep in mind that the water that has touched the bird can contaminate the sink."When it comes to determining whether Thanksgiving turkey is safe to eat, temperature matters."Cooking the poultry at a temperature that exceeds 165 is sufficient to prevent the risk of salmonella infection and other infections," de Almeida said.The USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service says turkey should reach a minimum internal temperature of 165 degrees Fahrenheit, measured with a food thermometer in the thickest part of the breast, innermost part of the thigh and innermost part of the wing. [fsis.usda.gov]If stuffing is cooked inside the turkey, the center of the stuffing should also reach 165 degrees. [fsis.usda.gov]Once Thanksgiving dinner is finished, food safety doesn't stop.Hoffman asked de Almeida how long people should keep digging into their Thanksgiving leftovers."Three days," de Almeida said. "So they have cooked the food on Thursday. They have Friday, Saturday, Sunday to get done with what was served."For additional context, federal food safety guidance gives a slightly broader window. The USDA advises refrigerating perishable leftovers within two hours and eating or freezing refrigerated Thanksgiving leftovers within three to four days. That makes the Monday after Thanksgiving the federal guidance's use-or-freeze deadline. [foodsafety.gov], [fsis.usda.gov]Leftovers should be reheated to an internal temperature of 165 degrees. [fsis.usda.gov]De Almeida advised people who are pregnant or immunocompromised to be particularly cautious with Thanksgiving leftovers."Women who are pregnant and immunocompromised people, they need to be extra cautious," de Almeida said. "And the rules for leftovers are more stringent, so they should consume the leftovers within one day."Food safety is especially important when preparing a large holiday meal with multiple dishes moving in and out of the refrigerator, oven and serving area.So while Thanksgiving is about good food, family and friends, keeping an eye on how that food is prepared, cooked, and stored can help ensure the holiday memories don't include a bout of food poisoning.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.summary: Truck-SUV crash cleared on Florida's Turnpike North in Martin County    WPEC
entry.article_text: A major multi-vehicle crash shut down all northbound lanes of Florida's Turnpike in Martin County on Tuesday afternoon, causing traffic disruptions for drivers. All northbound lanes were blocked, and the incident was classified as major. According to Florida 511, the crash is before mile marker 126 and mile marker 130. According to FHP, all northbound lanes reopened at 1:56 p.m. As of 3 p.m. the right shoulder is still blocked, according to Florida 511. The crash involved a medium-duty truck hauling a trailer loaded with pallets of mulch and a sport utility vehicle. Both vehicles were traveling northbound when the truck jackknifed and struck the wall and the SUV. Four individuals were transported to Florida Coast Medical Center, and one was transported to Martin Memorial South. Photos from the scene show multiple emergency vehicles and large trucks at the scene. Cars were also seen on the grass shoulder. The incident is classified as major. According to the Florida Highway Patrol , injuries are associated with the incident. See also: Boca Raton man accused of possessing, sharing 1TB of child, animal sex abuse material It is unclear what caused the crash.

entry.title: IRC sheriff renews push for unified 911 dispatch as Vero Beach weighs Amendment 3 cuts - WPEC
entry.summary: IRC sheriff renews push for unified 911 dispatch as Vero Beach weighs Amendment 3 cuts    WPEC
entry.article_text: Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers asked the Vero Beach City Council on Tuesday to take another look at merging emergency dispatch. He pitched it as a way to save money as the city prepares for revenue losses under Amendment 3 . Flowers said he first brought the idea to the council about two years ago. He said Brevard County has since moved to a unified dispatch system, and he told council members his offer still stands. "I'm not asking for anything specific today. I just want to make sure that it's known that it is my desire that we go to a unified dispatch system," Flowers said. He asked that it be considered "as a potential cost savings" as the city makes what he called "difficult decisions" under Amendment 3. Florida voters approved a ballot initiative that will slash non-school property taxes despite a campaign by local officials warning it would gut funding for public safety and other services. It will increase the homestead exemption from about $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Council member Tracey Zudans asked city staff to put numbers on the idea. "I'd love to see some numbers attached to it, not just response time numbers, but also some dollar numbers so that we can share that with our taxpayers as well," Zudans said. "I'd be happy to have my staff work with you guys," Flowers said. Mayor Aaron Vos said city staff will total what the city spends on dispatch now, and Flowers will bring back what it would cost the city to join a countywide call center. Vos said he expects a unified center would be run by the county, not the sheriff, similar to St. Lucie County's. Vice Mayor John Cotugno asked whether the dispatch center would be a county function or run by the sheriff's office. Flowers said the county technically runs dispatch, but most dispatchers work for his agency. "I have the bulk of dispatchers that work for me at the sheriff's office, so I can only offer it from my side," Flowers said. "You would have to ask the county if they were interested in maybe doing it differently." He added that the sheriff's office and the county are still discussing how Amendment 3 will affect their relationship. See also: 22-year-old West Palm Beach motorcyclist struck, killed by SUV in Loxahatchee That relationship has been strained before. In July 2025 a budget debate erupted during an Indian River County Commission meeting, prompting the board to call a 15-minute recess after tensions flared between commissioners and Flowers. Flowers was requesting $93.5 million that year, while the county recommended a budget closer to $83.5 million. Commissioners ultimately voted to raise the sheriff's budget by $6.8 million, far less than he requested. Flowers later sued the commission , which then held a special meeting over the sheriff's budget. "This is a very deep issue," Flowers said. "If we do it as a county, if we do it under me, either way, I'm just trying to get all of our dispatchers in the same room together." Council members took no action on the proposal. Vos said Amendment 3 means the city has to consider every option. "With the implications of Amendment 3, we have to look at all aspects of where we can save money," Vos said. "If it saves us money, that's what we need to do." But Vos said moving dispatch out of the police department could come with a hidden cost. "You could lose some of that rapport between the call center staff and the officers due to familiarity," he said. Vos said he talked with police leaders in Sebastian and Fellsmere after Flowers first pitched the idea. He said Sebastian police used the sheriff's call center until 2007, then went back to running their own. Vero Beach Police Chief David Currey said his position on keeping the city's dispatch center has not changed. Vero Beach and Sebastian police are the only agencies in the county that run their own dispatch. "The dispatchers know the officers. They know the community members," Currey said. "If we don't have that under our umbrella, then I don't have control over any of that." Currey said the department switched to a new computer-aided dispatch and records management system in June. He said the department is working with the sheriff's office to connect the two agencies' dispatch systems, which would let dispatchers see where deputies and officers are and handle calls without transferring them. Currey said the idea last came up around 2012. He said the sheriff at the time told the city that dispatching for Vero Beach would likely cost about the same, if not more. "We have ten dispatchers, and they have salaries, and they have benefits," Currey said. "That will cost him just like it'll cost us." Despite the uncertainty around Amendment 3, Currey said the department is not freezing hiring and is interviewing for a police officer position now.

entry.title: 4 men arrested after attempted home invasion at Martin County’s Evergreen Club - WPEC
entry.summary: 4 men arrested after attempted home invasion at Martin County’s Evergreen Club    WPEC
entry.article_text: A Palm City teenager's quick thinking may have stopped four men from breaking into his family's home at the Evergreen Club community off Murphy Road. The Martin County Sheriff's Office says the 17-year-old boy heard a noise outside their home on SW Bimini Circle at 3 a.m. Tuesday. He alerted his parents who called 911, interrupting the home invasion. When deputies arrived at the scene, the four suspects, three men and a teenager from Jacksonville, ran away in different directions. The sheriff's office says deputies set up a perimeter around the neighborhood with help from its aviation team, K-9 unit, and the Stuart Police Department. K9's were able to track down all four suspects hiding in separate locations throughout the community. The teen was found hiding in a bush outside the community. Two of the men were found hiding under a nearby bridge off Murphy Road. The fourth person was in a nearby parking lot who detectives believe was the getaway driver. The sheriff's office says at least one of the suspects was armed with a handgun. Sheriff John Budensiek said three of the four suspects have violent criminal histories. "These are bad, bad individuals who drove at least three and a half hours to Martin County to victimize a family that was going throughout their normal nightly routines," Budensiek said. Investigators said the suspects parked along the canal and walked half a mile into the neighborhood to target the home. The group is seen on home security video around 3 a.m. wearing dark clothing, masks and gloves. The sheriff said they tried to break in through a back door and covered a surveillance camera lens with a sticker. Deputies found masks, gloves and a firearm that had been stolen. Homeowners at the Evergreen Club community were shaken up. "I immediately woke up to Facebook and texts this morning, friends and family asked me if I was okay," said resident Katherine Willis. "Absolutely shocked that they would try to come in here. What are you going to get out of here? It's just very out of the ordinary for sure." The suspects were identified as: Nathaniel Phillip Wise Jr, 22 Za'kyri Isreal Emmanuel Crews, 21 Cameron Elijah Mapson, 21 Teenage boy, 16 All four were charged with attempted home invasion. Wise faces an additional charge of grand theft and possession of a firearm. They're all being held in the Martin County Jail without bond. See also: Boca Raton police arrest man after reported assault on El Rio Trail The agency is asking Palm City residents to check their homes and vehicles for missing property or signs of a break-in. Anyone who finds anything missing should call the sheriff’s office at 772-220-7060. "The Martin County Sheriff's Office is heavily invested in protecting our community," Budensiek said. "To these traveling criminals, we're gonna put you away forever if we can."

entry.title: 4 arrested after attempted home invasion at Palm City's Evergreen Club, sheriff says - WFLX
entry.summary: 4 arrested after attempted home invasion at Palm City's Evergreen Club, sheriff says    WFLX
entry.article_text: Four people from Jacksonville, including a 16-year-old, are in custody after the Martin County Sheriff's Office says a 17-year-old heard a suspicious noise outside his family's home in Palm City's Evergreen Club, prompting a 911 call and an extensive overnight search. Investigators say the group parked a vehicle near the C-23 Canal before walking into the gated community and targeting a home. Deputies later recovered masks, gloves and a stolen firearm during their investigation. WATCH: Teen's Alert Leads to 4 Arrests After Palm City Manhunt The sheriff's office is now asking residents in the Evergreen Club community to check their homes, vehicles and security cameras for anything suspicious as investigators try to determine why the group traveled from Jacksonville to Martin County and whether any other properties were targeted. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the incident began just after 3 a.m., when the family's 17-year-old son realized something was wrong. "The 17-year-old son heard a noise, woke up, knew something was wrong, but didn't quite know what it was," Budensiek said. "(He) went and talked to his parents." The family then began reviewing footage from security cameras around the property. According to Budensiek, one camera was no longer working properly. When the family went farther back through the recorded footage, he said they discovered people moving around the home. "They could see that one of their cameras wasn't working," Budensiek said. "They kept going further back in their search history, and saw where these three black males actually were circling the house." Budensiek said the video showed someone placing a sticker over a camera lens near the back door so activity there could no longer be seen. Deputies began searching the area outside the gated community and checked a parking lot near the C-23 Canal. "There indeed was a car parked there," Budensiek said. The sheriff's office said the suspects had parked along the canal before walking into the neighborhood. One person was taken into custody near the vehicle, while the others fled, according to the sheriff. Deputies established a perimeter and searched with assistance from aviation and K-9 units and the Stuart Police Department. Budensiek said two of the people who fled were ultimately discovered hiding beneath the bridge carrying Murphy Road over the C-23 Canal. "Two fled and ended up hiding under the bridge that crosses the C-23 Canal on Murphy Road," Budensiek said. "They were the last two to actually be apprehended after an extensive manhunt." The three adults arrested were identified as 21-year-old Nathaniel Phillip Wise Jr., 21-year-old Za'kyri Isreal Emmanuel Crews and 21-year-old Cameron Elijah Mapson. A 16-year-old was also arrested, but WPTV is not identifying the juvenile. All four face attempted home invasion charges, according to published reports citing the sheriff's office. Wise also faces grand theft of a firearm and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. As investigators retraced the route between the suspects' vehicle and the family's home, Budensiek said they recovered a handgun. "They recovered a handgun that was stolen with an extended magazine, and were able to corroborate again what the intended victim said," Budensiek said. The Sheriff's Office has also reported recovering masks and gloves during the investigation. Investigators are now trying to determine why this particular home may have been targeted. "We don't know why that house," Budensiek said. "We don't know if they went to any other houses potentially in the middle of the night." The sheriff's office is asking residents to review their security footage and inspect their homes and vehicles for missing property or possible evidence of another attempted break-in. Anyone who discovers missing property or signs of a break-in is asked to contact the Martin County Sheriff's Office at 772-220-7060. Investigators are also examining digital evidence as they work to establish why the four made the trip from Jacksonville to Palm City. "(He) went and talked to his parents."The family then began reviewing footage from security cameras around the property.According to Budensiek, one camera was no longer working properly. When the family went farther back through the recorded footage, he said they discovered people moving around the home."They could see that one of their cameras wasn't working," Budensiek said. "They kept going further back in their search history, and saw where these three black males actually were circling the house."Budensiek said the video showed someone placing a sticker over a camera lens near the back door so activity there could no longer be seen.The family called 911.Deputies began searching the area outside the gated community and checked a parking lot near the C-23 Canal."There indeed was a car parked there," Budensiek said.The sheriff's office said the suspects had parked along the canal before walking into the neighborhood.One person was taken into custody near the vehicle, while the others fled, according to the sheriff.Deputies established a perimeter and searched with assistance from aviation and K-9 units and the Stuart Police Department. Budensiek said two of the people who fled were ultimately discovered hiding beneath the bridge carrying Murphy Road over the C-23 Canal."Two fled and ended up hiding under the bridge that crosses the C-23 Canal on Murphy Road," Budensiek said. "They were the last two to actually be apprehended after an extensive manhunt."The three adults arrested were identified as 21-year-old Nathaniel Phillip Wise Jr., 21-year-old Za'kyri Isreal Emmanuel Crews and 21-year-old Cameron Elijah Mapson. A 16-year-old was also arrested, but WPTV is not identifying the juvenile.All four face attempted home invasion charges, according to published reports citing the sheriff's office. Wise also faces grand theft of a firearm and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. As investigators retraced the route between the suspects' vehicle and the family's home, Budensiek said they recovered a handgun."They recovered a handgun that was stolen with an extended magazine, and were able to corroborate again what the intended victim said," Budensiek said.The Sheriff's Office has also reported recovering masks and gloves during the investigation. Investigators are now trying to determine why this particular home may have been targeted."We don't know why that house," Budensiek said. "We don't know if they went to any other houses potentially in the middle of the night."The sheriff's office is asking residents to review their security footage and inspect their homes and vehicles for missing property or possible evidence of another attempted break-in.Anyone who discovers missing property or signs of a break-in is asked to contact the Martin County Sheriff's Office at 772-220-7060.Investigators are also examining digital evidence as they work to establish why the four made the trip from Jacksonville to Palm City.MORE PALM CITY: Judge rejects motion to dismiss animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki CamerlengoThis story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: FedEx aircraft overruns runway at Miami airport, closing all but 1 runway
entry.summary: A FedEx aircraft overran a runway at the Miami International Airport on Wednesday night, forcing all but one runway to temporarily close the day before Thanksgiving, according to the airport. There were no reports of injuries after the aircraft ran off the runway at about 8:40 p.m., the airport reported. Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units have responded. The incident happened almost three months after an Amazon cargo jet overshot another runway in Miami, killing five people on the ground. The McDonnell Douglas MD-11 was coming from Memphis, and flights will be resuming shortly, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. The administration will investigate. The airport recommended that passengers scheduled to fly Wednesday night should check with their airlines for the latest flight updates before traveling to the airport. We appreciate our passengers patience as we work to safely resume normal operations, the airport said in a statement. The runway this FedEx plane landed on Wednesday is different than the one the Amazon cargo plane overran in September. But three of Miamis runways converge at the west end, so the FedEx plane ended up close to where the Amazon plane careened across a road and struck a van filled with a plane cleaning crew. The MD-11 is the same type of cargo plane that crashed in Kentucky last year after an engine fell off a UPS jet as it was taking off, killing three pilots and 12 more people on the ground. The FAA said it approved Boeings proposed fix, and FedEx started flying them again in May. The National Transportation Safety Board said it had no information about Wednesday's incident.

entry.title: Martin County flood victims fear more devastation as county braces for another foot of rain - WPTV
entry.summary: Martin County flood victims fear more devastation as county braces for another foot of rain    WPTV
entry.article_text: Just weeks after historic flooding destroyed homes and displaced families in Jensen Beach, Martin County residents are bracing for another round of heavy rain — with up to 12 inches forecast over the next three days.For families still struggling to recover, the threat of more flooding comes as county commissioners work to determine what caused the initial disaster and how to help those who lost nearly everything.On Tuesday, flood victims packed a Martin County Commission meeting, pleading for financial assistance and answers.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Along Cheri Drive in Jensen Beach, the signs of destruction remain. Dumpsters line driveways, damaged belongings sit outside and families are still trying to salvage what's left of their homes.Lisa French, her husband, Jeremy, and their two young sons are among those displaced after floodwaters rose as high as 3 feet inside some homes two weeks ago."It's like we're kind of stuck," French told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey. French said her home had about 3 to 6 inches of flooding that sat inside for more than a week, causing mold to grow 3 to 4 feet up the walls. "So they, yeah, they tore the walls down in the house," said French. "They just chipped up the last bit of the tile, and it's empty." Now, with more rain approaching, French fears her family could face another disaster before recovering from the first."Of course, we're afraid because we all flooded in our houses," she said.New figures released by Martin County show at least 36 homes sustained damage, with an estimated $3 million in residential losses. Commissioners estimated another $14 million in damage to beaches, and at least $1 million in damage to roadways that now need repairs. For some residents, the destruction represents a lifetime of memories washed away."We've lost everything," one elderly Jensen Beach resident told commissioners. "We have 60 years of our life — kids, grandkids, everything. It's all gone."As residents demand answers about what went wrong, commissioners approved shifting $200,000 from the county's stormwater budget to investigate whether development and changes to local drainage systems contributed to the flooding.Commissioner Blake Capps called the investigation "a good starting point.""It may be that we need to augment the study beyond the $200,000 that we approve today," said Capps. Meanwhile, county crews are working around the clock to prepare for the next storm, lowering retention pond levels, deploying additional pumps and draining flooded properties."We have people 24 hours a day pumping that material down," Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said.Commissioners also approved financial assistance for eligible flood victims through the state's State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program.The assistance includes grants of up to $25,000 for income-eligible homeowners and loans of up to $75,000 secured by liens on their properties.But there's a catch: The grants are reimbursement-based, meaning homeowners must first pay for eligible repairs before receiving the money.For families who lost everything, that presents another obstacle."We don't have $25,000," French said. "A lot of people don't have $25,000, so it's great, and we're appreciative, but I mean, our house is empty, and $25,000 is not going to do much for us." The other problem: the county currently has just $1 million in SHIP funding available, and commissioners warned the money could run out quickly, even with additional state funding promised."They haven't given us the amount yet, but they have assured us that we will be getting some disaster relief funds," said Human Services Director Michelle Miller Strict income limits could also disqualify some flood victims who cannot afford to rebuild on their own. The income cap for a family of one is $86,040. The cap for a family of two is $98,400. For a family of four, it's $122,880. When reporter Kate Hussey asked Capps what would happen to those families, he acknowledged the county needs to explore other options."There are going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where someone barely missed the limit, and we're going to need to take a look at what we can do for those folks," Capps said.For residents like French, the need is immediate."We just need somebody to step up," she said. "We need funding." With another round of heavy rain approaching, Martin County is distributing sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park to help residents protect their properties, with a limit of 25 per person. The County's Emergency Operations Center is scheduled to be staffed beginning Tuesday at 2 p.m., and the county is coordinating with the National Weather Service and Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM).Fire Rescue is also standing by with multiple high-water rescue trucks.Commissioners also said a Federal Emergency Management Agency representative is expected to visit Nov. 30 to assess the damage — a potential step toward securing federal disaster assistance.But for families still displaced and facing the possibility of more flooding, the uncertainty remains.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie woman says flood damage left her 'landlocked' as road caved due to flooding - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie woman says flood damage left her 'landlocked' as road caved due to flooding    WPEC
entry.article_text: Frances Bertino has lived on Lakehurst Drive for nearly 30 years. For the past three weeks, a hole in the road outside her home has kept her from making the right turn out of her driveway. "I've been here since 1996 when we built the house," Bertino said. "I never had any problems until that. Until now." The hole is about five feet wide and sits in the middle of the road. It opened during the Nov. 2 storm that flooded much of St. Lucie County. The City of Port St. Lucie's flooded streets dashboard lists Lakehurst Drive between Sandia Drive and Prinville Street as "closed indefinitely due to infrastructure damage." Bertino said that when the road first closed, the barricades blocked her driveway. "They said if I got out of it, I was going to get arrested," she said. "I couldn't sleep at night thinking I'm landlocked." The barricades were later moved back. Now she turns around and drives out the other way. It seems funny at first," she said. Her neighbor, who often gives her rides, has had to change how he gets in and out. "Now he pulls in the driveway, now backs up and pulls out." See also: Travelers pack DJT airport ahead of Thanksgiving amid jitters over recent outages Bertino said she reported the damage to the city and was told a water pipe was involved. Asked whether she had heard anything since, she said, "No, I have heard nothing." On Wednesday afternoon, while CBS12 was interviewing her, city crews arrived to inspect the hole. "This is the first time they've been out to inspect it that I know of, because I didn't see anybody here," Bertino said. Three weeks." Asked whether the inspection gave her confidence the road would be fixed soon, she said, "I hope so." City spokesperson Scott Samples said a temporary fix for Lakehurst Drive is expected sometime next week. "The long-term fixes may take a little bit longer, but our goal is to try to get those temporary fixes in place as quickly as we can to make sure that people have access in and out of their homes," Samples said. Samples said the early November storm forced five road closures in the city, and two are still closed. The other is Ann Arbor between Pier Court and Jerico Lane. He said crews decide which roads to fix first based on how bad the damage is and how many people depend on that road. He said the repeated rain has slowed the work. Wednesday's Flood Watch is the third the city has prepared for since the start of the month. "This kind of weather makes it harder to continue to do those kinds of repairs," Samples said. He said supplies are another problem. Flooding up and down Florida's east coast has put many communities in need of the same repair materials at once. "A lot of those materials that we require to be able to fix those roads, it makes it harder to obtain those," he said. The storm also filled the swale outside her home. Bertino said she had seen water that high only once before, during Hurricanes Frances and Jeanne in 2004. "It was all the way to the top. I could not believe it," she said. "We're talking about Frances and Jeanne. And this is just a storm." Lakehurst Drive is one of two streets the city lists as closed indefinitely for infrastructure damage. The other is Ann Arbor between Pier Court and Jerico Lane. The closures come as federal help begins to reach the region. President Donald Trump approved Florida's request for a Major Disaster Declaration for the flooding that began Oct. 31. That makes FEMA individual assistance available to residents of St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River, Okeechobee, Palm Beach and Brevard counties. The aid can help pay for temporary housing, home repairs, and uninsured property losses. Homeowners, renters and small businesses can also apply for low-interest SBA disaster loans. FEMA says families should file insurance claims first, then apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or by calling 1-800-621-3362. The declaration does not yet cover St. Lucie County's local governments. Five of the six counties were also approved for FEMA public assistance, which pays local governments back for debris removal and emergency work. St. Lucie County was not on that list. The National Weather Service in Melbourne has St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River, Okeechobee and Brevard counties under a Flood Watch until 1 a.m. Thursday. Forecasters say 1 to 3 inches of rain is most likely, with 4 to 5 inches or more possible in some spots. They warn that heavy rain on already soaked ground could flood roads and low-lying areas.

entry.title: PSL police have a GTA VI release-day warning: Port St. Lucie is not Vice City - WPEC
entry.summary: PSL police have a GTA VI release-day warning: Port St. Lucie is not Vice City    WPEC
entry.article_text: The wanted level in Port St. Lucie should stay at zero, police say. As Grand Theft Auto VI arrives Thursday, the Port St. Lucie Police Department posted a playful safety briefing reminding fans that real life doesn’t come with a respawn button and that U.S. 1 and Crosstown are not racetracks. Five stars might be impressive in GTA , but trust us, you don’t want that kind of attention in Port St. Lucie, the department wrote. Its other reminders: patrol vehicles aren’t available for test drives, red lights aren’t suggestions, sidewalks aren’t shortcuts and the SWAT team isn’t a feature anyone wants to unlock. What happens in Vice City stays in Vice City, the post said. What happens in Port St. Lucie might come with a police report. The game officially launches Nov. 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. Rockstar’s fictional state of Leonida draws on Florida , with Vice City serving as its Miami-inspired centerpiece. The game follows Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, whose criminal plans pull them into a conspiracy spanning the state. CBS12 has been following the Sunshine State’s transformation into a real-life part of the game’s promotion. In September, a giant pink Welcome to Vice City sign went up on Miami’s Kaseya Center as part of a deal between Miami-Dade County and Rockstar Games. County officials said the arrangement was expected to bring in nearly $1 million in revenue and create marketing opportunities. Miami has also leaned into the Vice City connection with release-week events. The Miami Heat held a Night in Vice City celebration Wednesday, the night before launch. A release-day party is planned Thursday at the Clevelander South Beach, and Rockstar’s GTA VI : The Festival is scheduled for Saturday, Nov. 21, at Mana Wynwood. See also: Who’s responsible for improving drainage after St. Lucie County’s historic flooding? Police in other cities have also used the GTA VI release to remind players to keep the game’s crime on screen. The Atlanta Police Department posted that GTA is not a real place, but Atlanta is! and warned that reckless driving, drunk driving, auto theft and violence have real consequences. Keep it in the game, the department wrote . In South Florida, law enforcement leaders raised a different concern before release day. The Miami-Dade Association of Chiefs of Police opposed plans to promote the county as Vice City, saying the game depicts violence against women and law enforcement. Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz also questioned whether public agencies should promote a game built around crimes her department works to prevent. For drivers tempted to bring a little of the game’s chaos onto local roads, PSLPD’s advice is simpler: drive safe, play smart and leave the wanted level in the game. Could 'sick days' coincide with release? The release could affect more than gamers’ free time. A GameSquare survey of 1,000 U.S. employees found that 10% of full-time employees surveyed who identify as gamers planned to skip work on launch day, while another 30% were considering taking time off. Of those considering time off, 36% said they would call in sick. The survey also found that 42% expected the game to make them less productive at work. Surveyed gamers expected to spend about $400 on the game and related purchases, and anticipated playing a median of 15 hours during the opening weekend. The survey found 70% might skip watching sports to spend more time gaming, while 42% said they’d be less likely to watch NFL games that weekend. I ndian River County students have Thursday off , giving young GTA VI fans an unexpected chance to spend part of release day in Vice City. The district closed schools because of forecast conditions and flooding concerns, while St. Lucie schools reopened and Palm Beach County schools remained open, except for West Boca High School, which is closed because of heavy flooding in the parking lot.

entry.article_text: A Palm City teenager's quick thinking may have stopped four men from breaking into his family's home at the Evergreen Club community off Murphy Road. The Martin County Sheriff's Office says the 17-year-old boy heard a noise outside their home on SW Bimini Circle at 3 a.m. Tuesday. He alerted his parents who called 911, interrupting the home invasion. When deputies arrived at the scene, the four suspects, three men and a teenager from Jacksonville, ran away in different directions. The sheriff's office says deputies set up a perimeter around the neighborhood with help from its aviation team, K-9 unit, and the Stuart Police Department. K9's were able to track down all four suspects hiding in separate locations throughout the community. The teen was found hiding in a bush outside the community. Two of the men were found hiding under a nearby bridge off Murphy Road. The fourth person was in a nearby parking lot who detectives believe was the getaway driver. The sheriff's office says at least one of the suspects was armed with a handgun. Sheriff John Budensiek said three of the four suspects have violent criminal histories. "These are bad, bad individuals who drove at least three and a half hours to Martin County to victimize a family that was going throughout their normal nightly routines," Budensiek said. Investigators said the suspects parked along the canal and walked half a mile into the neighborhood to target the home. The group is seen on home security video around 3 a.m. wearing dark clothing, masks and gloves. The sheriff said they tried to break in through a back door and covered a surveillance camera lens with a sticker. Deputies found masks, gloves and a firearm that had been stolen. Homeowners at the Evergreen Club community were shaken up. "I immediately woke up to Facebook and texts this morning, friends and family asked me if I was okay," said resident Katherine Willis. "Absolutely shocked that they would try to come in here. What are you going to get out of here? It's just very out of the ordinary for sure." The suspects were identified as: Nathaniel Phillip Wise Jr, 22 Za'kyri Isreal Emmanuel Crews, 21 Cameron Elijah Mapson, 21 Teenage boy, 16 All four were charged with attempted home invasion. Wise faces an additional charge of grand theft and possession of a firearm. They're all being held in the Martin County Jail without bond. See also: Boca Raton police arrest man after reported assault on El Rio Trail The agency is asking Palm City residents to check their homes and vehicles for missing property or signs of a break-in. Anyone who finds anything missing should call the sheriff’s office at 772-220-7060. "The Martin County Sheriff's Office is heavily invested in protecting our community," Budensiek said. "To these traveling criminals, we're gonna put you away forever if we can."

entry.summary: A FedEx airplane overran a runway at the Miami International Airport on Wednesday night, forcing all but one runway to temporarily close the day before Thanksgiving, according to officials. There were no reports of injuries after the plane ran off the runway at about 8:40 p.m., the airport reported. The incident happened almost three months after an Amazon cargo jet overshot another runway in Miami, killing five people on the ground. By early Thursday, the Federal Aviation Administration was reporting hourslong flight delays. The FAA, which is investigating, said the McDonnell Douglas MD-11 was coming from Memphis. FedEx said the plane had 'an issue upon landing' and that it is coordinating with investigating officials. 'We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries,' the company said in a statement. FedEx had just started flying MD-11s again in May to deliver packages after that type of plane crashed in Kentucky last year as it was taking off. entry.title: Port St. Lucie woman says flood damage left her 'landlocked' as road caved due to flooding - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie woman says flood damage left her 'landlocked' as road caved due to flooding    WPEC
entry.article_text: Frances Bertino has lived on Lakehurst Drive for nearly 30 years. For the past three weeks, a hole in the road outside her home has kept her from making the right turn out of her driveway. "I've been here since 1996 when we built the house," Bertino said. "I never had any problems until that. Until now." The hole is about five feet wide and sits in the middle of the road. It opened during the Nov. 2 storm that flooded much of St. Lucie County. The City of Port St. Lucie's flooded streets dashboard lists Lakehurst Drive between Sandia Drive and Prinville Street as "closed indefinitely due to infrastructure damage." Bertino said that when the road first closed, the barricades blocked her driveway. "They said if I got out of it, I was going to get arrested," she said. "I couldn't sleep at night thinking I'm landlocked." The barricades were later moved back. Now she turns around and drives out the other way. It seems funny at first," she said. Her neighbor, who often gives her rides, has had to change how he gets in and out. "Now he pulls in the driveway, now backs up and pulls out." See also: Travelers pack DJT airport ahead of Thanksgiving amid jitters over recent outages Bertino said she reported the damage to the city and was told a water pipe was involved. Asked whether she had heard anything since, she said, "No, I have heard nothing." On Wednesday afternoon, while CBS12 was interviewing her, city crews arrived to inspect the hole. "This is the first time they've been out to inspect it that I know of, because I didn't see anybody here," Bertino said. Three weeks." Asked whether the inspection gave her confidence the road would be fixed soon, she said, "I hope so." City spokesperson Scott Samples said a temporary fix for Lakehurst Drive is expected sometime next week. "The long-term fixes may take a little bit longer, but our goal is to try to get those temporary fixes in place as quickly as we can to make sure that people have access in and out of their homes," Samples said. Samples said the early November storm forced five road closures in the city, and two are still closed. The other is Ann Arbor between Pier Court and Jerico Lane. He said crews decide which roads to fix first based on how bad the damage is and how many people depend on that road. He said the repeated rain has slowed the work. Wednesday's Flood Watch is the third the city has prepared for since the start of the month. "This kind of weather makes it harder to continue to do those kinds of repairs," Samples said. He said supplies are another problem. Flooding up and down Florida's east coast has put many communities in need of the same repair materials at once. "A lot of those materials that we require to be able to fix those roads, it makes it harder to obtain those," he said. The storm also filled the swale outside her home. Bertino said she had seen water that high only once before, during Hurricanes Frances and Jeanne in 2004. "It was all the way to the top. I could not believe it," she said. "We're talking about Frances and Jeanne. And this is just a storm." Lakehurst Drive is one of two streets the city lists as closed indefinitely for infrastructure damage. The other is Ann Arbor between Pier Court and Jerico Lane. The closures come as federal help begins to reach the region. President Donald Trump approved Florida's request for a Major Disaster Declaration for the flooding that began Oct. 31. That makes FEMA individual assistance available to residents of St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River, Okeechobee, Palm Beach and Brevard counties. The aid can help pay for temporary housing, home repairs, and uninsured property losses. Homeowners, renters and small businesses can also apply for low-interest SBA disaster loans. FEMA says families should file insurance claims first, then apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or by calling 1-800-621-3362. The declaration does not yet cover St. Lucie County's local governments. Five of the six counties were also approved for FEMA public assistance, which pays local governments back for debris removal and emergency work. St. Lucie County was not on that list. The National Weather Service in Melbourne has St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River, Okeechobee and Brevard counties under a Flood Watch until 1 a.m. Thursday. Forecasters say 1 to 3 inches of rain is most likely, with 4 to 5 inches or more possible in some spots. They warn that heavy rain on already soaked ground could flood roads and low-lying areas.

entry.title: 1 dead, 1 seriously injured in wrong-way crash on I-95 in northern Palm Beach County on Thanksgiving morning
entry.summary: A West Palm Beach man is dead and a Palm Beach Gardens man is seriously injured following a wrong-way crash on Interstate 95 in Palm Beach County on Thanksgiving morning, according to the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP). The crash was reported at 5:08 a.m. Thursday on I-95, just north of Military Trail. Investigators said a 37-year-old Palm Beach Gardens man was driving a white 2026 Chevrolet Equinox north in the southbound lanes of I-95 when he collided head-on with a gray 2017 Ford Expedition driven by a 46-year-old West Palm Beach man. The driver of the Chevrolet was transported to St. Mary's Medical Center with incapacitating injuries. The driver of the Ford was airlifted to the same hospital, where he was pronounced dead. FHP said his next of kin has been notified. As of 10 a.m., nearly five hours after the crash was reported, all southbound lanes remained closed, according to FL511, the Florida Department of Transportation's official statewide traveler information system. Drivers should seek alternate routes and anticipate delays as Thanksgiving travel continues. Motorists are also urged to move over or slow down for Road Rangers responding to the crash. Authorities have not released the names of either driver or determined why the Chevrolet entered the interstate traveling in the wrong direction. The crash remains under investigation. This is a developing story.

entry.title: Palm City family confronts masked intruders during attempted home invasion - WPBF
entry.summary: Palm City family confronts masked intruders during attempted home invasion    WPBF
entry.article_text: A Palm City family was shaken early Tuesday morning when three masked men, at least one armed, attempted to break into their home on Bimini Circle. The homeowner asked WPBF 25 News to not use their names but said his 17-year-old son was the first to hear the suspects as they tried to get in around 3 a.m. In an exclusive statement, the homeowner said, "My son heard them trying to jiggle open all three of our patio sliders fairly aggressively." The son woke his mother and father, and the father armed himself. "I grabbed my AR-15 and proceeded into the house as she called 911," he said. The homeowner believes the suspects got spooked after he turned off the outside lights. "They must have seen me through the windows and seen the lights go out and left," he said. "We're a bit shook from the experience but doing good and feel blessed and lucky." Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said his office deployed every resource they had to find the suspects. "We knew these were bad guys," he said. Authorities launched an extensive search for the suspects, using aerial resources and K-9 units. One suspect was found hiding in bushes outside the community, another near what they believe was the getaway car, and two others were discovered under a nearby bridge. The Sheriff's Office identified the suspects as 21-year-old Nathaniel Phillip Wise Jr., 21-year-old Za'kyri Isreal Emmanuel Crews, and 21-year-old Cameron Elijah Mapson. A fourth suspect is 16 years old. All four suspects are charged with attempted home invasion and are being held at the Martin County jail without bond. The sheriff said the suspects are from Jacksonville, and three of them have extensive criminal records. "These are bad, bad individuals who drove at least three and a half hours to Martin County to victimize a family that was going about their normal nightly routines," Budensiek said. One question investigators are still trying to answer is why the suspects chose this particular home. Budensiek said it's unclear if the attack was random or if the family was targeted. "We don't know the answer to that. We don't know why that house. We don't know if they went to any other houses potentially in the middle of the night," Budensiek said. Authorities are asking residents in the area to check their cameras, cars, and homes for any signs of suspicious activity and to contact the sheriff's office with any information.
