entry.title: Palm Beach County, Treasure Coast residents eligible for federal aid after storms, flooding
entry.summary: Federal disaster aid is now available for residents in Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast affected by recent flooding. FEMA announced late Tuesday that federal disaster assistance is available to individuals and families in Indian River, Martin, Okeechobee, Palm Beach, St. Lucie and Brevard counties as recovery efforts continue. U.S. Rep. Lois Frankel said in a statement the declaration unlocks critical federal recovery resources for residents, businesses and local governments devastated by the flooding. The assistance can include grants for temporary housing and home repairs, low-cost loans to cover uninsured property losses and other programs designed to help people recover from the disaster. Residents who suffered damage or other losses should first file a claim with their insurance provider. They can then apply for FEMA assistance through DisasterAssistance.gov , by calling 1-800-621-3362 or through the FEMA App . Those who use a relay service, including video relay or captioned telephone services, should provide FEMA with the number for that service when applying. Federal funding is also available on a cost-sharing basis to state, tribal and eligible local governments, as well as certain private nonprofit organizations, for debris removal and emergency protective measures. That assistance is available in Palm Beach, Martin, Indian River, Okeechobee, Brevard and Hardee, counties. Frankel said that Palm Beach County officials estimate that $53 million in disaster assistance is needed countywide nearly $35 million to help individuals and families recover and more than $18 million to help local governments cover emergency response and cleanup costs. Additional counties could be designated for federal assistance later, depending on the results of continuing damage assessments. What residents should do: File a claim with their insurance provider. Apply for federal assistance at DisasterAssistance.gov , through the FEMA App or by calling 1-800-621-3362. Severe storms and flooding have impacted parts of Florida since Oct. 31, prompting the state to ask for the federal disaster declaration.

entry.title: Fort Pierce boxing gym builds champions in the ring and community through discipline
entry.summary: In Fort Pierce, behind the doors of A Future Worth Fighting 4, they embody what the City stands for. Here, this community is a big fighting community. If youre from Fort Pierce, you know how we get down,' owner Darrion Henry said. How they get down at A Future Worth Fighting 4 was on full display at the 2026 Florida State Police Athletic League. WATCH: A local boxing gym brings the two C's: community and championships A local boxing gym brings the two C's: community and championships They finished with three state champions, a silver medalist, and a second-place overall team finish, and the star of the Tournament was none other than Justice Henry. He credits the gym's family-like atmosphere and tough-love environment for his success. This gym has been the biggest part of my life. Ive been boxing since I was eight years old, and this became a home for our own little community and us, with everyone we bring in here, said Henry. While Henry has been boxing since he was eight, he has a teammate, Frantzner Jean, whos just getting started but is already making a name for himself after winning his first fight by unanimous decision. It felt pretty fun; I just like the dopamine rush from it, said Jean. Every day after school, kids fill the gym to learn the sweet science of boxing, but there's one rule: you have to go to school every day. Im a teacher at Dan McCarty, so I can see how their behavior has changed, and now I have a lot of kids who show up to school because they know if they dont show up to school, Im going to get on them, said Henry. One of the kids taking the school-first approach is Michael Sanchez, whose dad signed him up for classes, but now hes ready to take this sport as far as it can go. I ended up liking it because I can learn from it, like discipline and hard work, said Sanchez.

entry.title: 1 dead, 6 others wounded in Thanksgiving morning shooting at Airbnb in Polk County, Florida
entry.summary: An 18-year-old was killed and six others were wounded in a Thanksgiving morning shooting at a Polk County Airbnb where investigators say dozens of young people had gathered for a party advertised on social media. Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said deputies responded to the shooting on Captiva Drive shortly before 1 a.m. Thursday. Investigators believe more than 50 people were at the rental property when gunfire erupted, with many of those attending being juveniles. He was shot multiple times and died at the scene, according to the sheriff. Six other people were shot, including teenagers ages 15, 16 and 17, as well as an 18-year-old and a 21-year-old. A 15-year-old girl who was shot in the chest was initially listed in critical condition and placed on a ventilator, Judd said. Investigators were later told she had stabilized and was expected to survive. The other victims suffered what Judd described as less serious gunshot wounds, including wounds to their arms and legs. According to Judd, the gathering was promoted on social media as a birthday pajama party for a juvenile. The advertisement included references to getting drunk and having shots available at the door. Investigators are still trying to determine who rented the property and how the rental was arranged. Judd said preliminary information indicates a 16-year-old girl was involved in organizing the gathering but could not have rented the property herself. Witnesses told investigators that an adult, possibly her brother or another young adult, rented it. Judd stressed that those details could change as detectives continue conducting interviews and gathering evidence. entry.title: 1 dead, 1 seriously injured in wrong-way crash on I-95 in northern Palm Beach County on Thanksgiving morning
entry.summary: A West Palm Beach man is dead and a Palm Beach Gardens man is seriously injured following a wrong-way crash on Interstate 95 in Palm Beach County on Thanksgiving morning, according to the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP). The crash was reported at 5:08 a.m. Thursday on I-95, just north of Military Trail. Investigators said a 37-year-old Palm Beach Gardens man was driving a white 2026 Chevrolet Equinox north in the southbound lanes of I-95 when he collided head-on with a gray 2017 Ford Expedition driven by a 46-year-old West Palm Beach man. The driver of the Chevrolet was taken to St. Mary's Medical Center with incapacitating injuries. The driver of the Ford was airlifted to the same hospital, where he was pronounced dead. FHP said his next of kin has been notified. All lanes were back open at about noon after the closure lasted about seven hours. Drivers should seek alternate routes and anticipate delays as Thanksgiving travel continues. Motorists are also urged to move over or slow down for Road Rangers responding to the crash. Authorities have not released the names of either driver or determined why the Chevrolet entered the interstate traveling in the wrong direction. The crash remains under investigation. This is a developing story.

entry.title: Palm Beach County, Treasure Coast residents eligible for federal aid after storms, flooding
entry.summary: Federal disaster aid is now available for residents in Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast affected by recent flooding. FEMA announced late Tuesday that federal disaster assistance is available to individuals and families in Indian River, Martin, Okeechobee, Palm Beach, St. Lucie and Brevard counties as recovery efforts continue. U.S. Rep. Lois Frankel said in a statement the declaration unlocks critical federal recovery resources for residents, businesses and local governments devastated by the flooding. The assistance can include grants for temporary housing and home repairs, low-cost loans to cover uninsured property losses and other programs designed to help people recover from the disaster. Residents who suffered damage or other losses should first file a claim with their insurance provider. They can then apply for FEMA assistance through DisasterAssistance.gov , by calling 1-800-621-3362 or through the FEMA App . Those who use a relay service, including video relay or captioned telephone services, should provide FEMA with the number for that service when applying. Federal funding is also available on a cost-sharing basis to state, tribal and eligible local governments, as well as certain private nonprofit organizations, for debris removal and emergency protective measures. That assistance is available in Palm Beach, Martin, Indian River, Okeechobee, Brevard and Hardee, counties. Frankel said that Palm Beach County officials estimate that $53 million in disaster assistance is needed countywide nearly $35 million to help individuals and families recover and more than $18 million to help local governments cover emergency response and cleanup costs. Additional counties could be designated for federal assistance later, depending on the results of continuing damage assessments. What residents should do: File a claim with their insurance provider. Apply for federal assistance at DisasterAssistance.gov , through the FEMA App or by calling 1-800-621-3362. Severe storms and flooding have impacted parts of Florida since Oct. 31, prompting the state to ask for the federal disaster declaration.

entry.title: Neighbors plead for help as repeated flooding threatens their Indian River County homes
entry.summary: People across South Florida and the Treasure Coast are bracing for yet another round of heavy rain , and one Indian River County community is pleading for help after battling repeated flooding this month. Joe Waters documented his frustration Saturday evening, recording on his phone in front of his mobile home in the Heritage Plantation mobile home park near Vero Beach as a car drove through floodwaters that almost covered its headlights. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Mobile home park residents plead for help after repeated floods Waters said the wake caused by passing vehicles crashed into the bricks that protect the undercarriage of his home, toppling them. 'The water came up probably about thigh high,' Waters said. 'Came up into the driveway, went into the house.' Waters and his wife were able to clean their home, but he said his car is still in the shop with $4,600 worth of damage, waiting on approval from the insurance company. When we showed up at Heritage Plantation Tuesday afternoon, a crowd of neighbors gathered fed up after battling multiple floods just this month. Dawn Carboni, the HOA president, told me she wants to be a voice for her neighbors, especially those who can't speak up. 'They just want to feel safe in their homes,' she said. The flooding has created dangerous conditions for emergency responders, Carboni said. 'We had a gentleman who needed EMS to come out, and they could not get to his home, so they had to park out on 82nd (Avenue), and then a large fire truck had to get to the home,' Carboni said. With more heavy rain in the forecast, Carboni said residents are frightened. 'People are afraid. It's horrible living in fear when you don't know if it's going to rain and you're going to be able to leave your home the next day.' She wants to spread awareness about what her community is going through. 'We need help, and we're asking for help,' Carboni said. Emergency managers in Indian River County tell me they're operating at a Level 2 emergency, meaning the Emergency Operations Center is partially activated. They've extended the state of emergency through Sunday, Nov. 30. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: More than a meal: Delray Beach man spends Thanksgiving feeding those in need
entry.summary: While many families gathered around the dinner table Thursday, Bill Caesar spent his Thanksgiving making sure those without a table to gather around weren't forgotten. Inside a Delray Beach home, about 40 volunteers worked together to pack 350 plates of hot food, complete with turkey, mashed potatoes and string beans. It's a Thanksgiving tradition Caesar has carried on for about 15 years through his charity, Coming Back to Give Back. 'I got here at 4 o'clock this morning,' Caesar said. For thousands of Floridians, Thanksgiving looks vastly different from the holiday many have come to know. More than 24,000 people are experiencing homelessness statewide, including more than 1,500 in Palm Beach County alone. Others face financial hardship, isolation or limited mobility. Caesar wants to make sure those circumstances don't keep anyone from enjoying a Thanksgiving meal. 'It's a great feeling whenever you can give back,' said Caesar. And for those who can't come to him, he goes to them. One of his stops Thursday was Lakes of Delray, a senior living community where he delivered 50 meals to residents, some of whom have difficulty leaving their homes or don't have family nearby. 'Cant get around, so we're bringing it to them,' Caesar said. From there, Caesar headed to a bus station, where he delivered a Thanksgiving dinner to a woman named Pauline, who has recently fallen on hard times. 'Special delivery!' Caesar said as he approached her. He handed her a plate of food, checked on her, and wished her a blessed Thanksgiving. Throughout the day, Caesar did more than distribute meals. He introduced himself, struck up conversations and connected with people throughout the community. For Caesar, the food is a way to offer something more: human connection. 'It's a great day brightening everybody else's day and making sure everyone's good,' Caesar said after sitting and talking with a man named Willie. 'He was like, ecstatic; he was like, 'Oh my god, I didn't have a meal, I didn't know what I was going to do today.' On a holiday centered around togetherness, even a brief conversation can carry meaning for someone accustomed to being overlooked. For people like Willie, Anthony and Jamie, whom Caesar visited Thursday, the greatest gift of Thanksgiving may not be what's on the plate, but the reminder that someone cares. Because sometimes, it's not just about having a place to get a meal. It's about feeling like you have a place in the world. This story was reported on-air by

entry.title: PBSO detective killed in I-95 wrong-way crash; FHP says driver was intoxicated, had 3 prior DUIs
entry.summary: A Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office detective was killed, and a Palm Beach Gardens man faces multiple charges following a wrong-way crash on Interstate 95 in Palm Beach County on Thanksgiving morning, according to the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP). The crash was reported at 5:08 a.m. Thursday on I-95, just north of Military Trail. Investigators said Raul Jonathan Espinoza Martinez, 37, of Palm Beach Gardens, was driving a white 2026 Chevrolet Equinox north in the southbound lanes of I-95 when he collided head-on with a gray 2017 Ford Expedition driven by a 46-year-old Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office detective from West Palm Beach. The driver of the Ford, whom the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office confirmed was an on-duty detective headed to work, was airlifted to St. Mary's Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead. FHP said his next of kin has been notified. The sheriff's office said the detective was driving an unmarked patrol car at the time of the crash. The detective's name has not been released. Espinoza Martinez was also taken to St. Mary's Medical Center with incapacitating injuries. All lanes were back open at about noon after the closure lasted about seven hours. The Florida Highway Patrol said at about 2:33 p.m., troopers arrested Espinoza Martinez in connection with the fatal wrong-way crash. The arrest took place at St. Mary's Medical Center, according to FHP. 'Troopers were joined by members of the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, who placed Espinoza Martinez in the handcuffs carried by the fallen detective,' FHP said in a statement. According to FHP, Espinoza Martinez was intoxicated at the time of the crash, with an active license revocation for 10 years and three prior DUI convictions. Upon his release from the hospital, FHP said Espinoza Martinez will be booked into the Palm Beach County Jail on the following charges: Vehicular Homicide DUI Manslaughter Aggravated Battery Aggravated Battery on a Law Enforcement Officer Driving While License Suspended or Revoked Causing Death or Serious Bodily Injury Driving While License Suspended or Revoked Subsequent Offense DUI Causing Damage to Property or Injury to Another Person Reckless Driving Causing Damage to Property or Injury to Another Person FHP said they are investigating the circumstances of the crash.

entry.title: Martin County flood victims fear more devastation as county braces for another foot of rain - WPTV
entry.summary: Martin County flood victims fear more devastation as county braces for another foot of rain    WPTV
entry.article_text: Just weeks after historic flooding destroyed homes and displaced families in Jensen Beach, Martin County residents are bracing for another round of heavy rain — with up to 12 inches forecast over the next three days.For families still struggling to recover, the threat of more flooding comes as county commissioners work to determine what caused the initial disaster and how to help those who lost nearly everything.On Tuesday, flood victims packed a Martin County Commission meeting, pleading for financial assistance and answers.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Along Cheri Drive in Jensen Beach, the signs of destruction remain. Dumpsters line driveways, damaged belongings sit outside and families are still trying to salvage what's left of their homes.Lisa French, her husband, Jeremy, and their two young sons are among those displaced after floodwaters rose as high as 3 feet inside some homes two weeks ago."It's like we're kind of stuck," French told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey. French said her home had about 3 to 6 inches of flooding that sat inside for more than a week, causing mold to grow 3 to 4 feet up the walls. "So they, yeah, they tore the walls down in the house," said French. "They just chipped up the last bit of the tile, and it's empty." Now, with more rain approaching, French fears her family could face another disaster before recovering from the first."Of course, we're afraid because we all flooded in our houses," she said.New figures released by Martin County show at least 36 homes sustained damage, with an estimated $3 million in residential losses. Commissioners estimated another $14 million in damage to beaches, and at least $1 million in damage to roadways that now need repairs. For some residents, the destruction represents a lifetime of memories washed away."We've lost everything," one elderly Jensen Beach resident told commissioners. "We have 60 years of our life — kids, grandkids, everything. It's all gone."As residents demand answers about what went wrong, commissioners approved shifting $200,000 from the county's stormwater budget to investigate whether development and changes to local drainage systems contributed to the flooding.Commissioner Blake Capps called the investigation "a good starting point.""It may be that we need to augment the study beyond the $200,000 that we approve today," said Capps. Meanwhile, county crews are working around the clock to prepare for the next storm, lowering retention pond levels, deploying additional pumps and draining flooded properties."We have people 24 hours a day pumping that material down," Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said.Commissioners also approved financial assistance for eligible flood victims through the state's State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program.The assistance includes grants of up to $25,000 for income-eligible homeowners and loans of up to $75,000 secured by liens on their properties.But there's a catch: The grants are reimbursement-based, meaning homeowners must first pay for eligible repairs before receiving the money.For families who lost everything, that presents another obstacle."We don't have $25,000," French said. "A lot of people don't have $25,000, so it's great, and we're appreciative, but I mean, our house is empty, and $25,000 is not going to do much for us." The other problem: the county currently has just $1 million in SHIP funding available, and commissioners warned the money could run out quickly, even with additional state funding promised."They haven't given us the amount yet, but they have assured us that we will be getting some disaster relief funds," said Human Services Director Michelle Miller Strict income limits could also disqualify some flood victims who cannot afford to rebuild on their own. The income cap for a family of one is $86,040. The cap for a family of two is $98,400. For a family of four, it's $122,880. When reporter Kate Hussey asked Capps what would happen to those families, he acknowledged the county needs to explore other options."There are going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where someone barely missed the limit, and we're going to need to take a look at what we can do for those folks," Capps said.For residents like French, the need is immediate."We just need somebody to step up," she said. "We need funding." With another round of heavy rain approaching, Martin County is distributing sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park to help residents protect their properties, with a limit of 25 per person. The County's Emergency Operations Center is scheduled to be staffed beginning Tuesday at 2 p.m., and the county is coordinating with the National Weather Service and Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM).Fire Rescue is also standing by with multiple high-water rescue trucks.Commissioners also said a Federal Emergency Management Agency representative is expected to visit Nov. 30 to assess the damage — a potential step toward securing federal disaster assistance.But for families still displaced and facing the possibility of more flooding, the uncertainty remains.

entry.title: Neighbors plead for help as repeated flooding threatens their Indian River County homes - WFLX
entry.summary: Neighbors plead for help as repeated flooding threatens their Indian River County homes    WFLX
entry.article_text: People across South Florida and the Treasure Coast are bracing for yet another round of heavy rain , and one Indian River County community is pleading for help after battling repeated flooding this month. Joe Waters documented his frustration Saturday evening, recording on his phone in front of his mobile home in the Heritage Plantation mobile home park near Vero Beach as a car drove through floodwaters that almost covered its headlights. Waters said the wake caused by passing vehicles crashed into the bricks that protect the undercarriage of his home, toppling them. “The water came up probably about thigh high,” Waters said. “Came up into the driveway, went into the house.” Waters and his wife were able to clean their home, but he said his car is still in the shop with $4,600 worth of damage, waiting on approval from the insurance company. When we showed up at Heritage Plantation Tuesday afternoon, a crowd of neighbors gathered — fed up after battling multiple floods just this month. Dawn Carboni, the HOA president, told me she wants to be a voice for her neighbors, especially those who can’t speak up. “They just want to feel safe in their homes,” she said. The flooding has created dangerous conditions for emergency responders, Carboni said. “We had a gentleman who needed EMS to come out, and they could not get to his home, so they had to park out on 82nd (Avenue), and then a large fire truck had to get to the home,” Carboni said. With more heavy rain in the forecast, Carboni said residents are frightened. It’s horrible living in fear when you don’t know if it’s going to rain and you’re going to be able to leave your home the next day.” She wants to spread awareness about what her community is going through. “We need help, and we’re asking for help,” Carboni said. Emergency managers in Indian River County tell me they’re operating at a Level 2 emergency, meaning the Emergency Operations Center is partially activated. They’ve extended the state of emergency through Sunday, Nov. 30. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

entry.title: PBSO detective killed in I-95 wrong-way crash; FHP says driver was intoxicated, had 3 prior DUIs
entry.summary: A Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office detective was killed, and a Palm Beach Gardens man faces multiple charges following a wrong-way crash on Interstate 95 in Palm Beach County on Thanksgiving morning, according to the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP). The crash was reported at 5:08 a.m. Thursday on I-95, just north of Military Trail. Investigators said Raul Jonathan Espinoza Martinez, 37, of Palm Beach Gardens, was driving a white 2026 Chevrolet Equinox north in the southbound lanes of I-95 when he collided head-on with a gray 2017 Ford Expedition driven by a 46-year-old Alan Smith, a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office detective from West Palm Beach. Smith, whom the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office confirmed was an on-duty detective headed to work, was airlifted to St. Mary's Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead. FHP said his next of kin has been notified. It is with profound sadness and heavy hearts that we announce the devastating loss our own, Detective Alan Smith. Detective Smith was fatally struck by a wrong way driver traveling southbound on I95 early Thanksgiving morning. Alan joined the Palm Beach County Sheriffs Office in January 2007. In 2012, he became a member of the Bomb Squad and graduated from the FBI Hazardous Devices School in September 2013. His commitment to law enforcement extended beyond his responsibilities as a Bomb Technician. He also served as a Task Force Officer (TFO) with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), specializing in explosives-related investigations. Alan was much more than a law enforcement officer and Bomb Technician. He was a college professor, and a lifelong scholar who was in the process of completing his doctoral degree. His passion for education, pursuit of knowledge, and commitment to mentoring others were evident throughout his personal and professional life. Above all his professional and academic accomplishments, Alans greatest pride was his family. He was a loving husband to his wife, Jennifer, and a devoted father to his 14-year-old son, Alexander. His passing is a tremendous loss to his family, the Palm Beach County Sheriffs Office, the Bomb Squad, the law enforcement community, and the countless individuals whose lives he touched through his service, friendship, and mentorship.   Alans legacy of service, knowledge, compassion, and dedication to others will never be forgotten. entry.title: The secret to a perfect Thanksgiving turkey? Okeechobee Steakhouse says it's butter
entry.summary: If you've ever admired a perfectly golden Thanksgiving turkey and wondered how professional chefs make it look so good, Okeechobee Steakhouse co-owner Ralph Lewis has a surprisingly simple answer. 'It's butter.' And not just a little butter. Secret to a golden Thanksgiving turkey? Butter, butter and more butter During a recent Thanksgiving cooking demonstration at Okeechobee Prime Meat Market, Lewis stood beside a giant inflatable stick of butter, worked from a table piled high with butter and seasonings, and even pulled a backup rubber stick of butter from his pocket. For Lewis, butter isn't simply an ingredient. It's the foundation of a great Thanksgiving turkey. 'Are you really supposed to have a budget with butter?' Lewis joked. 'Those two words do not go together.' The Butter Trick That Makes The Difference According to Lewis, the biggest mistake many home cooks make is putting all of their butter on the outside of the bird. Instead, he recommends carefully separating the skin from the breast meat and creating pockets beneath the skin. Once those pockets are created, it's time to start adding butter. Lots of butter. 'You just want to keep working it in there,' Lewis said. 'You can't put enough. You can't put too much. That's impossible, literally impossible, and that's a chef's code.' As the turkey cooks, the butter melts beneath the skin, helping keep the meat moist while contributing to the rich color and flavor many Thanksgiving hosts are trying to achieve. After working butter beneath the skin, Lewis also coats the outside of the turkey before adding seasoning. Pro Tip: Season The Butter First One of the most useful tips Lewis shared involves seasoning the butter before it ever touches the bird. Start by taking butter out of the refrigerator and allowing it to soften to room temperature. Then combine the softened butter with herbs and seasonings such as: Kosher salt Freshly ground black pepper Thyme Rosemary Sage Mix everything together until it forms a seasoned compound butter. Then spread that butter beneath the skin and across the exterior of the turkey. By combining the herbs and seasoning directly into the butter, the flavors are distributed more evenly throughout the turkey as it cooks. Lewis says it's a simple step that can make a noticeable difference in flavor. Step-By-Step Turkey Guide 1. Soften the butter Allow butter to come to room temperature. 2. entry.summary: Italian food, live music and family traditions return to Abacoa Town Center this weekend as the Galbani Feast of Little Italy celebrates its 25th anniversary Nov. 6-8 with three days of festivities and free admission, according to organizers. The festival runs from 4 to 10 p.m. Friday, 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. Saturday and 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. Sunday. This year's milestone celebration includes Italian food, cooking demonstrations, live entertainment, family activities and an unusual attempt to make festival history using string cheese. Italian favorites fill Abacoa Food is at the heart of the weekend. Festival organizers say guests can expect Italian-American favorites including pasta, sausage and peppers, Neapolitan pizza, zeppole, cannoli and gelato. The Galbani Cooking Stage will feature demonstrations throughout the weekend, giving festivalgoers a chance to watch chefs prepare dishes and pick up cooking tips. The published lineup includes Anthony Acampa, Sicilian Oven Chef Andrew, Galbani Chef Marco Sciortino (with special guest Joe Gannascoli from The Sopranos), Cooking with Vinny, Nina's Fresh Bakery and Michelin-starred chef Joe Isidori. Voga wine seminars are also scheduled during the weekend. Can Jupiter make string-cheese history? Saturday brings one of the festival's most unusual attractions. At 4 p.m., organizers are inviting festivalgoers to participate in an event billed as Let's Make Italian Festival History! The goal is to bring people together to simultaneously string string cheese. The public is encouraged to participate, turning a familiar snack into one of the quirkiest moments of the festival's 25th anniversary. Live music all weekend The 25th anniversary celebration also brings three days of live entertainment to Abacoa. entry.title: More than a meal: Delray Beach man spends Thanksgiving feeding those in need
entry.summary: While many families gathered around the dinner table Thursday, Bill Caesar spent his Thanksgiving making sure those without a table to gather around weren't forgotten. Inside a Delray Beach home, about 40 volunteers worked together to pack 350 plates of hot food, complete with turkey, mashed potatoes and string beans. It's a Thanksgiving tradition Caesar has carried on for about 15 years through his charity, Coming Back to Give Back. WATCH: More than a meal: Delray Beach man spends Thanksgiving feeding those in need Delray Beach man spends Thanksgiving feeding those in need 'I got here at 4 o'clock this morning,' Caesar said. For thousands of Floridians, Thanksgiving looks vastly different from the holiday many have come to know. More than 24,000 people are experiencing homelessness statewide, including more than 1,500 in Palm Beach County alone. Others face financial hardship, isolation or limited mobility. Caesar wants to make sure those circumstances don't keep anyone from enjoying a Thanksgiving meal. 'It's a great feeling whenever you can give back,' said Caesar. And for those who can't come to him, he goes to them. One of his stops Thursday was Lakes of Delray, a senior living community where he delivered 50 meals to residents, some of whom have difficulty leaving their homes or don't have family nearby. 'Cant get around, so we're bringing it to them,' Caesar said. From there, Caesar headed to a bus station, where he delivered a Thanksgiving dinner to a woman named Pauline, who has recently fallen on hard times. 'Special delivery!' Caesar said as he approached her. He handed her a plate of food, checked on her, and wished her a blessed Thanksgiving. Throughout the day, Caesar did more than distribute meals. He introduced himself, struck up conversations and connected with people throughout the community. For Caesar, the food is a way to offer something more: human connection. entry.title: PBSO detective killed in I-95 wrong-way crash; FHP says driver was intoxicated, had 3 prior DUIs
entry.summary: A Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office detective was killed, and a Palm Beach Gardens man faces multiple charges following a wrong-way crash on Interstate 95 in Palm Beach County on Thanksgiving morning, according to the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP). The crash was reported at 5:08 a.m. Thursday on I-95, just north of Military Trail. Investigators said Raul Jonathan Espinoza Martinez, 37, of Palm Beach Gardens, was driving a white 2026 Chevrolet Equinox north in the southbound lanes of I-95 when he collided head-on with a gray 2017 Ford Expedition driven by a 46-year-old Alan Smith, a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office detective from West Palm Beach. WATCH: PBSO detective killed in Thanksgiving wrong-way crash PBSO detective killed in I-95 wrong-way crash; FHP says driver was intoxicated, had 3 prior DUIs Smith, whom the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office confirmed was an on-duty detective headed to work, was airlifted to St. Mary's Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead. FHP said his next of kin has been notified. It is with profound sadness and heavy hearts that we announce the devastating loss our own, Detective Alan Smith. Detective Smith was fatally struck by a wrong way driver traveling southbound on I95 early Thanksgiving morning. Alan joined the Palm Beach County Sheriffs Office in January 2007. In 2012, he became a member of the Bomb Squad and graduated from the FBI Hazardous Devices School in September 2013. His commitment to law enforcement extended beyond his responsibilities as a Bomb Technician. He also served as a Task Force Officer (TFO) with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), specializing in explosives-related investigations. Alan was much more than a law enforcement officer and Bomb Technician. He was a college professor, and a lifelong scholar who was in the process of completing his doctoral degree. His passion for education, pursuit of knowledge, and commitment to mentoring others were evident throughout his personal and professional life. Above all his professional and academic accomplishments, Alans greatest pride was his family. He was a loving husband to his wife, Jennifer, and a devoted father to his 14-year-old son, Alexander. His passing is a tremendous loss to his family, the Palm Beach County Sheriffs Office, the Bomb Squad, the law enforcement community, and the countless individuals whose lives he touched through his service, friendship, and mentorship.   Alans legacy of service, knowledge
entry.article_text: Alan’s legacy of service, knowledge, compassion, and dedication to others will never be forgotten.— PBSO (@PBCountySheriff) November 26, 2026 The sheriff's office said Smith was driving an unmarked patrol car at the time of the crash. Espinoza Martinez was also taken to St. Mary's Medical Center with incapacitating injuries.All lanes were back open at about noon after the closure lasted about seven hours.The Florida Highway Patrol said at about 2:33 p.m., troopers arrested Espinoza Martinez in connection with the fatal wrong-way crash. The arrest took place at St. Mary's Medical Center, according to FHP."Troopers were joined by members of the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, who placed Espinoza Martinez in the handcuffs carried by the fallen detective," FHP said in a statement.According to FHP, Espinoza Martinez was intoxicated at the time of the crash, with an active license revocation for 10 years and three prior DUI convictions.Upon his release from the hospital, FHP said Espinoza Martinez will be booked into the Palm Beach County Jail on the following charges:Vehicular HomicideDUI ManslaughterAggravated BatteryAggravated Battery on a Law Enforcement OfficerDriving While License Suspended or Revoked Causing Death or Serious Bodily InjuryDriving While License Suspended or Revoked – Subsequent OffenseDUI Causing Damage to Property or Injury to Another PersonReckless Driving Causing Damage to Property or Injury to Another PersonFHP said they are investigating the circumstances of the crash.President Donald Trump made a statement about the crash during a press conference on Thursday, according to CNN."I just want to pay my respects to the family of a great police officer, uh, an expert at bombs and explosives who was killed today in an automobile accident while on duty and I'm not able to release his name yet. They, they're notifying the family and notifying a lot of people.

entry.title: Sheriff renews call for unified 911 dispatch as Vero Beach faces Amendment 3 cuts - Sebastian Daily
entry.summary: Sheriff renews call for unified 911 dispatch as Vero Beach faces Amendment 3 cuts    Sebastian Daily
entry.article_text: He said unifying dispatch across the county has been one of his goals since taking office. “One of my goals since being elected sheriff was to unify public safety dispatch for our entire county under one roof,” Flowers told Sebastian Daily . “St. Lucie and others have had this for decades, and it just makes sense from a safety standpoint, communications perspective, and an overall reduction of duplicative services. It’s my hope that with Amendment 3 passing, as cities look to find ways to reduce costs, a unified public safety dispatch system will be one of the first choices.” He originally raised the idea with the council about two years ago. Since then, Brevard County has moved to a single dispatch center. Flowers hopes the city will consider the concept as it works through what he called “difficult decisions” under the amendment. Voters approved Amendment 3 earlier this month to raise the homestead exemption on non-school property taxes from roughly $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and to $250,000 in 2028. Local officials had opposed the measure, warning it would cut into funding for public safety and other services. Council member Tracey Zudans asked for concrete numbers. “I’d love to see some numbers attached to it, not just response time numbers, but also some dollar numbers so that we can share that with our taxpayers as well,” she said. Flowers said his staff would work with the city on the figures. Mayor Aaron Vos said staff will first calculate what the city currently spends on dispatch, and Flowers will come back with an estimate of what it would cost the city to join a countywide center. Vos said he expects the county, not the sheriff’s office, would run any unified operation — the same arrangement used in St. Lucie County. Vice Mayor John Cotugno asked whether the center would be a county function or under the sheriff. Flowers said the county technically oversees dispatch, though most of the dispatchers work for his agency. “I have the bulk of dispatchers that work for me at the sheriff’s office, so I can only offer it from my side,” he said. “You would have to ask the county if they were interested in maybe doing it differently.” Council members took no formal action on the proposal. entry.title: 4 taken into custody after overnight burglary, manhunt in Martin County
entry.summary: A homeowner's quick call to 911 helped interrupt an attempted home invasion in Palm City early Tuesday, leading to the arrests of four people from Jacksonville, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The sheriff's office said the homeowner heard a noise outside a home on Southwest Bimini Circle in the Evergreen Club and contacted authorities. Investigators said at least one of the suspects was armed with a handgun. When deputies arrived, the four suspects scattered into the neighborhood, according to the sheriff's office. Deputies established a perimeter and, with assistance from the agency's aviation, drone and K-9 units and the Stuart Police Department K-9 unit, found all four hiding in separate locations throughout the community. Investigators believe the group parked near a canal and walked into the neighborhood to target the home. Deputies said they recovered a firearm, masks and gloves. Detectives later determined the gun had been reported stolen. The sheriff's office identified three of those arrested as 21-year-old Nathaniel Phillip Wise Jr., 21-year-old Za'kyri Isreal Emmanuel Crews and 21-year-old Cameron Elijah Mapson. The fourth person arrested is 16 years old. WPTV is not naming the juvenile. All four face attempted home invasion charges and were taken into custody, according to the sheriff's office. Wise also faces charges of grand theft of a firearm and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. The sheriff's office credited the homeowner's quick decision to call authorities with interrupting the alleged crime before anyone was hurt.

entry.title: Martin County approves $200,000 study to address Jensen Beach flooding - WPBF
entry.summary: Martin County approves $200,000 study to address Jensen Beach flooding    WPBF
entry.article_text: Martin County commissioners have unanimously approved $200,000 to fund a study that will analyze water movement during the recent flooding in Jensen Beach and identify ways to reduce future flood risks. Floodwaters earlier this month left homes and roads underwater in parts of Jensen Beach. The study will examine how water moved through the Savannas Preserve area during the storm, as some residents have questioned whether water discharged into the Blackwell Reservoir, which drains into the Savannas Preserve, contributed to the flooding. "What's happening now is not going to stop. This is an El Niño event that we are in through April. It's going to come and go," resident Jacqui Thurlow-Lippisch said during the Nov. 17 county commissioner meeting. Public Works Director James Gorton says the hydraulic model funded by the county will focus on two main objectives. "First one is model the storm event that we just had. We need to update, get some of the development that has occurred to our north, put into that model first and then model that storm, see where the weaknesses were, and then secondarily look at some solutions to reduce the risk," Gorton said. This initiative follows a separate study conducted by the county to analyze areas that have repeatedly flooded, aiming to understand the causes and identify potential solutions. Engineering permit manager and floodplain coordinator Christine Madsen said the analysis identified 53 repetitive loss areas. "We determined what some of the potential causes of the flooding were, and we used it to identify different projects that we could take and move forward within the future," Madsen said. One photo from the study shows flooding in the St. Lucie Settlement area along SW Salerno Road, where eight homes were elevated above the 100-year flood elevation with assistance from FEMA. Another photo shows one of the completed homes. "Flood losses are terrible. Just 1 inch of water can majorly impact a property. I mean it can cause up to $25,000 worth of damage," Madsen said. "We want to do whatever we can to help them." Residents can review the analysis on the county's website. Those with questions can call the county at 772-288-5956.

"(He) went and talked to his parents."The family then began reviewing footage from security cameras around the property.According to Budensiek, one camera was no longer working properly. When the family went farther back through the recorded footage, he said they discovered people moving around the home."They could see that one of their cameras wasn't working," Budensiek said. Budensiek said two of the people who fled were ultimately discovered hiding beneath the bridge carrying Murphy Road over the C-23 Canal."Two fled and ended up hiding under the bridge that crosses the C-23 Canal on Murphy Road," Budensiek said. A 16-year-old was also arrested, but WPTV is not identifying the juvenile.All four face attempted home invasion charges, according to published reports citing the sheriff's office. Wise also faces grand theft of a firearm and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. As investigators retraced the route between the suspects' vehicle and the family's home, Budensiek said they recovered a handgun."They recovered a handgun that was stolen with an extended magazine, and were able to corroborate again what the intended victim said," Budensiek said.The Sheriff's Office has also reported recovering masks and gloves during the investigation. entry.title: Fort Pierce boxing gym builds champions in the ring and community through discipline - WFLX
entry.summary: Fort Pierce boxing gym builds champions in the ring and community through discipline    WFLX
entry.article_text: In Fort Pierce, behind the doors of A Future Worth Fighting 4, they embody what the City stands for. “Here, this community is a big fighting community. If you’re from Fort Pierce, you know how we get down," owner Darrion Henry said. How they get down at A Future Worth Fighting 4 was on full display at the 2026 Florida State Police Athletic League. WATCH: A local boxing gym brings the two C's: community and championships They finished with three state champions, a silver medalist, and a second-place overall team finish, and the star of the Tournament was none other than Justice Henry. He credits the gym's family-like atmosphere and tough-love environment for his success. “This gym has been the biggest part of my life. I’ve been boxing since I was eight years old, and this became a home for our own little community and us, with everyone we bring in here,” said Henry. While Henry has been boxing since he was eight, he has a teammate, Frantzner Jean, who’s just getting started but is already making a name for himself after winning his first fight by unanimous decision. “It felt pretty fun; I just like the dopamine rush from it,” said Jean. Every day after school, kids fill the gym to learn the sweet science of boxing, but there's one rule: you have to go to school every day. “I’m a teacher at Dan McCarty, so I can see how their behavior has changed, and now I have a lot of kids who show up to school because they know if they don’t show up to school, I’m going to get on them,” said Henry. One of the kids taking the school-first approach is Michael Sanchez, whose dad signed him up for classes, but now he’s ready to take this sport as far as it can go. “I ended up liking it because I can learn from it, like discipline and hard work,” said Sanchez.

entry.title: Black Friday shoppers line up before dawn in West Palm Beach for exclusive Record Store Day releases
entry.summary: Black Friday shoppers were out early across South Florida on Friday, with some music fans waiting for hours to get their hands on limited-edition vinyl releases. About 80 people lined up outside Rust Wax record store in West Palm Beach as shoppers sought special limited-edition Record Store Day releases from artists including The Beatles, Cher, Sombr, the Grateful Dead and Stevie Nicks. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Vinyl fans line up for Black Friday releases T.A. Walker caught up with Diane of Palm Beach Gardens, a Stevie Nicks fan who arrived around midnight and scored one of the records on her wish list. She was among the first customers inside the store Friday morning and had her sights set on a special Stevie Nicks release of 'Bella Donna.' 'She took the face of the 'Bella Donna' album and imprinted it directly on the actual album itself,' Diane told Walker. 'So when you're listening to 'Bella Donna,' you're actually seeing Stevie Nicks.' The early-morning rush wasn't limited to record collectors. Shoppers were also heading to retailers and shopping centers across the area, including Walmart, Target, Best Buy, Macy's, Kohl's, The Mall at Wellington Green, The Gardens Mall, Town Center at Boca Raton and Treasure Coast Square. The crowds come as many consumers still plan to do at least some of their holiday shopping in person. According to holiday shopping research cited by Accenture , 66% of consumers plan to hunt for Black Friday or Cyber Monday deals at brick-and-mortar stores rather than doing all of their shopping online. The research also found the average consumer is expected to spend about $737 this holiday season. For the music fans waiting outside Rust Wax, however, Black Friday was about more than simply finding a discount. It was a chance to be among the first to grab a limited-edition release before it disappeared from the shelves. What do you want me to Shine A Light on? What are you most proud of where you live? entry.title: President Trump, FBI director pay tribute to PBSO detective killed in Thanksgiving wrong-way crash
entry.summary: President Donald Trump and FBI Director Kash Patel are paying tribute to a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office detective killed in a Thanksgiving morning wrong-way crash on Interstate 95. Speaking in Palm Beach on Thursday, Trump offered his condolences to the fallen detective's family. 'I just want to pay my respects to the family of a great police officer, an expert at bombs and explosives, who was killed today in an automobile accident while on duty,' Trump said. Authorities have since identified the fallen detective as Alan Smith, 46, of West Palm Beach. Trump did not identify Smith during his remarks Thursday, citing ongoing efforts to notify his family and others. In a statement posted on X, Patel revealed Smith had served nearly 20 years with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office and had extensive experience investigating explosives-related crimes. Smith graduated from the FBI Hazardous Devices School in September 2013 and served as a task force officer with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, according to Patel. 'This is yet another reminder of the sacrifices our law enforcement make standing their posts even on holidays to keep us safe,' Patel wrote. 'Never forget them and their families.' Smith leaves behind a wife and 14-year-old son. Driver accused of causing deadly crash had three prior DUI convictions The Florida Highway Patrol said Smith was driving an unmarked patrol vehicle south on I-95 just north of Military Trail shortly after 5 a.m. Thursday, when a driver traveling in the wrong direction collided with him head-on. Smith was on duty and headed to work at the time of the crash, according to the sheriff's office. He was airlifted to St. Mary's Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead. Troopers identified the wrong-way driver as Raul Jonathan Espinoza Martinez, 37, of Palm Beach Gardens. Investigators said Espinoza Martinez was intoxicated at the time of the crash and was driving despite three prior DUI convictions and an active 10-year driver's license revocation. 'He was going on the opposite side of the highway, if you can believe it. And so it's a terrible thing that happened.' And so it's a terrible thing that happened."Espinoza Martinez was hospitalized with serious injuries and arrested Thursday afternoon.Members of the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office joined troopers at the hospital, placing Espinoza Martinez in the handcuffs carried by the fallen detective, according to FHP.Troopers said Espinoza Martinez will be booked into the Palm Beach County Jail upon his release from the hospital on multiple charges, including DUI manslaughter, vehicular homicide and aggravated battery on a law enforcement officer.The Florida Highway Patrol continues to investigate the crash.

entry.title: Judge allows Hillsborough school bus camera lawsuit to proceed
entry.summary: A Hillsborough County judge has refused to throw out a lawsuit challenging the way drivers' ticket appeals are handled for Florida's controversial school bus cameras and the attorneys behind the case now want it to move forward on behalf of potentially thousands of other drivers. WATCH: Judge allows Hillsborough school bus camera lawsuit to proceed SCHOOL BUS CAMERA CLASS ACTION LAWSUIT FOLO The school bus stop arm cameras are designed to protect kids getting on and off school buses. But since they started rolling, Investigative Reporter Katie LaGrone and photojournalist Matthew Apthorp have exposed problems with what happens when drivers get a ticket and try to fight back. Stanley Shultz of Plant City was fined $225 last year after a school bus camera caught him passing the bus after its stop arm deployed. He said the bus' warning lights never flashed. So Shultz tried to challenge his violation and lost bringing his total fine to $270. But he's not done fighting, and neither is his attorney. 'He challenged the merits of the ticket. We're challenging the procedure,' said Shultz's attorney Gino Moreno. At issue: When a driver challenges one of these violations, who decides if it should be upheld or dismissed? Florida law calls for a 'local hearing officer' appointed by the school district or county. But in Hillsborough County, contested cases are being sent to state administrative judges through the Division of Administrative Hearings or DOAH and in most of these cases, the judges aren't in the same county where the ticket was issued. In Shultz's appeal, the judge who heard his appeal was in Tallahassee. And that's against the law, according to Shultz's lawsuit. 'If you're saying that it has to be heard by a local hearing officer, the hearing officer is being described as local. A state agency in Tallahassee is not local,' Moreno said. The Hillsborough County School District and its camera vendor, BusPatrol, tried to get the case dismissed. But recently, a judge said no, giving the green light for this camera lawsuit to keep rolling. Shultz's attorneys are now asking the court to certify the case as a class action, since there are thousands of other drivers in Hillsborough County whose appeals were also heard by judges outside the county. As of Oct. 2, nearly 5,000 school bus violations issued in Hillsborough County were contested with nearly 80% upheld by a DOAH judge, according to recent data provided by the Hillsborough County School District. But since they started rolling, Investigative Reporter Katie LaGrone and photojournalist Matthew Apthorp have exposed problems with what happens when drivers get a ticket and try to fight back.Stanley Shultz of Plant City was fined $225 last year after a school bus camera caught him passing the bus after its stop arm deployed. He said the bus' warning lights never flashed.So Shultz tried to challenge his violation — and lost — bringing his total fine to $270. But he's not done fighting, and neither is his attorney. "He challenged the merits of the ticket. We're challenging the procedure," said Shultz's attorney Gino Moreno.At issue: When a driver challenges one of these violations, who decides if it should be upheld or dismissed?Florida law calls for a "local hearing officer" appointed by the school district or county. But in Hillsborough County, contested cases are being sent to state administrative judges through the Division of Administrative Hearings — or DOAH — and in most of these cases, the judges aren't in the same county where the ticket was issued.In Shultz's appeal, the judge who heard his appeal was in Tallahassee. And that's against the law, according to Shultz's lawsuit."If you're saying that it has to be heard by a local hearing officer, the hearing officer is being described as local. A state agency in Tallahassee is not local," Moreno said.The Hillsborough County School District and its camera vendor, BusPatrol, tried to get the case dismissed. But recently, a judge said no, giving the green light for this camera lawsuit to keep rolling.Shultz's attorneys are now asking the court to certify the case as a class action, since there are thousands of other drivers in Hillsborough County whose appeals were also heard by judges outside the county.As of Oct. 2, nearly 5,000 school bus violations issued in Hillsborough County were contested — with nearly 80% upheld by a DOAH judge, according to recent data provided by the Hillsborough County School District.Last year, one of those judges revealed to Reporter LaGrone why the law makes it difficult for drivers to win appeals."It doesn't give us any discretion do anything but uphold the citation or void the citation," Judge John Van Laningham told LaGrone last year. For nearly two years, LaGrone and Apthorp have exposed problems with these cameras, which have generated nearly $30 million in paid fines in Hillsborough County alone.First, they discovered drivers were getting ticketed without a way to contest their fine. Then lawmakers had to adjust the law just to ensure drivers could appeal.It could take several months before a judge determines whether to certify this lawsuit as a class action. While this court battle is based in Hillsborough County, Moreno could expand the lawsuit to other Florida counties where DOAH judges are also being used to hear driver appeals.BusPatrol did not respond to our request for comment about this latest ruling but a spokesperson previously called the lawsuit "baseless." A spokesperson for the Hillsborough County school district said it does not comment on pending litigation. Shultz's attorney calls the lawsuit necessary for drivers to get a fair shot at fighting back what these buses capture on camera."You opened up this program before you set up a hearing program, then you changed the law, and then you still can't follow the law. That's ultimately what our position is: just get it right," Moreno said.

entry.title: Flood victims demand answers as FEMA delays disaster decision amid millions in damage
entry.summary: Dumpsters line driveways, bulldozers tear through debris and homes sit gutted along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach, where families are still picking up the pieces after historic flooding devastated parts of Martin County. For some residents, the water is still receding. For others, the cleanup has only just begun. Now, as another round of rain threatens the Treasure Coast, families already facing thousands of dollars in repairs are asking a question they can't afford to leave unanswered: How will they pay to rebuild? WATCH REPORT BELOW: Flood victims demand answers as FEMA delays disaster decision 'It's like an apocalypse here' For Linda Weisbecker, the destruction is difficult to put into words. 'It's like an apocalypse here,' she said, standing amid the devastation in her neighborhood. For nine days, Weisbecker and her neighbors navigated waist-deep floodwaters, unable to begin assessing the full extent of the damage. 'Once we got through that and the water came out, we just all started pitching in, going in to see what we can salvage from each home,' said Weisbecker. Neighbors worked together, sorting through waterlogged belongings and salvaging whatever they could. Now, the home she once knew is little more than an empty shell. 'We are fully gutted. Our house is empty,' she said. 'We lost everything, from pictures of our children and their lives, our friends, our grandkids, now we have great-grandkids. Everything [my husband] had since he was 13 on is gone.' Demolition is supposed to be the first step toward rebuilding. But for Weisbecker, it's also a painful reminder of how much work and money lies ahead. 'You do think about that process and you sit there and you say to yourself, how am I gonna do this?' Weisbecker said. Weisbecker was approved for a $25,000 grant through Florida's State Housing Initiatives Partnership, or SHIP, program, which provides housing assistance to eligible residents. While the grant offers some relief, the cost of rebuilding a flood-damaged home can quickly exceed that amount. And not every family will qualify for the same assistance. 'This is very urgent for people to get back into their daily lives,' Weisbecker said. 'This is total devastation. For everyone.' Millions in damage but no federal disaster declaration New estimates released by Martin County reveal the staggering financial toll of the flooding. According to county officials, the storm caused: $14 million in beach damage Nearly $1 million in damaged roads that now
entry.article_text: For everyone."New estimates released by Martin County reveal the staggering financial toll of the flooding.According to county officials, the storm caused:$14 million in beach damageNearly $1 million in damaged roads that now need to be repaved$3 million in residential losses affecting families still struggling to recoverAdditional costs in county staff overtime associated with the emergency responseThose figures put the known damage at approximately $18 million, not including additional expenses.A federal major disaster declaration could open the door to FEMA assistance for the public infrastructure repairs and potentially provide additional relief to affected residents.But so far, no such declaration has been approved.Without federal reimbursement, County Spokesperson Martha Ann Kniess said Martin County could be left responsible for covering millions of dollars in public recovery costs itself, forcing officials to find funding elsewhere in the county budget or identify other sources of assistance.And that uncertainty comes as residents are already struggling to afford repairs to their own homes.During an emotional Martin County Commission meeting Tuesday, flood victims pleaded with local leaders to do more to secure financial assistance."Please. Fight for us!" one resident urged commissioners.Others questioned why help was taking so long, particularly as more rain threatened their already damaged properties."And the answer from this dais is wait 13 more days?!?" another resident asked.Commissioner Eileen Vargas of District 1 told residents she is doing everything she can to try to expedite the process, but 'doesn't have all the answers.'"I did, through contacts, reach out to FEMA to try and get this going," Vargas said.According to Vargas, a new FEMA director is expected to take office Nov. 30, which she hopes will turn the tide. "He is going to personally petition President Trump to declare our area a disaster," Vargas said.However, a federal declaration is not guaranteed, and even if approved, not all damages or recovery expenses would necessarily qualify for reimbursement.WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey contacted FEMA, questioning the length of the response and when residents could expect answers.In its response, FEMA confirmed it had received the major disaster declaration request and that the request remains under review.The agency referred additional questions about the response and recovery timeline to the Florida Division of Emergency Management.WPTV also contacted the state agency but had not received a response as of Wednesday.In the meantime, Martin County is working to distribute emergency housing assistance through Florida's SHIP program.The county currently has approximately $1 million in SHIP funding available, with eligible residents able to apply for grants of up to $25,000.Additional assistance may be available through loans of up to $75,000, though those loans are subject to repayment requirements and liens.County officials acknowledged that the existing funding could run out quickly, particularly given the scale of the destruction.Michelle Miller, Martin County's human services director, told commissioners the state has promised additional disaster relief funding, but doesn't know when that funding could come in. "They haven't confirmed the amount yet but has assured us we will be getting some disaster relief funds," Miller said.But there are limitations.Some programs require homeowners to pay for repairs upfront before seeking reimbursement.

entry.title: Mary Peltola projected to flip Alaska Senate seat, giving Democrats 56-44 majority
entry.summary: Democrat Mary Peltola is projected to defeat Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, according to the Associated Press, delivering a significant pickup for Democrats. ANALYSIS | The significance of Peltola's election win The significance of Peltola's election win Peltola's victory marks the first time since 2008 that a Democrat has won a U.S. Senate election in Alaska, and gives Democrats a 56-44 majority in the Senate though two lawmakers identify as Independents and simply caucus with the Democrats. 'As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first,' Peltola said in a statement. 'As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaskas working families. Thank you Alaska. Lets get to work. Peltola, who made history in 2022 as the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, focused her Senate campaign on lowering the cost of living and addressing economic challenges facing everyday Alaskans. She previously served in the U.S. House of Representatives, where she became known for emphasizing issues important to Alaska, including the state's fishing industry and economic development. The race drew national attention as Republicans fought to defend their Senate majority. Sullivan, a military veteran seeking a third term, received support from President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance. Sullivan aligned his campaign with the Trump administration's tax and spending priorities and advocated for expanding fossil fuel production. The race in Alaska was complicated by the presence of another Dan Sullivan on the ballot. Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, ran as a long shot Democratic candidate for Senate. Both Dan Sullivans running prompted a legal fight early in the campaign, and President Donald Trump later called the former teacher's campaign 'fake' and 'a hoax by the Democrats.'

entry.title: DeSantis says Florida will seek another federal disaster declaration after historic flooding
entry.summary: Gov. Ron DeSantis said Florida is preparing to seek additional federal disaster assistance after a second round of historic flooding inundated communities across the state, with the St. Johns River reaching record levels and hundreds of people requiring rescue. Speaking Monday in Brevard County alongside state and local emergency officials, DeSantis said parts of Cocoa Beach and surrounding communities received 15 to 20 inches of rain in recent days. Many of those areas were still recovering from severe flooding earlier this month. WATCH BELOW: Florida seeking more federal aid after historic flooding, according to DeSantis DeSantis says Florida seeking more federal aid after historic flooding DeSantis said the St. Johns River near Cocoa reached nearly 19 feet on Saturday, surpassing the previous record by more than a foot. He warned that because the river moves slowly, flooding could take weeks or even months to fully recede. 'There could be more flooding that happens in the near future,' DeSantis said. 'The St. Johns River is a major concern just given how high it has gotten.' Florida preparing another disaster declaration request Florida previously requested a major federal disaster declaration following the first round of flooding earlier this month. DeSantis said that request is awaiting action from the federal government. The state is now collecting damage assessments from the latest flooding and plans to submit another request for a major disaster declaration. DeSantis said the second request will cover a broader area because more counties and communities were affected by the latest rainfall. "The St. Johns River is a major concern just given how high it has gotten."Florida previously requested a major federal disaster declaration following the first round of flooding earlier this month. DeSantis said the second request will cover a broader area because more counties and communities were affected by the latest rainfall.Florida Division of Emergency Management Executive Director Jared Perdue said the state could have enough damage information to move forward with the request as soon as Monday or Tuesday.DeSantis said he expects the request to warrant federal approval."It's basically just the damage assessments trying to show that there's been enough damage to justify federal intervention," DeSantis said. "And I think in this case that that has been the case."DeSantis also said individual assistance included in the state's initial request could provide some relief to residents with damaged homes, including those who did not carry flood insurance. However, he cautioned that federal assistance may not cover the full amount of a homeowner's losses.State agencies, including the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, Florida National Guard, Florida State Guard and Florida Highway Patrol, have completed nearly 500 floodwater rescues, according to DeSantis.The Florida National Guard has mobilized 421 personnel and conducted 417 welfare checks, while deploying 54 high-water vehicles across six counties.Another 173 FWC officers are deployed, along with more than 200 FHP troopers assisting flooded communities, stranded motorists and disabled vehicles.Nearly 160 Florida State Guard personnel have also been mobilized. State Guard crews have helped with "muck and gut" operations at more than 250 properties in Brevard and Okeechobee counties, removing water-damaged material from flooded homes.The state has distributed more than 22,000 boxes of water, 7,500 ready-to-eat meals, 1,200 flood cleanup buckets and 1,300 tarps to affected communities, according to Perdue.Emergency officials warned that high water remains a threat even as conditions begin to improve.Perdue said State Road 50 in Brevard County and State Road 46 in Seminole County remained underwater as of Monday."If there are any state roads or local roads that are underwater, please do not drive or walk through the water," Perdue said. "It can be very dangerous. You just can't see what's down there."The Florida Division of Emergency Management has deployed more than 10,000 feet of temporary flood barriers to protect critical infrastructure, including government buildings and lift stations in Seminole County and HCA Florida Lake Monroe Hospital in Sanford.The state has also deployed 90 pumps and 22 vacuum trucks during the response in Brevard, Broward, Indian River, Flagler, Palm Beach, St. Lucie and Volusia counties.FDOT has more than 750 personnel working on flood assessments and pumping operations across Central and South Florida, DeSantis said.A shelter remains open at the Joseph N. Davis Community Center in Melbourne.Four multi-agency resource centers have also been established across three counties, including two in Brevard County. DeSantis said more than 1,600 residents have already received assistance through the centers. The centers will be closed on Thanksgiving.Residents whose homes are uninhabitable because of flooding can also apply for the state's temporary travel trailer program through emergencyRV.org.DeSantis said state resources will remain in affected communities throughout the recovery."Our folks aren't going anywhere," DeSantis said. We're going to see through the federal assistance and make sure that people can get back on their feet."

entry.title: More than 140 fall ill aboard cruise ship that departed Fort Lauderdale
entry.summary: More than 140 passengers and crew on board a cruise ship that departed from South Florida last week have reported becoming sick with a mystery gastrointestinal illness, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says. According to information provided by the CDC, the Princess Cruises ship Caribbean Princess departed Port Everglades in Fort Lauderdale on Nov. 11 on a 12-night journey. The outbreak was then reported days later on Nov. 15. RELATED STORY | Nearly 200 passengers rescued after tanker hits river boat in New Orleans: 'Miracle on the Mississippi' At least 134 of 2,936 passengers and 14 of the 1,132 crew members have reported symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhea, according to the CDC. In response to the outbreak, Princess Cruises and the crew on board the ship said there have been increased cleaning and disinfection efforts according to their outbreak and response plan. In addition, passengers and crew who are sick have been isolated. 'Norovirus is often the cause of gastrointestinal illness outbreaks on cruise ships, but we don't always know the cause of the outbreak when we begin an investigation,' the CDC said on its website. 'Finding the agent that caused an outbreak (causative agent) can take time.' So far, the cause of the illness is unknown. 'Princess Cruises can confirm that a limited number of guests aboard Caribbean Princess have reported mild gastrointestinal illness,' the cruise line said in a statement to CBS News Miami. 'Our crew responded promptly by implementing enhanced sanitation protocols across the ship, including comprehensive cleaning and disinfection measures.' RELATED STORY | CDC sidelines itself as hantavirus cruise ship outbreak grabs global attention The statement says that while most guests remain unaffected by the illness, it is continuing to monitor the situation. According to the CDC, cases of illnesses that have been reported are totals for the entire voyage. 'It does not mean all people are sick at the same time, such as when they arrive or leave a port or ship,' the CDC continued. The Caribbean Princess departed Fort Lauderdale on a round-trip, 12-day Panama Canal trip that is expected to return on Nov. 23.

entry.title: TRICARE allows emergency prescription refills in 20 Florida counties after flooding
entry.summary: The Defense Health Agency has authorized temporary emergency prescription refills for TRICARE beneficiaries in 20 Florida counties affected by fall flooding. The waiver remains in effect through Nov. 29. The counties covered by the waiver are Brevard, Broward, DeSoto, Duval, Flagler, Glades, Hardee, Hendry, Highlands, Indian River, Martin, Miami-Dade, Monroe, Okeechobee, Palm Beach, Putnam, Seminole, St. Johns, St. Lucie and Volusia. How TRICARE beneficiaries can get emergency refills Beneficiaries who need an emergency refill should take their prescription bottle to any TRICARE retail network pharmacy, according to the Defense Health Agency. If the prescription bottle is unavailable or its label is damaged or missing, beneficiaries should contact Express Scripts or a retail network pharmacy for assistance. Beneficiaries can find a network pharmacy through the A potentially unsafe link has been removed or by calling Express Scripts at 1-877-363-1303. When possible, beneficiaries should visit the pharmacy where the prescription was originally filled. Prescriptions filled by a retail chain may also be filled at another location operated by the same chain. If the prescribing clinician is available, beneficiaries can also ask the clinician to call a new prescription into a network pharmacy. Urgent and emergency care during flooding TRICARE beneficiaries other than active-duty service members may receive urgent care from any TRICARE-authorized urgent care center or provider without a referral, according to the Defense Health Agency. The option allows beneficiaries to seek nonemergency treatment if their primary care provider is unavailable because of an emergency. Anyone who reasonably believes they are experiencing a medical emergency should call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room. entry.title: GTA 6 finally arrives as Florida gamers prepare for one of the most anticipated video game launches ever
entry.summary: It's the most anticipated video game in the last 10 years. At midnight Thursday, video gamers in Florida will finally have an opportunity to play Grand Theft Auto 6. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Grand Theft Auto 6 Releases at Midnight 'Everything I'm seeing so far looks like the hype has been worth it,' said Adriano, who was outside Skinny Louie restaurant in West Palm Beach on Wednesday. The restaurant has been rebranded as Burger Shot, a fictional fast-food place featured in the game. GTA 6, as it is being called, is set in a place that looks very much like South Florida. The game reportedly had a $1 billion budget and has generated so much buzz among fans that the Wall Street Journal estimates 1.5 million may skip work on Thursday. Sportsinsider.com reports Florida ranks first in the nation for people expected to use a PTO or vacation day to play the game. 'No work tomorrow or for the next five days,' said Laury, who was grabbing lunch Thursday at the West Palm Burger Shot. 'It's a little bit of a religious experience. It's a little crazy.' GTA 6 sells for $79.99 for the standard edition and $99.99 for the ultimate edition for PlayStation 5 and Xbox. WATCH BELOW: Could GTA 6 become best-selling game of all time? Could Grand Theft Auto VI become the best-selling video game of all time? 'It's really reached this level of like mainstream awareness that's pretty unprecedented for a game like this,' Jordan Minor, principal writer at PCMag, said. Minor wrote a review of the game , calling it 'a masterpiece I never want to leave.' 'For a lot of other people, this is going to be the only game they play all year or all next year,' Minor said. 'It may be the only game they've played in like the past five years.'

entry.title: New 24/7 animal cruelty hotline in Florida already getting results just hours after its launch
entry.summary: A new 24/7 animal cruelty hotline in Florida is already getting results just hours after its launch was announced. Big Dog Ranch Rescue CEO and founder Lauree Simmons said the hotline went live Monday, and the organization received more than 30 calls. It also led to the rescue of an abandoned and neglected dog in Bay County. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Big Dog Ranch applauds Florida's new animal cruelty hotline The hotline gives people a place to report suspected animal abuse, including cruelty, abandonment and dog fighting.
