entry.article_text: Just weeks after historic flooding destroyed homes and displaced families in Jensen Beach, Martin County residents are bracing for another round of heavy rain — with up to 12 inches forecast over the next three days.For families still struggling to recover, the threat of more flooding comes as county commissioners work to determine what caused the initial disaster and how to help those who lost nearly everything.On Tuesday, flood victims packed a Martin County Commission meeting, pleading for financial assistance and answers.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Along Cheri Drive in Jensen Beach, the signs of destruction remain. Dumpsters line driveways, damaged belongings sit outside and families are still trying to salvage what's left of their homes.Lisa French, her husband, Jeremy, and their two young sons are among those displaced after floodwaters rose as high as 3 feet inside some homes two weeks ago."It's like we're kind of stuck," French told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey. French said her home had about 3 to 6 inches of flooding that sat inside for more than a week, causing mold to grow 3 to 4 feet up the walls. "So they, yeah, they tore the walls down in the house," said French. "They just chipped up the last bit of the tile, and it's empty." Now, with more rain approaching, French fears her family could face another disaster before recovering from the first."Of course, we're afraid because we all flooded in our houses," she said.New figures released by Martin County show at least 36 homes sustained damage, with an estimated $3 million in residential losses. Commissioners estimated another $14 million in damage to beaches, and at least $1 million in damage to roadways that now need repairs. For some residents, the destruction represents a lifetime of memories washed away."We've lost everything," one elderly Jensen Beach resident told commissioners. "We have 60 years of our life — kids, grandkids, everything. It's all gone."As residents demand answers about what went wrong, commissioners approved shifting $200,000 from the county's stormwater budget to investigate whether development and changes to local drainage systems contributed to the flooding.Commissioner Blake Capps called the investigation "a good starting point.""It may be that we need to augment the study beyond the $200,000 that we approve today," said Capps. Meanwhile, county crews are working around the clock to prepare for the next storm, lowering retention pond levels, deploying additional pumps and draining flooded properties."We have people 24 hours a day pumping that material down," Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said.Commissioners also approved financial assistance for eligible flood victims through the state's State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program.The assistance includes grants of up to $25,000 for income-eligible homeowners and loans of up to $75,000 secured by liens on their properties.But there's a catch: The grants are reimbursement-based, meaning homeowners must first pay for eligible repairs before receiving the money.For families who lost everything, that presents another obstacle."We don't have $25,000," French said. "A lot of people don't have $25,000, so it's great, and we're appreciative, but I mean, our house is empty, and $25,000 is not going to do much for us." The other problem: the county currently has just $1 million in SHIP funding available, and commissioners warned the money could run out quickly, even with additional state funding promised."They haven't given us the amount yet, but they have assured us that we will be getting some disaster relief funds," said Human Services Director Michelle Miller Strict income limits could also disqualify some flood victims who cannot afford to rebuild on their own. The income cap for a family of one is $86,040. The cap for a family of two is $98,400. For a family of four, it's $122,880. When reporter Kate Hussey asked Capps what would happen to those families, he acknowledged the county needs to explore other options."There are going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where someone barely missed the limit, and we're going to need to take a look at what we can do for those folks," Capps said.For residents like French, the need is immediate."We just need somebody to step up," she said. "We need funding." With another round of heavy rain approaching, Martin County is distributing sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park to help residents protect their properties, with a limit of 25 per person. The County's Emergency Operations Center is scheduled to be staffed beginning Tuesday at 2 p.m., and the county is coordinating with the National Weather Service and Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM).Fire Rescue is also standing by with multiple high-water rescue trucks.Commissioners also said a Federal Emergency Management Agency representative is expected to visit Nov. 30 to assess the damage — a potential step toward securing federal disaster assistance.But for families still displaced and facing the possibility of more flooding, the uncertainty remains.

entry.title: 37th Stuart Air Show draws big crowds for picture-perfect weekend
entry.summary: The 37th Stuart Air Show brought aviation fans young and old together for a picture-perfect weekend filled with aircraft, family traditions, and appreciation for veterans. Organizers said the weekend got off to a strong start Friday night with a drone and fireworks show and continued with large crowds throughout the weekend. 'Stuart Air Show has had an amazing weekend Friday night with our drone and fireworks show. We had a great turnout,' Chrissy Valvano said. 'Sunday, we're looking at a record turnout for Veterans Appreciation Day, and this weather could not be better.' For some families, attending the Stuart Air Show has become a tradition passed down through the years. 'The Stuart Air Show has been a part of our community for many years,' Sarah Naylor said. 'We have many memories of coming in the past, as long as I can remember.' For younger aviation fans Wyatt and Ivy Rotan, some of the biggest attractions were the military aircraft. 'I like coming to the Stuart Air Show because I like to see the C-17 and the F-16 fly,' Wyatt said. 'I like seeing the C-17,' Ivy added. The event also gave young people a chance to learn more about aviation while honoring those who served. 'You get to have a lot of fun around here, just going around and seeing a bunch of planes,' John Gefell said. 'Also, because I'm working on my aviation merit badge as a Boy Scout and my grandpa was a veteran, so its just real fun to come out here and just have a lot of fun.' With beautiful weather and a strong turnout, the 37th Stuart Air Show once again brought the community together, giving longtime fans and a new generation of aviation enthusiasts a weekend to remember.

entry.summary: Weeks after historic flooding devastated homes in Jensen Beach, Martin County families are still cleaning up and rebuilding, with volunteers, churches, firefighters, contractors and local leaders joining the recovery effort. Water marks remain visible on some homes, showing how high floodwaters rose. Residents are now removing damaged drywall, clearing debris and collecting donated supplies while seeking financial assistance and answers about the area's drainage systems. Jensen Beach families rebuild as neighbors rally after historic flooding Neighbors step in to help Jensen Beach families Before-and-after video from the Jensen Beach neighborhood shows the extent of the flooding, which left several homes under feet of water. Weeks later, homeowner Lisa Marie French said cleaning up has been a major undertaking. We first told you about French's circumstances last week. 'Its a lot of work. entry.title: Port St. Lucie extends boil water notice for 21,000 customers after main break
entry.summary: About 21,000 customers in Port St. Lucie remain under a precautionary boil water notice after a contractor damaged a water main earlier this week. The city announced it is extending the notice for the Tradition and west Port St. Lucie areas following Tuesday's water main break near Glades Cut Off Road. The notice covers all of Tradition, including Western Grove, Riverland, Wilson Grove and Southern Grove, as well as areas west of Interstate 95 south to Becker Road. Communities along Glades Cut Off Road, including Copper Creek, Wylder and Verano, are also affected. City officials said the notice will remain in place until water quality testing is successfully completed and the city determines it is safe to lift. With an estimated 21,000 customers affected, officials said a significant number of water samples must be collected and tested to ensure the water is safe. The city is asking residents not to tamper with clearly marked hydrants or pipes that are flushing water, warning that interference could delay testing and extend the notice. According to officials, the break was caused by a contractor working on a construction project unrelated to the city. Crews responded and repaired the damaged 36-inch water main within hours before beginning the required flushing process. The city is investigating the incident and expects to pursue appropriate action to recover costs from those responsible. There is no estimated time for when the boil water notice will be lifted. Residents can find updates at CityofPSL.com .

entry.title: St. Lucie County schools closed Friday as heavy rain threatens morning commute
entry.summary: St. Lucie Public Schools will be closed Friday, Nov. 20, because additional heavy rainfall is expected overnight and into the morning, district officials announced Thursday. ADDITIONAL CLOSURES: Indian River County schools closed Friday due to flooding, heavy rain Palm Beach County schools to close Friday amid heavy rain, flood watches The district said it made the decision out of an abundance of caution because heavy rain could coincide with the morning arrival period while areas throughout the county are already saturated. The safety of our students and staff is at the forefront of this decision, Superintendent Dr. Jon R. Prince said. Given the potential for heavy rainfall during the morning arrival period and the already saturated conditions throughout our community, we believe closing schools is the safest decision for our students, families, and employees. After-school activities also canceled All after-school programs scheduled for Friday are canceled, including aftercare, activities and athletic events, according to the district. The closure means students will begin their Thanksgiving holiday early. Students are scheduled to return to school Monday, Nov. 30. Saturday SAT decision pending The district has not yet determined whether the SAT scheduled for Saturday, Nov. 21, will take place. Officials said a decision on the SAT will be made later Friday and communicated to families as soon as possible. This story has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Port St. Lucie restores water service, but boil water notice remains
entry.summary: Water service has been fully restored to the Tradition and western Port St. Lucie areas following a major water main break Tuesday, but a precautionary boil water notice remains in effect. The break happened near Glades Cut Off Road when a contractor working on a construction project unrelated to the city damaged a 36-inch water main, according to city officials. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Tradition water service restored after water main break Crews completed repairs Tuesday evening and began flushing the water main shortly afterward. The city initially recommended a 48-hour precautionary boil water notice Tuesday at noon for the Tradition area, including Western Grove, Riverland, Wilson Grove and Southern Grove, west of Interstate 95 to Becker Road. The notice also covers communities along Glades Cut Off Road, including Copper Creek, Wylder and Verano. City officials said water quality testing began Wednesday. Because of the number of customers affected, a significant number of samples must be collected and tested before the notice can be lifted. Residents should continue boiling water until the city confirms it is safe to use without boiling. Restored water service does not mean the boil water notice has ended. The city is investigating the incident and expects to pursue appropriate action to recover costs from those responsible. Updates will be posted at CityofPSL.com .

entry.title: Woman dies after Port St. Lucie hit-and-run; police say driver was playing 'ding dong ditch' beforehand
entry.summary: A 24-year-old woman has died from injuries she suffered after she was struck while riding an electric scooter in a hit-and-run crash in Port St. Lucie , police said Wednesday. The woman died at approximately 9:23 p.m. Tuesday, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Teen Charged in Port St. Lucie E-Scooter Hit-and-Run | WPTV The crash happened around 5:10 a.m. Monday near the intersection of Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. Police said the woman was riding an electric scooter when a vehicle struck her. Investigators allege the driver left the scene without stopping to help her or notify law enforcement. The department's Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit later identified the vehicle as a gray Chevrolet Tahoe and located it at a Port St. Lucie home, according to police. Investigators identified the alleged driver as 18-year-old Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer. Police said investigators learned Sanchez-Chasmer had been playing 'ding dong ditch' with friends shortly before the crash. According to the department, the group was leaving a home where they had been participating in the prank when the vehicle struck the woman. Sanchez-Chasmer was arrested and charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, a second-degree felony, police said. Following the woman's death, police said they anticipate the State Attorney's Office will pursue enhanced or additional charges as appropriate based on the circumstances and the outcome of the investigation. Police did not identify the woman in Wednesday's news release.

entry.title: Another flooding threat tests St. Lucie County as leaders brace for Amendment 3 budget cuts
entry.summary: As the threat of another round of November rain and flooding takes aim at Florida's east coast, many local governments are once again preparing for what may be ahead. 'I think everybody is well aware now that this storm drain system was not designed for the flooding we're getting nowadays,' St. Lucie County spokesman Erick Gill said. 'There were probably 50 to 100 staff members out there, including crews in public works, out in the field working during the storm. That's unbudgeted overtime,' Gill said. This week, the county offered free sand , donated by Dickerson Infrastructure and Stewart Materials, for residents to bag. Other services cost money, and Gill said budgeting is already on the minds of county leaders now that the Amendment 3 tax cuts are coming. What is uncertain is how the loss of revenue will affect things like storm preparation and response. 'We still don't know what the total impacts will be for, you know, with Amendment 3 with the additional homestead exemption,' Gill said. 'We're looking at the early estimates in this next upcoming fiscal year to be about a $60 million shortfall and then about $120 million once the exemption goes up.'

entry.title: St. Lucie Public Schools closed Wednesday due to flooding concerns
entry.summary: St. Lucie Public Schools will close all schools and district offices Wednesday, Nov. 18, as officials prepare for the potential for significant rainfall and localized flooding. The district announced the closure Tuesday, saying forecasts from the National Weather Service still have some uncertainty surrounding the exact timing, location and amount of rainfall. However, with the ground already saturated across the community, district leaders said they are taking a cautious approach in the interest of students, families and employees. All after-school activities, aftercare programs and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday are also canceled. District officials said they will monitor rainfall, flooding and road closures throughout the day Wednesday. They will also evaluate access to schools, bus stops and transportation routes. A decision on whether schools will reopen Thursday, Nov. 19, is expected to be announced Wednesday evening. The district said updates will be posted on the official St. Lucie Public Schools website and its social media channels. A flood watch is in effect for the entire Treasure Coast through Friday evening.

entry.title: Amendment 3 task force tries to get the message to Florida residents
entry.summary: Indian River Countys Tax Collector and Property Appraiser have formed Task Force 3, to get the word out for residents to qualify the new Homestead Exemption coming with Amendment 3. What people really need to understand is, there's less than five weeks to get a driver's license to become a resident of the state of Florida, said Property Appraiser Wesley Davis. WATCH: Amendment 3 task force tries to get the message to Florida residents Indian River Co Launches Amendment 3 Task Force Florida residency is a key component to being able to qualify for the exemption, which is rising to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, after voters approved the referendum on election day. New homeowners coming into the state after January 1, 2027 will have to wait five years for the new full exemptions. Current renters in Florida can still qualify for the new exemption on any future home they buy. The sense of urgency right now is that you don't need to have a homestead by the end of the year, Davis says. What you need to do to qualify for the homestead exemption is you must be a resident of the state of Florida by the end of the year.' That also includes current residents who have failed to get a Florida ID and still hold a driver's license from their previous state, says Tax Collector Carole Jean Jordan. They can establish residency in an apartment, and then when they buy a home, they can file for homestead. The local officials also pointed out county offices will be closed around the upcoming holidays. The impact of Amendment 3 will be felt in future county budgets, and both department heads acknowledge there are already discussions about budgeting next year. Estimates are that the county could lose about 20-30 million dollars over the first couple of years under the amendment. This will not end property taxes, Davis says. About half of everybody's tax bill goes to education, and education is not affected by this at all.

entry.title: Indian River County schools closed Thursday as heavy rain raises flooding concerns
entry.summary: All School District of Indian River County public schools and district offices will be closed Thursday, Nov. 19, because of expected heavy rain and potential flooding, district officials announced Wednesday. Officials cited already saturated ground and concerns about whether students and employees could safely travel to and from schools. The storm system is expected to affect Indian River, Brevard and Volusia counties between 3 a.m. and 3 p.m. Thursday, according to the district. Saturated ground raises travel concerns Indian River County remains under a flood watch as another round of rain moves through the Treasure Coast. The National Weather Service forecast calls for a 95% chance of precipitation Thursday, with about 1.74 inches of rain possible. The district said saturated conditions were a key factor in its decision to cancel classes and close offices. 'With ground conditions already saturated, we cannot be confident that students and staff will be able to travel safely to and from school,' the district said. 'Weather conditions may also affect staff members' ability to report to work.' The closure comes about two weeks after prolonged rainfall caused significant flooding in Indian River County. Flood watch remains in effect A flood watch for Indian River County remains in effect through Friday evening. The National Weather Service is also reporting a high surf advisory and rip current statement for the area. Indian River County officials have warned residents that roads not officially listed as closed could still have standing water or other hazards. Drivers should obey barricades and never attempt to drive through floodwater. The school district said student, family and employee safety remains its highest priority. Officials will continue monitoring conditions and said any additional information will be released through official district communication channels. entry.title: PBSO detective killed in I-95 wrong-way crash; FHP says driver was intoxicated, had 3 prior DUIs
entry.summary: A Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office detective was killed, and a Palm Beach Gardens man faces multiple charges following a wrong-way crash on Interstate 95 in Palm Beach County on Thanksgiving morning, according to the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP). The crash was reported at 5:08 a.m. Thursday on I-95, just north of Military Trail. Investigators said Raul Jonathan Espinoza Martinez, 37, of Palm Beach Gardens, was driving a white 2026 Chevrolet Equinox north in the southbound lanes of I-95 when he collided head-on with a gray 2017 Ford Expedition driven by a 46-year-old Alan Smith, a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office detective from West Palm Beach. WATCH: PBSO detective killed in Thanksgiving wrong-way crash PBSO detective killed in I-95 wrong-way crash; FHP says driver was intoxicated, had 3 prior DUIs Smith, whom the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office confirmed was an on-duty detective headed to work, was airlifted to St. Mary's Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead. FHP said his next of kin has been notified. It is with profound sadness and heavy hearts that we announce the devastating loss our own, Detective Alan Smith. Detective Smith was fatally struck by a wrong way driver traveling southbound on I95 early Thanksgiving morning. Alan joined the Palm Beach County Sheriffs Office in January 2007. In 2012, he became a member of the Bomb Squad and graduated from the FBI Hazardous Devices School in September 2013. His commitment to law enforcement extended beyond his responsibilities as a Bomb Technician. He also served as a Task Force Officer (TFO) with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), specializing in explosives-related investigations. Alan was much more than a law enforcement officer and Bomb Technician. He was a college professor, and a lifelong scholar who was in the process of completing his doctoral degree. His passion for education, pursuit of knowledge, and commitment to mentoring others were evident throughout his personal and professional life. Above all his professional and academic accomplishments, Alans greatest pride was his family. He was a loving husband to his wife, Jennifer, and a devoted father to his 14-year-old son, Alexander. His passing is a tremendous loss to his family, the Palm Beach County Sheriffs Office, the Bomb Squad, the law enforcement community, and the countless individuals whose lives he touched through his service, friendship, and mentorship.   Alans legacy of service, knowledge
entry.article_text: Alan’s legacy of service, knowledge, compassion, and dedication to others will never be forgotten.— PBSO (@PBCountySheriff) November 26, 2026 The sheriff's office said Smith was driving an unmarked patrol car at the time of the crash. Espinoza Martinez was also taken to St. Mary's Medical Center with incapacitating injuries.All lanes were back open at about noon after the closure lasted about seven hours.The Florida Highway Patrol said at about 2:33 p.m., troopers arrested Espinoza Martinez in connection with the fatal wrong-way crash. The arrest took place at St. Mary's Medical Center, according to FHP."Troopers were joined by members of the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, who placed Espinoza Martinez in the handcuffs carried by the fallen detective," FHP said in a statement.A judge on Friday ordered Espinoza Martinez to be held on a $1.7 million bond.According to FHP, Espinoza Martinez was intoxicated at the time of the crash, with an active license revocation for 10 years and three prior DUI convictions.Upon his release from the hospital, FHP said Espinoza Martinez will be booked into the Palm Beach County Jail on the following charges:Vehicular HomicideDUI ManslaughterAggravated BatteryAggravated Battery on a Law Enforcement OfficerDriving While License Suspended or Revoked Causing Death or Serious Bodily InjuryDriving While License Suspended or Revoked – Subsequent OffenseDUI Causing Damage to Property or Injury to Another PersonReckless Driving Causing Damage to Property or Injury to Another PersonFHP said they are investigating the circumstances of the crash.President Donald Trump made a statement about the crash during a press conference on Thursday, according to CNN."I just want to pay my respects to the family of a great police officer, uh, an expert at bombs and explosives who was killed today in an automobile accident while on duty, and I'm not able to release his name yet. They, they're notifying the family and notifying a lot of people.

entry.article_text: Martin County commissioners have unanimously approved $200,000 to fund a study that will analyze water movement during the recent flooding in Jensen Beach and identify ways to reduce future flood risks. Floodwaters earlier this month left homes and roads underwater in parts of Jensen Beach. The study will examine how water moved through the Savannas Preserve area during the storm, as some residents have questioned whether water discharged into the Blackwell Reservoir, which drains into the Savannas Preserve, contributed to the flooding. "What's happening now is not going to stop. This is an El Niño event that we are in through April. It's going to come and go," resident Jacqui Thurlow-Lippisch said during the Nov. 17 county commissioner meeting. Public Works Director James Gorton says the hydraulic model funded by the county will focus on two main objectives. "First one is model the storm event that we just had. We need to update, get some of the development that has occurred to our north, put into that model first and then model that storm, see where the weaknesses were, and then secondarily look at some solutions to reduce the risk," Gorton said. This initiative follows a separate study conducted by the county to analyze areas that have repeatedly flooded, aiming to understand the causes and identify potential solutions. Engineering permit manager and floodplain coordinator Christine Madsen said the analysis identified 53 repetitive loss areas. "We determined what some of the potential causes of the flooding were, and we used it to identify different projects that we could take and move forward within the future," Madsen said. One photo from the study shows flooding in the St. Lucie Settlement area along SW Salerno Road, where eight homes were elevated above the 100-year flood elevation with assistance from FEMA. Another photo shows one of the completed homes. "Flood losses are terrible. Just 1 inch of water can majorly impact a property. I mean it can cause up to $25,000 worth of damage," Madsen said. "We want to do whatever we can to help them." Residents can review the analysis on the county's website. Those with questions can call the county at 772-288-5956.

entry.title: Boil water notice lifted for 21,000 Port St. Lucie customers after water main break - WPEC
entry.summary: Boil water notice lifted for 21,000 Port St. Lucie customers after water main break    WPEC
entry.article_text: Thousands of Port St. Lucie residents can put away their pots after city officials lifted a precautionary boil water notice Saturday afternoon. The City of Port St. Lucie announced the all-clear at 3:15 p.m. Saturday after water quality tests confirmed the water was safe to drink. The notice affected approximately 21,000 customers in Tradition and areas west of Interstate 95 following a water main break Tuesday near Glades Cut Off Road. See also: A helping of hope: 600 turkeys bring Thanksgiving cheer to South Florida families Residents in the following communities no longer need to boil their water: Tradition Western Grove Riverland Wilson Grove Southern Grove Copper Creek Wylder Verano The affected area stretched west of I-95 south to Becker Road, including communities along Glades Cut Off Road. According to city officials, the break occurred when a contractor working on a construction project unrelated to the city damaged a 36-inch water main. City crews responded immediately and completed repairs within hours. Flushing and required water quality testing followed. After tests confirmed the water was safe, officials lifted the precautionary notice. The city thanked the roughly 21,000 affected customers for their patience throughout the disruption.

entry.title: Flooding leads to partial road collapse in Port St. Lucie - WPBF
entry.summary: Flooding leads to partial road collapse in Port St. Lucie    WPBF
entry.article_text: A road and nearby property in Port St. Lucie have partially collapsed following historic flooding, leaving residents concerned about the growing damage and the safety of surrounding homes. “All this was flooded,” said Yoshi Duran, a neighbor who showed the damaged area near her home. From aerial views, the extent of the collapse is clear, with sections of the road and property having fallen into the hole. “It’s not anything to laugh about. It is a dangerous situation because they’re not knowing when it can cave in,” Duran said. The collapse occurred during the flooding, as water poured in and the land buckled until it finally gave way. Duran said the hole has been expanding daily since then. Because what’s going to happen, you know? What’s going to happen to the houses that are around this area?” Duran said. City officials are aware of the issue and are working to address it. “We want to repair these as quickly as we possibly can. Unfortunately, it takes some time,” said Scott Samples, public information officer for Port St. Lucie. Samples explained the damage was caused by excess water both on the road and in a culvert below it. He said the city is currently determining the best way to fix the problem. “You want to make sure you’re doing it as well and as correctly as you possibly can. So that may require some studies to take place before you actually start the work,” Samples said. For Duran, that work can’t come soon enough. We understand everybody is short-staffed. But we need answers,” Duran said. City officials said there is no timeline for the repairs since they're still trying to figure out the best way to fix the problem.
